en: The Dance of Reasoning (Tarkatāṇḍava)
The Introduction, adorned with the commentary titled *Nyāyadīpa* composed by Śrī Rāghavendra Tīrtha.
For those who have conducted critical investigations into the works known as the *Candrikā*, *Nyāyāmṛta*, and *Tarkatāṇḍava*, which are celebrated under the names of the three Vyāsas:

It is not unknown that we proclaim how the skill in deliberation of the Mahodayas, the eloquence of their own established doctrines, and the excellence of their well-founded principles become easily accessible.

Among these three, this work titled *Tarkatāṇḍava*— the sovereign among treatises on debate— is intended for the benefit of newcomers to the traditions of the science of logic (*tarka-śāstra*) which have been accepted by the learned for their service to the Vedas (*nigama*).
“The Vedas were composed by someone;
they are not authoritative.
Rather, only that which possesses the power of auxiliary factors (sahakārin) is authoritative.”

He establishes through reasoning alone the refutability of those treatises which propound such non-Vedic subjects as "the Lord possesses limited qualities" and "liberation is the destruction of suffering"— subjects that detract from the majesty of the Veda— and he demonstrates the acceptability of those [treatises] whose intent is not in contradiction with the Veda.
That which is in his name:
the *tāṇḍava* of logic,
the *taṇḍava* of reasoning.

The term *tarkatāṇḍava* is to be analyzed in three ways: by means of the locative case (*saptamī*), it denotes the locus of the act of subjugation; by means of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it denotes the relationship belonging to the *tāṇḍava*, which consists of the manifestation of being and specific types of exertion.
Through the word "reasoning" (tarka), which is joined with inference and logic, the attainment [of the goal] is easily obtained.
Only one doubt remains: how can there be fearless movement and respect on this path through the forest of conceptual construction?
To that end, we shall extend our finger toward the direction of its explanation.
The name of this commentary, the *Tātparyacandrikā*, has not been stated by means of a name signifying something that assists in dancing, as is the case with the *Prakāśa* and the *Sudhāparimala*.
Moreover, with the desire to explain even his own name by its very root,
he [states that] it "kindles" or "burns" dry logic, and thus "illuminates" sound reasoning.
It is illuminated by *nyāya* (reasoning) and *yukti* (logic); thus, it is easily explained as being named *Nyāyadīpa* (The Lamp of Reasoning).
Not only this much, but there are also statements within this volume;

specifically, on the second page, starting from the fourteenth line with the words “In this treatise devoted to the investigation of *nyāya*,” up to: “Because it is devoted to the investigation of the logic of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) useful for determining the objects of knowledge taught in the *Brahmatantra*, it [is so called] precisely because of its subject matter and so forth.”
In the third volume, at the ninth mark, it says: "He composes the *pūrvaraṅga* (preliminary ritual) which introduces the performance of the *tāṇḍava*.

And in the second volume, by means of the two words expressing the relevant inquiry (*upayuktacintā*), there is an investigation into the correctness or incorrectness of the logical principles (*nyāya*) that are either favorable or unfavorable to the *Brahmatantra* (the Vedāntas).
From the sequence of the third enclosure, it is easy to understand the intention to explain the purpose of the dance, as well as the pursuit of logical reasoning throughout.
We now publish the first volume of this work of such great magnitude; therein,
we shall first provide a brief introductory preface concerning the book and its author.
Let aside for now this extensive investigation of the text;
our own inclination toward investigating even the author is but limited.
For the venerable Somanātha Kavi, an ancient scholar, praised him most extensively in his vast poem titled *Vyāsavijaya*.
And we have now obtained this poem in its printed form.
Of this [author], who is skilled in the discernment of well-examined investigation and who possesses the armor of logic:
[the works of] others—1. *Nyāyāmṛta*, 2. *Tātparya-candrikā*.
3. *Tattvavivekaṭīkā-mandāramañjarī*, 4. *Upādhikhaṇḍanaṭīkā-mandāramañjarī*, 5. *Māyāvādakhaṇḍanaṭīkā-mandāramañjarī*.

The authors of these works— namely, the *Mithyātvānumānakhaṇḍanaṭīkāmandāramañjarī* and the *Bhedojjīvana*— are the venerable sages Vyāsarāja, who were experts in the science of words, sentences, and logic, and proficient in the meaning of the traditional doctrines.
Among these, those who bestow the state of renunciation [are as follows]:
"May the preeminent swan, ever attached to the lotus feet of the slayer of Kaṃsa,
known as the King of Teachers Devoted to Brahman, abide within my mind."

Thus, the venerable Tīrtha Munivarēnya, who is honored in the *Tātparya-candrikā* and other works, was a preceptor of learning (*vidyā-guru*) expert in all the scriptures and endowed with qualities such as knowledge, devotion, and dispassion; he is renowned as Śrī Pādarāja, the sage Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. The authors of these very texts also intend this same point.
In the Nyāyāmṛta: "I bow to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Muni, who possesses auspicious qualities such as knowledge, dispassion, and devotion, and who is my preceptor in learning."
Many disciples attended them;
among them were the renowned Vādirāja Svāmin and Vijayīndra Saṃyamīndra, the authors of one hundred and four works, including the *Gurvarthadīpikā* and the *Yuktimallikā*.
The conclusion established by the inscription is that they adorned this land of Bhārata in person during the sixteenth century of the Christian era.

For it is stated in the inscription: "In the year one thousand four hundred and thirty-nine of the Śaka era, the village of Gaurapurābhida was granted by King Kṛṣṇadevarāja, the sovereign of Vijayanagara, to the venerable Vyāsarāja. Thus, indeed, the inscription says.
By these compositions, they especially benefit all who do not assist them; thus, all followers of the Madhva school are indeed in a state of debt to them.

Furthermore, this summary of the narrative has been extracted from the *Bhūmikā* (introduction) of the work titled *Candrikāprakāśaprasara*, composed by the eminent scholar Gauḍagori Veṅkaṭapamaṇārya, who was honored with the title *Paṇḍitaratna*.
We ascertain from the study of the songs (*gānagāthā*) composed by these [teachers] that Vyāsatīrtha was well-versed in the science of music (*ganaśāstra*) and in the poetic art of Karṇāṭaka.
Consequently, there are two lineages of disciples for them.
There is one lineage of those who propagate the doctrine of Dvaita in the Sanskrit language,
and another of those who propagate the doctrine of Dvaita in the Kannada language.
Among these, the first tradition consists of eminent scholars such as Vijayīndra and others, who are counted as the foremost.
In the second [category] are those such as the most famous Purandaradāsa and others,
by whom all students of singing first rely on songs already composed;
even Purandaradāsa and the others have studied various compositions of the gods (gīrvāṇa).
Only those who had thoroughly studied the Vedānta scriptures composed treatises in the Karṇāṭaka language for the benefit of the world hereafter.
Therefore, we shall now investigate this present work.
Regarding its title *Tarkatāṇḍava* (The Dance of Reasoning) and its correspondence with that meaning, I have already written something previously.
Now, here is the division of the treatise:
That which is to be established, as well as the sequence of its establishment, we shall lead forth for examination.

Division: At the outset, a division is made by way of the names of the chapters (*pariccheda*) into three parts—the Chapter on Direct Perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*), the Chapter on Word (*śabdapariccheda*), and the Chapter on Inference (*anumānapariccheda*).

On pages 487 (lines 7), 490–12, and 505–5 of the commentary, the names following the word *pariccheda* become clear through the use of the terms "first," "second," and "third. There is something intended here.
Thus, this is very clearly established.
In this work, upon close study, various commentaries on the passages defining the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) from the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya* are found.

Therein, after praising Hari with the verse beginning “*sadāgamaika*” (the one whose sole authority is the true tradition), there follows an effort to establish the attributes mentioned therein as well as those included within that category; the division [of the work] is made according to the very names of its chapters (*pariccheda*).
These three also indeed proceed in this very way.
Here too, first is the verse beginning with “by their own means of valid cognition” (*svataḥpramāṇaiḥ*);
therein it exists for the purpose of establishing those who have entered the category of the attributes of the illustrious Rāmaṇa.
We conjecture that even the composition of the three sections conforms to the establishment of those [categories].

By examining the final passage of this composite work, it will become very clear that this entire treatise is intended for the purpose of establishing what was stated in the first half of the verse beginning with “*svataḥ*”.

Thus, since the apprehension of a *varṇa* (phoneme) as a quality is impossible according to the aforementioned reasoning, [the treatise aims to establish] that which consists of a collection of *varṇas* whose nature is eternal and all-pervading substance.

"In the root text it says, 'It is logical that the Veda is not of human origin. And in the commentary it says: 'The sense is that it is well said [in the verse] that "thus, by means of the scriptures which are devoid of a beginning," [the Veda's authority] is established as correct.'"
Within these very sections, we also encounter six intermediate subdivisions, designated by names ending in the suffix "-vāda" according to their respective subject matter. They are as follows:
1. *Prāmāṇyavāda* (The Doctrine of Validity);
2. *Vedāpauruṣeyatvavāda* (The Doctrine of the Non-human Origin of the Vedas).
3. The doctrine of God (īśvaravāda);
4. The doctrine of caste (varṇavāda); 5. The doctrine of inherence (samavāyavāda).
6. The Doctrine of Non-conceptuality (*Nirvikalpavāda*). Thus, there are thirty-two divisions among these six [schools].
According to the principle that “in one's own system, the definition is established by itself,” the names corresponding to their respective subjects are observed to be written at the end of each.
These are clear in the table of contents (*viṣayānukramaṇikā*).

Just as the term "section" (*pariccheda*) is common among the names of the major divisions (*mahāvibhāga*), and as the term "chapter" (*vāda*) is [common] among the names of the intermediate divisions (*madhyavibhāga*) which are smaller than those,
so too it is [common] among the names of the final divisions (*antimavibhāga*).
There may indeed be some word that is consistent and conveys a non-contradictory meaning.
By attaching it to the numerals "first," "second," and so forth, the phrase "let us call [him]" (*āhvayāma*) becomes further appropriate.
The venerable Bādarāyaṇa, in the *Mahābhārata*, uses words such as *pauloma* and *āstika* at the ends of the parvas to denote minor divisions.
By such terms as "Ādisabhā" and others, he adopted numerous divisions;

it appears to us that even these "wild sages" (vyālamuni) accept the word "vāda" at the end of names composed of small groups of both [types of followers] for the sake of a non-contradictory meaning, and thus this path is not our own invention,
but has its footprints marked by the author of the Nyāyadīpa itself.

In that regard, on the fourth panel, at the eighth mark, it says: "Here, up to the doctrine of the self-evident validity of cognition (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya-jñapti-vāda*). On the one hundred and eighth panel, in the eleventh line, it says: "As in the past, according to the direction stated here in this doctrine, for the sake of unhesitating engagement."
In the sixth line of the 378th folio, we observe: "And this is clearly [stated] in the very work *Vādānta*.
This same method is also followed in the *Nyāyāmṛta*, a treatise on independent discourse (*svatantravāda*).

In the commentary on this work, titled *Nyāyāmṛta*, in the section "The Argument Establishing that the Non-existent is the Counter-positive of Negation," those who examine the sentences would accept [the reading] found on page 459, line 8.
Furthermore, in some manuscripts of the root text (*mūla*), on page 184, line 9, it reads: "In the section 'The Doctrine of the Self-Origination of Cognition'."
Let this deliberation suffice;
thus ends the determination of the number of atomic theories set forth within the great systems of doctrine.
In the first [section] on the theory of validity (prāmāṇyavāda), there are eighteen [verses], 18;
in the second, the latter three, 3;
in the third, immediately following, only one, 1.
In the fourth [row]... then six... 6;
in the fifth... two above... 2;
in the sixth... the remaining two... 2. Thus.
It is to be established.
At the very outset, by means of the pretext of defining the name, the subject matter has already been presented in its general outline.

However, the primary intention of the author of this work is solely to reconcile those points of disagreement regarding the nature of knowledge and the instruments of knowledge that exist between the Naiyāyikas and those who do not follow the Vedas.
At the time of revealing each of those various compendia, we shall specifically demonstrate those respective subjects.
This specific subject matter pertains to the *Prakṛtasaṃpuṭa*.

Furthermore, within this *Saṃpuṭa*, which is designated by the terms "Pratyakṣakhaṇḍa" and "Pratyakṣapariccheda," [the discussion concerns] direct perceptions (*pratyakṣajñāna*) and their means (*sādhana*).

The investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) has been accomplished through reasoning. Since the means for knowing and the objects of knowledge can be easily understood through the very treatises on the definitions of the means of valid cognition, such as the *Paddhati*, the discussion of validity (*prāmāṇya*) alone remains.

Even there, no such dispute exists regarding the essential nature of validity; rather, it concerns only how its production and its cognition occur. Therefore, we clearly perceive that this very subject, in its general form, is the traveler upon the path of inquiry, for what has been examined in its general aspect is not [exhausted] by its specific aspects, such as the validity of perception and so forth.
It is not established.
In the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pariccheda*), an investigation into the validity of direct perception alone is appropriate,
and not that of verbal testimony (*śābda-pramāṇya*) and so forth.
True.

If he had intended to define each specific validity (*prāmāṇya*) in its respective determination, then the doubt would have remained: "If the general validity is not intrinsic (*svataḥ*), how could a particular validity be so?

Therefore, since the doubt regarding particulars is pacified by the very investigation of the general at the outset, we perceive that the definition of the general validity right here is not untenable.
In that regard as well—
(a) the Vedāntins hold that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*),
while the Naiyāyikas hold that it is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
(kha) The Vedāntins hold that the Vedas are authorless and eternal, whereas the Naiyāyikas maintain that they were uttered by God and are non-eternal.
(ga) The Vedāntins maintain that the omniscience and other attributes of God are established solely through the Vedas.
The Naiyāyikas [hold] that [the existence of sound is established] by inferences that do not apprehend the property itself;
the Vedāntins [hold] that phonemes are eternal and all-pervading substances;
the Naiyāyikas [hold] that they are impermanent qualities.
(Ṅa) The Vedāntins hold that color is to be known through conjunction (*saṃyoga*),
whereas the Naiyāyikas maintain it is through inherence (*samavāya*).
(Ca) The Vedāntins maintain that indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) does not exist.
"There is [a self]," say the Naiyāyikas;
thus there are sixteen conflicting views.
It is for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion regarding these that the formal debate (vāda) is accepted.

Having stated that this chapter concerns the subject of validity (*prāmāṇya*), the following objection arises: "What is the relevance of an investigation into the Veda, the Lord (*Īśvara*), and so forth?
To this, we reply as follows.

Since objections arise regarding the inherent validity (*prāmāṇya-svatastva*) once it has been introduced, and since the final doctrine (*siddhānta*) cannot be firmly established unless these are resolved, one must resort to five arguments;
thus, each preceding argument is followed by each succeeding one.

When the self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of cognitions and the means of cognition is to be established, it follows that this also applies to the Veda; thus, the Veda's status is well-settled through its eternity and lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*).
The composition of the second discourse, concerning the non-human origin of the Veda, is intended to dispel the doubt that "this [self-validity] is inconsistent if the Veda were of human origin.
When an opponent objects, "I shall resolve in this way the very inconsistency that arises if there is human authorship," the third discourse begins.
To the question that because the individual phonemes (varṇas) are impermanent, the Vedas—which consist of an aggregate of them—are also impermanent; [the answer is:
sound (śabda) is an eternal and all-pervading substance, whereas articulated sound (dhvani) is a quality of space (ākāśa).
Thus, for the fourth [proponent] who maintains this position:

"If sound is not a quality of space, then it has no relation of inherence (*samavāya*) with space, which is the auditory organ; therefore, who could perceive it through the auditory organ?"—and for the fifth [proponent], who seeks to suppress the clamor by denying inherence:

"In the absence of inherence, the two-fold nature of perceptional valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramā*), distinguished as non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*), would be uprooted"—this is the first [point of] the sixth [proponent], who proclaims his own desired conclusion.

The sequence of exposition. We shall demonstrate the method for remaining steadfast regarding the object of knowledge by indicating the general direction within the doctrine of the validity of cognition (*prāmāṇyavāda*) in one particular section.
In the verse beginning with "svataḥpramāṇaiḥ," the intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) of validity (*prāmāṇya*) is introduced.

If the word *pramāṇa* is derived in the sense of a state (*bhāva-sādhana*), then validity is a property of cognition (*jñāna-dharma*). If, however, it is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*), then it is a property of the means of producing cognition.
Regarding this twofold validity (*prāmāṇya*), there are two views: self-validity in its cognition (*jñapti*) and self-validity in its production (*utpatti*).

Ultimately, there is self-validity in the cognition of that which resides in knowledge, self-validity in the production of that which resides in knowledge, and self-validity in the cognition of that which resides in the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Thus, a fourfold classification has emerged, including [the views of] origination from self;
the investigation of these will now be undertaken in their proper order.
And as for that— what indeed is this so-called "intrinsic validity" (svatastva),
and what is the inconsistency in any other alternative?
What is the means of valid cognition?
How are the logical impossibilities resolved? Why is there no dependence on another?
Thus, through these questions and answers, the stream of inquiry pursues the matter in that very manner, thinking it will become perfectly clear.
In all cases, the essence of "being intrinsic" (svatastva) is either being innate (sahajatva) or being the natural rule (autsargikatva), and not being produced through dependence on something else.

For this very reason, it is stated on the twelfth folio: "Because [validity] is innate (*sahaja*), the self-validity (*svatastva*) consisting in the spontaneous apprehension of validity is not established"; and on the two hundred and third folio:
"The power that produces valid cognition is innate, but unlike the power that produces error, it is not something acquired (*ādheya*)."
1. The self-validity (*svatastva*) of the cognition of the validity of knowledge—this has been explained in three ways.

One [view] is as follows: "The necessity that the validity of each respective cognition, which consists in its correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*), is the object of a witnessing consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*) directed toward that very cognition which is the locus of such validity, provided that this cognition is not accompanied by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that presents something contradictory to the validity of the object to be grasped."

"Another [definition] is: 'the fitness of the validity of each respective cognition to be the object of a witnessing consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*) which has as its object that very cognition upon which the validity of the apprehended [object] depends.

Here, that which the Naiyāyikas consider to be the *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent reflective awareness) regarding the form of a cognition is precisely what is designated by the term 'witnessing consciousness' (*sākṣin*).
If that witness were to grasp the cognition, it would necessarily grasp its validity as well."
Just as for a traveler elephant, the removal of thorns is merely the motive (prayojaka) and not the instrument (karaṇa), so too is the warding off of that which presents obstacles to validity.
This is the final meaning established by the first definition.
By the second [type of cognition], however, there exists a power to apprehend validity, just as fire has a burning power;
yet, just as fire may fail to burn due to an obstructing factor, this [second cognition] may also fail to have validity as its object.
Nevertheless, just as palm-leaf and other such things are combustible, validity is also apprehensible by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).
Thus, it follows that self-validity (*svatastva*) consists in the fitness for being an object of direct perception;
as for the third etymological derivation, let it rest, as it is not unique to our own system.
2. Impossibility under another interpretation:
"Self-validity (svatastva) consists in being apprehended by the entire causal complex that apprehends the cognition along with what apprehends its invalidity;
the absence of this is other-validity (paratastva)."
Thus, in the *Maṇi*, the Mīmāṃsakas’ doctrine of intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) has been explained in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Here, its ultimate refutation is stated as follows:
by the word “that” (*tat*), the validity of that cognition of a jar—which arises in a particular context—is [established].
It does not appear; rather, it is known as a sublation because another cognition is apprehended.

Even the refinement—that "it is the state of being the object of a produced cognition which is not produced by a cognition whose object is that [original] cognition"—is untenable in its intended meaning, because even the desired *anuvyavasāya* (reflective awareness) is produced by some unproduced cognition of God (*īśvara-jñāna*).

Therefore, when it is stated that "it is the knowledge produced by the knowledge of that [object]," or when "non-producedness" is defined in a way favorable to one's own position by abandoning the words "produced by the knower of both," the very fault of contradiction (*bādhā*) and so forth has been stated.
When the sentence "all knowledge is a quality" is employed, precisely such a verbal cognition arises.
The established position is that its validity is apprehended by the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).
The essential point here is that this reflective awareness does not possess the same qualifier that was stated [in the initial cognition].
3. Proof for intrinsic validity (*svatastva*):

"The validity of cognition is apprehended intrinsically, because it is apprehended while not being apprehended by another; whatever is apprehended while not being apprehended by another is apprehended by that [very thing], just as color, which is not apprehended by another, is apprehended by the eye. And so forth.
The first [position] was stated in accordance with the refutation of intrinsic validity (*svatastva*);

and the second was stated in accordance with [the following inference]: “The subject of dispute—the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*)—is capable of being the object of the validity of the knowledge it apprehends, because it is a subsequent cognition, like another subsequent cognition whose object is the same as that of a prior cognition whose validity has been apprehended. And so forth.
Since it is not easy to provide a graceful verbal restatement of those subjects that are established solely through the path of logic, we therefore leave them exactly as they are.
4. Refutation of the impossibility of the self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) [of cognition]:
"I know this is silver"—this is one subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).
Immediately following this, there is no doubt as to whether silver is a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition or not.
Therefore, having silverness as its qualifier is not an external object; rather,
this is the object of the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya),
nor does any doubt arise regarding that which is qualified by silverness.
Therefore, the qualification by "silver-ness" (rajatatva-vaiśiṣṭya) is an external object;
it is not the object of the subsequent cognition (anuvyavasāya).
The qualification by "silver-ness" and so forth resides within the status of being a valid cognition (prāmāṇya).

Therefore, how can it be established through inferences proving the self-validity (*svatastva*) of validity that validity is the object of the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*)? To this objection—that [the inference] is thus sublated—one might reply: "By what means of knowledge is the absence of the apprehension of the qualification of silverness in the primary awareness (*vyavasāya*) established? It is by the subsequent reflective awareness."
If the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) does not have that [object] as its object, then its very establishment would not occur;
this is the manner of the refutation.
5. When knowledge arises, there might initially be a doubt as to whether it is valid or not;
that [doubt] would not arise, because at the very moment of apprehending the cognition, its validity is not abandoned.
Thus, there is no other possibility.
It has been stated that the restriction regarding the apprehension of validity occurs precisely when there is an absence of an obstructing factor, and not when an obstructing factor is present.

In a case where there is doubt regarding validity, the contradictory [cognition] exists; therefore, validity does not become the object [of that cognition], and thus it is a doubt—this is the manner of refutation by others.
6. Regarding the reasons stated for the self-validity (*svatastva*) of authority, let them be; they may not establish the probandum.
To this objection that [the reasons] are irrelevant (*aprayojaka*), the following is the refutation.
In order to engage with unwavering resolve in great undertakings such as sacrifices, the authority of the Veda and other scriptures must necessarily be known;
thus, the authority of one is established by another, and that of the latter by yet another.

In that case, there would be an infinite regress due to the phrase "by another"; therefore, having abandoned the extrinsic nature (*paratastva*) of validity, one must accept its intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) alone.
Why is extrinsic validity (*paratastva*) not accepted?

7. Regarding the extrinsic nature of validity (*prāmāṇyaparatastve*), since the determination of validity is necessary in order to dispel the doubt regarding invalidity (*aprāmāṇyaśaṅkā*), the aforementioned infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is one defect.
8. If validity were itself to be inferred, how could there be a cognition of validity at the outset?
Since the probandum would not be established, this is another fault.
9. "The validity of a cognition— which is the object of a doubt that occurs in the third moment relative to a certainty regarding its own substratum and object—

is not apprehended by the very cognition that apprehends its own substratum, because it is the qualifier of the qualifier of the form of the cognition to be grasped, and because it is the qualificand of that [cognition]."
Because it is a member of a doubt that occurs in the third moment, is co-located with its own substratum and object, and is delimited by them—
just like invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*)—
invalidity is not apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
Because a doubt regarding invalidity arises in the third moment immediately after [the cognition of] knowledge;

likewise, because a doubt regarding validity arises in some cases in the third moment immediately after [the cognition of] validity, the essential point is that validity, too, is not intrinsic (*svataḥ*). This is another counter-argument.
The reversal of that [position] is as follows:

in this proof, the term "all cognitions that apprehend their own substratum" includes even the inference desired by oneself; therefore, the proof of its non-apprehensibility is overwhelmed by the fault of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Furthermore, there is sublation (*bādha*) and contradiction (*vyāghāta*).

By this same method and through the very same lack of discipline, other inferences as well are flawed; thus, the suspicion that the validity of the cognition of a defective rule is extrinsic (parataḥ) is not well-founded.
Regarding the self-validity (*svatastva*) of the truth of knowledge at the time of its origination:

in this definition of self-validity, such an elaborate effort is not required. Since that [self-validity], which is the opposite of the probandum, will be easily understood through the inference of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself, it is not defined here; rather, on the eighth line of the one hundred and fifty-fourth folio, it is stated: "The state of having an origin dependent solely upon that which produces the knowledge... (*jñānajanakamātrādhīnajanmatvaṃ*).
It has been stated that [the property] "belongs to itself."

In the preceding examination of intrinsic nature (*svatastva*), the *anuloma* (direct) method was adopted by stating the favorable arguments and then refuting the unfavorable ones; now, the *pratiloma* (reverse) method is employed by first refuting the unfavorable arguments and then establishing the favorable ones.

Thus, first, there is the refutation of the theory of extrinsic validity (*paratastva*). There exist the following inferences establishing extrinsic validity: "Invalid cognition is produced by causes other than those of [valid] cognition, because, while being an effect, it is a particular instance thereof, like invalidity," and so forth.

Just as invalid cognition (*apramā*)—which is a specific type of cognition—is produced by defects (*doṣa*) over and above the general causes of cognition, so too is valid cognition (*pramā*) that is non-eternal produced by excellences (*guṇa*) and so forth; such is the meaning [of the opponent's position]. This is the objection.
For valid cognition (*pramā*) is indeed knowledge (*jñāna*);
it is undisputed that its cause is the cause of knowledge.
Even so, if you were to prove that it is produced by a cause distinct from that [cause of knowledge], then there would be contradiction (*virodha*) and sublation (*bādha*) in your own inferences.
There is no quality whatsoever that can fulfill the status of being an effect of valid cognition;
likewise for other inferences as well—this is merely an illustration of the point.
Such is the rebuttal.

11. Even if a general quality (*guṇa*) may not exist in valid cognition (*pramā*) as such, it is clearly demonstrated that for every instance of non-eternal valid cognition, qualities such as the absence of a connection with what is non-existent (*avidyamānāsaṃsarga*) and so forth constitute its quality.

Nevertheless, since the mere non-apprehension of non-relation is easily available even in error, one might say that [the opponent] intends to mean the existence of the object itself by means of a non-existent qualifier;
however, the existence of the object is a cause common to all cognitions,
and therefore it does not contradict the doctrine of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*).

12. Let there not be a single concomitant property (*anugata-guṇa*) in non-eternal cognitions; rather, let cognition arise through many non-concomitant [causes] alone. "The state of being a non-eternal valid cognition (*anityapramātva*) resides only in those effects whose causal status is counter-correlative to a causality delimited by a property residing only in its own substratum; it resides only in those effects that are not producible by anything other than the substratum of such a causality."
In this regard, there is the following inference as proof: "Because it is a property [of cognition], like invalidity (*apramātva*).
Invalidity requires an additional cause beyond the general causes of non-eternal cognition; whatever effect depends on that [additional cause] is restricted to its own occurrence.

Therefore, those properties—such as being a produced perceptual error—which reside in the states of error generated by their own substratum, are the loci of the effect-nature delimited by each of those [properties], such as produced perceptual errors and the like.
It exists only in that [subject].
And thus—the error of impermanence—is not an effect of a single kind;
rather, it is manifold through the distinctions of perception, inference, and so forth.
It follows, therefore, that the causes are likewise manifold;
and in the same way, even impermanent cognitions produce various effects,
and their respective causes are also manifold.
It follows, therefore, that the respective qualities corresponding to each [effect] are the causes in their respective instances.
This is a doubt based on the inference that [the Vedic text] consists of only five words as stated by the Lord of Sacrifice (Yajñapati). The refutation of this is as follows.
Granted that there may be various causes for non-eternal cognitions;
however, these are not qualities (*guṇas*),
but rather the respective prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*) of those cognitions, which are precisely what we maintain.

Nevertheless, since the connection between the probandum and the reason is already established in the aforementioned inference, the fault here is that of proving what is already proven (siddhasādhana). Thus [it is said].

13. The property of being a valid means of cognition (*pramātva*) for the perception of the impermanent is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of "being an effect" (*kāryatā*), because—provided there is no subverting evidence—it resides in all effects, just like "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Pot-ness resides in every effect; therefore, it is the delimiting factor of "being an effect."
In this way, there would also be the status of being a valid perception (*pratyakṣapramātva*) regarding impermanence.

This same sequence applies to the status of being a valid inference (*anumitipramātva*) regarding impermanence and to the status of being a valid verbal cognition (*śābdapramātva*). Such is another objection.
In the case of all direct perception (*pratyakṣapramā*), neither sense-object contact (*indriyasaṃnikarṣa*) nor the object (*artha*) is the cause [of validity].

For when one sees mother-of-pearl and errs, thinking "this is silver," since both the contact and the object in the form of mother-of-pearl are present there, it would follow that the cognition "this is mother-of-pearl" would be a valid cognition (*pramā*).
If it is argued that the defect (*doṣa*) does not manifest the mother-of-pearl, [the response follows...]
"In that case, let the mere absence of defects be what is efficacious for valid cognition;
let there be no other cause. This is the reply.

14. Invalidity (*apramātva*) is that which is necessitated by the state of being non-eternal knowledge (*anityajñānatva*), provided it requires more than that as its necessitating factor; for when such an additional necessitating factor exists, invalidity arises, and when it does not exist, it does not arise—just like [the case of] invalidity itself.

By this inference, in the perceptual valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramā*) of an object consisting of gross parts, the contact of the sense organ with many parts (*bhūyo 'vayavendriyasannikarṣaḥ*) is the cause.
In that case, following doubt and error, specific valid cognition (*viśeṣapramā*) is the cause;
in an inference that is necessarily of the nature of valid cognition, the consideration of the logical mark (*liṅgaparāmarśa*) is the cause;
and in such verbal cognition, the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārthajñāna*) is the cause—this is the conclusion reached in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
I suspect that for one suffering from jaundice, although there occurs both the cognition of yellowness and whiteness in the conch-shell and repeated sensory contact with its parts,
he nevertheless perceives the conch-shell as yellow and errs;
he does not correctly cognize it as white.
Therefore, there is the fault of the deviation of positive concomitance (*anvayavyabhicāra*) in the claim that "the effect does not exist at all when the cause exists.
For instance, there arises a doubt as to whether what stands before one is a post or a person;
subsequently, by perceiving hands and so forth, or feet and so forth, the certain conviction arises that it is indeed a person.
That [subsequent cognition] is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*).
In this case of valid knowledge following a doubt, where is there any application of the cause you favor—namely, the form of a specific valid knowledge? It is nowhere.
Therefore, since the effect has arisen despite the absence of the cause, there is also the fallacy of deviation in negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*).
Thus is the resolution.
15. Let the mere absence of defects be the cause;
even so, the claim that validity is intrinsic (svataḥ) is not well-supported.

For just as in the case of a staff, its being a staff, its solidity, and so forth, although they are useful for the effect [of holding], they lack the status of being the [actual] cause, the same can be explained here as well.
By this much, even the objections against the intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) of the production of validity have been refuted.

What is the proof for the intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) of the production of validity? The following inference serves as the proof: "The state of being an impermanent, true cognition is not a non-delimiting property of the effect that is not delimited by the state of being an impermanent cognition, because it lacks the absence of occurrence in impermanent cognitions, just like the state of being a cognition (*jñānatva*).
Such is the inference.
The state of being knowledge (*jñanatva*) does not reside in impermanent knowledge;
therefore, it is devoid of non-residence therein.
Consequently, that which resides everywhere in everything qualified by the state of being impermanent knowledge— [is the subject].
The meaning is that in that case, being an effect is not a non-delimiting factor;
thus, it is not stated that "cognition has arisen in the form of cognition-ness.
In the same way, it is certainly not the case that the property of being an impermanent true cognition does not reside in an impermanent cognition.
Therefore, regarding the general property of non-eternal knowledge (*anityajñānasāmānya*), that which is its "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) is not delimited [by specific qualities].
Knowledge arises in the form of being non-eternal, being true (*yathārtha*), and so forth; thus, it is not called by those names. This is the demonstration of this point.
Thus, it follows that valid cognition (pramā) does not require any cause beyond what is necessary for the production of knowledge;
and so, on page 154, in verse 8, the establishment of self-validity (svatastva) is stated as "having its birth dependent solely upon that which produces knowledge."
17. Non-validity (or error) would also be intrinsic; moreover, let the defect in the case of valid cognition be considered simply as a quality.
Thus, this counter-objection is to be answered as follows:
when there is a defect, there is error; when there is an absence of a defect, there is no error.
Thus, since there is no way whatsoever to abandon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the fault that consists in being a cause of invalid cognition is indeed unavoidable.

Regarding the intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) of the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the intrinsic validity of the cognition (*jñāna*): since the refutation of the opponent's position is equally easy to accomplish regarding the intrinsic validity of the instrument through the very same arguments used for the intrinsic validity of the cognition, no separate effort has been made here for that purpose.

18. The validity of an instrument (karaṇa) consists precisely in its being the means for the cognition of an object as it truly is. Its "self-validity" (svatastva) with respect to its apprehension consists in its being apprehended by whatever apprehends the fact of its producing that cognition.
Just as the power to produce knowledge resides inherently in the sense organs, so too does the power to produce knowledge of objects as they truly are possess inherent existence,
or rather, it is non-different from them at the time of their arising.
All of this is merely an exposition of the *Tattvanirṇaya*, which states: "Validity is indeed intrinsic, for otherwise there would be an infinite regress; invalidity, however, is extrinsic."
From the very beginning, through this much of a discourse:

"I worship the Lord of the Glory of Infinite Auspicious Qualities, who has been described by means of self-evident authorities and the Vedic traditions, which are free from beginningless [defects], with great reverence."

Thus, by means of the introductory verse stated here following the salutation to the deity and the guru, that which was demonstrated—that the venerable Rāmaṇa possesses infinite auspicious qualities proclaimed by the Veda, which is itself a valid authority independent of any author—is not untenable;
for even though the Veda is not of human origin, its innate validity remains unimpaired.
Thus the conclusion is reached.

Therefore, at the conclusion of the discussion on validity, he showed the summary: "Consequently, because validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), even the Veda, though not of human origin, is indeed a means of valid cognition."
An investigation of the commentaries:
Two commentaries on this work have come into my hands— first, one titled *Yuktiratnākara*.
2. This other work, called the *Nyāyadīpa*, was composed by Vijayīndra, the author of the *Yuktiratnākara*.
He was a disciple of the original author (Mūlakāra), the teacher of the authors of the *Nyāyadīpa*, and his spiritual preceptor (*paramaguru*) in the *āśrama* tradition.

This commentary is also extensive in its verbal expression; for it says in the fourth folio of the *Nyāyadīpa*: “The detailed exposition here, up to the discussion on the cognition of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇyajñapti*), is to be seen in the *Yuktiratnākara* composed by the venerable Guru.
We are left in doubt as to whether this is complete or whether it extends only this far.
This detailed exposition is complete in just this much; thus, it is indeed included within the statement of the *Nyāyadīpa*.
Furthermore, we do not perceive it as being entirely complete.
Therefore, it is logical to take the side of the position that [the world] is incomplete.
In this regard:
"There is indeed a commentary composed by the venerable teacher (Gurupāda), but it is extremely extensive;
therefore, this commentary is being composed for the sake of those with dull intellects, covering the entire scope [of the subject]."
Thus, the second verse found in the Nyāyadīpa and other works is also authoritative evidence.
The authors of this work titled *Nyāyadīpa* are Rāghavendra Svāmins;
regarding this, there is no objection whatsoever.
Regarding their lives and conduct, the poem titled *Rāghavendravijaya* and the hymn titled *Guruguṇastava* are already well-known today.
The authors of the *Guruguṇastava* were the grandsons of Raghavendra Svāmī during his householder stage, and his great disciples during his ascetic stage; they were masters of debate (*vādīndra*).
The primary author is Vijayīndra, and his [disciple] is Rāghavendra; by this, their period is also almost fully revealed.
Their Vṛndāvana shines in the village named Mantrālaya, situated near the city of Rāyacūru, where he excels in fulfilling the desires of his devotees.
Unlike other renunciants, these were not ushered into Vṛndāvana after death; rather,
desiring to transcend even the range of all vision, they entered within by fashioning a mental Vṛndāvana and caused it to be established.
Such is the doctrine of truth according to the followers of the Sāṃpradāyika school.
They remember the assistance rendered to the Madhva school by these [teachers] as follows:

"The seed sown by Vyāsa upon the soil of the Śruti, its sprout-glory obtained from the feet of the Blessed Lord (Madhva), was slightly made to flourish by the ancients; then it was fully developed with spreading branches by the victorious Jayatīrtha."
"This victorious tree of the Madhva Siddhānta has sprouted from Maunīśa Vyāsārāja, it has blossomed under Śrī Indrācārya, and today it bears fruit under Śrī Rāghavendra. Thus [it is said].
Let it suffice that this poem and hymn, composed regarding his deeds which exceed even this, serve as a guide for the path. Thus ends [the work].

The meaning is: "by those which produce valid cognition" (*pramājanakaiḥ*), precisely because they possess the capacity to generate such knowledge, namely, the validity of that respective knowledge which consists in its correspondence with reality (*yāthārthyarūpa*).

The meaning of *āṅ* is primacy (*mukhyatva*). The sense is that it is stated by primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) preceded by intention (*tātparya*).
This is evident when it is expressed through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Regarding this, the detailed exposition up to the theory of the self-evident nature of the cognition of validity (*svataḥprāmāṇyajñaptivāda*) is to be found in the *Yuktiratnākara* composed by the venerable Guru.
The self-evident nature (*svatastva*) of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whose form is the Veda is to be known through the cognition of its ascertained validity.

Likewise, the self-evident nature of the production (*utpatti-svatastva*) depends upon the establishment of the self-evident nature of the production of the validity of the cognition generated by that [Veda]; thus it is understood sequentially in the case of cognition (*jñapti*).

And in order to establish that very point first, while explaining the statement made by the author of the *Ṭīkā*—"Self-validity (*svatastva*) consists in being apprehended solely by the apprehender of cognition"—he defines self-validity with respect to the act of knowing (*jñapti*) as follows: "Of that which has the nature of correspondence (*yāthārthya*)," etc.
"Object" (*artha*) means the knowable.
"Yathārtha" means existing without transgression [of the object]. It is an *avyayībhāva* compound meaning "according to similarity. The state of being according to the object is *yāthārthya*.

The meaning is that "of that nature" refers to the non-deviation from the object of knowledge (*jñeyāvyabhicāritva*), which consists in taking as its object the knowable exactly as it exists. This has been stated as "of this [cognition] which is the validity of cognition" by accepting that such non-deviation resides in every single instance of valid cognition (*pramiti*), whether it be mediated (*parokṣa*) or immediate (*aparokṣa*), produced or unproduced. The underlying intention is that [other definitions], such as being either the means of proof (*sādhana*) or the substratum (*āśraya*) for the establishment of validity as "being an experience" (*anubhūtitva*) or "reaching an unknown object" (*anadhigatārthagantṛtva*), are flawed due to defects such as being too narrow (*avyāpti*) or impossible (*asaṃbhava*). Thus, the essence of validity is established as residing in all cognitions.

Although this [validity] is common to all cognitions by virtue of its being a subsequent measure (*anupramāṇa*), it has been stated that the validity of a cognition consists in its having the object of knowledge as its domain through the power of the scripture (*sātra*).

Furthermore, the qualification "this and that" (*tattat*) is applied to each specific cognition in order to illuminate the self-validity (*svatastva*) of validity residing in every instance of valid cognition, emphasizing that each [instance of validity] is indeed distinct from the others.

Self-validity (*svatastva*) consists in the necessity that a particular cognition, which is the substratum of the apprehended validity and which is not accompanied by a causal complex that presents a contradiction to that apprehended validity, must be the object of the witnessing-consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*). Nevertheless, because it is necessary to have a means for ascertaining the validity— such as the perceptual cognition that grasps the nature of that [original] cognition, the inferential cognition produced by reasoning that supports it, and the cognition of its validity itself— the validity of the cognition is also included as the subject (*dharmin*).
Alternatively, one should not be misled into thinking— as in the view of ancient logicians— that validity is intrinsic in some cases and extrinsic in others;
rather, it is so in all cases.

In the view of the Navīnas (the Neo-Nyāya school), since it is accepted that [validity] is everywhere extrinsic (*parataḥ*), one should understand that this is stated "in order to exclude that" [extrinsicality]. Regarding the term *grāhya* (to be apprehended): the meaning is that there is a necessity regarding its being an object [of apprehension] in this sense—that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*), which does not have as its object those specific cognitions that serve as the substratum for the apprehended validity (*grāhyapramāṇya*) because they are not conjoined with the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of the suspicion of defects (*doṣaśaṅkā*) and so forth that presents that [validity], indeed apprehends it. Thus, there is a certainty regarding its being an object of that [witness-consciousness].

Since the *Nyāyāmṛta* establishes that cognitive error (*vipratipatti*) is not necessary [for the occurrence of doubt], it has stated only one alternative— that there is no certainty [regarding its presence].

Here, although the nature of contradiction— consisting in being the absence of validity (*prāmāṇya*) or being pervaded by it— is absent in any one of the four [factors] such as the absence of validity,

that which constitutes "contradiction with the apprehended validity" (*grāhyaprāmāṇyavirodhitva*) is the state of being the object of that cognition, upon whose occurrence the ascertainment of validity is obstructed.
This is to be understood in the case of the absence of validity (*prāmāṇyābhāva*) and so forth.

And he will state later, in the discussion on the fact that the ascertainment of validity is the motivator for action: “Because absences [are defined] as the absence of that which is opposed to the ascertainment of validity,” and so on.

[The nature of an obstacle] consists either in being an impediment to the ascertainment of validity, or in obstructing some property conducive to it, or in being pervaded by the non-arising of that [ascertainment].

Although the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇya-niścaya*) is eternal knowledge by virtue of its nature as a witness (*sākṣin*), its having validity as its object and so forth are indeed produced; thus, it is not difficult to account for the non-arising of an ascertainment of validity qualified by those [properties].

In the phrase "that which brings [the object] to mind" (*upasthāpaka*), it should be understood that the meaning is "not conjoined with either the presentation of a contrary [cognition] or the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces it."

and the doubt that there is a contradiction because the witness-consciousness, while grasping the cognition of a jar, does not grasp the validity of the cognition of a cloth, is addressed by what remains.

In my view as well, the objection— that there would be a contradiction because the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) fails to apprehend validity when an obstacle exists, namely the presence of a causal complex that apprehends a factor contradicting the apprehended validity, such as the suspicion of a defect— is also refuted. Here, although it might seem inappropriate to maintain the restriction that "objecthood" belongs only with respect to the cognition of the witness-consciousness;
In my view as well, since validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not apprehended by inference,
it is nonetheless logical that there is a rule that [validity] is simply the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*) with respect to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*). Furthermore,

this is because [validity] lacks the nature of being a cognition of a cognition (*jñānajñānatva*), such as having the form of "having that mode as its mode" (*tatprakāraprakārakatā*), which is what is intended here.
Regarding the phrase "tattajjñāna" (that specific cognition):

even if one were to state "having as its object the locus of the validity of the apprehended," the aforementioned defect would remain unchanged because a cognition of a jar could still apprehend a cloth; therefore, it is restated as "having as its object that specific cognition.
For this very reason, the term "that specific" (*tattat*) is also used in the designation of the subject (*dharmin*).

The point is this: if it were not stated that [the witness-consciousness] is the substratum for the apprehension of the validity of the object (*grāhya-pramāṇya-āśraya*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of even a cognition that is the substratum of invalidity being grasped by the term "that particular cognition. Consequently, since the witness-consciousness directed toward that [invalid cognition] would not grasp its validity, there would be a direct contradiction (*bādha*). Even though the witness-consciousness is one, the apprehension of the validity of the cognition of a cloth is contingent upon the apprehension of the cognition of the cloth itself; it is not contingent upon the apprehension of the cognition of a jar. Therefore, the suspicion of contradiction is indeed appropriate.

Regarding the phrase "doubt regarding defect" (*doṣaśaṅkā*): it means the doubt that [the cognition] is produced by a defective instrument, which takes the form of either the ascertainment of that [defect] or its cause and so forth.

Since it is possible to interpret the [text's] "by the witness alone" (*sākṣiṇaiva*) in two ways—as being grasped by the witness or as being grasped indeed by the witness—the author states the intended meaning with the word "here" (*atra*).
The meaning is "in the case of etymological interpretation"—that is, by means of inference.
The meaning is that an inference arises for Maitra and others in the form: "Caitra’s cognition is valid because it accords with the object," and so forth.
(Note: *ṇya* for *ṇya-grahaṇāt*; *ktam* for *uktam*; *sāmagryā* for *sāmagryāḥ*);
*sva-jña-sva-ni.* (abbreviation for *sva-jñāna-sva-niyata*).)

Alternatively, *svatastva* (self-validity) is the fitness of the validity of each respective cognition to be the object of a witnessing consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*) which has that very cognition as its object and which is based on the validity of the apprehension of that cognition. [Objection: But if the witnessing consciousness, which apprehends the cognition, apprehends its validity only by depending on the absence of a contrary causal complex (*virodhisāmagrī*), then it is impossible for it to possess *svatastva*, defined as being apprehended by the cognition-apprehender independently [of such factors]. To this, he says: "Even by the theory of extrinsic validity (*paratastva*) and so forth. This means: even according to the theory of extrinsic validity and other such views.
For there is a fault [in the theory] if the non-occurrence of the causal complex that presents the contradictory [cognition] is the cause for grasping validity;
however, there is no fault if it functions as a mere *prayojaka* (indirect cause), like the removal of a thorn by an elephant capable of walking. Thus Bhava has stated: "as a *prayojaka*. 1.

Previously, the etymological definition was provided by specifying the causal agent with reference to the presence of a result; now, however, he states another method by abandoning such a qualification—namely, "or else" (yadvā).

Or, he says "or else" (yadvā) in order to establish that validity is intrinsic (svataḥ) in all cases and at all times. Now, if intrinsic validity consists in being apprehended by the unimpeded witness-consciousness (sākṣin), then the general rule (utsarga) is simply this: "The witness, which apprehends cognition, grasps it as valid"—and it is only through the exception (apavāda) characterized by non-correspondence (visaṃvāda) that it grasps invalidity.

By stating that there is no contradiction with the principle of "generality" (autsargikatva) as set forth in the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā* and other works, the following objection is raised: even with the aforementioned qualification, there would be a sublation (bādha) because validity is not apprehended by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*) during the state of obstruction.

Furthermore, by the term "witness," [the author] refers to the knowledge of a jar produced by words such as "there is a knowledge of a jar," as well as to the knowledge produced by the non-sensory (alaukika) generalization (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) regarding the aspect of that very knowledge.
Regarding the apprehension of validity—[in the case of] 1.

*grahe* (in the apprehension)—*mu.*, *ca.*; 2. *sāraka-*—*ā.*; 3. *pakṣā-*—*ā.*, *mu.*; 4. *pakṣe-*—*mu.*; 5. because even with the aforementioned qualification, the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) does not apprehend invalidity in a situation where there is an obstructing factor—*mu.*—[this is] its own cognition, [its own] determination.
Regarding the theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*):

fitness (*yogyatva*) consists in being the delimiting factor, by means of the knowledge of its own object, with respect to the innate capacity for apprehension residing in the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).
[Objection: There is a fear that this would result in a contradiction, because fitness could never be an object [of that apprehension].

By the expression "having as its object those respective cognitions which are the substrata for the validity of the apprehended," the doubt that there is a sublation—on the grounds that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), while apprehending the cognition of a jar, never apprehends the validity of the cognition of a cloth, and thus lacks the requisite fitness—is likewise dispelled; the sense is that this is logical as before.
Here too, the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) is used, as previously, to exclude [the possibility of the witness being] the essential nature, the sense organ, or an error.

The meaning is that even the status of being a witness (*sākṣitva*)— whether it consists in having as its qualificandum that which possesses the aforementioned qualifier by way of having a mode of determination that has that [qualifier] as its mode, or whether it consists in the nature of a perceptual cognition regarding that object, or whether it consists in the nature of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) regarding the portion of the cognition— is indeed nothing other than the nature of a sensory perception (*laukikapratyakṣatva*) regarding the portion of the cognition. Here too, as in the previous case, one should understand that the function of the phrase "by the [cognition] which is the substratum of the apprehended validity" is to be understood in the same way.
Surely, it might be argued that here "self-validity" (svatastva) means the fitness to be apprehended by the very cognition that apprehends its own substrate;
and this [fitness] exists even for invalidity (aprāmāṇya).
Nor is it correct to say there is no fault because, in that case, the cognition is known by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), whereas invalidity is inferable.

Alternatively, because it will be stated later that the apprehension of invalidity occurs through the *sākṣin* (the internal witness) alone, whose capacity is established by the discrepancy (*visaṃvāda*), [the author] says this;

or else, if "fitness to be an object of the *sākṣin*" were defined as being capable of entering into empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) produced by the *sākṣin*, then this would ultimately result in the actual production of that effect, and thus the self-validity (*svatastva*) of validity at the time of its obstruction would not be secured. Therefore, he says: "And fitness is innate... (*yogyatvaṃ ca sahajām*).

With respect to the innate power of making [an object] its own content, the "delimiting nature" (*avacchedakatva*) of the witness (*sākṣin*) or its power toward that object— which is the cognition (*jñāna*) consisting in the locus of the apprehended validity— is its function as a differentiator by way of being the object (*viṣayatayā*).

The meaning is that the fitness of validity to be an object of the witness consists precisely in its capacity to induce the conventional usage "the power to grasp validity," just as one speaks of "the power to grasp cognition."
The power of the witness (sākṣi) grasps the validity residing in that [cognition] only through the medium of the cognition itself,
not directly.

Just as perception grasps a universal (jāti) only through the medium of the individual (vyakti) and not directly, it is therefore said [in the text] "through the medium of the cognition of its own object."

The Theory of Validity (*Prāmāṇyavāda*)—[Section on] Self-Cognition and Self-Awareness—Page 12. 1. *prāmāṇyasya* — *kha*. 2. *ca* — *kuṃ*. 3. *ca* — *kuṃ*. 4. *gyā* — *kuṃ*. And thus, even in a state of obstruction, just as there is the capacity for burning in the palm of the hand and so forth, there is indeed the capacity for the apprehension of validity (*prāmāṇya*).
Consequently, because the power to apprehend validity is innate, the claim that the apprehension of validity is merely "default" (*autsargika*) is unestablished.
And it has been said by the authors of the *Ṭīkā*: “The witness-consciousness itself is capable of taking both the cognition and its validity as its objects.”

The state of being the object of the single power that apprehends knowledge is the validity's fitness to be an object of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). This does not exist in invalidity, because their objects are distinct; this will be made clear later.
Gurupāda, however, explains it as follows: "By the word *sva* (self), validity (*prāmāṇya*) is meant;
it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
It refers to that very knowledge which has itself as its object, namely, the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*)."

They say that since validity does not have the power residing in the witness (*sākṣin*) as its direct object, it was stated [in the text] "by way of a cognition whose object is itself. Alternatively, even though the "power" (*śakti*) is not established in the opponent's view, this may be intended to show that it is unique to one's own system; or, thinking "I shall make the opponent accept the power," it means that [validity] is the delimiting factor for the mere causal complex that grasps the cognition, by way of the cognition whose object is itself; or, it means having a grasping function delimited by a property that serves as the delimitor of the grasping of the cognition.
Or rather, the sense is that it is for that purpose.

Now, one might ask: even by this much, how is the self-validity (*svatastva*) of the validity of a cognition—which has fallen into a state of obstruction—attained, such that all means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would possess self-validity? To this, he says: "And thus... (*evaṃ ca*).
The meaning is: "given that self-validity (svatastva) consists in the form of capacity (yogyatā)," or alternatively, "given that capacity has the aforementioned form"—thus [he says] "dāha" (burning).
The meaning is: "like the fitness for being the object of burning.
He states "and likewise" (*tathā ca*) to show that another point is also supported by the second definition—the meaning being:
"when there is a definition containing such fitness as has been stated"—namely, regarding its being the general rule (*autsargikatva*).

The meaning is that it is the general rule (*autsargikatva*) as stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā* and other works, namely: "The witness (*sākṣin*), which grasps cognition, perceives [it] precisely as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); this is merely the default state. And so it has been said.

The meaning is that it has been stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā* that validity (*prāmāṇya*) has as its object an innate capacity (*sahaja-śakti*), and that there is fitness (*yogyatā*) in the case of an obstruction.
