[End of section] svapna-jña-sva-ni. (Self-cognition of dreams).
However, [the opponent argues]: "But [the cognition] apprehends only the knowledge itself as it is restricted [by its object], and it does not intend to apprehend its validity. // 2 //
Alternatively, *svatastva* (intrinsic validity) is the necessity that [validity] is the object of a cognition distinct from any cognition whose object is not established as valid for both [parties].

Even if the reading there were "obstructed by the occurrence of another cause" or "by a mental error," this would still be a restatement of a portion [of the definition], and thus there is no fault. // 2 //
Out of confidence, he states another alternative position, which is common to all who maintain that [the self] is not self-proven, with the words "Or else."
The phrase "of the validity of each respective cognition" is to be supplied [to the end of the sentence].

In the probandum (sādhya), it should be understood as "having as its object each respective cognition which is the locus of the validity of that which is to be apprehended. For indeed, there are many proponents of the theory of intrinsic validity (svatastvavādin).
The author of the *Grantha* alone is Bhaṭṭa,
who maintains that cognition is supersensible;
the Guru is the proponent of the view that cognition is self-luminous by its very nature.
Miśra, however, like the Naiyāyika, maintains the theory that the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) is not self-luminous (*asvaprakāśa*).

In this regard, the term "both" (*ubhaya*) refers to being accepted by both the Siddhāntin and the Tārkika, or by both the Bhaṭṭa and the Tārkika, or by both the Guru and the Tārkika, or by Miśra and the Tārkika, or by Māyi and the Tārkika; such is the meaning, because it is impossible for one person to engage in debate with several parties at once.

That which is established for both parties (*ubhayasiddham*) refers to a cognition that does not have validity as its object (*prāmāṇyāviṣayakam*), and which is agreed upon by both as being such a cognition— namely, cognitions in the form of "this is a jar" (*ayaṃ ghaṭaḥ*) and so forth, as well as cognitions in the form of "the apprehended" (*grāhya*) and so forth. Furthermore, this includes the witness-consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*) of the nature previously described in the Siddhānta, the inference of cognition (*jñānānumiti*) in the Bhaṭṭa school, and the self-luminous cognition of jars and the like in the Guru (Prābhākara) school.
According to the view of Miśra, there is an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) of that [cognition];
thus, the necessity of its being an object—namely, that it is indeed grasped by that [after-cognition]—is established in his system.

Nor should it be suspected that, according to the Guru’s (Prabhākara) view, since all cognitions are admitted to be both true (*yāthārthya*) and self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*), there is no cognition whatsoever that does not have validity as its object; for this...

In cases where there is the superimposition of non-validity upon a cognition—such as in the phrase "the validity of knowledge"—it is accepted by both the Guru (Prabhākara) and the Tārkika (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika) that such a cognition does not have validity as its object. (Note: The variants indicate that the word "tat" is absent in manuscript *mu* and *cha*; "hi catvāraḥ" is present in *kuṃ*; and the remaining markers indicate omissions in *kuṃ*.)

“On the theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*)— 14. @-- ----- -- -------- ---------- — therein, by the statement ‘non-different from a cognition that does not have validity as its object,’ [it is shown that] with respect to a perceptual cognition having a jar or the like as its object, such as ‘this is a jar,’ there is a cognition produced by words such as ‘knowledge is a quality’ and by words such as ‘cognition of a jar,’ which has cognition itself as its object.”

Even according to the view that self-validity (*svatastva*) applies both to the cognition itself and to the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) bound to it—[it remains that] in the Guru’s system (*Prabhākara*), "superimposition" (*āropa*) consists in the non-apprehension of the non-relation of invalidity (defined as having a qualifier residing in a different locus), whereas in the Nyāya system, it is a qualified cognition; this is another matter. In this regard:

By the expression "having as its object that specific cognition which is the locus of the apprehended validity," it is intended that the state of being distinct from the aforementioned form of cognition applies to that very portion [of the object]. Thus, when a cognition having a cognition as its object is accepted as valid, there is no fault, because it is distinct from [the initial cognition] while not having validity as its object. Alternatively, the theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*) refers to each respective validity that is to be apprehended.
And thus, as stated in the original formulation, there is no fault in that instance.

Here, if it were said that there is a necessity of being the object of a cognition whose content is the validity established for both parties—without introducing two *nañ*s—then there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of such an inference and so forth.
Therefore, the expression “distinct from that which does not have [the object] as its content” is employed.

In this context, he explains the function of the remaining words as follows: "Therein," [the first term] "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is intended to dispel the doubt that there would be a contradiction because validity is not apprehended by a cognition of a jar, etc., which is distinct from the jar, etc., having the form already described;

whereas the final [term] is intended to dispel the doubt that there would be a contradiction because of the absence of being an object of a jar, etc., which is distinct from such a cognition. Thus he says: "Therein."

If one were to state only that there is a necessity of being the object of a cognition established for both parties, without specifying "distinct from a cognition whose object is validity," then it must be asked: by the term "cognition established for both parties," is perceptual cognition intended,
or verbal cognition, or else cognition in the form of an after-cognition (anuvyavasāya)?

Regarding the second [alternative] as well, one must consider the following options: is it a cognition having [another] cognition as its object, or a cognition having a cognition conjoined with its object as its object?

Or, keeping in mind the alternatives such as: is it a cognition grasping the object, or a cognition grasping the cognition, or a cognition grasping both, or a perception in the form of an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) that grasps both?
He refutes them in succession, beginning with the words "This is a jar," and so forth.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: because the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of [a cognition] such as direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*) is not an object [of that perception].

According to the Guru’s view (*gurumata*), since validity is apprehended even by a cognition such as "this is a jar," the phrase "in relation to a cognition" (*pratīti*) should be understood as referring to a cognition such as "this cognition is invalid.
(Note: *janya* — *mu.* and *ca.* editions)

The theory of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇyavāda*): Since the three types of cognition already mentioned do not have validity as their object, they lack the property of being distinct from that [validity].

By the statement "established for both," the objection that there is a *arthāntara* (shifting the subject) because the opponent's intended property—being the object of an unimpeded after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*)—is not established; since, according to the Nyāya view, even an unimpeded after-cognition does not have validity as its object and thus lacks the quality of being distinct from it, is hereby refuted. He clarifies this dismissal of the objection with the words: "of the threefold [validity] mentioned."

As for the claim that validity—consisting in having "potness" as its qualifier in that which possesses potness—is grasped by the cognition produced by the words "this is the cognition of a pot," that is incorrect because it is the meaning of individual words (*padārtha*) rather than the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "with respect to the obstructed after-cognition" (*pratibaddhānuvyavasāyam pratīti*): in the Guru’s (Prabhākara) system, this refers to the perception of an obstructed cognition such as "this cognition is invalid"; whereas in the Bhaṭṭa system, it refers to the inference of an obstructed cognition.
The object of meditation.

Regarding the phrase "stated as being established for both": when it is stated [in the definition] that the object is "validity" (*prāmāṇya*), then— by taking as the object that knowledge which consists of an unimpeded after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) and is established for only one of the two parties— the doctrine of the self-evident nature (*svatastva*) of validity would not be established as a final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The meaning is as follows: because that [unrestricted after-cognition] lacks the absence of being non-objective with respect to validity (*prāmāṇya*), when "established for both" is stated, since an unrestricted after-cognition lacks establishment for both parties by virtue of not having validity as its object, there is indeed the state of being distinct from such knowledge established for both; thus, there is no fault of proving the unintended (*arthāntaratva*).

The mention of "after-cognition" (*anuvyavasāya*) is illustrative; it should also be understood to include unimpeded inferential cognition (*apratibaddhajñānānumiti*) and unimpeded self-luminous cognition (*apratibaddhasvaprakāśajñāna*). The same applies hereafter.
And "unimpededness" (apratibaddhatva) consists in the non-presence of that which is opposed to validity and its causal complex.
He clarifies the method for dispelling doubt with the words: "unimpeded."

The meaning is that, since [the cognition] such as "the sun established for both parties" does not have validity as its object, it is possible for it to be distinct from what is established for both parties. (Note:
*svamajñasvanni* refers to the section on self-cognition and the knower of oneself.)
Regarding the theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*):

although in the Nyāya system an unimpeded after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) has validity as its object, in my view it is possible for it to be distinct from that [validity], because it is established by both parties that it is different from the cognition whose object is validity.

By the statement "necessity" (*naiyatya*), [it is shown that] in the Nyāya system, such an inference of validity regarding validity itself— [The text appears to be a fragmentary manuscript or draft containing technical philosophical arguments concerning the nature of self-awareness and the determination of truth in the context of Nyāya epistemology.]

The doubt that [the argument] might be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)— because [the self] is the object of some subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*)— is thereby dispelled.
It should be understood that here, the first two positions are unique to our own system (*svamata*),
whereas the third is common to the systems of the Mīmāṃsakas and others.

It is with reference to these very three positions that it is stated in the *Sudhā*: “The self-validity (*svatastva*) consists in the fact that the correctness residing in a cognition is apprehended by whatever apprehends the cognition itself.

Here, regarding the first position, the term “cognition-apprehender” (*jñānagrahaka*) used in the *Sudhā* refers precisely to the substratum of the apprehended validity—[as indicated by the phrase] “of such a kind.”

In this context—meaning, within the three definitions of self-validity (*svatastva*) previously stated—it refers to [the following]: with respect to the inferential cognition, "This cognition is valid because it is the cause of successful activity," which is a cognition distinct from a cognition whose object is not the validity established by both parties;

[this inference occurs] with respect to the *vyavasāya* (primary cognition) brought forward by memory, as well as with respect to the *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent cognition) that apprehends the validity brought forward by memory, and the *anuvyavasāya* whose object is a cognition of the same class as the one whose validity has been grasped. This is the meaning.
"His own view" (*svamata*)—the meaning is that although it is common to the systems of the logicians (*tārkika*), it is not common to the three types of Mīmāṃsakas.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "Mīmāṃsakas etc.," one should understand either Bhaṭṭa, Kumārila, and Prabhākara; or, as the proponent (*siddhāntin*), Śrīdharamiśra; or those who maintain the doctrine of Māyā (*māyāvādin*) and so forth.
He establishes these three positions as they appear in the *Sudhā* text with the words "this" (*etad*) and "as stated" (*ukte*).
The meaning is that it was stated during the occasion of the commentary on the *Anuvyākhyāna* in the passage beginning with: “For the authority of scripture is indeed intrinsic, just like perception.
He clarifies that point with the words beginning with “here,” and so forth.

As for what was stated in the *Maṇi*: “Self-validity (*svatastva*) is the state of being apprehended by the entire causal complex that apprehends the cognition while not apprehending its invalidity; and the absence of that [complex] is extrinsic validity (*paratastva*). That is not correct.
In his own system (svamata), [the author] provides the definition of self-validity (*svatastva*) regarding the cognition itself (jñapti).
// 1 // Having restated the definition of self-validity as propounded by others—which is common to all three types of Mīmāṃsakas—he refutes it with the words "As for that which... (*yattu*).

In the *Maṇigrantha*: "Regarding the cognition 'this is a jar' (*ayaṃ ghaṭaḥ*) which is the locus of the validity of knowledge, whatever collection of causal factors (*sāmagrī*) apprehends that cognition but does not apprehend its invalidity—be it, according to the Guru’s (Prabhākara) view, the form of the contact between the eye and the jar and so forth which generates a self-luminous determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) of the form 'I know this jar'; or, according to the Miśra (Bhaṭṭa) view, the form of the contact between the mind and [the soul] and so forth which generates a subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*); or, according to the Bhaṭṭa view, the form of the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth which generates an inference such as 'the jar is the object of knowledge, because it is the locus of cognizedness (*jñātatā*)']..."
The meaning is that its being apprehended by that [cognition] constitutes its self-evident nature (*svatastva*).

In this etymological explanation, by the use of the word "there" (*tatra*), it refers to those cognitions such as the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, where—following the inference of invalidity based on signs such as non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*)—there arises a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form: "I know this [silver] to be invalid."

In that context, there is a concern that there would be a contradiction (*bādha*), because the validity residing in the inference— which is constituted by invalidity in the form of "having invalidity as its qualifier" when applied to a cognition lacking validity— would be apprehended by the very after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) that apprehends the invalidity residing in the first cognition. This concern is addressed by the phrase "not apprehending invalidity," because in cases such as "this cognition is invalid," the validity residing in that cognition is not apprehended by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that apprehends invalidity.

By the statement "as long as" (*yāvad*), the apprehension of validity (*prāmāṇya*) by the inferential complex that grasps knowledge (*jñānagrāhakānumitisāmagrī*) or by subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the Nyāya system— which would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)— is refuted.

It should be understood that those [conditions] which prevent sublation (*bādhavāraka*) in the positive alternative (*vidhikoṭi*) serve to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established in the negative alternative (*tadabhāvakoṭi*), and conversely, that which prevents the fallacy of proving what is already established serves to prevent sublation.

“Prāmāṇyavādaḥ pu- 19. (Note: The text provided consists primarily of critical apparatus indicating variant readings from different manuscript traditions.)

In the Guru’s system (*gurumata*), although all cognitions are valid, it is possible to have a memory of the form "this cognition is invalid"—where invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), defined as having a qualifier that does not exist in the object qualified by it, is well-known through desire—and thus it is possible to grasp an invalidity whose non-connection has not been previously grasped; therefore, even in his view, the phrase "not grasping invalidity" is not redundant.

Regarding what was stated here— that the word "therein" (tatra) has the meaning "in the cognition which is the locus of the apprehended validity," in order to exclude sublation by the apprehension of validity— that is not correct. For there is sublation [of the opponent's position] by a cognition such as a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) whose object is a single cognition having two fires as its content— such as "these two are fires"— which, due to a defect, apprehends the invalidity of one part while nevertheless apprehending the validity of the other part.

As for the claim that there is no fault because the phrase "of that which is desired" (yattu tadiṣṭasya) means "of the cognition that is the locus of the apprehension of validity regarding the object-part [of the knowledge]," that is not correct. Even so, since the apprehension of non-validity—which consists in the absence of validity regarding that part, such as "this cognition is not valid"—is sublated by the apprehension of non-validity as a positive entity, it falls prey to the fault stated in the root text. Furthermore, as for the argument that the word "tat" refers to the apprehended object...

The claim that there is no fault because the term *sat-prāmāṇya* (validity of the true) is construed with the meaning "contradictory to the validity of the object to be grasped" is also not tenable. For if that were the case, it would result in the designation *atat-prāmāṇya* (invalidity of that), and thus the word *tat* in the aforementioned designation would lack syntactic connection (*asāmarthya*) with the word *prāmāṇya*. Furthermore, in the view of the Guru (Prabhākara), although the recollection "this cognition is invalid" (*idam jñānam apramā*) apprehends invalidity, the apprehension "this is a cognition" (*idam jñānam*) acts as an obstacle to the recollection of invalidity.

This is because, by not apprehending validity (*prāmāṇya*), there would be the consequence of sublation (*bādhā*), and thus the stated definition of self-validity (*svatastva*) could not be made applicable to the Guru’s system (*gurumata*).

Nor is it the case that in the section on the arising of validity (*utpatti-prāmāṇya*), the author of the *Maṇi* himself—under the heading "The Prābhākaras, however," etc.—while discussing the demonstration of the impossibility of doubt in the Guru’s system, accepted that there is an apprehension of validity even in cases such as "Is this cognition valid or not? and thereby demonstrated that the doubt has a different object; for [he did so] even in such instances.
It should not be suspected that there is no sublation because of the existence of the apprehension of validity;
for if that were the case, it would follow that the term "non-apprehender of its invalidity" would be redundant in that [opponent's] own system.

By way of an example: even though a cognition of a cognition—which does not apprehend invalidity (defined as having a qualifier in that which lacks it)—has as its object the absolute absence of validity (defined as having a qualifier in that which possesses it), it nonetheless does not apprehend validity. Therefore...
Because of sublation (*bādhāt*).

Even if, by the term "invalidity" (*aprāmāṇya*), one intends that which is opposed to validity (*prāmāṇya*)—that is, even if, in such a case, one accepts the apprehension of validity and intends by the term "non-apprehender" (*agrāhaka*) the non-occurrence of the causal complex for its apprehension (*grāhakasāmagryasamavadhāna*)— [The text continues: ...[the opponent argues that] there would be no fault [in the definition], because in cases where validity is not apprehended due to the absence of the causal complex for its apprehension, the term "invalidity" would indeed apply to that which is opposed to validity. However, this is not so; for in such a situation, since the causal complex for the apprehension of validity is absent, the very apprehension of validity is precluded, and thus the term "invalidity" cannot be applied to it. Therefore, the definition remains faulty. Furthermore, if one were to maintain that the term "invalidity" refers to the non-existence of validity itself, then in a case where validity is apprehended but subsequently sublated, the term "invalidity" would incorrectly apply to that very object of cognition, as the non-existence of validity would still be present there. Thus, the definition is untenable. Consequently, the opponent's position is refuted. Therefore, the term "invalidity" must be intended to refer to the non-apprehension of validity. And if one intends by the term "non-apprehender" the non-occurrence of the causal complex for that apprehension, then... [the argument proceeds].

Furthermore, in the view of Miśra and others, in a case where there is a grasping of non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*), since the causal complex for that [non-validity] is absent, the grasper of the cognition would not grasp its validity even though it is not produced by that [complex].
Thus, there is indeed a sublation (*bādha*). Since such refutations are obvious, they are set aside;

rather, in the stated definition, since it is sufficient that [validity] be the object of a cognition whose object is the cognition itself, the mention of "the causal complex of the grasper" (*grāhakasāmagrī*) is redundant.

Having accepted [the objection] out of respect, he states the fault regarding the meaning of the term *aprāmāṇya* as it was heard [in the opponent's view]—either by omiting the words "grāhakasāmagrī" (the causal complex of the apprehender) and using the word "jñāna" (cognition) instead, or by restating it as it stands—by saying: "tadabhāvavatī" (that which possesses the absence of that).
"Of that which apprehends non-validity as well."

It should also be understood that [the term] "not having as its object" refers to that which is pervaded by the absolute absence of invalidity (aprāmāṇya) in the form of the aforementioned state. By this, one should also consider that the intention to express non-existence (*abhāva*) through the negative particle (*nañ*) is employed.

Now, if the negative particle has the meaning of opposition (*virodha*), there is no stated fault; for it is possible to include under the term "invalidity"—which denotes what is opposed to validity—the absence of validity, its pervader (invalidity), and its pervaders (those subsumed under invalidity), all of which are indeed opposed to validity.

With the intention that contradiction consists in being the object of a cognition that obstructs the ascertainment of validity, [the author] restates the intended meaning as formulated by Pakṣadhara and others, and then refutes it, saying: "By invalidity... etc.
By the word *api*, he indicates this:
although the attainment of that which is incompatible with the validity of the apprehended object does not occur merely by this much,
there is still no attainment because of the incapacity even when combined with that word.
[This] is the cause for being merely contradictory;
nevertheless, this is an accepted [position]—thus [it is stated] in such sentences as "bādha" and so forth.

Regarding the theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*):

because the cognition produced by the sentence "knowledge is a quality" (*jñānaṃ guṇaḥ*), etc., as well as the cognition of a cognition produced by general perception (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) such as "knowledge is an object of valid cognition" (*jñānaṃ prameyam*), do not have validity as their object, the defect of sublation (*bādha*) remains as before. Furthermore, even if one intends by the term "cognition-apprehender" (*jñānagrāhaka*) a state of being an apprehender of cognition through its inclusion of its own object—as in the case of the cognition "this is a jar" produced by words—[the same defect persists].
Since the cognition of a cognition (*jñānajñāna*) does not have the validity [of that cognition] as its object, there is indeed a contradiction.

The phrase "of the cognition of a cognition" connects with the rest of the sentence; the meaning is: of that [cognition] which has as its qualificandum a cognition whose qualifier is "being a quality" (*guṇatva*), etc., and which is produced by sentences such as "Cognition is inherent" (*jñānaṃ samavetam*) or "Cognition is an entity" (*jñānasamūrtam*).

One might argue that "not having as its qualifier a property that pervades being directly known" (*sākṣājjñānatvavyāpakadharmāprakāraka*) should also be a qualification of the apprehender; therefore, it was stated: "the cognition 'the object of knowledge' (*jñānaṃ prameyam*)."

The meaning is this: when knowability (*prameyatva*) is known within a cognition, it becomes a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*) and, through the relation of self-qualifierhood (*svaviśeṣaṇatā*), presents all things in the form of cognitions which serve as its own substrata; thus, a cognition whose qualificandum is a cognition having knowability as its qualifier possesses the property of being a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) regarding the cognition that is the substratum of knowability.
In order to avoid the aforementioned fault, he raises an objection with the words: "by the term 'the grasper of cognition'."
"By way of not having validity as its object."

The point is that because [the property of being a pot] is not the meaning of a word (*apadārtha*) and is not the meaning of a sentence (*avākyārtha*), it cannot in any way manifest as the qualificand (*viśeṣyaka*) and so forth, just like the "pot-ness" [in the cognition of a pot].

As for the view conceived by Pakṣadhara—that even though validity is not presented by a word, it manifests in the cognition "this is a cognition of a pot" as the delimiting factor of the relation (*anvayitāvacchedakatayā*)—that has been refuted by him himself; thus, having accepted this, it was stated:
"Thus [it is]. And this has been explained by the venerable teacher (Gurupāda).
If it is argued that there is an intention to include the apprehension of a cognition as having its own object as a constituent—provided that it is distinct from the word [itself]—this is not so.

For even then, there would be a contradiction because the knowledge of a knowledge produced by an inference such as "This person possesses the knowledge of a jar, because he behaves accordingly" does not have validity as its object.
Furthermore, it would follow that the knowledge produced by the words "Knowledge is valid" would likewise fail to have validity as its object; this is the intended meaning.

Now, it might be argued that by the term "cognition-apprehender" (*jñānagrāhaka*), what is intended is the status of being an object of that [cognition] by virtue of having as its qualifier the mode of the cognition which is the locus of the apprehended validity, and by virtue of having as its qualificandum that which possesses that mode.

And here, by the two qualifiers, there is the cognition having "your pot" as its qualificandum and the cognition having "pot-ness" as its qualifier; and thus, by the two words [“your pot” and “pot-ness”], [the cognition of] the pot...

If it is argued that the two objections—that the validity of the cognition of the object of knowledge and the cognition itself are not the objects [of the subsequent reflective cognition], and thus there is a contradiction—are refuted in sequence, we reply as follows:

The "objectivity" (viṣayatva) you have described—namely, being the qualificandum possessing that mode by way of being the mode of the cognition which is the locus of the apprehended validity—is in fact nothing other than having validity as its object.
This is because the nature of validity consists precisely in being the qualificandum of that which possesses its own mode.

Well then, let us accept the view stated by Yajñapati: that validity is apprehended by its own substratum through having its own mode as its mode (*svāśrayaprakārakatayā*) and through having its own substratum’s qualificandum as its qualificandum (*svāśrayaviśeṣyaviśe�ṣyakatayā*).

Even so, according to the literal reading, since even a cognition such as "something has potness as its mode and something [else] as its qualificandum" would not apprehend validity, it must be stated [more precisely] that [validity is apprehended] through having the mode of its own substratum as its mode (*svāśrayaprakāraprakārakatayā*) and through having as its qualificandum that which possesses the mode of its own substratum (*svāśrayaprakāravadviseṣyatayā*).

In that regard, concerning the phrase "as having that mode" (*tatprakāravad*), since the mode (*prakāra*) would otherwise incur the previously mentioned defect if it were merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), it is stated that [the cognition] has as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) that which is qualified by that mode. With the intention that "therefore no defect whatsoever arises," he raises an objection with the words "But surely...
(*nanu*). [The phrase is] "as having that mode."

The meaning is "by way of having that mode as its qualifier" (tatprakāraviśiṣṭaviśeṣyakatayā); this refers to having that as its object, i.e., being the object of a determinate cognition (vyavasāya). With the words "In this view," etc., he clarifies the function of the two members [of the definition] in order to reinforce the fault that will be stated later—namely, with the words "herein" (atra ca).

And thus, it would be said that "self-validity" (svatastva) consists in being apprehended by whatever causal complex has validity as its object.

In that case, since such self-validity exists even under the theory of extrinsic validity (paratastva), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). Furthermore, if one were to prove extrinsic validity—which is the absence of this [self-validity]—there would be the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (apasiddhānta).

For, according to the opponent's position, validity is not only not the object of an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), it is also not the object of the inference of validity. Objection: Is it not the case that even the apprehension of invalidity—consisting in the presence of a qualifier in a locus where that qualifier is absent—is in fact an apprehension of the fact that the object has that as its qualificandum?
For the status of having that as the qualificandum (*tadvad-viśeṣyakatva*) is cognizable through the cognition of the presence of that qualifier (*tat-prakārakatva*).

This is because, if the status of having that as the qualificandum does not appear [in consciousness], it is impossible to apprehend the presence of that qualifier. As for what was stated by Narahari: “In the phrase ‘aprāmāṇyāgrāhaka,’ by transposing the negative particle (nañ), it means ‘that which apprehends the absence of invalidity’; this results in the meaning ‘that which apprehends validity.

Thus, the meaning of the positive alternative (vidhikoṭi) is that validity is apprehended by whatever apprehends the cognition. This too is refuted by the author’s own statement: “If you maintain that [validity] is apprehended by whatever totality of conditions (sāmagrī) has validity as its object, then you would be asserting that it is apprehended by that very [totality],” for this results in the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). Thus, it is rejected by the author’s own words.

Nor should it be argued that because the term "grāhya" (the apprehended) is intended independently as that which is apprehended, the fault of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) is absent by virtue of the word "yāvat" (as far as/as long as); for if that were the case, the property of being the object of a subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) would not exist according to the Nyāya school. Furthermore, if the negative particle (*nañ*) were taken to mean the absence of validity (*prāmāṇya*), it could not be compounded with the preceding term.
One should consider that [the opponent's position] is untenable because of the redundancy of the two negative particles (*nañ*) and the redundancy of that term [“non-apprehension”].
This very point is stated: “The qualification ‘not apprehending non-validity’ is redundant.”

Now, an objection: Just as for the apprehension of a cognition, whatever is required by the causal complex that apprehends the cognition is also required for the apprehension of its object—that very same causal complex which apprehends the cognition is [simultaneously] the apprehender of the object-possessing cognition.
The intended [cause] is the causal complex for reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).
This is because the very contact with the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) required for the apprehension of that cognition is likewise required for the apprehension of its object, such as a jar.

If it is argued that the expression "the cognition of a jar" (ghaṭajñānam) requires the power residing in the word *jñāna* for the apprehension of the cognition, but requires the power residing in the word *ghaṭa* for the apprehension of the jar, we say: no. [The author] refutes the doubt stated by Pakṣadhara, beginning with "nanu" (but if...).
"Only for that long."
The meaning is: that very [cognition] in which the apprehension of the object is necessarily conditioned by the apprehension of the cognition itself.

And in this view, the qualification "not apprehending invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyāgrāhakatva*) is purposeful for the sake of avoiding the objection regarding error, because the cognition produced by the word "error" does not apprehend validity.

Furthermore, the qualification "as long as" (*yāvat*) is included to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since the cognition produced by the word "valid cognition" (*pramā*), which apprehends the cognition as colored by its object, does indeed apprehend validity in the aforementioned form.

He clarifies, in sequence, that there is neither sublation (bādha) nor proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā), by means of the phrase "the totality of the conditions for reflective awareness" (anuvyavasāyasāmagrī).
This is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound;
the meaning is "the conjunction of the self and the mind," and so forth.

The causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of self-luminous determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) and the like is also to be understood as included within the conjunction that constitutes the determinative cognition.
The meaning is that [the relation] is specifically the *saṃyuktasamavāya* (inherence in what is conjoined) between the determination (*vyavasāya*) and the mind.

The point is that, just as there is a requirement for the proximity consisting of the form of the determination when grasping an external object as its content, so too there is an equal requirement for the determination when generating a subsequent determination (*anuvyavasāya*), because the status of being an object is identical in both cases.

The specific qualification *jñāna* (cognition) is included in each respective word for cognition (*tattaj-jñāna-pada*) in order to secure the quality of directly taking an object of knowledge as its domain, thereby distinguishing it from other means of valid cognition such as the eye and so forth.
The meaning is that validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in the form of a cognition whose object is a pot and whose mode is "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).
However, when the word "validity" (*prāmāṇya*) is used to denote validity in its absolute sense, then the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) serves to clarify the meaning.
For this very reason, in the *Sudhā*, the statement of the thesis is simply "validity," [qualified by] "is intrinsic" (*svataḥ*).

The meaning is that [the cognition] is indeed an object of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) which has as its object that very knowledge produced by a causal complex that does not include anything that would present a contradiction to the validity of the apprehended object.
The function of the qualifiers is as explained previously.
And the witness-consciousness is precisely the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form of ordinary perception and so forth; thus, [validity] is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

In such arguments as "Validity is apprehended extrinsically because it is subject to doubt," the probandum (sādhya) intended by the opponent—consisting of the state of being apprehended by something other than the specific witness-consciousness mentioned—is defined as being apprehended by [a cognition] distinct from that. This is the meaning of the phrase "being apprehended" (*grāhyatva*) and so forth, which occurs in the absence of that [specific witness-consciousness].
1. *ghrāṇādi* — Kuṃ. Cha. Ka. 2. *ta* — Kuṃ. 3. The word *eva* is absent — A. 4. *jñāna* is not present — Ā. 5. *kṣānu* — Kuṃ. Ā.

The theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*): [Page 35] The cognition "I am experiencing pleasure" is the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) of a cognition that is not marked by the suspicion of defects and the like.
Or (pa 2).

Therefore, even if [the nature of Brahman] is graspable by inference and so forth, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*). Furthermore, there is no room for the refutation stated in the *Maṇi*—namely, that "for another it is self-established, while for itself it is established by another," and so on. However, some maintain that being graspable by another means: (1) not being graspable by perception characterized as previously described; or (2) being the object of a first cognition produced by something other than the witness-consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*).
"Grasped by another" means that it exists when that [other] is absent.
Therefore, they say that even if validity is grasped by inference and so forth under the theory of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), there is no lack of proof regarding the qualifier.
In this context, the qualification "being real" (satyam) is stated because the mere fact of being apprehensible (*grāhyatva*) is not a sufficient reason [for the conclusion].

The qualification "being real" is included in order to eliminate the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), for although smell and other qualities residing in a jar are indeed apprehensible, they are not apprehended by the aforementioned type of perception which apprehends its own substratum.
In order to dispel the difficulty of accounting for occasional doubt and so forth regarding the intrinsic apprehension of validity (*prāmāṇya*), he states specifically as well: "Happiness," etc.
The meaning is that it is a cognition in the form of a witness (*sākṣin*), whose object is the direct perception of one's own present happiness through its own function.

One should not suspect that this constitutes a different subject matter (*arthāntaratva*) because it is inconsistent with the dispute as to whether, regarding the aspect of knowledge, a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form of ordinary perception and so forth has validity as its object or not.
He states other alternative views, common to both external and internal [schools], beginning with "doṣa" (defect).

The meaning is: [the definition applies] to the cognition of a jar or similar object which is produced by a defective instrument (*duṣṭakaraṇa*) and is not overwhelmed by doubts regarding its invalidity or certainty, such as "Is this invalid? or "Is this certain?".
Nor should it be suspected that this is identical to the final position (*antyapakṣa*);

for in that case [the former], it is a qualifier of the *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent reflective awareness), whereas here it is a qualifier of the *vyavasāya* (primary perceptual judgment), and in that case it is defined by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that presents what is opposed to validity.

But here, because of the extreme difference due to the entry [of the object] as the cause of that [cognition], namely, the apprehension of defects in its effects and so forth, it is called the "causal complex of the presenter."
The meaning is that the causal complex for its [the cognition's] presence has been established.

[Self-validity (svataḥ-prāmāṇya): The Doctrine of Validity, page 36. (Note: The phrase "not being graspable by perception" is absent in Kuṃ., Ā., and A. This item is absent in Kuṃ. This line is absent in manuscript A. Doctrine of Self-Validity, page 36.

Either the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) of a cognition that serves as the cause for unshakable activity (*niṣkampapravṛttihetubhūtajñāna*), or a reflective awareness that is not accompanied by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that presents a factor contradictory to validity (*prāmāṇyavirodhyupasthāpaka*),
[is the apprehender] of the validity of the cognition it itself grasps.

It should be understood that in all these cases, by the phrase "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*), what is intended is knowledge in the form of valid cognition (*pramā*) not produced by defects; therefore, although the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) whose object is an error such as "this is silver" depends upon [the initial cognition], there is no contradiction [with our position] even if that [reflective awareness] were to apprehend validity in that instance.

This is because, according to our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the apprehension of validity therein occurs through mental perception (*mānasa*), whereas validity is not apprehended by the reflective awareness whose object is an error.

Alternatively, according to the direction that will be stated, since the property of being an *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent reflective awareness) does not exist in the *anuvyavasāya* of an error, there is no sublation (*bādha*) because that [property] is absent from it.

For this very reason, since the *anuvyavasāya* intended here is understood as being of the nature of ordinary perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*) regarding the aspect of cognition, one should not suspect "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) in the Nyāya system by taking an *anuvyavasāya* whose object is validity brought forward by memory.
"Grasped by oneself."

The knowledge that is apprehended by its own *anuvyavasāya*—in the first established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is the witness-consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*) itself, which has happiness as its object and is self-luminous; in the view of others (*paramata*), it is mental in nature and consists of the determination (*vyavasāya*) of happiness;
and in the other three positions, it is of the nature of a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) having objects such as a jar, termed *vyavasāya*, and distinct from the witness-consciousness.

That [validity] is lost; the meaning is that [the validity] consists in having "the property of being a pleasure" as its qualifier (prakāraka) when the object is a pleasure, or "the property of being a jar" as its qualifier when the object is a jar.

To exclude the possibility of sublation—since the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) of the cognition of a jar does not have the validity of the cognition of a cloth as its object—it is stated: "of the cognition apprehended by itself" (svagrahyajñāna).

Alternatively, by stating simply "having as its object validity," one might fall into the fault of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) in the final view by taking as the object the validity residing in itself; therefore, [the author] says "a cognition grasped by itself" in order to avoid this deviation from the intended meaning.
And thus, there is no difference in meaning.
[Self-Validity (svataḥ-prāmāṇya): The Discourse on Validity (prāmāṇyavāda), page 37. *Note: 1. niṣkalaṅka – Ka; 2. tā – Kuṃ; 3. Not found in the Kuṃ manuscript.*
— [The cognition] has that as its object (sā. 1) or possesses that as its qualifier (sā.

2). — Nor should it be suspected that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), because it lacks the property of having the validity of its own apprehended determinative cognition (vyavasāya) as its object.

Because there is no deviation of the reasons with respect to the aspect of direct perception (*sākṣyaṃśa*), by virtue of obtaining the status of being a grasper of validity for as much as is grasped by itself and by others;

or else, the expression "the validity of the cognition grasped by itself" is stated in order to obtain a validity consisting in the nature of being a cognition whose qualificandum is "pleasurability" (*sukhatva*) and so forth.

Furthermore, the probandum is the state of having validity as its object (*prāmāṇyaviṣayatva*); and this should not be understood according to that view in which the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is indeed what is known by the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*).
However, in the view that even that which is cognizable is not cognizable by itself, it is intended that validity has existence (*sattva*) as its object;
therefore, there is no room for the objection that, under that position, one would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
For this very reason, he will state: "By virtue of its existence, there is the mention of that..."
This is because [the existence of the object] is what is to be proven (*sādhyatvāt*).

Nor should it be suspected that the qualification "by the proponent as being existent" (*satvena*) is redundant, on the grounds that there is no established counter-instance (*vyāvartyāprasiddheḥ*) to be excluded;

for according to our own system (*siddhānte*), even in the case of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, there exists a mental perception (*mānasadarśana*) whose object is the validity [of that cognition], yet which does not determine the existence of its own object.
Furthermore, it is logically consistent that something may be excluded merely by virtue of being established for another;
for in inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the removal of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) for the opponent is also a purpose of the proponent.

Moreover, just as "being produced" (*janyatva*) serves as a qualifier for the Mīmāṃsaka in the case of the definition "not produced by an agent's effort" (*ajanya-kṛti-ajanya*), so too here, "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and the like can serve as qualifiers for the proponent by way of being an adjunct (*uparañjaka*).

And it is stated in the *Maṇi* [the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*] regarding the theory that origination is the means of valid cognition (*utpattiprāmāṇyavāda*): “What is required is the exclusion of what is established for both parties; however, the establishment of the excluded object for both is not required, because of the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*).”

Regarding the state [of being]: against one who argues that validity (*prāmāṇya*), although it is the object of a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), does not function as a qualifier (*prakāra*) because it was not previously present, he says: "or [the cognition] having that as its qualifier."
The meaning is: "that which has as its qualifier the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the cognition of its own object.

The intention is that the status of the cognition of a qualifier as a cause [of the qualified cognition] will be refuted in the section on the critique of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpa-bhaṅga*). Regarding the phrase "contrary to that" (*tadviruddha*):

it means "provided that it does not have as its object that which is contrary to the validity of the apprehended object—namely, the absence of validity (*prāmāṇyābhāva*) and non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*) which is pervaded by it."

@---------- ----------- -------- Because, while not having as its object that which is contradictory to it (*tadviruddha*) and while not having as its object that which is pervaded by it (*tadvyāpya*), it is a cognition that opposes doubt regarding it (*tatsaṃśayavirodhipratyayatvāt*). (He. 1)
(He. 2) Because, while not having as its object that which is pervaded by it, it is a certainty opposed to the certainty of its absence; (He.
3) because it is a cognition that serves as the cause for linguistic usage regarding that [object]; and (He.
4) because it has that as its object by virtue of having the qualifier of that cognition as its own qualifier and having as its qualificandum that which possesses that qualifier.

The inference begins with "like the inferential cognition of validity" and so forth. Furthermore, contrariety (*viruddhatva*) consists in being the object of a cognition that obstructs the cognition of that [probandum]—that is, being pervaded by it (*tadvyāpya*).

The meaning is that it is pervaded by validity (*prāmāṇya*), which consists in having as its qualificandum a state of being a pleasure characterized by the experience of pleasure and so forth; thus, it is the opposite of doubt regarding that [validity].
The nature of being an opponent to doubt regarding validity should be understood as consisting in being pervaded by the non-arising of such doubt, and so forth.
The functions of the qualifiers will be made clear later; [the phrase] "having that as its object" refers to this.
The meaning is "having validity as its object"—that is, "in that cognition."

The meaning is "the cognition which is the locus of the validity of the apprehended object. The refutation of the qualification by the probandum (*sādhyavaiśiṣṭya*) will be clarified later, because [the cognition] has that as its object.
The meaning is "because it has resolution as its object"—just like the inferential cognition of validity (*prāmāṇya*).

The meaning is that this knowledge is valid because it is the cause of successful activity; thus, there is the existence of both the four reasons and the two probanda mentioned in the inference for validity (*prāmāṇyānumiti*).

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the inferences stated in the *Sudhā* such as: "Validity is apprehended by the very same means that apprehends the cognition, because it is a property inherent in a cognition other than invalidity, like cognitivity (*jñānatva*).

Although the first qualification [of the reason] cannot be established according to its literal sense due to the impossibility of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), the second qualification is not impossible; for if [the cognition] does not have an object contradictory [to the truth],...

Having accepted the general pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti) that "that which, while having a pervaded object, is a cognition opposed to doubt regarding that [object], has that as its object," he states the purpose [of the following]. *Prāmāṇyavāda*, Chapter 1: *Svata-anu* (Intrinsic Nature), Page 39. In this regard, regarding the first reason: because it was stated as "not having for its object that which is contradictory to it," [it excludes] the ascertainment of invalidity, which is contradictory to validity;

because it was stated as "not having for its object that which is pervaded by it," [it excludes] the ascertainment of smoke-possessiveness, which does not have that [fire] as its object; and because it is opposed to doubt regarding that [object], [it refers to] the ascertainment of smoke by way of its being pervaded by that [fire].

There is no deviation [in the definition] because it has been stated that [the cognition] is opposed to doubt regarding that [object], because it has been stated that it is a "cognition" (*pratyaya*) in the case of the cognition of a jar and so forth, and because there is no deviation in cases where the knowledge of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) or the recollection of the alternatives (*koṭi*) is absent.
Nor is there deviation in the case of a cognition of another object that is intensely vivid.

Because the very causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for that cognition—consisting of the movement of the mind toward another object and so forth—is itself opposed to it; [the term "vahnyamattvāviṣayaka" means] "not having non-existence of fire as its object."

In the case of the inference "This [mountain] possesses fire because it possesses smoke," once there is the certain cognition "This possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire," the doubt "Does this possess fire or not? does not arise. Consequently, even though the stated form of the reason is present, since there is an absence of the property of not having "possessing fire" as its object, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) therein;
such a suspicion is refuted by the qualification "not having that [pervader] as its object. This is the meaning.

However, it should be understood that in the case of a qualified pervasion (*viśiṣṭavyāpti*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—even in a certainty that has as its qualificandum something possessing a conch-like neck (*kaṃbugrīvādimad*) which is a pervader of that [truth], provided that this certainty is contrary to doubt regarding that [truth] even though it does not have the form of validity consisting in having a pot-ness-possessing thing as its qualificandum; this is because the subject (*dharmin*) is unknown.
The meaning is that there is an absence of knowledge regarding the substratum (dharmin) whose nature is the object of determination.

The point is this: since the knowledge of the substratum is a cause of doubt, the absence of that [knowledge] is pervaded by the non-arising of its effect; therefore, the cause [of doubt] is not present there.
He says "the alternatives" (koṭi), according to the view that the knowledge of the substratum is not the cause of doubt.
The meaning is that there is an absence of recollection of [the object's] limit (koṭi).
This is also an illustration;

it should also be understood that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases such as the conjunction with cow’s ghee, which manifests saffron fragrance and the like, and which is opposed to doubt regarding them.
Anticipating an objection regarding the deviation (vyabhicāra) even of a qualified reason, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not).
It is from the causal complex alone.
And thus, the meaning is that because the state of being a condition (*pratyayatva*) is absent there, the reason (*hetu*) itself is non-existent.
[Self-Validity of Cognition] (svataḥ-prāmāṇyavādaḥ), p. 40.
Now, even so, the cognition of the manifestor—such as hands, feet, and so forth—is, by its very nature, opposed to doubt regarding the manifested genus of "man" and the like;
it is not [opposed] by way of being a pervader (*vyāpyatayā*).

If it is argued that there is no deviation [from the rule] because the cognition of the lamp and so forth, like light itself, serves as the cause for the cognition of the manifested object by its very nature, and yet that [cognition of the lamp] does not have the manifested object as its content, we say: not so.
For doubt regarding the manifested object is indeed twofold.

Just as there is doubt regarding a pot situated in darkness due to the absence of that cognition which serves as its manifestor, or due to the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), [so too would it be here].
Nor does the fact that the causal complex is opposed [to doubt] imply that the cognition produced by that complex must also be opposed to doubt simply by virtue of being opposed to the complex;
for we observe that the status of a certainty opposed [to doubt] as an obstructer is itself caused by its being an obstructer of the causal complex for a certainty opposed [to doubt].
It should not be argued that "whatever causal complex is an obstacle to one [cognition] is an obstacle to another," according to the statement of Pakṣadhara;
for the certainty of a contradictory [cognition] functions as an obstacle precisely by apprehending the absence of the object to be grasped, and thus it is not caused by anything else.
The point is that even though the causal complex for inference might obstruct perception when the objects are distinct, inference is not observed to be so obstructed.
He anticipates an objection regarding deviation in another instance, saying: "Now, [nanu]..."
By its very own nature.
The meaning is "by means of the hands, feet, and so forth"—that is, by way of being pervaded.
The meaning is: "by way of being attainable through the state of being a person" (puruṣatva) and so forth.
Having stated the existence of the reason, he says "And that... to show that the probandum does not [follow].
It should be understood that this objection regarding deviation is also raised only by accepting a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*).
To explain meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through its distinction [from concentration], he says: "The manifest," and so forth.

With the intention that [the non-apprehension] is either caused by the absence of the causal complex for certainty, or, when that complex is present, caused by defects that obstruct it, he clarifies its twofold nature with the words "vyañjaka" (manifesting).
Regarding the word "jñāna": it means knowledge.
The meaning is "certainty"; [it refers to] the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
The meaning is: "because of the absence of the causal complex for certainty"—as follows:
1. *karaṇaṃ*—ka. 2. *sthaghaṭa*—kuṃ, cha, ka. 3. The phrase *“sāmagrīpratibadhyasya virodhiniścayapratibadhyatva”* is added—kuṃ. 4. *bodhyam*—kuṃ, a. 5. The word *“tat”* is not present—kuṃ.
Or [it arises] from defects such as distance;
for example, the doubt regarding whether a post is a person.
In the first case, the very collection of conditions for the ascertainment of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is what opposes doubt;
and since validity (*pratyayatva*) does not reside in that [collection], there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

When two cognitions have the same qualificandum and the same qualifier, the validity consisting of the qualificandum and the qualifier is one and the same.

Thus, although the aforementioned *anuvyavasāya* (after-cognition) does not depend on a second cognition that takes as its object the first cognition which is the locus of the apprehended validity, it nevertheless depends on a cognition that takes the first cognition as its object; therefore, [the opponent's objection] that there is a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) because [the validity] is not established by that [second cognition] is not correct.

This is because, in the debate over whether the validity of the *vyavasāya* (primary cognition) is the object of the *anuvyavasāya* or not, the proof is merely for the sake of establishing that it is an object of the *anuvyavasāya*.

And because there is an illustrative example for that [self-validity], and because self-validity—as expressed by the phrase "having as its object the knowledge of that" and so forth—is also established by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
The meaning is: when only the knowledge of the aforementioned form is intended by the word *tat*, and when validity is a single entity; [the argument follows] because it is dependent.
The intended meaning is that [the reason] functions as a bringer of the qualifier "having the nature of validity"; thus, there is a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalyam*).

The meaning is as follows: regarding the dispute (*vipratipatti*) as to whether the validity of a cognition is apprehended by a cognition not produced by a cognition whose object is that [first] cognition, the proponent of *svataḥ-prāmāṇya* (intrinsic validity) seeks to prove precisely that it is apprehended by such a cognition.

However, since that [second-order] validity is absent in the validity of the second cognition, the probandum—in the form of "having as its object the validity of the cognition apprehended by itself, while being not produced by a cognition whose object is that [first] cognition"—is absent in the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) of that [second cognition]. Thus, the point is established.
He states that there is no fault even if [the self-luminosity] is taught by another, saying: "tajjñāna... (in the verse).

In order to ensure that the probandum (*sādhya*) follows in the example, even when the probandum is formulated as "having as its object the validity of the cognition apprehended by itself," the desired specific probandum will nonetheless be established. This is because the reason—namely, being an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) whose object is the determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) that serves as the cause for unshakable practical activity—is indeed present in the subject (*pakṣa*), which consists of the after-cognition directed toward the first cognition.

Furthermore, even in that case, there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) according to the view of the new school of Nyāya (*navīnanyāyamata*), because intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) is absent there as well.
For if that were the case, then regarding its validity, there would necessarily arise at some point one of the following: doubt, error, or a sublating cognition (*vyatirekapramā*).

The sense is this: since the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) does not depend on another cognition whose object is the cognition of that [initial] cognition, it is established that the state of having the validity [of the initial cognition] as its object is indeed of the aforementioned nature.
In accordance with the view of the ancients that the validity of inference and so forth is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), he says: "Or else... (*yadvā*).

By this statement— speaking of "distinct and non-distinct views"— it is indicated that, just as in my view intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) applies everywhere, in your view extrinsic validity (*paratastva*) does not apply everywhere,
since you admit intrinsic validity in some cases. Thus, it is suggested that one should abandon this "half-old-woman" approach (*ardhajaratīya*) and accept intrinsic validity everywhere.

Now, as for what was stated by the Teacher in the *Maṇi*: "Since inference has all suspicion of error eliminated, its validity is apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*); that is, the property of being a cognition of fire in a smoky place—which is invariably concomitant with the validity of the inference—is presented in the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*). Therefore, due to the perception of this specific feature, there is no suspicion of invalidity therein."
The intention is that, just as there is no doubt regarding invalidity once validity has been ascertained, one determines the object and engages in unshakable practical activity (*vyavahāra*).

Having raised the objection—thinking, "Since it has already been stated that the older view has a different intended meaning, how can this example apply to that view?"—the author accepts it even from that perspective, beginning with the words "yat ca" (and that which...).

Regarding the term "saṃśaya" (doubt): the doubt would be whether the inferential cognition (*anumiti*) is valid or not; the misconception (*viparyaya*) would be that it is indeed invalid; and there would be no valid cognition regarding the absence of validity (*prāmāṇyavyatireka*), such as "it is not a valid cognition. This is because the certainty of validity (*prāmāṇyaniścaya*), which is the opposite of those states, would not arise. Nor is this an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Because this would contradict the statement that "all delusions have been cast aside.

[The opponent] objects: "But surely, since the nature of being a valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) in the case of the cognition of fire is grasped by the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*)—namely, as the state of having smoke as its qualificandum (*viśeṣyaka*) while possessing fire as its qualifier (*prakāraka*)—there can be no doubt in that regard. [The author] replies:

No. Because the inferential cognition (*anumiti*) has as its object merely the possession of fire (*vahnimattva*), and because there is no means of bringing the external object's "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) to mind, it is not an object of the after-cognition. Thus, [the validity] is not grasped there.
The sense is that [the opponent's position] fails because it results in the cognition of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and because [the required certainty] is not established.
For this very reason, there is no justification for [the opponent's view] through ignorance of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) and so forth,
since they admit that there is never any absence of error.
In this context, it is appropriate to say "one or the other" (*anyatara*) because doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*) are grouped together as a single category.
He anticipates the objection stated by Maṇi regarding the means for the cessation of doubt and so forth, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*).
"Of that which is fixed."

The sense is that there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that: "wherever there is the state of having smoke as the qualificand while fire is the qualifier, there is the state of having fire-possessor as the qualificand while fire is the qualifier.

Now, does one claim that the state of having smoke as the qualificand is grasped by the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) precisely because it was presented by the inference? Or is it presented by the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection)? Having thus considered these alternatives in the mind, he refutes the first with the words: "of the inference" and "presenting [agent]."
The meaning is that [the cognition] does not appear as a positive entity in the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).
This is also an *upalakṣaṇa* (an elliptical indication),
because even if validity were not manifest as such, doubt would still be excluded.

It should also be understood that since the external object— the fact that having "smoke-possessing" as its qualificandum is pervaded by having "fire-possessing" as its qualificandum— does not appear at all in the inferential cognition, it cannot be an object of the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) because there is no means of bringing it to mind (*upanāyaka*). As for the claim that the cognition of a property pervading truth (*prāmāṇya*) in its own form alone is what opposes doubt and the like, and that this must be postulated here precisely because there is no other way, that is not correct.

Because there is no other possible recourse even when validity is established through intrinsic nature (*svatastva*). By this very [argument], the following view is refuted: that when the state of possessing smoke has been presented by a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the subsequent inference—which arises with the state of possessing fire as its object—is a cognition of a "qualified-qualifier" (*viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya*) type (like the cognition "this is fragrant sandalwood") due to the power of its causal complex; and that it has as its object the inferendum as qualified by the mark (*liṅgopahita-laiṅgika*), such that this [inference] itself is the "presenting agent" (*upanāyaka*).

Because of the force of the experience that the inferential cognition has as its object merely the state of possessing fire (*vahnimatva*), the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is restricted specifically to perceptual knowledge. Alternatively, if there were no such restriction, then when the inferential after-cognition (*anumity-anuvyavasāya*) grasps the validity (*prāmāṇya*)—in the form of having "smoke" as its qualifier—in that which possesses smoke, the inference would be established as a self-evident instance of validity regarding the aspect of "possessing smoke. Alternatively, the validity of the cognition "I am happy" is the object of its subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya), because, while that [reflective awareness] exists, it is not devoid of manifestation, just like the primary cognitive act (vyavasāya).
Nor is this reason unestablished; for if it were otherwise, doubt and the like would occasionally arise regarding that validity.

By the use of the particle *eva* in the phrase "prāmāṇyameva" (only validity), it is shown that since the absence of doubt and so forth is admitted only with respect to the factor of validity (*prāmāṇyāṃśa*), it is logical to accept the certainty (*niścaya*) regarding that very factor, and not the acceptance of certainty regarding the factor of pervasion (*vyāpyāṃśa*). This is because, even by virtue of being pervaded by validity, the certainty [of the pervading factor] necessarily follows. or else, the validity of each respective cognition is fit to be the object of a subsequent reflective cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) that has that [original] cognition as its object, because it is a property of a cognition delimited by an adjunct (*upādhi*) that is fit to be the object of such a [reflective] cognition—just like the "cognition-ness" (*tattajjñānatva*) of each respective cognition.
Thus, the self-validity (*svatastva*) is to be established in a general sense.
Nor is the final reason unestablished;

for the existence of the object, which is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of validity, is fit to be the object of a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) by virtue of being the object of the primary determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*).

The two negatives are employed to exclude any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding properties such as being either a valid or invalid cognition, which are constituted by limiting adjuncts that are both fit and unfit [to be objects].
The meaning is that it is like its qualificand (*viśeṣya*). [The formal argument is:
“Validity is apprehended by whatever apprehends the cognition, because it is a property residing in cognitions other than invalidity, just like ‘cognition-ness’ (*jñānatva*)”;
and “validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), just as perception is.”
Having refined the inference stated in the *Vyākhyānasudhā*, he says: "tattajjñāna...
[and] "yogyam."

And it should be recalled that what was stated previously—that "fitness" consists in being a delimiting factor with respect to the innate power of apprehension residing in the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) by means of the cognition of its own object—is intended here.
By the statement "not constituted by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) unfit to be its objects," the category other than invalidity found in the *Sudhā* is explained.
By this, the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding validity in the form of "having no qualifier that does not reside in the qualificand" is refuted.
In general.

The meaning is that [the validity] is established either by commonality with both the related and the unrelated, or by commonality with validity in general; it is not established specifically, as in the case of the validity of the cognition "I am happy.
Since the dispute concerns only the non-inclusion of the existence of the qualifier (*vaiśiṣṭya*), he says: "of the existence of the object" (*viṣayasatvasya*).
"In the case of being either one or the other," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: if it were stated that [validity] is a property of cognition constituted by an adjunct (*upādhi*) capable of being its object, then even in the aforementioned instance where the subject (*dharmin*) exists, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent; therefore, the phrase "not constituted by an adjunct capable of being its object" is used to exclude that possibility.

And as for the nature of *anuvyavasāya* (reflective awareness), there is no fault whatsoever, whether it be defined as being a perception of that object by way of having the qualifier of the qualifier of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) as its own qualifier and having as its qualificandum that which possesses such a qualifier, or as being a perceptual cognition of the portion consisting of the [primary] cognition itself, or as being a worldly perception (*laukika-pratyakṣatva*) regarding the portion of the cognition.

The meaning of the phrase beginning with "etc. (*ādi*) is: not being delimited by a qualifier that is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in the qualificandum, and possessing that qualifier in that which possesses it.

The point is that if one were to state only "because it has the nature of cognition" (*jñānadharmatvāt*), there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to invalidity (*apramātva*) and so forth.

Now, if in all these inferences the intended property of being a "subsequent reflective awareness" (*anuvyavasāyatva*) consists in being a cognition whose object is a cognition, then there is the fault of sublation (*bādhādi*) in the case of a verbal cognition such as "this is a cognition.

However, if it consists in being a cognition whose object is a cognition possessing an objective content (*saviṣayaka*), then there is a fault in the case of a verbal cognition such as "this is the cognition of a jar."

If [the property to be proven] were "being a direct perception whose object is a cognition," there would be a contradiction (*bādha*) and other fallacies in the case of the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) whose object is the scope of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as well as in the case of the direct perception whose object is the cognition produced by the universal-connection (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*).

Furthermore, if [the property] were "being an eternal cognition whose object is a cognition," one would incur the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking the cognition of God (*īśvarajñāna*) as the locus; therefore, he says: "And [the property is] being an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāyatva*)."
By this, what was stated previously—that "the *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent cognition) accepted by the logicians (*tārkika*) is precisely our *sākṣin* (witness)"—should be understood as explained.
Here, the function of each term has already been made clear.

Now, one might object: "If the nature of *anuvyavasāya* consists in having the qualifier of the qualifier of the mode of the *vyavasāya* (primary cognition), then this is simply the state of having validity as its object; thus, there is the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). This is not so.
In this position, what is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*) is the mention of validity (*prāmāṇya*) by way of its existence;
however, when it is held that the probandum is merely the state of having validity as its object, he states it in another manner in that position: "in a portion of the cognition" (*jñānāṃśe*).

**The Doctrine of Intrinsic Validity (Svataḥ-prāmāṇyavāda)** Invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), however, is apprehended only when there is a subsequent consideration of non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) and so forth; therefore, its apprehension is not intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
The distinction is that the cognition of validity is observed even without the investigation of corroboration and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Since it is established that in cases where no doubt arises regarding the invalidity of another cognition having the same object as a cognition whose invalidity has already been apprehended, this must be known through after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*); therefore, by analogy, the same should hold elsewhere, and thus the cognition of invalidity would also be intrinsic (*svataḥ*). This is not so.

Because the absence of the object of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*), which serves as the limiting condition (*upādhi*) for invalidity, is not presented [to consciousness] by that [primary cognition], it is unfit to be the object of a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).
Furthermore, "worldly" (*laukika*) means not being produced by generalizing perception (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*) and the like.

The qualification "with respect to the aspect of cognition" (*jñānāṃśe*) is intended to exclude sublation and other defects in cases such as the following: when a past cognition of a jar is presented by memory, there arises a cognition—"I possess the cognition of a jar"—which is a worldly perception with respect to the aspect of the self (*ātmāṃśe*); the qualification is used to avoid invalidating that instance.

[The opponent says: "But if that is so, since there is no distinction between [the cognition] being a property of knowledge (*jñānadharmatva*) and being external and noble (*bāhyāryatva*), and since the dependence on non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvādāpekṣatva*) is equal in both cases, then invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) would also be apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*). Therefore, what is the distinction of validity (*prāmāṇya*)?
To this, he says: "But invalidity... (*aprāmāṇyaṃ tu*).
And this will be explained in the "Treatise on the Impossibility of Inferring Validity" (*prāmāṇyānumityasambhavavāda*), where it says: "is seen."
The sense is that this refers to a stage where [the cognition] has reached the state of habitual practice (*abhyāsa*).
Now, it may be argued: "An after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) is incapable of taking the invalidity of the knowledge it apprehends as its object, because it is an after-cognition."

Having raised the objection that there is a parity with fallacious cases—namely, that it is like a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) which takes as its object another cognition that has already apprehended its own invalidity—he refutes this with the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*).
Regarding "vyavasāya" (resolution): it refers to the firm determination to act.

The meaning is as follows: in the determination (*vyavasāya*) "this is silver" and similar errors, there is an absence (*abhāva*)—namely, the absence of silver-ness (*rajatatvābhāva*)—which is not an object [of that cognition]. Since invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) consists in having a qualifier (*prakāra*) where that [qualifier] is absent, it takes the form of an adventitious property (*upādhi*) included within that [invalidity]. Because such an absence is not manifested in the cognition "this is silver," but is manifested only in the cognition "this is not silver," how could the former be fit for reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*)?
