**The Doctrine of Self-Validity (*Svataḥ-prāmāṇyavāda*)** As it was stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda: “Validity is indeed intrinsic (*svataḥ*); otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).”

The word "is known" (*jñāyate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The meaning is that it is impossible for the stated reasons—which are to be established by the aforementioned inferences—to reside in the subject (*pakṣa*) [of the argument] otherwise. Thus end the inferences regarding intrinsic validity (*svatastva*). // 3 //
Now, it might be argued that the aforementioned correspondence with reality does not belong to the witness (*sākṣin*).
And thus, the sense is that in that case, sublation (*bādha*) itself is the defect; as it has been said:
The meaning is that it has been stated in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya* that these inferences regarding intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) are faultless.
Having quoted that [text], he states the meaning consistent with the present context: "And validity... and so forth.
Inferences for [the theory of] intrinsic validity (svatastva) // 3 // Now,

just as it is argued that the invalidity [of a cognition] is contradicted by the fact that its constituent condition— the absence [of defects]— is not an object of the primary apprehension (*vyavasāya*), and thus cannot be known by the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), so too [it might be argued] regarding the validity [of a cognition]: even though its constituent condition— the qualification of the locus (*dharmin*)— is indeed an object of the primary apprehension...

It is not the object of that after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), because that [after-cognition] has an external thing as its object; otherwise, just as with the aspects of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), there would never be any doubt as to whether the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) exists or not—this is the intended meaning. With this in mind, [it is said]: "Let this validity be for now; nevertheless, immediately following the after-cognition, [there arises] the cognition..."

Keeping in mind what the author of the *Maṇi* has stated—that "since doubt regarding the validity [of a cognition] and its possessing the object is established by experience, the possession of the object is not its [the doubt's] object"—he raises an objection with the words "But surely... (*nanu*).
The meaning is that it consists in the nature of a cognition whose object possesses that [qualifier] and which has that as its mode (*tatprakāraka*).
This statement is made for the sake of facilitating the material cause (*upādāna*) to be mentioned later.
He says "of the witness" (*sākṣiṇaḥ*), relying on the established tenet (*siddhānta*) that the witness is self-luminous knowledge (*svarūpajñāna*).

Relying on the view that "the experience of mental cognition is *anuvyavasāya*," he says: "or the object of *anuvyavasāya*. [From] *Svatastvanumāneṣu Bodhoddhāraḥ Prāmāṇyavādaḥ*, page 63. Or [it is] the object of *anuvyavasāya*.

If it is argued that the inferences for self-validity (*svatastva*) have their objects sublated— because while no doubt is observed regarding the fact that [a cognition] has "silver-ness" as its qualifier, a doubt is observed regarding its having "that which possesses silver-ness" as its qualificand, and thus it lacks the capacity to apprehend the external object consisting of "that which possesses silver-ness"— we say no. This is because, since properties such as "possessing happiness" are not external objects, the self-validity of cognitions of happiness and so forth, which are known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), remains unimpeded.

Furthermore, is the qualification by silver-ness (*rajatatva*) and so forth not an object of the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) at all, or is it an object of the after-cognition by virtue of being an object of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*), yet not an object of it independently?

Furthermore, it is impossible to abandon the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) of the appearing distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*) as already established and instead postulate a specific *svarūpa-sambandha* (essential relation);
for there is also the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*): "I know this as qualified by silverness."

The meaning is that the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) appears in the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) in the same manner as it is an object of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*), namely, by way of its existence.

The point is that even though the relation of qualification is an external object, since it is an object of the primary cognition, it is logical that its status as a qualifier—consisting in being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)—should appear in the after-cognition.
He says "of what is already established" because the specific relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) with the cognition is not an external object.
The point is that in cases such as the past, it is impossible for there to be a differentiating character (*vyāvartakatva*) consisting of the capacity to generate a cognition of exclusion;

furthermore, under the view that the cause of [the cognition] is the knowledge of the qualifier, since a second [qualifier] is impossible, the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) is already established as being of the nature of "appearing therein" (*tatra bhāsamāna*), and so forth.

Since it was previously established by the statement, "It is proven by experience that the state of having the relation of specificity (*vaiśiṣṭya*) as its object also appears," he says: "This [is in the form] *rajatatve*... (in silver-ness).

If it is argued that the meaning of this [statement] is indeed "I am one who possesses a cognition having as its qualifier the relation of silverness to a qualificandum," and that the relation (*vaiśiṣṭya*) is not a qualifier in the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*), because—
due to not being previously presented— it appears solely through the mode of relation (*saṃsarga-maryādā*), we say: no.

The sense is that since the status of the cognition of a qualifier as a cause [of the subsequent determinate perception] will be refuted in the refutation of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpakabhaṅga*), there is no obstacle to the manifestation of the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*)—even though it was not previously present—as a qualifier in the determinate perception (*vyavasāya*), just as "silverness" appears [as a qualifier].

Now, one might object: even though in the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) there is the manifestation of the qualified nature residing in the primary cognition (vyavasāya)—namely, the state of having as its object that which is qualified by silver-ness—the state of having as its qualificandum that which possesses silver-ness, which resides in the primary cognition and is included within the definition of validity, is not manifested.

If this were the case, it would follow that even regarding the objective constituent (*dharmyaṃśa*) of a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), there would be an absence of the nature of certainty regarding its validity, and consequently, doubt might occasionally arise even in that regard. Furthermore, in a case of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) whose object is identical to that of a cognition whose validity has already been apprehended, even the cognition being known as valid appears independently.

Now, one might object: "Independence (*svātantrya*) consists precisely in appearing as a qualifier of the cognition while not being a qualifier of its [own] qualifier—a property residing in a cognition whose existence is necessarily determined by the existence of its object.

The absence of this is independence. Even if such independence were present in cases like "I am possessed of the valid cognition of a jar," it would not be so in cases like "I am possessed of the cognition of a jar," where it does not appear independently.

In that case, since [the object] appears precisely as a qualifier of the cognition of the object, and because there is a dispute regarding whether mere subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) has validity as its object, he says: "When the object exists... (*arthasattve*).

Now, if [the truth] does not appear independently, how can the subsequent cognition (anuvyavasāya) be opposed to doubt regarding its validity, or how can it be the cause of unhesitating activity? To this, he says:
"Also from independence."

[Objection: Even so, if validity were intrinsic (*svatastva*), there would be no doubt during the stage of non-habituation [of a cognition], because validity would be apprehended along with the cognition itself. [Response:

He raises the objection—expressed in the *Maṇi* and other works—regarding the refutation by counter-arguments (*pratikūlatarka*) against the aforementioned inferences, beginning with "nanu": Even so, if validity were intrinsic, there would be no doubt during the stage of non-habituation, because validity would be apprehended along with the cognition itself.
Nevertheless.
The meaning is: "even in the absence of defects in the form of powerful sublation"—that is, "because of the apprehension of validity."
The meaning is that otherwise, the doctrine of self-evident validity (svataḥ-prāmāṇya) would be undermined; this applies even in the case of non-apprehension (agraha).
The word "of knowledge" (jñānasya) is to be supplied [to the end of the sentence].

For just as in your view— despite the rule that a genus and its individual instance are necessarily cognized by a single cognition— a non-apprehension of the nature of mother-of-pearl occurs due to a defect in the case of the error "this is silver," so too in my view, despite the rule that a cognition and its validity are necessarily cognized by a single cognition.

Even in a case of doubt, although there is the apprehension of the cognition, the fact that its validity is not apprehended by it does not constitute a refutation of the theory of intrinsic validity (*svatastva*).
[Note: *bhrama* is not the term used;
*svasaṃvedanaṃ* is the reading.]

Regarding the theory of intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*): [Objection: If there is no apprehension [of validity], then because there would be an absence of knowledge of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*), [validity could not be known]. [Reply: This is not so.

It has been stated that intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) consists either in the necessity of being cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedyatva*) in the absence of an obstacle, or in the fitness for being cognizable by the witness-consciousness.

And in a case where there is doubt regarding invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-saṃśaya*), it is precisely the causal complex for the apprehension of invalidity that acts as an obstacle to the power of apprehending validity (*prāmāṇya*). Otherwise, doubt regarding invalidity would be impossible. Thus, even if the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) apprehending the cognition fails to grasp its validity due to the obstruction of that power, our stated definition of "self-validity" (*svatastva*) is not lost; for even under the theory of self-validity, the ascertainment of the validity of the cognition of the subject (*dharmijñāna*) [is maintained].

And because of its possible occurrence, doubt is indeed appropriate. With the thought that our own position regarding self-validity (*svatastva*) applies there as well, [the author] explains the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*: "Even when the substratum (*dharmin*) is perceived, since contradictions and the like are observed, the witness (*sākṣin*) is obstructed; thus, doubt arises in the mind regarding the object of validity. Thus he comments.
He provides the explanation: "when there is no obstruction."
The meaning is: "provided that there is no presence of a causal complex that brings about what contradicts validity.
In all these cases, the witness should be understood as being exactly of the form previously described—namely, "the apprehension," etc.
The meaning is "certainly"—otherwise [it would not be so].
The meaning is: "the absence of the causal complex (sāmagrī) of the kind previously described.
To the question, "Let there be the causal complex; what follows from that?", he says: "And if this is so... (evam ca).
The meaning is: "when there is the presence of a causal complex that brings about the apprehension of a factor incompatible with validity"—this refers to the cognition of the locus (dharmijñāna).
The meaning is: "of that [cognition] which is the cognition of the subject (dharmin) in the form of a resolve when there is doubt"; thus, doubt is indeed appropriate.

This [cognition] is to be understood as mental (*mānasa*), and not as being of the nature of a witness (*sākṣirūpa*), because the latter consists of a very firm ascertainment (*sudṛḍhanirṇaya*). [Notes: 1.
*t* — *kuṃ*; 2. *tihyu* — *cha-ka*; 3. *grāhaka* — *cha*; 4. the word *rūpa* is absent — *ā*.
(Regarding self-validity: The theory of intrinsic validity (prāmāṇyavāda), page 83.

Indeed, even the fact that the non-apprehension of "cognition-ness" (jñānatva) and "validity" (pramātva) share the same subverting factor and are sublated by the same [obstructing condition] is not included within the definition of intrinsic validity (svatastva).

Even though the two capacities for grasping that [cognition] are distinct, the capacity for grasping validity is innate, just like the capacity for grasping the nature of cognition; it is not acquired, as is the case with the capacity for grasping invalidity. It is precisely by this much that validity is *svataḥ* (intrinsic).
Furthermore, it is observed that although the capacities for burning and illuminating coexist in fire, there is a distinction in their respective obstructors.

Or, let it be that there is only a single power of apprehension for those two; nevertheless, [the author] clarifies what was stated [in the verse], namely that "it is not from this [power] that self-validity is said to be lost," by saying: "For not... (na hi).

If the meaning [of the opponent's position] were that "in the absence of an obstacle, there is the necessity that knowledge is invariably cognizable by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin)," and that "when an obstacle exists, neither the knowledge nor its validity is grasped by the witness," then the doctrine of intrinsic validity (svatastva) would be lost;
however, the intention is not stated in this way. This is the sense.

Now, if one accepts the identity of the cognition-ness (*jñānatva*), the truth-ness (*pramātva*), and the capacity for apprehension, then it follows unavoidably that if one is not apprehended by another means, neither of the two will be apprehended. On the other hand, if they are distinct, the doctrine of intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) is surely lost,
because [truth] would then be apprehended by a capacity distinct from the capacity for apprehending the cognition itself.

Otherwise, it would follow that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is also intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Therefore, since the position of difference is understood from the statement in the *Prakṛtinayasudhā*, “The capacity of a means of knowledge (*māna*) to apprehend validity is obstructed by the suspicion of defects,” and the position of non-difference is understood from the statement in the *Jijñāsānayasudhā*, “The fact that instruments produce truthfulness [of cognition] solely through their power to produce [cognition] is their intrinsic nature (*svatastva*),” this is the case in both positions— both difference and non-difference.
He states [the definition of] meditative absorption (samādhi): "by the grasping of that."
But it does not have the capacity to apprehend invalidity.
The term "innate" (*sahaja*) is carried over [from the previous context].
However, the meaning is that it is produced by defects (*doṣāhita*).
In such cases as "do not burn this," it is logical that there can be both obstruction and non-obstruction of the power to burn depending on the difference in the object;
yet, in this way, there is no *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) because of the introduction of an additional cause consisting of the absence of an obstructer.
This is because, according to the Nyāya school, validity is apprehended even by a subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) that is itself unobstructed.
Nor is there a deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

For it is stated in the *Ṭīkā*: “Even if we admit that the absence of causes for apprehending invalidity is also a factor conducive to the apprehension of validity, there is never any loss for us. Furthermore, this will be explained in the discussion on the intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) of the production [of knowledge], where it will be shown that “the absence of an impediment is not a cause.”
Regarding the phrase *mā dahepi*: the word *mā* here has the sense of negation according to the rule “*amānonā* [express] negation. It is not the particle *māṅ*;
therefore, the absence of the *luṅ* (aorist) tense prescribed by the rule “*māṅi luṅ*” is correct, as stated in the *Ṭīkā*.
This is a paraphrase, by way of meaning, of what is stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*.

Indeed, the reading there is: “In the present case, there is no loss whatsoever for us. And thus, that statement in the *Ṭīkā* is consistent even as a concessive argument (*abhyupagama-vāda*), meaning that there is no loss regarding the present matter—the non-human origin of the Veda.

And if, in this way, the apprehension of validity were dependent upon causes other than those for the apprehension of the cognition itself, how would the intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) of validity not be lost? To address this, the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā* states:
"For the mere fact that the absence of burning produces a bamboo sprout from a bamboo seed does not mean that the absence of burning is the cause of the bamboo sprout.
Rather, when an effect contrary to it [burning] fails to arise, the bamboo seed produces the sprout by its own inherent power."
Keeping in mind the preceding statement—"otherwise, neither general rules nor exceptions would exist anywhere"—he says: "pratibandhaka... (obstructing...).

In a case where, although there was previously no suspicion of a defect or the like, a doubt subsequently arises due to the occurrence of another cause, validity is indeed ascertained at that time; for at that moment, the obstructing factor is absent. Thus, having accepted that the ascertainment of validity is [normally] hindered by an obstacle and thereby explained the possibility of doubt, [the author] now explains the possibility of doubt even while accepting the ascertainment of validity in certain cases—starting with the words "yatra" (where).

Alternatively, let it be granted that in a situation where there is the convergence of a causal complex (sāmagrī) that presents factors contradictory to validity, doubt is possible even when validity is ascertained, because the intended "self-validity" (svatastva) is not lost.
But how is this the case at a time prior to the convergence of that causal complex?
For in that case, if validity is not ascertained, self-validity is indeed lost.

Because there is no absence of the principle that "whatever cognition is an obstacle to a certain [cognition], its causal complex is also an obstacle to that [cognition]," and because otherwise the aforementioned doubt would not arise regarding the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇya*), he says: "In which... (*yatra*).
It is indeed ascertained.
The meaning is "by the mind," and not "by the witness," because it is a firm determination;
that in which the determination is very firm is to be known as "witness-observation."
In mental perception there would be no defects, just as in the perception of a witness.
It should be understood that this is based on the statement in the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the *Jñānapāda*: "For whatever perception might be erroneous in some cases, that is indeed mental [perception].
By this, it should be known that the objection raised in the *Maṇi*—"Even when validity is ascertained, doubt may arise therein due to other defects"—is refuted.
The objection that "this would lead to the consequence of [constant] activity" is refuted;
for at the time of ascertaining validity, activity is indeed desired since there is no obstruction,
whereas subsequently, activity does not occur because that [validity] has perished and because of obstructions.
By this, the objection— "How can there be doubt when the ascertainment of validity is present?"— is refuted;
for that [ascertainment] perishes at a later time,
and because doubt is logically established by the presence of doubt regarding validity even when validity has been ascertained.

As for the statement in the *Maṇi*: “Nor should it be said that, just as there is doubt regarding an object due to doubt about its validity, there is doubt regarding validity due to doubt about the cognition of validity;

for even in the case of the cognition of validity, if its own validity is apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*), doubt would be untenable,” that too should be understood as refuted by this very [argument].

In a situation where defects have arisen, when there is certainty regarding the validity of a mental cognition, it is possible for doubt to arise because validity is not ascertained due to the influence of those defects.
Prāmāṇyavāda, Part II – 86.
However, some [maintain] that because the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) is not a cause of doubt, the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) arises in the very form of a doubt.

Even if the cognition of the locus is not a cause [of the doubt], the restriction to a specific locus within that doubt is justified solely by the restriction of the factors that produce the cognition of the locus.

Having thus demonstrated the presentation of doubt as it is actually stated in the root text and other sources, [the author] now addresses the following point: with the intention that the refutation found in the *Maṇi*—namely, the passage stating, “The cognition of the locus (*dharmin*) is a cause of doubt; otherwise, there would be no restriction to the locus and no mention of the alternatives (*koṭi*)”—which seeks to establish the absence of doubt through the absence of the cognition of the locus, is also not valid, he states two resolutions by way of bold assertion (*prauḍhi*) under the guise of another topic.
"Some," and so forth, [is stated] up to "because of the lack of a cause."

Since that [doubtful cognition] arises from the very same general causal complex (*sāmānyasāmagrī*)— consisting of the contact between the qualifier and the sense organ, the recollection of the class-attribute (*koṭi*), the knowledge of the qualifier, and the non-apprehension of the non-relation (*asaṃsargāgraha*) between those two—
it is unnecessary to postulate an additional specific causal complex (*viśeṣasāmagrī*) in the form of the knowledge of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) for doubt.

Thus, the point is that in cases of doubt, since the ascertainment of validity is possible through the mere non-cognition of the object's ascertainment (*vyavasāya*), it is logical for the proponents of intrinsic validity (*svatastvadī*) to maintain that doubt regarding validity and so forth is appropriate.

[Objection: "But surely, when a person traveling at speed on horseback or the like has sensory contact with many trees, doubt regarding their being *panasa* trees or the like arises only in some instances and not everywhere; thus, such a restriction (*niyama*) regarding the locus (*dharmin*) itself establishes that the cognition of the locus is a cause of doubt.
To this, he says: "Even though the cognition of the locus is not a cause... [etc.]
The jar-like state of the knowledge of the substratum.

For even according to you, although proximity (*sannikarṣa*) is indistinguishable everywhere, you must state that the greatness of the object (*viṣaya-māhātmya*) and so forth is the restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*) for why the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) occurs in some cases and not in others.
Let that very [greatness of the object] be the restrictive factor in the case of doubt as well.
According to the maxim, "Let the cause of that [cognition] itself be the cause; what is the use of an intermediate step?", let it be the cause directly.
The meaning is that even though these [individual instances] do not share a commonality, a commonality is possible because they all serve as causes for the cognition of the subject (*dharmijñāna*).
*Sva-saṃdanaṃ* (Self-ascertainment):
*Prāmāṇyavāda*, p. 87.

However, when there is a connection with the two extremes (*koṭi*), since the extreme is not in contact with the locus (*dharmin*), the cause is simply the observation of frequent co-occurrence (*bhūyassāhacaryadarśana*) with a common property such as "uprightness" (*ūrdhvatva*) that is unknown [to reside in either alternative].
It is not, however, the observation of frequent co-occurrence with a common property known to reside in the locus of doubt; for that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
They say, however, that the cognition of common properties such as "uprightness" and so forth is of the nature of memory, produced by causes such as indeterminate perception (*adṛṣṭa*) and the like.

As for the statement of the *Śāradāmaṇi*: "If [the cognition of the subject] is a cause by virtue of being the causal complex for the cognition of the subject (*dharmijñāna*), then for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), let it be a cause simply by virtue of being the cognition of the subject itself"—that is not correct.

Since the [required] state of affairs is established by the mere collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*), it is cumbersome to postulate that the cognition of the subject (*dharmijñāna*) is a cause [of doubt].
[Objection: But if the cognition of the subject were not a cause, then the property of being "associated with a side" (*koṭyuktaṭatva*) would not belong to doubt;

for since that [property] does not occur pervasively (*avyāpyavṛtti*), it cannot be a universal (*jāti*), and thus [doubt] would consist merely in the perception of multiple properties co-occurring with the sides of doubt within the subject of doubt.

Alternatively, since it is untenable that such [doubt] would lack a cause in the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*)—given that the alternative (*koṭi*) must be expressed either as a property perceived as residing in the locus of doubt or as the state of being connected to an alternative through the observation of frequent co-occurrence—he says:
"But as for the state of being connected to an alternative... (*koṭyuktatve tu*).
The logical connection is that perception alone is the cause—by virtue of being untouched by doubt regarding the subject (dharmin).
The meaning is: "by way of not being connected with the property-bearer (dharmin).

Now, one might object that since the perception of a common property is a cause of doubt, knowledge of the property-bearer is necessary for the sake of knowing the property; to this he replies: "common [to all], such as verticality, etc."

The seed of the lack of conviction in the statement "some [say]" is as follows: since the substratum (dharmin) whose nature is doubt—being of the character of a volitional determination (*vyavasāya*)—exists only when known, like pleasure and so forth, there is no obstacle to its being grasped by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) prior to the recollection of the alternatives; therefore, the knowledge of the substratum is necessary, and it is only according to the direction we have stated that the explanation of doubt is sound.
However, it should be understood that this is not due to the non-acceptance of the cognition of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*).
For this very reason, he will state later: "Cognition must necessarily be known.
The rest, however, is in the *Guruṭīkā*.
[Self-validity] (svasaṃvedana): The theory of intrinsic validity (prāmāṇyavāda), page 88.

However, others [hold that] although the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) is a cause for error elsewhere, in the case of invalid cognition—which consists of a non-determinate form (*avyavasāya-rūpa*) having as its object a present determinate cognition (*vartamāna-vyavasāya*)—there is a reversal of the status of being valid (*pramātva*).

Just as that [cognition] is not a cause [for doubt], so too in other cases, even though the knowledge of the property (*dharmajñāna*) exists, it is logical that it is not a cause when there is doubt regarding its validity.
Nor should it be argued that because the superimposition of validity is not present [in the case of a valid cognition], there can be no such superimposition;

for according to the theory of intrinsic validity (*svatastva*), just as validity is cognized in a true cognition, the superimposition of validity upon an error likewise does not depend upon that [external factor]. Thus they say.
"Elsewhere" means: regarding objects such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

The sense is that since the superimposition of "silverness" and so forth occurs only upon the mother-of-pearl and not elsewhere, it is necessary for the cognition of the mother-of-pearl to be the cause of that superimposition by virtue of its possessing qualities such as glitteringness (*cākacakyam*) residing in the silver;
this is the point established by the phrase beginning with "present," etc.

The meaning is as follows: just as in the case of a valid cognition (pramā) such as that of a jar, its validity—which consists of the possession of that [object] and so forth brought forward by the primary cognition—is apprehended by its subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya), so too, even in the case of an invalid cognition (apramā) such as that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, its validity—consisting of the possession of that [object] and so forth brought forward by its own anuvyavasāya—is determined at the very next moment without requiring a cognition of the locus (dharmijñāna).
It is accepted that this is exactly the same.
Anticipating the objection—"How can there be a superimposition of that [validity] when validity itself is not present?"—he refutes it with the words beginning "na ca" (nor is it...).

For this very reason, it was stated by the author of the *Maṇi* in the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) argument: “Even invalid cognition is grasped as being valid,” and so forth; such is the intended meaning.

However, the seed of dissatisfaction here should be understood as follows: since the apprehension of cognition is performed by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), whereas doubt regarding its validity is a mental state (*mānasa*), one must follow the previously mentioned method in order to avoid the consequence of undermining the doctrine of intrinsic validity (*svatastva*), which would arise if validity were not apprehended along with the apprehension of the cognition itself.

Having accepted that [the cognition] is the cause for the knowledge of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) and that it determines validity (*prāmāṇyaniścaya*), he demonstrates the possibility of doubt by means of another method, stating: "But other...
(*anyat tu*). [This concludes] the *Sva-saṃdana*, the *Prāmāṇyavāda*, page 89.

Others, however, maintain that even in a case of doubt, since the causal complex [for knowledge] exists according to the aforementioned reasoning, there is an ascertainment of validity by the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) at the very outset; yet, immediately after the cessation of that after-cognition, when the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) is presented by memory, a doubt regarding it is indeed appropriate.
For it cannot be known—without the attainment of yoga and so forth—that doubt arises only at the time of the after-cognition and not in the moment immediately following it.
They say that even according to the opponent's view, there is no determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) at the time of doubting its validity;

for the determinative cognition perishes precisely at the time of the recollection of the alternatives (*koṭi*) occurring immediately after the knowledge of the subject (*dharmin*). Regarding the word "stated" (*uktā*): it means by the method set forth in the section of the text dealing with the removal of sublation (*bādhoddhāra*).
In that case, since even the subject (*dharmin*) of the determination would have perished, there could be no doubt; therefore, he says: "smṛti" (recollection).
The meaning is that [the object] is presented by a memory produced by a mental impression (saṃskāra) deposited by a subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya).
Now, one might ask: how can that which is merely presented appear as the substantive (viśeṣya) in a doubt? To this he says: "Even in the opinion of the opponent."

In this view as well, since the apprehension of the cognition (*jñāna*) serves as the witness (*sākṣin*) in cases of doubt, and the apprehension of its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is mental (*mānasa*), even when the mental ascertainment of validity has perished, there exists at all times the experience of the nature of the self during deep sleep— which is established by the subsequent recollection occurring in the moment immediately following the apprehension of the cognition.

Since it is impossible to account for doubt through the destruction of that [apprehension] by assuming that the apprehension of validity occurs via the apprehension of the cognition, [the opponent's position remains untenable].
Since the proof of that [point] must be carried out in the very manner previously stated, what is the use of this present method?
Furthermore, the cognition of a cognition is not mental;
for if it were so, there would arise the possibility of doubt and the like regarding whether or not it is indeed a cognition of that [object] at any given time.
For it is said in the Jñānapāda:
"Desire, knowledge, pleasure, pain, fear, fearlessness, compassion, and so forth, are established by the witness; for no one anywhere has any doubt regarding them."
This is the seed of [the opponent's] lack of conviction, which should be meditated upon.
Even though these three positions are not consistent with our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), they serve as refutations against the logician (*tārkika*).
[Notes: 1. In place of *yasthale*—Ā.; 2. *grāhaka*—Ā.; 3. *autpattikā*—Ā.]
This has also been stated by the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth.

The meaning is that if power were not innate simply because an effect is not produced during the state of obstruction, then it would be impossible to establish that the power to burn and so forth is innate when fire is present.
The demonstration of doubt regarding [knowledge] being self-evident (svatastva).
The intention is that this [objection] is presented here with the thought that it is capable of being stated; such is the sense of the phrase "this too."
The meaning is that, according to the method stated, the justification for intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) even in cases of doubt is established.
This concludes the justification for intrinsic validity in the face of doubt.
[Verse 5] Furthermore, the reasons for intrinsic validity are not inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).

If validity were extrinsic (*paratastva*), then the validity of the cognition of validity would itself have to be grasped by another cognition—such as an inference produced by signs like corroboration—and likewise, the validity of that [second] cognition would have to be grasped by yet another; thus, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) with respect to the result. Nor are these [reasons] unconvincing (*aprayojaka*).

The meaning of "na ca" (and not) is that there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—namely, "let the reasons exist, but let the probandum in the form of being apprehended by itself (*svato-grāhyatva*) be absent"—because there is no favorable reasoning (*anukūla-tarka*) for establishing the probandum.

Although previously (in verse 2), the removal of the charge of the reason being non-conclusive (*aprayojakatva*) was performed in its specific form, there is no fault here, as this is a general removal;
for this very reason, the expression "the reasons" is used.

While explaining the *Ṭīkā* passage, "If one accepts that its validity is also apprehended by another, there would be an infinite regress," he states the two types of infinite regress according to the reasoning found in the *Maṇi* and other works, beginning with the words "paratastve" (if [validity] were extrinsic).
The meaning is that [the cognition] is apprehended by anything whatsoever, other than the cognizer and the witnessing consciousness; this is what is meant by "result-oriented" (phalamukhī).

Thus, if validity were to be inferred, then because of the consequence of "unestablishedness" (*asiddhi*) and so forth if the validity of the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*), its pervasion (*vyāpti*), and so on were not ascertained, one would have to accept another mark for the sake of ascertaining that [validity],

and the ascertainment of the validity of the cognition of that [other mark], and so on ad infinitum; thus, due to the occurrence of two types of infinite regress regarding both the cause and the primary object.

Nor should it be argued that there is no infinite regress because the requirement for corroboration (*saṃvāda*) occurs only where there is a suspicion of defect (*doṣa-śaṅkā*) and so forth; for if that were the case, the requirement for corroboration would be solely for the purpose of removing obstacles (*pratibandha-nirāsa*) and not for the purpose of apprehending validity (*prāmāṇya-graha*), which would result in the consequence of entering into my own [Mīmāṃsaka] position. The statement regarding the determination of the "non-establishment" (*anavasthā*)—whether as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the non-availability of other causes, or for the sake of determining the non-occurrence in a single instance, or in accordance with the opponent's own admission—is an expression intended to establish the necessity of inference (*anumeyatva*).
Previously, however, having accepted the general [view], it was stated that "it is from another," and so forth; but the object of meditation was not specified as being "by way of the cause."
This is to be explained as before.

According to the ancient view, the validity of cognitions is apprehended through inference (*anumiti*), whereas the validity of that inference itself is intrinsic (*svataḥ*); some maintain that this is stated even though it pertains to the cause (*kāraṇa-mukhī*) because there is no infinite regress regarding the result (*phala-mukhānavasthā*).
Others, however, hold that since intrinsic self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) is absent in any case according to that view, the infinite regress exists there as well.
For this very reason, they say that the general statement is "extrinsic nature" (*paratastva*), and not the specific one, "the state of being inferable" (*anumeyatva*).

However, regarding the case where there is a doubt about validity due to a suspicion of invalidity within the cognition of validity, the *Maṇi* states that in such cases, the certainty of validity arises precisely from the ascertainment of the validity of the cognition of validity; [the author] raises this objection: "No..."
And where [it says] "ca yatra" (and where).
Regarding the word "defect" (doṣa):
The meaning is that [the cognition] takes the form of a doubt, such as "being produced by a defective instrument" (*duṣṭakaraṇajanyatva*).

The mention of "expectancy" (*ākāṅkṣā*) is because it imitates the *Tattvanirṇaya*, which states: "And there is no infinite regress (anavasthā) because, only when there is expectancy, is there dependence on another means of valid cognition. For it has been said:
1. ṅganta – cha. 2. sthādyu – ā.
(Regarding the state of being *pra-ni-pra-kṛtva*):
The theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*)—page 92.
It has indeed been stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda: “Because expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) itself consists of a defect of the intellect.”

Nor does the mere negation of validity lead— out of fear of the "stick" of contradiction— to the conclusion that validity, defined as having a qualifier residing in the qualificandum,

is established only in a general sense; rather, it culminates specifically in the case of the cognition of fire as "having the qualifier 'fire-ness' in that which possesses fire-ness," and so forth, by the force of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in the cognition of the probandum.

But has it not been stated here in the *Maṇi* that "the first cognition of validity [is established] by a negative inference (*vyatirekin*)"? To this, he replies: "Because [the probandum] is unestablished" (verse 2).
The sense is that when the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, there can be no knowledge of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) defined by it.

Now, one might object: "The distinctness [of a cognition] will indeed be established as being of the nature of validity (*prāmāṇya*) through the inference: 'It is to be proven by a cause distinct from the causes of successful activity, because it has an effect distinct from those'. To this, he says:
"pravṛtti..."—the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes being the mode of a successful activity directed toward a qualificand capable of burning, and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that [the reason] might be unestablished in another way, he states the refutation:
"And not"— meaning there is no cognition having a qualifier residing in the qualificand—
because a negation such as "there is no valid cognition" or "there is no means of knowledge" is untenable without the prior establishment of a valid cognition somewhere;

for if one were to accept its establishment for that purpose, it would entail the punishment of contradiction (vyāghāta), and thus, out of fear of that, the establishment of its existence somewhere must necessarily be admitted.
It has been stated that [this] is established in a general sense.

"Being established" (sādhyamānam) means that the cognition of fire is being established by means of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) as having a qualifier (*prakāra*) residing in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), because it is the cause of successful purposeful activity (*samarthapravṛttihetutvāt*). [Notes: 1. From *taḥ* to *siddhaṃ*: *kuṃ*, *ga*, and *kha* manuscripts read *taḥ siddhaṃ*. 2. Regarding *aprasiddha*: the *mu* manuscript reads *aprasiddha iti*. 3. Regarding *ṣyakatvādi*: the *kuṃ* manuscript reads *vahnyavṛttiprakārāvacchinnatvādirādipadārthaḥ*; the *a* manuscript reads *ṣyakatvādi*. 4. Regarding *dvyana-pastve-praprā-ṇyātya-bhavaḥ*: [This appears to be a scribal corruption or fragment]. The meaning is that the cognition of fire is being proven by a negative inference to possess a qualifier that subsists in its object, on the grounds that it serves as the cause for effective action. This concludes the section.
And thus, it should not be said that there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) nor the fallacy of being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*);
this applies first in the case of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
Because contradiction does not arise,
and because a negation by oneself is preceded by the cognition of that [object],
nor is there in that case any such establishment consisting of memory produced by impressions from a previous life.
Since the validity of the first cognition of validity is established by its very nature as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*), there is no evidence to postulate [an extrinsic source for it].

Now, suppose that the first [cognition]—this experience as "fire"—possesses the property of having "fire-ness" as its qualifier (*vahnitva-prakārakatva*)... nor is there the fault of being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇya*); the sense is that because the probandum is not ascertained in a particular individual instance, there is no determination of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

Now, one might object: even if a contradiction by another person does not enter into an inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), the establishment of that [contradiction] would nonetheless occur simply because it is impossible to deny one's own validity; to this, he says:
Regarding the word "itself" (*svayam*): the sense is that it must be investigated how that very cognition could be [valid] in such a manner.

As stated by the author of the *Maṇi* (Gangeśa) and his followers who know the tradition: "Validity consists in either the absence of a qualifier residing in the qualificand due to impressions from a previous birth, or in being a cognition that possesses a qualifier in what possesses that [qualifier]; that alone is what is to be established in the case of the cognition of fire and so forth. This is what has been said.
Having restated the opinion, he refutes it.

"And not there"—this means in the case of the first inference of validity (*prāmāṇyānumiti*). "In the justification" (*upapattau*)—the meaning is that the manner of its justification has been stated both in the section on the removal of sublation (*bādhoddhāra*) and in the section establishing doubt (*saṃśayopapādana*). He raises the objection against the position favored by the author of the *Maṇi* (Gaṅgeśa), which was stated in the passage beginning, "We, however, say that the very absence of validity in the first instance is what is to be proven by the negative inference (*vyatirekin*)": "Now... (*atheti*).
The statement "this" (*iyam*) is for the purpose of excluding error.
The statement "as fire-ness" (*vahnitvena*) is for the sake of avoiding sublation (*abādha*) when there is an experience of fire as a substance (*dravyatva*) and so forth.

Regarding the theory of extrinsic validity (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya-vāda*), on page 112: by means of the inference— "That which has as its qualificandum something lacking fire is not [valid], because it does not produce successful activity, unlike invalid cognition"— the very absence of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyābhāva*) is what is to be inferred.
For it is precisely from that [perception] that an unshakable cognitive activity (*niṣkampapravṛtti*) arises.
Furthermore, even in that case, the fault of the "non-establishment of the probandum" (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) does not apply;

for in a purely negative inference (*vyatirekin*) where the probandum is a non-existence, one apprehends the pervasion of the absence of the reason by the presence of the probandum—which is the nature of an existent entity—even without the prior establishment of the probandum itself.

Regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) stated in the *Maṇi* as "not having the qualifier 'fire-ness' in that which lacks fire-ness," the explanation of its meaning according to Yajñapati’s commentary is as follows: the portion ending with the word "satī" (in the phrase "provided that there is the state of having fire-ness as a qualifier," etc. is not a qualifier of the absence (*abhāva*) which constitutes the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*).

Consequently, in the cognition "this is fire-ness," even though there exists the state of having fire-ness as its qualificand in that which lacks fire-ness, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because the probandum—in the form of a qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) caused by the absence of the qualifier—is present.
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Maṇi*: [text fragment].

The statement beginning with "samartha" (capable) as a reason is made in accordance with his own subsequent text: "given that [the cognition] produces an effort directed toward an object capable of burning, yet lacks the capacity to produce an effective activity characterized by the mode of 'fire-ness' (*vahnitva-prakāraka*) and so forth.
Otherwise, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) in the probandum (*sādhya*) would be redundant.
The term "having fire as its object" (*vahniviṣayaka*) is intended to qualify "effective activity" (*samarthapravṛtti*).
Therefore, there is no deviation [of the definition] in the case of the cognition of a jar and so forth.
If it is argued that even so, there is still a deviation in the cognition "there is fire-ness here," then in that case,
the qualification "provided that it has fire-ness as its qualifier" (vahnitva-prakārakatve sati) must be added.
Now, one might ask: "In the absence of a certainty regarding validity, how can there be purposeful activity? To this, he says: "Precisely from that."

The meaning is that it is known through the absence of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). The point is that even for one who maintains [the view] that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is an object of cognition, its utility lies precisely therein; thus it is said to "have non-existence as its probandum" (*abhāvasādhyaka*).
For the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is indeed for the sake of knowing the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists only between the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) and the absence of the reason (*hetvabhāva*).

Or rather, the probandum (*sādhya*) is simply "that which does not have as its qualificand that which lacks the nature of fire" (*vahnitvābhāvavad-viśeṣyakaḥ na*). (This concludes the discussion on the theory of validity, page 113.)
The absence of invalidity is established by the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Nor is it an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason because of its exclusion from similar instances (*sapakṣa*) such as a jar and so forth, since that [uncommonness] is a fault only with respect to impermanence; if this is argued, it is not so.

When the means for apprehending the validity of the first [cognition] has been asked, it is irrelevant to state the means for apprehending the absence of invalidity; therefore, the knowledge of those two alone is necessary. And therein, the absence of the probandum is indeed invalidity itself.

The point is this: that cognition of the counter-positive (pratiyogin), which consists of the absence of the very nature of the thing to be negated, does not depend upon [the prior cognition of] the absence of that [counter-positive]. Therefore, even if that [absence] is unestablished, it is possible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), namely: "wherever there is invalidity, there is an absence of being a generator of successful activity. Thinking that the qualifier "provided it has fire-ness as its mode" (*vahnitvaprakārakatve sati*) is redundant, he states the refinement of the probandum (*sādhya*) as formulated by Pakṣadhara and others, beginning with "Or else" (*yadvā*).
How, then, is the absence of invalidity—defined as having a particular qualifier in that which lacks it—established? To this he says: "In the subject," etc.

Because of the reason stated, the negation of invalidity—consisting in the state of having "fire-ness" as its qualifier—is a negation of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇābhāva*). Since a negation of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭaniṣedha*) results only by taking the negation of the qualified entity (*viśeṣyābhāva*) due to sublation (*bādha*), the negation of the qualified entity is established when one proves the mere absence of that [invalidity].
In this case as well, the qualification of the reason should be understood as before.
Therefore, there is no aforementioned deviation [of the reason] from the similar instances (sapakṣa), such as a jar and so forth.
The meaning is that, because it lacks an objective referent (*nirviṣayakatvena*), the existence of the probandum (*sādhyasattva*) is ascertained therein; thus [it is called] "impermanent" (*anitya*).

The meaning is that it is a defect only at the time when a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*) is absent; however, since here there exists a favorable argument in the form of a sublation of the counter-example (*vipakṣabādhaka*) consisting in the destruction of the reason (*hetūcchitti*), it is not a defect—because [the other case] would be irrelevant (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*).
The sense is that this results in the fallacy of "shifting the subject" (*arthāntara*) as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Furthermore, it should be noted that in cases such as "this is an object of valid cognition" (*prameyam*), since the absence of being an object of valid cognition (*prameyatvābhāva*) is unestablished, an inference regarding the absence of invalidity—which is constituted by that [absence]—is impossible.

1. *dityarthaḥ* — Ā. Kuṃ. 2. *vahnitvā* — Ā. Mu. 3. And here, it should also be understood that the qualification of the reason (*hetu*) is "because it is a certainty having 'fire-ness' (*vahnitva*) as its qualifier" — A.

Nor should it be said that the aforementioned negative inference (*vyatirekin*) alone grasps validity—consisting in having a subject qualified by fire-ness—as a result of the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatābala*).

[For] it is only a previously unknown particular (*viśeṣa*) that is manifested, which is presented by the pervasion (*vyāpti*) as being delimited by the delimitor of the pervader (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*).

Because the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) establishes the connection with the subject, it lacks the capacity to bring about the cognition of that connection for the aforementioned form of validity (*prāmāṇya*), which has not been established in such a manner.

By this [argument], it is shown that immediately after the inference of the absence of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyābhāva*), [the following cannot be established]: "This experience as fire has as its qualificandum a locus possessing fireness, provided that it does not have non-fire as its qualificandum..."

Now, [one might object]: "In the case of two contradictory modes, if there is an absence of having a subject that lacks that [property], the conclusion must ultimately rest on having a subject that possesses it;

otherwise, the connection of the reason with the subject would not be possible. With this intention, [the author] says: "The absence of the absence of having that mode in what lacks it, being established, is established by taking recourse to having that mode in what possesses it."
Anticipating the objection raised in the *Maṇi*—namely, that "there is no third possibility"—he refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
"By pervasion."

The meaning is this: when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a thing delimited by a certain property (*dharma*) is apprehended as being delimited by another property, then through the presence of that [reason] in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), there can be the establishment of only that which is delimited by that [latter] property;
it cannot be the establishment of validity (*prāmāṇya*).
Nor should it be suspected that this rule applies only to positive reasons (*anvayin*) and not to negative ones (*vyatirekin*).

This objection may be raised based on the view that positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) is apprehended through negative concomitance (*vyatirekasahacāra*); or, even in the case of a purely negative inference (*vyatirekin*), such a statement is made with the intention that it necessarily has as its object the absence of the probans pervaded by the absence of the probandum. This refers to "that" [inference]. "This... [is the beginning of the subsequent argument].

By the words "by this," he refutes another alternative position stated in the *Maṇi*: "The cognition having 'fire-ness' as its qualifier has as its object that which possesses fire-ness," and so forth.
Since his own commentary states that the term *viṣaya* refers to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it is said to be "having that as its qualificand" (*tadīyaviśeṣyaka*). [Notes on variants:
1. *sthita* — *ga*. 2. *sthi-* — *kuṃ-ca.ga*. 3. *yadvedaṃ* — *a*. [The phrase:
*pastve-praprā-ṇyātya-bhavaḥ*.
The argument that validity is established by another negative inference (vyatireki) because [the cognition] has a particular as its qualificandum is refuted;

for on the view that the relation of qualification (vaiśiṣṭya) is known through after-cognition (anuvyavasāya), the probandum is unestablished in the subject (pakṣa) according to the theory of extrinsic validity (parataḥ).
Furthermore, if invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) were also inferable, how could it be established?

For [inference] would require the cognition that the absence of the probandum—in this case, invalidity—is the counter-positive of the absence that pervades the reason proving the absence of invalidity.

If, however, after a sublation (*bādhā*), one determines invalidity through the mind regarding an error presented by memory—thinking, "A cognition of fireness occurred to me with respect to what lacks fireness"—then, subsequently to the efficacy of the activity (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*),...
Regarding the phrase "because the probandum is unestablished":
nor should it be suspected that this fault does not apply because [the cognition] follows from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous existence,
for that has already been refuted.
It should also be understood that since such an inference is possible from the very beginning, the initial inference of the absence of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) would be redundant.

With the intention of showing that even in the inference of the absence of invalidity, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished due to the non-apprehension of the negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*), he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
Anticipating the objection that invalidity is not established in the second reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), he says: "But if... (*yaditviti*).
The meaning is that "this is not fire" constitutes another sublation—namely, the one involving memory.
The meaning is: "the memory produced by the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) of the erroneous cognition of fire"—that is, non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*).
The meaning is that [the object] is presented by a memory produced by the experience of the form of the negation (*bādharūpa*).
He says "then" (*tarhi*) to address the objection that validity (*prāmāṇya*) itself might also be known through a fifth-order reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*).

And thus, having taken the fifth counter-argument (*anuvyavasāya*), since it is possible for the inference of validity (*prāmāṇya*) itself to be primary through the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*), what is the point of the inference of the absence of validity? This is the sense. Furthermore, this was stated while conceding the opponent's position; in reality, however, the inference of validity itself is untenable.
1. *parapakṣe* – mu. 2. *bodhyam* – mu.a. 3. *ke* – mu. 4. *anumāne* – kuṃ. In the opponent’s view:

let the mind itself determine, through the mediation of memory, that the determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) brought forward by memory has as its object the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*). Or rather, let that very fact of the determinate cognition having as its object the qualification of "fire-ness" brought forward [by memory] be determined at the very outset by the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) itself. What is the use of this elaborate hypothesis?
By this, the claim that the property of having "fire-ness" as its qualificandum is established by the mind in the case of desire and so forth is refuted;
for if that were the case, then according to the reasoning already stated, it would be possible for the mind itself to determine validity.

Furthermore, the causal relationship between valid cognition (*pramā*) and successful purposeful activity (*samartha-pravṛtti*) is inherently characterized by necessity (*niyama*). And this necessity does not reside merely between two individual instances due to the problems of infinite regress and deviation (*anantya-vyabhicāra*).

With the intention that, if one accepts [the object] as being known by the fifth reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), it is all the more established that it must be accepted as being known by the first reflective awareness—as has already been demonstrated—he says: "Or rather, at the very beginning."
"By a poorly constructed [argument]," etc.

The meaning is that there is a fabricated sequence such as first inferring the absence of non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*), then inferring validity (*prāmāṇya*), and subsequently following the fifth-order after-cognition (*anu-vyavasāya*) for the sake of establishing non-validity, and so forth.

Now, one might object: "In the after-cognition 'I desire [the object] as fire' regarding something possessing the property of fire-ness, the possession of that [fire-ness] (*tadvattva*), brought forward by the desire, is apprehended within the desire;
likewise in the case of aversion and so on. Therefore, let it be established in that cognition of fire."
And thus, because there is no lack of established proof, he says: "By this..."
"In the manner stated."
The meaning is "of that which is presented by the determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*)," according to the method stated in the *Bādhoddhāra* treatise.

Thus, having stated the non-establishment of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) defined by that [subject] through the assertion of the non-establishment of both validity and invalidity under the view that [validity] is inferable, he states the non-establishment of the probandum (*pramiti*) for the reason—beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
He restrains.
The meaning is that there is a rule of this nature: "whatever is valid cognition is preceded by an efficacious activity"—[this is stated] because of the two [types of] deviation.

The meaning is that even in the absence of this particular instance of validity (*prāmāṇya*), one observes activity [toward the object] by means of another instance [of validity]. *Prāmāṇyavāda*, page 117. (End of the section on the non-existence of the absence of validity).

But if [it is argued that it is] "by way of being delimited by truth" (*pramātvāvacchedena*), then there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*): once truth is known, there is the knowledge that [truth] is the cause of purposeful activity, and by that very [knowledge], truth is known.

Nor is there a restriction [of validity] determined by being produced by a quality (*guṇa*) and so forth; for you yourself have stated in the *Utpattiprāmāṇya* section that "the restriction does not apply to two individuals alone, because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and because of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). The point is that this results in a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).

If it is argued that there is no circularity because the apprehension of validity by the mind in some cases is due to the apprehension of its being a cause for activity, then let validity itself be apprehended by the mind at the very first instance; what is the need for inference? This is the sense.
And this was stated assuming that the cognition of validity is the cause of activity.

In the view that the cognition of the absence of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyābhāvajñāna*) alone is the cause of purposeful activity, the term "validity" (*pramātva*) should be understood as referring to the absence of invalidity. Alternatively, as stated in the passage: “The absence of the property of having a [certain] qualifier in what lacks that [qualifier], being established, is established by taking up the property of having that qualifier in what possesses it;

for, since there is no third possibility, it is impossible to conclude the probandum without that,” the use of the term "validity" refers to the very inference of validity through the inference of the absence of invalidity.

By this, the following reason is also refuted: "because it is a certainty having 'fire-ness' as its qualifier (vahnitvaprakārakaniścayatva), while being the producer of an effort directed toward an object capable of burning.
This is because, first of all, the status of being a producer (janakatva) is difficult to ascertain.

Furthermore, reasons such as "because it is a certainty having 'fire-ness' as its qualifier with respect to an object capable of burning" are already virtually refuted, since it has been stated previously that the property of having an object capable of burning as its qualificand (dāhasamarthaviśeṣyakatva) is likewise difficult to ascertain at the outset.
Furthermore, since reasons such as "being capable of burning" do not lead to the inference of the general property of being a means of valid cognition (*pramātva*), one might object:
"Let there be the apprehension of that [validity] by way of a property co-extensive with *pramātva*. Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*).

By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), there is the inclusion of [the properties] such as being produced by the absence of defects, being non-defective, and being produced by non-defective instruments—[all of which belong] to validity (prāmāṇya).
The meaning is: "of one who is established in the knowledge of impermanence.
(1. *pramātva* — *mu-a*; 2. *nasya* — *kuṃ*; 3. *nyānu* — *mu*.
[The phrase *pastve-praprā-ṇyātya-bhavaḥ* is a scribal corruption.]
The Theory of Validity (prāmāṇyavāda), Part 2—118.

Because it is difficult to ascertain that a cognition possesses validity (*pramātva*) as the delimitor of being produced [by a cause], specifically because it is difficult to ascertain that it is produced by a quality (*guṇa*).
Furthermore, validity is not inferred through the efficacy of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*),
because such efficacy is absent in the cognition of the moon, stars, and so forth;
and because activity itself depends upon the knowledge of validity, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Furthermore,
because there is deviation in the case of mistaking the luster of a gem for the gem itself;
nor [is it established] by correspondence.
Because there is deviation in the case of correspondence with another cognition;
because correspondence with a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*) remains unestablished even now;
and because the mere absence of non-correspondence exists even in the case of an error where no sublation has yet arisen.
Furthermore, because the absence of the capacity for non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda-yogyatva-abhāva*) is difficult to ascertain without knowing that [the cognition] is valid (*pramātva*),

and because being produced by excellences (*guṇa-janyatva*), being produced by the absence of defects (*doṣa-abhāva-janyatva*), and not being produced by defects (*doṣa-ajanyatva*) are all inferable from the effect in the form of validity— such that excellences and the like are difficult to ascertain without knowing the validity that delimits the nature of being produced—
there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*).
Following the direction stated in the *Yuktipādīya-sudhā* and the direction stated in the *Vādāvalī*, he sets forth the seven reasons that infer validity—beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
By way of capacity.
The meaning is "in the form of the acquisition of an object.
To the proponent who suggests that something other than that [acquisition] might be the subject of the thesis (pakṣa), he replies with the words "of activity" (pravṛtteḥ).
"By virtue of being dependent upon the knowledge of validity."
The sense is that even in the opponent's view, [the cognition of validity] must be required for the purpose of the absence of the cognition of invalidity (aprāmāṇya-jñāna).
To one who says in our own view that mere activity does not depend on the cognition of validity, he replies with the word "maṇi" (gem).
Because of deviation.
The intended meaning is that it is an error that is corroborated by another error.
[Objection: But even in your own view, since invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), there would be the fallacy of the unestablished probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) in that inference.
3. *etannāsti*—mu. 4. *abhāvajñānārtham*—mu.

In my view, however, although the witness (*sākṣin*) apprehends validity as a general rule (*utsargataḥ*), it also apprehends invalidity following sublation (*bādhānantaram*), due to the exception (*apavāda*) characterized by non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*), according to the manner described above.
For it has been stated in the *Sudhā*:
A witness also perceives invalidity when there is the presence of a detractor.

As for the statement in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇayaṭīkā*, “Invalidity is indeed inferable,” that was made with the intention that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) necessarily requires a contradiction (*visaṃvāda*) when apprehending invalidity.
For this very reason, it was stated in that same work: “But it is not the case that [invalidity] is apprehended merely by whatever apprehends the cognition. And in the *Vādāvalī*:
Having stated, "Because the non-validity [of the cognition] is determined through inference," he says—

"But in my view"— in order to show that even for him, the effect [of the subsequent cognition] is the same, whether it consists in the following of impressions from another birth, or the following by means of first inferring the absence of validity, or the following of what is established by the fifth-order reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*), and so forth.
As a general rule.
The meaning is: "by the power of their own respective natures.
To the objection, "Let it be so by itself; what is the use of [assuming] a discrepancy? he says: "in the manner stated."

The meaning is: "in accordance with the method stated there," because it has been stated in the *Svatastvanumānavāda* (the treatise on the intrinsic nature of validity) that "invalidity is apprehended only when there is a subsequent consideration of non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) and so forth," and because it was further stated therein that "there is no capacity for the apprehension of invalidity intrinsically" (*svato 'prāmāṇyagrahe asāmarthyāt*).
This is what is meant by the phrase "for it has been said."
In the first quarter [of the verse]:
"For the validity of scripture is indeed intrinsic, just like perception;
otherwise, there would be an infinite regress, and likewise invalidity would result from something else."
The meaning is: "at the occasion of explaining this.
This is a restatement, by way of meaning, of the words from the *Sudhā*: "the witness," and so forth.
This is called "utterance."
The meaning is that this refers to the occasion for explaining the statement: "Only those of wicked intellect entertain no suspicion regarding the non-existence [of the soul].

In the theory of intrinsic validity (*jñapti-svatastva*), there is a refutation of extrinsic inference (*paratastvānumānabhaṅga*). [From] *Prāmāṇyavāda*, page 121: **Thesis 1:** Validity (*prāmāṇya*)—which is the object of a doubt that is co-located with its occurrence—is not apprehended by any cognition that apprehends its own substrate, insofar as it is characterized by having the qualifier of the mode of the apprehended cognition as its qualifier and having the qualificand of that [apprehended cognition] as its qualificand.

Even regarding the statement in the *Maṇi*: "The locus of dispute (*vivādapada*) is not [the subject], because even when its own substratum is apprehended and ascertained, it is doubted in the third moment following that—without a doubt regarding invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*)—just like invalidity itself," one should understand that what is to be proven here is the absence of that [doubt], according to the method stated by Pakṣadhara and others in their commentary on that [text]: "Just as the probandum was stated in the case of conflicting opinions (*vipratipatti*), so here the absence of that [doubt] is to be known as the probandum."
He provides a restatement of its application, preceded by the necessary equipment, as follows: "svāśraya... (belonging to its own substratum).

It should be understood that because it was not known by what delimitation (*avaccheda*) the subject of dispute is defined, he himself has clarified the intended delimitor of the thesis (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*)—which regulates the dispute—even though it was not mentioned in the *Ṭīkā* or other such works. The meaning is as follows: the "locus" (*āśraya*) is the determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) of one's own validity;
and the validity of the cognition is that which is the object of the doubt which co-occurs with the certainty regarding that [determinative cognition].

The qualifiers [in the definition] are provided because [the probandum would otherwise be] unestablished (*asiddhi*) in the following cases: (1) regarding validity that is not the object of doubt; (2) regarding validity that is ascertained as such; (3) regarding the object of a doubt that has a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*); (4) regarding the object of a doubt existing at the fourth moment; and (5) regarding the object of a doubt existing at any third moment whatsoever.

Since an additional portion, namely the validity of the cognition itself, is introduced here, one should not suspect that there is a "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) due to the identity of the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). The expression "validity of the cognition" (*jñānaprāmāṇya*) is stated specifically to exclude the charge of *siddhasādhana* in the case of invalidity.

The phrase "as far as" (*yāvat*) is used regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in order to exclude sublation (*bādha*), since such [erroneous] inferential cognitions and the like do not have [the true nature of the object] as their apprehended content (*grāhya*).

Although the state of not being apprehended by cognitions produced by words such as "knowledge" or "cognition of a jar" exists even when [the nature of the object] is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), the expression "a mode (*prakāra*) of the knowledge that is apprehended" is employed [to specify the intended meaning].
The function of the two components [of this definition] has already been made clear.

1. varti-ka-ga-ca. 2. kuṃ-cha-ga-ka. 3. jñānagrāhakāgrā - ka-cha. 4. vā-kuṃ-a-ā. 5. ya-kuṃ-a. 6. tathā-a. 7. hetupa-a-ā. 8. retyādyu-kuṃ-a-ā. (The refutation of the opponent's view regarding the nature of cognition; the theory of intrinsic validity [prāmāṇyavāda], page 122. 1. *varti-ka-ga-ca*: "The lamp-flame, the eye, and the object. 2. *kuṃ-cha-ga-ka*: "The jar, the cloth, the pot, and the pillar. 3. *jñānagrāhakāgrā - ka-cha*: "Cognition, the grasper, and the non-grasper. 4. *vā-kuṃ-a-ā*: "Or, the jar, the cloth, the pot, and the mat. 5. *ya-kuṃ-a*: "The cloth, the jar, and the mat. 6. *tathā-a*: "In that manner. 7. *hetupa-a-ā*: "The cause, the effect, and the non-effect. 8. *retyādyu-kuṃ-a-ā*: "By this and so forth, the jar, the cloth, the pot, and the mat.

This is because it possesses the property of being the object of a doubt that occurs in the third moment relative to a certainty having its own substratum as its object. And because it is not the object of a doubt produced by that [cognition].

Here, considering that the single probandum stated by Maṇi in the *vipratipatti* (disagreement) is also an illustration for other probanda mentioned there, he himself states [the following] for the sake of ease in refutation: "tajjñāna... etc.
The meaning of that [term] and the function of the qualification are clear from the refutation of the definitions of "self-proven" (*svataḥ*) as stated by others.

Since the knowledge of God exists in both systems of thought, the two co-located terms—"certain" (*niścaya*) and "limit" (*avadhika*)—are used respectively to prevent the fallacies of non-establishment (*aprasiddhi*) and contradiction (*bādha*).
The meaning is "limited by the moment of its own arising.

Therefore, one should not suspect a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the object within the alternative of doubt about the object occurring in the third moment, limited by the moment of the persistence of the certainty whose object is its own substratum.

"Even though its own substratum has been ascertained, it is still being doubted in the third moment following that"—accepting this first meaning stated in the *Maṇi* commentary, which attains grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through the force of the locative absolute (*sati-saptamī*), one reason has been stated.
Then, accepting "simultaneity with the same pillar" (*samānakīlīnatā*) as another distinct meaning, he states a second reason: "having as its object its own substratum," and so forth.
The phrase "because it has doubt as its object" means, as before, "because it is a member of the alternative of a doubt.
Therefore, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in this case or in the previous one regarding determinate cognition (vyavasāya).

He clarifies the reason stated in the *Maṇi*—namely, "because it is being doubted even when its own substratum is ascertained, provided there is no doubt regarding its invalidity"—with the words beginning with "svāśrayaviṣayaka-kiñcit... and so forth.
By the term "ascertainment whose object is its own locus" (*svāśrayaviṣayaka-niścaya*), Maṇikaṇṭha does not intend every kind of ascertainment.

He states another alternative for the subject, as mentioned in the *Maṇi* [the Nyāyamañjarī], beginning with "the validity of this cognition in its state of non-habituation" (*anabhyāsadaśāpannaitajjñānaprāmāṇyam*), by saying: "or rather, the validity of this cognition" (*yadvaitajjñānaprāmāṇyam*).

therefore, the meaning is that there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*) for the reasons. The phrase ending in "kālinā" (temporal) is included to exclude sublation (*bādha*), as indicated by the word "pūrva" (prior).

In the *Jñapti* [section], the refutation of the opponent’s view (*parastv-anabhaṅga*) regarding the theory of intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*), page 124:
The disputed validity of the primary cognitive act (*vyavasāya-prāmāṇya*) is not cognizable by its subsequent reflective awareness (*tad-anuvyavasāya*).

Because of the three reasons stated beginning with "the third [moment] relative to that," one should apply the qualification "like invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyavat*). Therefore, the inferences for intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) are contradicted by inference.

In this regard, the purpose of the qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇa*) has already been largely explained in the discussion on the definition of self-validity (*svatastva*). Regarding the first reason (*hetu*), there is the state of being an object of doubt occurring in the third moment, delimited by the object itself in its form as silver-ness (*rajatatva*); likewise, there is the state of being an object of doubt occurring in the fourth moment, delimited by the certainty of its own substratum (*svāśraya*).

Likewise, because there exists the state of being the object of Maitra’s doubt— which occurs in the third moment relative to the determination of Caitra’s own substratum— there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case. immediately thereafter, following the non-conceptual [cognition] of the nature of knowledge—without the aspect of [the object as] knowledge—there arises the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), which is conceptual regarding the aspect of the jar, takes the form of Narasimha, and consists of the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*).
Immediately after that, in the second moment, which is the moment of the subsistence of that after-cognition, there is the recollection of the alternative possibilities (*koṭi*).
