In the first [case], by means of the first two parts, there is the avoidance of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) with respect to the verbal cognition and the cognition itself, namely: "your cognition has potness as its qualifier" and "your cognition has that which possesses potness as its qualificand."

By the use of the word "yāvat" (up to), in the first case, the result is the exclusion of sublation (*bādha*) regarding the fifth type of reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) and so forth, according to the Nyāya school. By the two terms in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the exclusion of sublation results because such a cognition of God lacks the property of being graspable; this is the meaning of what has already been stated. The point is that even for the cognition of a cloth (*paṭajñāna*), because it serves as the locus for the validity of its own object, it lacks the probandum [of being self-evident] since it is apprehended by a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that takes it as its object— this is what is meant by "specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*).
Even so,

regarding the validity of a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya-prāmāṇya*), there is a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) because it is the object of a doubt produced by a doubt concerning its own validity, which is based on an inferential cognition of validity (*prāmāṇyānumiti*) directed toward that very locus.
To exclude that [case], the qualification "something" (*kiñcit*) is added.

And thus, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*). For even when there is doubt regarding the validity of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) due to doubt about the validity of the inference, there is no such doubt [regarding the primary cognition] because of the absence of doubt regarding the validity of the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*).
However, being the object of a doubt not produced by a doubt regarding validity is not the probans (*hetu*).
This is because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since even the object itself is the object of a doubt that is not produced by that [doubt regarding validity].
In all these cases, the sublation (*bādhaka*) consists precisely in the elimination of the probans from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

However, under the view that [validity] is known through itself (*svataḥ*), since the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) itself consists in the ascertainment of validity, there can be no doubt regarding validity in the third moment—due to the absence of the causal complex for doubt that is constituted by the non-existence of that [ascertainment] at the second moment when it [the subsequent cognition] persists.

Thus, because that [subsequent cognition] is also apprehended by the subsequent cognition, and because there is an absence of the reason (given its suitability to produce a doubt generated by a doubt concerning validity regarding that subject), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*); this is the sense—that [the reason] is not unestablished (*asiddhi*).

The sense is that, because there is no absence [of the probans] in an undivided [locus], the fact that it does not exclude the unestablished (asiddhi) is not a fault—this is with reference to the *anuvyavasāya*.

The sense is that, because its validity is fixed by necessity, there can never be any doubt regarding it. He clarifies the destruction of the [opposing] reason with the words beginning "svatastu" (but by itself).
"Regarding the ascertainment of validity."
And thus, the sense is: how can there be doubt when the specific characteristic is perceived?—this is expressed by the words "in the absence of that."

The meaning is: the absence of the perception of the qualifier in the form of the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇyaniścaya*). (Note on variants: 1. *prāmāṇyapadaṃ na* is found in manuscripts Kuṃ, Ka, Kha, Ga, Cha; 2. *anumitiprāmāṇyasaṃśayenevānuvyavasāya* is found in manuscript Ga;
3. *dūṣaṇaṃ* is found in manuscript Ā; 4. *prāmāṇyasaṃ-* is found in manuscripts Mu, A, and Ā.)

In the case of the theory of intrinsic validity (*jñapti*), there is no violation [of the rule] "parastvāna-bhaṅgaḥ" (the subsequent [cognition] does not destroy [the first]). This is because, at the moment when the certainty of validity is established in the second [cognition], the causal complex for doubt—which consists of the absence of that [validity]—is absent; therefore, it is impossible for validity to be the object of a doubt produced by a causal complex that is simultaneous with the certainty of its own substratum.

If the *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent reflective awareness) were the apprehender of the validity [of the primary cognition], then, given the rule that a doubt regarding the object to be grasped (*grāhya*) necessarily follows from a doubt regarding the validity of the apprehender (*grāhaka*), there would be a doubt regarding the validity of the *anuvyavasāya* itself at the very moment of inferring the validity of the *vyavasāya* (primary cognition). Furthermore, due to this doubt regarding the validity of the *anuvyavasāya*, a doubt regarding the validity of the *vyavasāya* would occasionally arise;
yet such an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) is not accepted.
Because there is a rule that the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya) possesses validity.
It is said:
if the first [proposition] were to be proven, there would be an *apasiddhānta* (departure from established tenets), sublation (*bādha*), and contradiction (*vyāghāta*).
Precisely for this reason: the meaning is "because the ascertainment of validity is itself that very ascertainment."
The second [term] is explained as "the moment of persistence" (sthitikṣaṇa).
The third clarifies the destruction of the cause—namely, that of the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya).
First, he states the faults of the thesis (pratijñādoṣa) with the words beginning "The first is the thing to be proven" (ādyo sādhya).

Since, in the manner described, the property of apprehending its own substratum consists in the apprehension of validity (*prāmāṇya*), and since even in the opponent's view it is established that [validity] is apprehended by such [cognitions] as inference, to prove the absence of that [apprehension] would constitute a departure from one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

Furthermore, if it were stated that "validity is not apprehended by that which apprehends validity," the contradiction and the self-defeating nature (*vyāghāta*) of the claim would be perfectly evident.
Even if one specifies "independently" (*svātantryeṇa*), there remains precisely the same contradiction, according to the method set forth in the *Bādhoddhāra* commentary.

The point is that since the probandum (sādhya) in its stated form would also exist in the case of an object [that is not a cognition], there would be the consequence of deviation (vyabhicāra); therefore, the qualification of the reason intended to exclude that [deviation] would be redundant.
"Portion."

"All knowledge is a quality" means that the portion consisting of the validity of the knowledge produced by words [is the subject]; the intention is that this has already been stated as the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkaraṇa*).
(Note: 1. *tiprā* – Kuṃ.; 2. *sya* – Ka, Kha, Cha.)
In the case of the *jñapti* (cognition), there is no sublation (*bhaṅga*) by the word "past" (*apastvāt*). [This concludes] the theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*), page 129.
In the second part, there is the proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
And this has been established in the "Refutation of the Definition of Self-Existence" (*Niruktibhaṅga*), which addresses the self-existence (*svatastva*) asserted by others.

Furthermore, regarding the term "its own" (*svaśabda*) in the probandum (*sādhya*), does it refer merely to the validity of that which has been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*), or does it refer to that which is co-referential (*samabhivyāhṛta*) with it? Not the first.

The latter [alternative] is not tenable, because non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*) is apprehended by the cognition that apprehends its locus— that is, the cognition which has as its qualifier the non-validity residing in that which possesses non-validity— and thus the probandum, which consists in being unapprehended by that [cognition], is absent from the example, namely non-validity itself. Furthermore, since there is no possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to an object such as a jar, the third term in the reason (*hetu*) is redundant.
For in this view, the pot itself, as uttered in co-utterance (*samabhivyāhṛta*), is the meaning of its own word.
It is for this very reason that he says: "And this has been established."

Although sublation (*bādha*) and contradiction (*vyāghāta*) were not explicitly mentioned by name, they are said to have been "established" because they have been established for all practical purposes.
He states the faults regarding the example and the reason according to the distinction of the thesis (pakṣa), beginning with "furthermore" (kiñca).
Regarding "of invalidity" (aprāmāṇyasya): [it refers to the non-existence of validity].

The meaning is as follows: after the error of silver-ness (*rūpyatva-bhrama*) regarding mother-of-pearl, when a sublation occurs, there arises a reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) that "this cognition is invalid. In this case, the validity consisting in being a cognition whose qualifier is invalidity with respect to an object that possesses invalidity is itself the subject (*pakṣa*). Since the apprehender of the locus of that validity must necessarily apprehend the invalidity that constitutes its very essence, there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in that instance.

Regarding the phrase "like invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyavat*), although the commentary on that [text] explains it as meaning "like the invalidity which constitutes one alternative of the doubt concerning the validity that has been made the subject (*pakṣa*)," the intended sense is that the same applies even to that which constitutes such validity;
this clarifies the absence of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
This is stated in the phrase "in this position" (*asmin pakṣe*).

1. *Paratastva* etc.—Kuṃ, Ka, Ga, Cha. 2. The word *mātra* is not present—Kuṃ, Ga. 3. *Hetāv iti* is not present—Kuṃ, Ka, Kha, Ga, Cha. 4. *Sya*—Mu, A, Ā. [The refutation of the view that validity is extrinsic (*paratastva*) in the context of cognition. *Prāmāṇyavāda*, page 130.

Furthermore, in the case of a jar, the probandum—in the form of "not being graspable by any cognition that grasps the constituent potsherds which are the substrata of the jar"—is indeed present; so how could there be any possibility of a deviation (vyabhicāra) in that instance? Moreover, what is being proved by these inferences: is it the absence of fitness for direct apprehension by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), or the absence of the result in the form of a definitive ascertainment (niścaya)? It cannot be the first, because, as you have stated, just as in the case of the locus (dharmin), even in the case of the qualifying relation (vaiśiṣṭya), according to your view, there is a lack of fitness consisting in not being presented by the determinative cognition (vyavasāya), whereas according to my view, once that [relation] has been presented by the determinative cognition, there exists an innate incapacity on the part of the witness-consciousness to perceive it.
Because of sublation (*bādha*);

because doubt is logically established precisely by the absence of a result in the form of certainty; and because [the reason] would be irrelevant (*aprayojakatva*) for proving the absence of fitness (*yogyatva*).
Even in the latter case, does the proof of the absence of the result consist in the presentation of something that opposes validity, such as the suspicion of a defect?

If it is objected that, since the term "cognition of the apprehended" (*grāhyajñāna*) in the phrase "the mode of the cognition of the apprehended" (*grāhyajñānaprakāra*) also refers to its own substratum, then because the shard—which is the substratum of the jar—is a mode without a [further] mode, it would follow that every cognition apprehending the substratum of the jar (i.e., the shard) would have that [shard] as its qualificandum; and thus, such a cognition is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). We reply:
No. The very fact that such a cognition is unestablished constitutes its being the "apprehended" (*grāhya*) therein, because the probandum—in the form of the absence of that [cognition]—is present.

For this very reason, it was stated that "the probandum (sādhya) certainly exists. Alternatively, since the non-establishment of such a cognition regarding the subject (kāpāla)—which is the absence of the result consisting in having that [cognition] as its object—is not established in the case of the jar, there would be no possibility of a deviation (vyabhicāra) therein; thus, expressing dissatisfaction with that [previous argument], he says: "Furthermore" (kiñca).

The phrase "the aspect of the property" (dharmyaṃśa) is an elliptical expression; the meaning is "as in the case of both the property and the substratum of the property"—that is, "in this [instance]."
The meaning is that it has the aspect of distinction as its object—by virtue of having been so stated.

In the *Bādhoddhāra* [treatise]: "It is not obstructed. [Commentary: Regarding the cognition [of the object], there is no destruction [of the means of knowledge] even after [the object] has been known. (Note: This passage addresses the objection that if an object is already known, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be redundant; the response is that the means of knowledge does not perish once it has produced the cognition.)
The theory of validity (prāmāṇyavāda), page 131:
[Does it arise] through the convergence of causal factors when there is no obstruction, or when there is an obstruction?
Not the first.
In that case, regarding validity, [the reason] would be unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) due to the absence of doubt,
and it would also be unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*); thus,
the latter [alternative] is not tenable.
This is because such an admission is acceptable; nor does the absence of capacity follow merely from the absence of a result,
since it has already been stated that there is sublation (bādha).

For just as fire possesses the inherent power to burn, yet its failure to burn occurs due to an obstruction such as a magical gem (*maṇi*), so too the apprehension of validity possesses an inherent power to grasp validity, yet the non-apprehension of validity occurs due to obstructions such as the suspicion of defects (*doṣa-śaṅkā*).

This has been stated by the authors of the *Ṭīkā*: "Even though the apprehension of validity is innate, just as the non-burning [of fire] is possible due to an obstruction such as a magical gem, the apprehension of validity is logically established as being obstructed by the suspicion of defects."
"For the elephant's power of movement is not dependent on another [factor] merely because it requires the clearing of the path by oxhoof grass.

The point is that since it was not stated that [the reason] is ungraspable at the time of doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), there is room for two alternatives; thus, [the opponent claims] this is a case of "proving what is already accepted" (*iṣṭāpatti*).

The meaning is that our intended definition of self-validity—either as being directly perceivable by the witness-consciousness without dependence on another, or as being fit for such witnessing—remains unimpaired.

[Objection: But surely, since the self-validity [of cognition] is lost through the inference that there is no capacity [to produce a result] due to the absence of a result, [the author] says: "And not..."
Because sublation has already been stated.
The meaning is: "according to your view," and so forth.
Since it is illogical that there should be a non-apprehension of that [capacity] when its existence as a capacity and its fitness are present, he says: "In the case of fire," etc.
To the objection, "If it depends on the absence of an obstacle, how is its self-sufficiency not lost?", he says: "For it has been said..."
The meaning is "in the Vādāvalī.

Now, one might object: since the reasons stated by [Śrīharṣa] in the *Maṇi* are presented here as counter-arguments to the reasons stated by [the author] himself, then—under the view that an *upādhi* functions as a counter-argument—the presentation of an *upādhi* against a counter-argument would be as useless as presenting another counter-argument against a counter-argument. Therefore, relying on the opinion of the author of the *Maṇi*, he says:

— [The phrase] "due to the deviation of the limiting adjunct" (*upādheḥ vyabhicārāt*), etc. [In the case of] cognition (*jñapti*), there is no sublation (*bhaṅga*) because of its being perceived (*upalabdhatvāt*). (Note: The manuscript *ka* contains only the portion ending with "due to the possibility of [the cognition] of the [object]" (*ṇasyopapatteśca*).)

Furthermore, there is a refutation by means of the aforementioned reasoning (tarka), namely, the form of infinite regress and the impossibility of apprehending the validity of the first [cognition]. Moreover,

on the view that the adventitious condition (upādhi) brings about deviation, the upādhi consists in being composed of an adventitious condition that lacks the fitness to be an object of reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya).
Furthermore, being constituted by a limiting adjunct that is not grasped by that [cognition] is unintelligible without that [adjunct] itself being ungrasped;
for such is observed in cases such as "possessing heaviness" when the heaviness is constituted by a heaviness that is not grasped by perception.

1. Your reason (*hetu*), however, is established even when that [cognition] is apprehended, precisely by the absence of the fruit consisting of apprehension; thus, the *upādhi* (limiting condition) pervades the probandum (*sādhya*).

Since it has been demonstrated that fitness exists even in the aspect of the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*)—just as it does in the case of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*)—the fact that the subject (*pakṣa*), namely validity (*prāmāṇya*) which possesses the probans (*sādhana*), is not constituted by an *upādhi* devoid of fitness for reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) clearly establishes that the *upādhi* does not pervade the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*).

To explain how there is pervasion by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*), he clarifies its being the efficient cause (*prayojakatva*) with respect to the probandum: "that which is graspable by it" (*tadgrāhya*).
This is a restatement of the previously mentioned qualification without modification.
He states the lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*) of the reason with the words "tvadīya" (your own).
"Even in the case of being graspable by that"—the meaning is "even in the case of being fit for apprehension by that.

And thus, by stating the presence or absence of a favorable *tarka* (reductio) regarding the limiting condition (*upādhi*) and the reason (*hetu*), [it is shown]: "When the probans is accompanied by a favorable *tarka*..."
Since the pervasion by the probandum is destroyed, there is no possibility of a limiting condition (upādhi) in that case.
With the thought that there is no room for such an objection, he says: "It pervades the probandum."

Since even the aspect of "being knowledge" regarding the object of knowledge that possesses conditions (*sākṣaṇa*) is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), he refutes what has been stated by others in order to establish that [point], beginning with: "Furthermore...
(Refutation of the destruction of the knower in the act of cognition)
Furthermore, if the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) were in the form of "Narasiṃha" (the man-lion), the doubt would be whether it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding a jar,
and not whether the cognition regarding the jar is valid or not.
This is because the property of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) is not known as the delimiting condition of the subject (*dharmitāvacchedaka*).
Furthermore, it is unestablished that doubt exists at the third moment;

for since one who is not omniscient is unable to determine the number of supersensible and extremely subtle moments, doubt occurs precisely at the third moment relative to the determination of its own substratum, and not at the fourth or subsequent moments.

Because it is impossible to determine [the certainty of validity]. However, if— on the grounds that the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) lacks the nature of a determination of validity— one assumes that doubt occurs in the third moment due to the presence in the second moment of the causal complex for doubt, which consists in the recollection of alternative possibilities qualified by the absence of such a determination, then, since the doubt exists in the third moment, [there would be no certainty] for the after-cognition.
If extrinsic validity (*paratastva*)—in the form of the absence of the nature of certainty regarding validity—is what you seek to prove, there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*).
[This is because] it would be due to ignorance.

And thus, the point is that if one accepts another cognition characterized by the nature of being a cognition (jñānatva) for that purpose, then [the property of] "occurring in the third moment delimited by the ascertainment of its own substratum" remains unestablished.
Now, if it is argued that by the word "ascertainment" (niścaya) only conceptual cognition (savikalpaka) is intended, he says: "Furthermore" (kiñca).
Having stated the defects common to all three reasons, he also states the defect in their specific forms: "Furthermore, regarding the first... and so forth.
"It is unestablished."
The meaning is "already burnt and established.
[Regarding the term] "mutual dependence" (*anyonyāśraya*):
1. The word *rūpa* is not present in Kuṃ, Ga, Kha, and Cha. 2. Or rather, it is *evaṃ* in Mu, A, and Ā.

In the case of the cognition [of validity], there is no destruction [of the initial certainty] by doubt occurring in the fourth or subsequent moments; thus, the theory of intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*) remains unrefuted. Furthermore, the extrinsic nature (*paratastva*) of validity is not established even by a doubt occurring in the fourth or subsequent moments.

Although doubt does not arise in the third moment due to the presence of the recollection of the alternative (koṭismaraṇa) produced in the second moment— which, in the form of a certainty regarding validity, acts as an obstacle— nevertheless, it is possible for doubt to arise in the fourth moment because of that recollection of the alternative, which exists in that same moment as a causal complex (*saṃśayasāmagrī*) qualified by the destruction of the obstacle produced in the third moment.

The meaning is: if it is established that reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) lacks the capacity to ascertain validity, then the existence of doubt at the third moment cannot be established; and if that [existence] is established, then this [lack of ascertainment] is established. Now, one might object: "Let there be no certainty regarding the reason; let the stated probandum be established by taking as its object a doubt occurring in the fourth moment or thereafter. To this, [the author replies]: "By means of the reflective awareness in the form of the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) in the first moment..."

He states with the words "na ca" and so forth that even if validity has been ascertained, doubt regarding it in the fourth moment and thereafter is not untenable; thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (aprayojaka).
"Secondly," it says.
The meaning is: "by that which has arisen at the moment of the persistence of the subsequent reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya)"—that is, in the form of a certainty regarding validity (prāmāṇya).
The meaning is that it consists of the ascertainment of validity known as the cognition of the previously mentioned subject; this is what is meant by "at that moment."
The meaning is "at the third moment";
[it refers to] that which has the nature of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

In that case, according to their view, even if the cognition of the subject (*dharmijñāna*) has perished, it serves only as a means for the recollection of the alternative (*koṭi*), and thus its absence is not a defect.
Furthermore, even if that cognition has perished, a doubt arises as to whether the resulting cognition is valid or not, since the object is presented by memory.
Nor should it be argued that the presentation by memory occurs only because the object was previously experienced as being valid; for such was not the case in the prior experience.
Because it is possible for a defect to obstruct the aspect of validity [in the case of cognition].
(In the case of the apprehension [of validity], there is no destruction of the [required] conditions.)

Regarding the second reason as well: once it is established that non-apprehension (*anuvyavasāya*) has validity (*prāmāṇya*) as its object, then at the moment of the subsistence of the second *anu-vyavasāya*,
there is (1) an absence of certainty regarding validity, because (2) the causal complex for doubt— in the form of the recollection of a qualified alternative— is present.
The proof that this [cognition] is simultaneous with the certainty in the form of an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) is established;

and once that is established, it follows that validity is not established as an object of the after-cognition by virtue of being the object of a doubt produced by the aforementioned causal complex—thus there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).

Likewise, regarding the third reason, if the restriction of the after-cognition to validity were established, then the doubt as to whether "only a true cognition is grasped as valid" or "only a false cognition [is grasped as valid]" would necessarily have the inferential cognition of validity itself as its locus.

In reality, however, in my view, since the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*) in the case of an error is known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), and its validity is known through the mind (*mānasa*), the presentation of that [validity] alone is not contradictory; this is the intended meaning.
The same applies to the second reason as well.

It should be understood that the state of being simultaneous with the ascertainment of its own substratum (*svāśrayaniścaya*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of doubt and error. Now, one might object: "Since the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*), which consists of the ascertainment of the locus (*dharmin*), has as its object the validity [of the cognition], it is known that the causal complex consisting of the recollection of alternative possibilities (*koṭi*) qualified by the non-perception of distinguishing features (*viśeṣādarśana*) is present at that time; therefore, this [simultaneity] is difficult to establish. To this, he says: "Of the after-cognition," and so forth. This is the second [point].
The meaning of this is that the moment of subsistence belongs to the after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*);
thus it is also in the case of the third reason.

It should be understood that it is difficult to know [the truth] when there is doubt regarding validity (*prāmāṇya*) whose locus is the *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent reflective awareness). To the objection that it is easily known simply because the *anuvyavasāya* is invariably valid, he says: "Of the *anuvyavasāya*... [etc. (Note: 1.
*yasthi* — *ka*, *kha*, *cha*; 2. *rūpapratibandhakābhāva* — *kuṃ*, *ga*; 3. *tasyāniścaya* — *ka*, *kha*, *cha*; 4. *daprā* — *kuṃ*.)
However, by establishing the fact that [the cognition] has the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) as its locus,

one establishes that it is not an object of doubt arising from a doubt regarding the validity residing in the subsequent cognition— [a doubt] which would otherwise stem from a doubt regarding the validity of the primary cognition (*vyavasāya*). Consequently,
since the rule that the subsequent cognition possesses validity with respect to that [primary cognition] would depend on this, there is indeed a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).
By this [argument], validity is known extrinsically (*parataḥ*), because in the state of non-habituation it is subject to doubt, just like invalidity.
Furthermore, that very "extrinsic nature" which is denied by the opponent is what is being proven here;
and in this case, partial unestablishment (*bhāgāsiddhi*) is not a logical fault.
And when that has been accomplished...
The phrase "of the validity of the determinate cognition" (*vyavasāyaprāmāṇyasya*) and so forth refers to the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

The intended meaning is that, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there is no necessary rule that the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) of validity in cases such as doubt must itself be a valid cognition (*pramātva*).

Thus, having refuted the inferences stated by [Śrīharṣa] in the *Maṇi*, he now refutes the inference mentioned by Udayana in the second chapter of the *Kusumāñjali* and suspected in the *Sudhā* with the words "by this" (*eteneti*).

The connection [of the words] is "is rejected. Now, one might object: since otherness (*paratva*), which consists in being different, can be established as intrinsic (*svatastva*) by virtue of its being a property inherent in a single locus, this would result in proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*). Therefore, he refines that point: "And as for extrinsicness (*paratastva*)... [and so forth].

The meaning is that by the phrase "tatprakāraprakāra... and so forth, the status of being an object of cognition (*grāhyatva*) for the previously mentioned form of knowledge is negated; thus, it is that very [point].

And so, there is no room for the refutation stated in the *Maṇi*—namely, "Even if it were its own object of cognition, it might sometimes be the object of another's cognition, since even 'self' is 'other' in relation to something else"—this is the intention behind the words "atra ca" (and here).

If it is objected: "But how can there be a suspicion of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*), given Vardhamāna’s statement that the phrase ‘in the state of non-repetition’ is intended to exclude partial unestablishedness?"—we reply: No. Since it has been stated that the subject (*pakṣa*) is validity in general, and because this is inherently doubtful, the phrase ‘in the state of non-repetition’ was introduced to account for cases where [the reason] is unestablished in some instances. For even in the case of the validity of a cognition produced in the state of repetition, there is an absence of doubt in every instance of that portion of the subject which arises from the state of non-repetition.

It should be understood that when there is a suspicion of partial non-establishment (*bhāgāsiddhi*), one states that it constitutes a fallacy according to the view of the ancients. (Note: The variants for the following terms are as follows:

1. *ṇyasyānu*—kha, cha, ca; 2. *tu*—mu, ca, ga; 3. ‘*sādhyate*’—na, kuṃ, ga, cha; 4. *syāpramātvādi*—ni, a; 5. *jñānagrā-*—mu; 6. *ktyā*—a; 7. *nne*—a. (Regarding the cognition [of the reason], there is no refutation because [the reason] exists [in the subject].)

In the *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava*, First Chapter, page 176:

Because of the assistance of reasoning (*tarka*), there arises the inference that [the Veda] has a single author; and since the aforementioned excellence (*guṇa*) exists therein, it would be recognized as valid knowledge (*pramā*).

Nor should it be said that the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*)—accompanied by such excellences as the correct reflective awareness (*satyaparāmarśa*) and so forth—is the [probans]. This is because validity can be established by the mere absence of sublation alone, since that is necessary; thus, the excellence cannot be proven to be the cause [of validity].
The meaning is: in the inference "clarity (*prasāda*) has an agent, because it is an effect, like a pot," [the reason] is stated.
The meaning is that, in reality, this has already been stated by the words "possessing the pervader of the probandum" (*sādhyavyāpyavat*) and so forth.

By this, the claim of Rucidatta—that the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) in a subject (*pakṣa*) which possesses what is to be known under the delimitation of the subject-delimiter (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) is a merit (*guṇa*)—is refuted;
for it does not transcend the defects already stated by the words "having multiple agents" (*anekakartṛka*) and so forth.
Because, in fact, validity can be established simply by the cognition of the subject as possessing the property to be known,
and because that [cognition] is not a quality since it is conditioned by the existence of its object;

by this very argument, the statement of Pakṣadhara— that in the case of a valid inference whose probandum is not incompatible with the delimiting condition of the subject, the "correct consideration of the middle term" (*yathārtha-liṅga-parāmarśa*) is the quality— is also refuted.

In the case mentioned regarding the prior non-existence of fragrance (*gandhaprāgabhāva*), even though the quality (*guṇa*) you have described is present, [the inference fails] because it is sublated by the existence of a valid cognition of the probandum that does not contradict the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).
Furthermore, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the case of the thundering of clouds.

As it is said: "And it is observed that even in the absence of a quality, the speech of an unreliable person (*anāpta*) that happens to coincide with the truth produces a cognition that accords with reality."
Explaining the statement from the *Tattvanirṇayaṭīkā*, he refutes the previously mentioned view that there is a concomitant quality even in verbal valid cognition, saying: "In this way... (evam).
When it should have been said, "A jar exists," the statement "A cloth exists" uttered through negligence and so forth is the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). (pradi-prasu-pratyeta-guṇaḥ)
*Prāmāṇyavāda*, Part II—177.

Thus, in the case of a cognition produced by the words of a deceiver or by the words of a parrot, etc., where there is a correspondence with reality (*yādṛcchika-saṃvāda*), there is no knowledge of the object of the sentence as it truly is (*yathārtha-vākyārtha-jñāna*).
Nor should it be suspected that even in those cases, such [knowledge] exists in God.

Furthermore, there would be the over-extension [of the definition] that, just as validity (*prāmāṇya*) arises from being produced by a cause residing in a different locus, so too invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) would arise from being produced by a defect residing in the same locus;
and moreover, that [defect] is not the direct producer of verbal valid cognition,
because valid cognition arises in the listener even when that defect residing in the speaker has long since perished.
Alternatively, it resides in the speaker by means of the composition of the sentence; yet, with respect to that composition, there is no causal agency [on the part of the speaker],
because such [composition] is established merely through the cognition of a series of words, as in the case of parrots, children, and the like.

[Objection: "But surely, even if such a quality is absent in that particular sentence, it exists in another sentence of the same class; therefore, it cannot be the cause [of validity] even in that case. To this, he says: "Furthermore" (kiñca).
The phrase "even though it has long since perished" is to be construed with what precedes.

Now, it may be argued that the knowledge of the Lord, which serves as the cause for every effect, being of the nature of knowledge of the meaning of sentences as they truly are, may function as a cause for valid cognition (*pramā*) by way of composing [the sentence].
Therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of accidental valid cognition,
nor is the composition of a sentence possible without it.

He raises this objection with the following thought: because [the Lord] is the cause of the mere effect [of speech] by way of being the cause of its composition and of the valid cognition produced thereby;

and because, even in the case of the valid cognition produced by the words of a parrot and the like, there is no deviation [from the rule] if one takes the valid cognition of the Lord himself into account—this being the intent of his own commentary, which states:

“In the case of the words of a deluded person, a deceiver, or a parrot, it is the knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence belonging to the Lord alone that is the generator [of the cognition]. (Nyāyamañjarī).

1. This passage does not exist in Kuṃ, Ga, Kha, Ka, and Cha. 2. *vākyādī* — Kuṃ. 3. The additional passage beginning with “*yathārthajñānajanakatvam iti tatvanirṇayaṭīkāṃ vivṛṇvānaḥ*” exists in Ā. 4. Nor should it be argued that, even in that case, the cause [of the scripture] is the knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence residing in God, mediated by the act of composition;

for such knowledge serves as a cause only through its being immediate with respect to the material cause (*upādāna*), just as it does in the case of ordinary cognition and error, and thus lacks the specific character required to be the cause of valid knowledge (*pramā*).
Otherwise, there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) already mentioned;

furthermore, since even error is postulated as the cause for composing sentences that are inconsistent with reality—such as those uttered by parrots and the like—it would follow that, just as there is eternal valid cognition, there must also be eternal error.
If it is objected: "In verbal cognition, either semantic competency (*yogyatā*) or the resulting valid cognition itself is the excellence (*guṇa*);
and since neither exists in every authoritative sentence, [your argument fails]," we say no.

For if you were to prove that [verbal cognition] is produced by such an excellence—which does not contradict the Vedas' being non-human (authorless) as I maintain, yet which contradicts the establishment of an *Īśvara* as you maintain—then your argument would result in proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*).
And it is not even there.
The meaning is: "even in the case of one that coincides by chance"—thus it was said.
The meaning is that it has been stated [in the verse] beginning with "otherwise than this" (anyathāsmādādi).

He raises an alternative view stated in the *Maṇi*, which begins with "But we say," and continues: "In verbal cognition, the speaker’s knowledge of the object as it truly is is not the *guṇa* (excellence);
rather, it is [the sentence's] compatibility (*yogyatva*) and so forth, or that true knowledge itself.
He anticipates this objection.
"Is it not so? (nanu) //

It has been stated that "your desired [view]—that fitness, being existent in its own right, is not the cause [of truth], and therefore it is not a quality, and thus there is no valid cognition [arising from it]"—is refuted.
"Because the production and dissolution of valid cognition (pramā) depend upon another [cause], there can be no confidence in anything other than that;
therefore, no other alternative is possible.

By this statement from the *Kusumāñjali*, since it is accepted that the extrinsic nature of validity (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*) serves as the means for establishing God, [there follows] the knowledge of the true meaning of the sentence.

The point is that since the quality of being a property (*guṇatva*) exists in the Veda as a subject, God is established by the fact that there is knowledge of such a true sentence-meaning [in the Veda]. (Note: The manuscript variants indicate the following corrections:

Furthermore,
regarding semantic competency (*yogyatā*): is it the existence of the relation conveyed by the words, or is it some other property invariably concomitant with the existence of that relation?
The first [alternative] is not tenable: because neither verbal cognition nor its object is the producer of that [verbal cognition];
and because, since being an object is included within the nature of valid cognition (*pramātva*), it cannot be its cause;

and furthermore, because even in the case of perceptual and other forms of valid cognition, there exists the presence of a determinate object, your proposed definition of verbal cognition would lack the required exclusivity (*asādhāraṇya*).
Furthermore, even in the case of invalid cognition (*apramā*), it would follow that the existence of the object itself is the defect (*doṣa*).

[Objection]: But surely, since the author of the *Maṇi* stated that "the existence of God is not established by the fact that Vedic valid cognition is produced by excellences (*guṇa*)," in this system the establishment of God must proceed by means of another reason; to this, he says: "Moreover" (*kiñca*).

"The compatibility [of the sentence] with the non-sublation of the sentence-meaning is *yogyatā* (compatibility)"—this is the first alternative, according to the statement in the *Maṇi* within this very discussion on validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*).
The second alternative—that it is a distinct property (*dharmāntara*)—follows from the mention of "sublation" (*bādha*) regarding *yogyatā*.
The meaning is that in the final case, it would be common to [all three times], such as the past and so forth;
and because it is impossible for it to be the cause of that.
The intended meaning is "because it would reside in itself" (ātmāśrayāt); [this refers to] "only the existence of the object" (viṣayasattvasyaiva).

Since a fault (*doṣa*) is precisely that which is opposed to a quality (*guṇa*), and because [the fault] must be capable of following [the object], you too must admit the appearance of even what is non-existent (*asat*) in an error (*bhrama*). Otherwise, it would not be an error at all; this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: "But surely, in the case of a valid cognition produced by the words of Śuka, Bāla, and others, since there is an absence of any other factor that serves as the cause for its validity, one must admit—since there is no other recourse—that even the 'existence of the object' (viṣayasattva), which is itself the 'fitness' (yogyatā), is the excellence (guṇa).

To this, he replies: "By the necessary [excellence]. 1. The word *kiṃ* is not present in manuscript *cha*. 2. This passage is not found in manuscript *kha*. 3. The phrase *niyatapadaṃ* is not present in manuscripts *ca* and *cha*.

4. *bdapramāsā-mu-ca*. 5. *ṇeśvara-ā*. 6. *vādo-kuṃ*. 7. The word *abhāva* and so forth are additionally present in *kuṃ*. 8. This line is absent in *a*. 9. *pyasa-mu-a*. 10. The word *api* is not present in *ā*.
And because validity (*pramātva*) is established by the very fact of being necessarily faultless (*nirdeṣatva*). *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 180).

Not the last [alternative]. For you have stated that *yogyatā* (semantic competency) consists either in the absence of being the qualificand of a cognition (*pramā*) that is the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in the other word-meaning while there is a relation with the first word-meaning; or else, it consists in the absence of a property that delimits the counter-positiveness of an absolute non-existence residing in the other word-meaning while there is a relation with the first word-meaning.

The meaning is that since the speaker may possess defects such as error, deception, and the like, and since even the capacity [of the words] would be absent [in that case], it is necessary to depend upon that [capacity] for the sake of [understanding] the meaning; this is the point.
He states what was said in the *Yogyatāvāda*: "One... and so forth.

In expressions such as "he sprinkles with water," there is a single entity in the form of the act of sprinkling; regarding its relation, there exists a valid cognition (*pramā*) whose qualifier is the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence residing in the other entity, namely the water. Since the absence of being the qualificand (*viśeṣyatva*) of that [cognition] is present, such a sentence is "fit" (*yogya*). However, in cases such as "he sprinkles with fire," [the conditions are not met].

Since the cognition arises that "the relation of sprinkling is the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in fire" with respect to the relation defined by sprinkling, there exists therein precisely the state of being the qualificand of a valid cognition whose qualifier is the property of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in another object; thus, such a sentence is unfit [for the definition],
and consequently, there are no cases of under-extension (*avyāpti*) or over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

In this context, regarding the appropriate statement "sound is in space," the property of being the qualificandum of a valid cognition whose object is the counter-correlativity of absolute non-existence residing in sound exists in space—which is a category that does not possess [sound]—and thus there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*). To avoid this, instead of saying "one category" (*eka padārtha*), it is stated as "the relation of this category. Since the relation with space is not like that, there is no fault.

They say that since the definition would be complete by merely stating "the absence of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in another entity," the phrase ending with "the absence of being the object of a valid cognition [of such counter-positiveness]" was stated on the basis of the view that "being the object of a valid cognition of such counter-positiveness" is the obstructive factor.

5. There is no word for *seka*—a-ā. 6. Those [cognitions] which, because of their being valid cognitions (*pramātva*)—that indeed—taddhi-ā. 7. ṣyābhāḥ—kuṃ. 8. But, thus not—mu. 9. What is it?—pa—a-ā. (prati-prasu-pratyeta-guṅgaḥ)
Regarding the theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*), page 181:

In that regard, in the first position, there is a contradiction with the cognition of the syntactic connection (*anvaya-pramā*). In the second [position], in the case of "he sprinkles with water," the *yogyatā* (semantic competency) is established as the absence in the water of those properties—such as "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) and so forth—which serve as the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the non-connection with the act of sprinkling.

In this regard, although these two are invariably concomitant with the existence of a relation (*saṃsarga*) and yet are not themselves the nature of the relation, the previously mentioned fault does not apply.

However, Narahari stated that if one were to say merely "the absence of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence" (i.e., *atyantābhāvapratiyogitvābhāva*), then semantic competency (*yogyatā*) would be nothing other than the meaning of the sentence itself; therefore, he said it is "the absence of being the counter-positive of a non-existence qualified by that [relation].
We shall clarify this in the discussion on semantic competency (*yogyatāvāda*).

Since the property of being the object of the valid cognition "the relation with a jar is the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the house" exists even in the relation with the jar, this would exclude the sentence "there is a jar in the house" from the definition; therefore, to avoid this under-extension (*avyāpti*), it is stated that there must be an absence of being the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) of such a valid cognition.

Because it is impossible to ascertain the absence of being the qualificandum of a valid cognition (pramā) common to both oneself and others, and because there are defects such as the excessive complexity (gaurava) involved in introducing "valid cognition" [into the definition], the second definition is adopted.

For the property of being the relation with fire (*vahnisaṃsargatva*) is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma*) of the absolute non-existence residing in the object denoted by the word "sprinkling" (*seka*); since the absence of that [property] exists in the contact with water (*jalasaṃyoga*), the sentence "he sprinkles with water" and the like is semantically competent (*yogya*).
The statement "by fire" (agninā) is unsuitable; thus, there is no fault such as non-pervasion (avyāpti).

Here, because the absence of being the counter-correlate (pratiyogitva) in the form described above culminates in the existence of the relation (*saṃsarga*) within the sentence-meaning, the cognition thereof is not a cause for verbal valid knowledge (*śābdapramā*). Therefore, it is stated that [the word] is devoid of the property that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakadharma*) of this [absence];
hence the term "non-connection" (*ananvaya*).

The meaning is that when there is a relation with one word-meaning, the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in another word-meaning constitutes a form of non-connection— namely,
"fireness" and so forth.
Fire, the seasons, stones, and so forth.
1. *vyastaṃ padaṃ* — Kha, Ga, Ka, Ca, Cha. 2. *ktā doṣāḥ* — Cha. 3. *sarge 'stī* — Ā.
4. *ata uktaṃ* — Mu. 5. *tākābhā* — Ā.
Nevertheless, the resulting meaning here is that,

between these two views, the excellence (*guṇa*) consists either in the absence of the cognition of non-connection, or the cognition of the absence of the cognition of non-connection, or the state of being devoid of the property that delimits the counter-correlativity of non-connection, or the cognition of that state of being devoid of it.

And that is incorrect; for since validity is established by the necessary quality of being faultless alone, there is no need for [the following]: its being pervaded by relation (*saṃsarga-vyāpyatva*), the absence of a valid cognition of the absence of relation (*saṃsargābhāva-pramā-viraha*), the valid cognition of that [absence], or the absence of the property that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-dharma-śūnyatva*) of the absence of relation, or the valid cognition thereof.
Alternatively, there is excessive complexity (*atigaurava*) in postulating [the absence of defects] as a quality (*guṇa*).
For, when defectlessness is present, no absence of verbal valid cognition is observed apart from those two [defects and their absences], or apart from the cognitions of them.

[Regarding the statement] "fire-ness and so forth": because the property of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absolute absence residing in sprinkling—which has the relation of connection (*saṃsarga*) with fire as its locus—is based on properties such as fire-ness, it is said that "fire-ness and so forth" [are the delimitors].
They also say that the phrase "delimiters of counter-correlativity" (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) means "delimiters of locusness" (adhikaraṇatāvacchedaka).
He states "or the absence of the cognition of non-connection," etc., in accordance with the two previously mentioned alternatives: "fitness" (yogyatā) or "the cognition thereof" (tatpramā).
"By means of what is necessary."
The intended meaning is that the absence of the aforementioned valid cognition (pramā) and so forth is possible precisely through the faultlessness of the sentence.
The phrase "of that which pervades the connection" (*saṃsargavyāpyasya*) is an adjective qualifying that absence of valid cognition.

Now, one might object: "Since it is impossible to abandon the causal status of those two [the absence of defects and the absence of valid cognition], which is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just as it is for faultlessness. To this, he says:
"Indeed not."
"Of those two."
The meaning is: [the absence of the property of being devoid of the aforementioned form of valid cognition and the absence of the property of emptiness].
Even in the case of the speech of a parrot and the like, which is non-concordant with reality, faultlessness is not established;
for even in the absence of defects such as delusion and so forth, there is another [factor].

The sense is that it must be postulated for someone [as the cause]. He says, "And not verbal," because that [the Veda] is postulated solely on the grounds that its production by [human] qualities would otherwise be inexplicable.
"Even now," it says.
The meaning is: "even at the time of conceptualizing the qualities that follow [the object]."
(Pradīpa-prasū-pratyeta-guṇaḥ) The Theory of Validity (prāmāṇyavāda), p.
183. Furthermore, it has not yet been established that verbal cognition (śābdapramā) is produced by a causal excellence (guṇa).
By which [reason] the quality of being a *guṇa* (excellence) is postulated for those two, or for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that produce them, in order to bring about that [result].

Furthermore, even in the case of perception and other means of knowledge, since there exists— concomitant with the existence of the object— the absence of valid cognition due to the non-existence of the object and so forth, that very [absence] would have to be the "excellence" (guṇa).

If it is argued that it is improper to state that the contact between sense-faculties and supersensible objects, etc., constitutes an excellence, because there is no evidence for its being a producer of cognition despite its existence there, then the same applies to the present case as well.

Even if this [ocular defect] were not a valid cognition (*apramā*), the valid cognition of the absence of the object—which is invariably concomitant with the non-existence of the object—or the possession of a property that delimits the non-existence of the object, would constitute the defect in those two [types of cognition]; however, glass and the like would not.

He states "furthermore" (*kiñca*) to show the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that results from postulating causality even in the absence of independent positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

By the phrase "due to the absence of valid cognition" (*pramāvirahādeḥ*), the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes both the absence of the property that delimits that valid cognition and the absence of that valid cognition itself—this refers to "contact" (*sannikarṣādeḥ*).
The meaning of the word "etc. is the consideration of a correct logical mark (*salliṅgaparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, it is as follows: "Moreover, in this way" (*apicaivam*).

The meaning is that "guṇatva" (the state of being a quality) is that which is inseparable from the non-existence of the object; that is, "inseparable from the non-existence of the object" is a qualifier of the valid cognition (*pramā*) of the absence of the object.
The meaning is "the state of being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of that valid cognition"—this refers to the phrase "of those two."

The meaning is: "between the state of being the object of a valid cognition of the non-existence of the object and the state of possessing a property that delimits the non-existence [of that object]"—but not, as it were, [in the sense of being identical].
Furthermore, in that case, the statement by Maṇi and others—that glass and the like are defects (*doṣa*) in the context of error—would be untenable;
moreover, there would be a contradiction with their positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). This is the intended meaning.
Furthermore,
if verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*)— which is a valid cognition of relation (*saṃsarga-pramā*)— were necessarily produced by a cognition pervaded by the relation, it would be an inference (*anumiti*).

Furthermore, if the *guṇa* (excellence) is held to be either the absence of a cognition of non-relation (*asaṃsargapramāviraha*) or the cognition of the absence of a cognition of non-relation (*asaṃsargapramāvirahapramā*), then in cases such as "one should sprinkle with fire," there would be a cognition of relation for the listener even at a time when there is an absence of a cognition of relation.

Now, one might object: "Since a defect (*doṣa*) is a cognition of a property that is invariably concomitant with the non-existence of the object, how can it be a defect given that it contradicts the illusion of the object's existence? To this, he states another objection against the position that the *guṇa* is a cognition of a relation-pervaded [property], namely: "Moreover, the verbal cognition of a relation... [is the issue].
The intended meaning is that it is like a valid cognition [arising] from the conjunction of a mountain with fire, and so forth.
If it is objected that, like a perceptual cognition following a doubt, even that which is produced by the knowledge of the pervaded (vyāpyadhī) is not of the nature of inference, we say no.
In that case, [the inferential cognition] lacks the status of having a pervasion-cognition as its cause because it possesses a stronger means of production (balavat-pratyakṣa-kārakatva).
Furthermore, if it were invariably produced by a pervasion-cognition here, it would follow that it has that [pervasion-cognition] as its cause;
for even inference from the consideration of the middle term (parāmarśa) is not stronger than the causal complex of perception (pratyakṣa-sāmagrī).
Nor is it the case that [the cognition] lacks the nature of an inference because it is not produced by a cognition having "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) as its qualifier;
for if it were necessarily produced by such a cognition, it would possess that very nature,
since its being produced by that [cognition] is inevitable.

Otherwise, even by virtue of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) and so forth, that knowledge would incur the status of being a quality (*guṇatva*) of its corresponding valid cognition (*tatpramā*).
This is because, compared to [the property of] being a valid cognition of the absence of the non-connection [of the qualifier with the qualificand],
the property of being a valid cognition that is pervaded by connection (*saṃsargavyāpyatvapramātva*) is simpler (*laghutvāt*).
The point is this: because causality has been established for it in another form;

and because the status of being a cause—by way of being the absence of the cognition of non-relation (*asaṃsarga-pramā*) or by way of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*)—depends upon the proof that valid cognition is produced by a quality (*guṇa*), which would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Having rejected the position that "a quality is a valid cognition pervaded by relation," he states the flaw in the position that "the absence of the cognition of non-relation is the quality" with the words: "Furthermore, the absence of non-relation... (*kiñcāsaṃsarga...*)

In some places, however, there is also the reading: "or the cognition of the absence of non-contact [or] the cognition of the absence of valid cognition. (Note: Variants include *bdīyasaṃ* for *bdīya-saṃ*; *nanvayapramāvirahadaśāyām* for *nanvayapramāvirahadaśāyām*; *bhramā-* for *bhramā-*; the word *rūpa* is omitted in one manuscript; this section of the text is missing in another; and *yā* for *yā*.)
(Pradīpa-prasū-pratyeta-guṇaḥ) Pramāṇyavāda, p. 185.

Nor should it be argued that even when the listener lacks that [knowledge], there exists for God a valid cognition (*pramā*) of non-connection, and that [cognition] acts as an obstacle to the listener’s valid cognition of connection.
For if that were the case, it would be impossible to abandon the ancient doctrine that for God, the truth of the meaning of his words is a quality (*guṇa*).
Furthermore, the cognition of the Lord (*īśvara*) as being non-concomitant (*ananvaya*) cannot, first of all, act as an impediment by making known the non-existence of its object;

for it is impossible for a cognition residing in the Lord—which is established as existing in its own nature (*svarūpasatya*)—to make known that [non-existence] to a listener, as they would be in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Nor can it be made known by that [cognition] when it is known as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Even though the manifestation (*utthiti*) is the cause for activity directed toward the object standing before one, since this would entail that the knowledge of the qualifier-qualificand relation (*vaiśiṣṭyajñāna*) is also a cause, the view that non-apprehension of difference is the cause of activity would be abandoned; therefore, the meaning is that its status as a delimiting factor of causality (*hetutāvacchedakatva*) is exactly like that [of the manifestation].
He states [this] according to the Nyāya school: "by way of being an object."
"In this context, it is perception."
This means that such is the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The theory of validity (prāmāṇyavāda), p. 205:
[This is] because it would involve the conceptual complexity (gaurava) of postulating both the absence of defects as the cause and the delimiting condition of that causality;

and furthermore, because there is a deviation in negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra) regarding general validity, since validity is observed even when a defect is present according to the aforementioned reasoning.

For it is stated in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇayaṭīkā*: “The absence of defects is also not the cause of validity, because valid knowledge arises even when a defect is present in cases of accidental correspondence.”

Furthermore, it has been stated that since in common worldly usage there is no treatment as a cause when an obstacle is absent, "otherness" (anyathāsiddhi) should be defined as something distinct—namely, the state of being an adversary that subverts the operation of a cause in its default effect-producing capacity.
Having stated the "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhi*) fallacy, he states the "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) as well: "It has been said," etc.

Furthermore, the meaning is according to the method stated in the passage beginning with, "Moreover, [the cognition] produced by the error of [seeing] feet and so forth in what is actually hands and so forth."

[Objection: Since a defect acts as an impediment, the positive and negative concomitance of its absence with the effect must be independent; therefore, the "otherwise-established" status (anyathāsiddhi) mentioned previously is not tenable. To this, he says: "Furthermore... (kiñca).

The meaning is that you have previously been defeated by the argument that, having abandoned the etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*) of the word *anyathāsiddha*, you have instead provided a threefold technical definition (*paribhāṣikārtha*) in accordance with worldly usage; therefore, here too, in accordance with usage, you should define "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) as something other than the three types of *anyathāsiddhi* stated by you.
This is what is meant by the phrase "for it has been said."

The meaning is that the claim that the absence of defects cannot be considered a cause because it is established otherwise has been stated in the *Sudhā* commentary on the verse beginning with "And its validity is like perception" (*pratyakṣavacca prāmāṇyam*) in the *Jijñāsādhikaraṇa*.

1. *tadavacche-ka-kha-cha*. 2. *mājñā-kuṃ*. 3. *virahatārū-ka-khṛcha*. 4. The phrase “*ityuktam*” does not appear in *cha-kha*. It has indeed been stated in the *Sudhā*: “If it is argued that ‘in that case, the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*) must be the cause,’ we say no.”
For if that were the case, it would follow that there could never be any general rules or exceptions whatsoever.
Nor should it be suspected that there is a contradiction between this commentary (*bhāṣya*) and the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā* (Sudhā) or the *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā*.

This is because, in the *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, the term "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is intended solely in the sense we have stated: namely, being the counter-positive of an absence whose occurrence is conditioned by the absence [of the effect], which is common to the potter, the father, and so forth, with respect to a jar.

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). The meaning is that it was stated in the *Vādāvalī*: “If it is argued, ‘Since validity is necessarily concomitant with the absence of defects, why should its extrinsic nature (*paratastva*) not be established?’—we say no; because even in cases of accidental correspondence (*yādṛcchika-saṃvāda*), the causal status [of the absence of defects] is undermined by the absence of the absence of defects. The meaning of the passage beginning with “utsarga,” however, should be understood as already explained by the preceding text beginning with “the causality of that which is opposed to burning” (*dāhavirōdhino hetutva*), according to the *Bhāṣya-ṭīkā*.
The meaning is "of that which was previously mentioned"—namely, by means of the *sudhā* (nectar).
It should also be understood as "and by means of the *vādāvalī* (the series of arguments)"—that is, by means of its distinction (*tadvyatireka*).

The meaning is that the nature of being a causal factor (*prayojakatva*) for validity consists in its being the counter-positive of an absence that is itself conditioned by the absence of defects. The resulting meaning is that the nature of being a causal factor consists in having an effect whose absence is conditioned by its own absence. For it has been said: 1. *doṣābhāvavyatirekaprayuktavyatirekapratiyogitvaṃ prāmāṇyasya yattadrūpaṃ prayojakatvam* 2.
*sviviraprayuktavirahapratiyogikāryakatvarūpaṃ yatprayojakatvam iti phalitorthaḥ* 3. *uktaṃ hi* (Note: The numbers refer to the original text's enumeration.)
The meaning is that in the *Vārttika*, the status of the absence of defects as a causal factor (*prayojakatva*) has been stated in the aforementioned manner.
"Due to the absence of those" means due to the absence of defects which are dependent upon excellences (*guṇa*).

The absence of that twofold lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*)—which consists either in non-cognitiveness or in erroneous cognitiveness, and [furthermore] consists either in erroneous cognitiveness or in non-performance—is what is meant.
The meaning is that, by the removal of the absence of defects— which serves as a counter-exception to invalidity—
the general rule (utsarga) that valid cognition arises from the causal complex of knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*) alone remains unbroken.
(Prayāṃ-dobhāsya-heṅgaḥ) *Prāmāṇyavāda*, p. 207:

“Therefore, from excellences (*guṇa*) follows the absence of defects (*doṣa*); from their absence follows the absence of the two forms of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). Thus, the natural validity (*utsarga*) is not sublated.”
Thus—it may be asked: how then can a defect (doṣa) also function as an impediment?
For even when that [defect] is present, valid cognition (pramā) is observed in that very same case. If this is argued, we say no.
This is because there is an absence of the obstructor— which is qualified by the absence of an excitant— due to the presence of an accidental objective entity acting as that excitant.
Nor should it be argued that, because it is necessary, the mere existence of the object (*viṣayasattva*) alone is the cause of valid cognition (*pramā*), and not the absence of defects;

for at the time of the error of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, even though the object—namely, the "shell-ness" (*śuktitva*) and so on—is present, there is an absence of the valid cognition of "shell-ness" due to the obstruction caused by the defect.

Alternatively, just as in cases such as "Do not burn this," where there is a specific individual intended by the mantra, it is precisely in those instances where there is an absence of the existence of the object of a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*) that [the absence of the defect] acts as a preventer. In a situation where the existence of the object is merely accidental, there is simply the absence of a preventer. However, if the absence of defects were a cause in its own right (*svarūpeṇa*), then a deviation in negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyabhicāra*) would be difficult to avoid; therefore, the absence of defects is not a cause.

With the thought that the "otherwise-accomplished" (anyathāsiddhi) consisting in being the opposite of the previously mentioned obstructer is untenable, the following objection is raised: "But surely... (nanu).
Regarding that: "therein."
The meaning is that it is concordant by mere coincidence.
The meaning is that there would be this fault: "May he not burn."
Its validity should be understood as stated in the *Saṃśayopapādavana* section of the *Grantha*: namely, that there is a deviation in the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyabhicāra*).
The meaning is that it is "coincidental" (*yādṛcchika*). Therefore—[from this]... [End of fragment].

Therefore, there is no proof whatsoever for the view that [knowledge] arises from another.

This has also been stated by the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth. The meaning is that if even the absence of defects— which consists in the removal of exceptions to a general rule (*utsarga*)— were to serve as a logical reason (*hetu*), it would be impossible to establish the distinction between what is a general rule and what is an exception.
The refutation of the view that the absence of defects is a cause for valid cognition (pramā).
This means that because there is no such thing as a recurring positive quality (guṇa), and because the absence of defects is not a cause [for valid cognition].

The Refutation of the Causal Role of the Absence of Defects in Valid Cognition // 15 // Regarding the view that validity is intrinsic (*svatastva*), in the position that there exists a quality (*guṇa*) which accompanies all non-eternal valid cognitions, the state of being a non-eternal true cognition is the delimiting factor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) that is not delimited by the state of being a non-eternal cognition. [Commentary on the phrase] "Regarding the view that validity is intrinsic": [This refers to the following: In the theory of intrinsic validity, it is held that there is a specific excellence (*guṇa*) inherent in every instance of non-eternal valid knowledge. Consequently, the property of being a non-eternal true cognition serves as the defining characteristic of the effect, without being restricted merely by the general property of being a non-eternal cognition. This implies that while the mere nature of being a non-eternal cognition is common to both true and false cognitions, the status of being a true cognition requires the additional presence of a causal excellence (*guṇa*). Thus, the property of being a non-eternal true cognition is the specific determinant for the production of such a result, rather than being subsumed under the broader category of non-eternal cognition.
The term "māna" (means of valid cognition) is carried over [from the previous context];
the meaning is that it is "stated.

The phrase "in the case of the alternative of qualities not being included" is stated for the sake of discernment, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

He states a counter-inference against the inference formulated in the *Maṇi*: "The property of being non-eternal invalidity (*anityāprāmāṇya*) is the delimitant of an effectness that is the counter-correlate of a causality distinct from the causality whose counter-correlate is an effectness delimited by non-eternal cognition-ness; because it is a property that delimits an effectness pervaded by non-eternal cognition-ness, like [the property of] invalidity. This is expressed as: "anitya... etc.

The qualification "non-eternal" (*anitya*) is applied to the subject (*pakṣa*) in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since the mere qualificand (*viśeṣya*) exists eternally and could thus serve as the delimiting property of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*).
The mention of "corresponding to reality" (*yathārtha*) serves the same purpose of avoiding that fallacy.

Regarding the arguments for intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) at the time of origination: [validity] is like "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*), because it is devoid of the absence of occurrence in non-eternal cognitions.

Because it is constituted by a property that is invariably concomitant with it, whatever is thus is so; for example, being-a-pot (*ghaṭatva*), which is constituted by the form of having a broad base and belly, is not the delimitor of the effectness that is not delimited by potness.

The qualification "impermanent" in the subject (*pakṣa*) is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), [namely] by way of [the probandum] not being the delimitor of the effectness residing in eternal cognition.
The mention of "as-it-is" (*yathārtha*) is likewise solely for the purpose of avoiding that same fallacy.

The qualification "of an eternal [entity]" (*anitya*) and so forth is applied to the property of being an effect (*kāryatā*) in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), [namely] that the property of being an effect residing in an eternal cognition (*jñāna*) does not have [eternality] as its delimiting factor (*anavacchedaka*).
The phrase "residing in valid cognition" (*pramāniṣṭha*) should also be added [to the definition].
By this, there is no *siddhasādhana* because the property of being an effect residing in a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth does not have [eternality] as its delimiting factor.

The two negative particles (*nañ*) in the reason—such as "being a sense-organ" (*indriyatva*) and so forth—are intended to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) and the like, which serve as the delimiters of the effectness (*kāryatā*) that is counter-correlative to the causality residing in the sense-organs.
This is because, in those cases, there is also the presence of "subsisting in non-eternal cognition," and thus the absence of that [subsistence] does not obtain.
The mention of "non-eternal cognition" (*anityajñāna*) is also stated precisely for the sake of removing the aforementioned fault.
The term "impermanent" (*anitya*) is used to exclude the charge of unestablished reason (*asiddhi*), [the example being] "like cognition-ness" (*jñānatva-vat*).

The intended meaning is that because [cognition-ness] exists eternally, it cannot be a delimiting factor for being an effect (*kāryatānavacchedakatva*), and yet it does reside in impermanent cognitions. Thus, [the property] is "similar to that" (*tatsama*).

The meaning is that it is because it is constituted by that property which is co-extensive with the state of being a means of knowledge for the impermanent—namely, the state of being a cognition of the impermanent.

The point is that even in the case of an error (*bhrama*), within the objective aspect (*dharmyaṃśa*), there exists a mutual relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the state of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*) and the state of being an impermanent valid cognition (*anityapramātva*) or the state of being an impermanent cognition (*anityajñānatva*).

For this very reason, in order to highlight that [the definition] is composed of properties co-extensive with that [state], the author did not designate the subject as "the state of being an impermanent valid cognition" (*anityapramātva*), but rather stated it as "the state of being an impermanent true cognition" (*anityayathārthajñānatva*)—as expressed by the words "that which is thus" (*yadevam*).

The meaning is that whatever is constituted by a property that is co-extensive (samaniyata) with another, that [latter] is the delimitor of the effect-ness (kāryatāvacchedaka) of that [former] without being itself delimited—this is illustrated by the term "pṛthubudhna" (broad-based).
The property of being a pot (*ghaṭatva*), which has the form of a broad base and belly, is a name-property (*nāmadharma*).

Because it is constituted by the property of potness which is restricted to its own [substratum], the effectness residing in cloth and so forth—which is not delimited by that [potness]—is not delimited by it; such is the meaning.
