Alternatively, [the property in question] is not the delimitor of the effect-ness of residing in error, because it resides in error, like the nature of being an error (bhrāntatva).
Nor is there a lack of proof for those reasons,
because even in the case of an error, validity exists with respect to the objective aspect (dharmyaṃśa),
and because validity is constituted by the nature of being a cognition (jñānatva).
Nor is there a lack of probative force;

for when it is necessary that only one of two co-extensive properties serves as the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), it is more appropriate—by the natural inclination of the evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of parsimony—that the lighter property, namely "non-eternal cognition-ness" (*anityajñānatva*), be so designated.

In the case of error (*bhrama*), since the properties of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) and being a valid cognition (*pramātva*) are both either pervasively present (*vyāpyavṛtti*) or non-pervasively present (*avyāpyavṛtti*), it is logical—even if they are produced by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*)—that they coexist [in the same locus], just as velocity (*vega*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) do in your own view.
He states another probandum (*sādhyāntara*) while still indicating the previous position: "not occurring in error" (*bhramāvṛtti*).

The meaning is as follows: "being an effect residing in error" refers to the state of being an effect (kāryatā) that resides in valid cognition (pramā), while "that which does not delimit it" means that which is not the delimitor of such an effect-ness.

The probandum is that "the state of being a non-eternal true cognition" is not the delimitor of the effect-ness residing in such a cognition. Thus, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of "non-eternal cognition" as the cause; for that [non-eternal cognition] is indeed the delimitor of the effect-ness defined by causes such as the contact between the self and the mind (ātmamanaḥ-saṃyoga).
And because it occurs in error, it is stated as "not occurring in error.
Furthermore, there is no fault, since the property of being non-eternal cognition is not a delimitor of the effect-ness residing in such things as jars; thus, [the phrase] "nor of these" is used.
The meaning is "of the three.

By the phrase "even in the case of error," the refutation of the [objection regarding] the non-establishment of the beginning and the end is provided—namely, that of the status of being a valid cognition (*pramātva*).
The meaning is that the property of being a means of valid cognition for the impermanent is constituted by the property of being a cognition of the impermanent.

Alternatively, since it is established as a matter of fact that if validity (*pramātva*) is constituted by "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*), then non-eternal validity must be constituted by "non-eternal cognition-ness," the term "of validity" (*pramātvasya*) alone was used [in the original], meaning "of that which is simpler" (*laghunaḥ*).
The sense is that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is cumbersome because it is constituted by the existence of the object (*viṣayasattva*).

however, in my view, it is appropriate that its absence occurs because of the presence of a defect that subverts the validity of the cognitive factor.

Invalidity (*anityapramātva*) is the delimiting property of the effect-ness that stands in the relation of being counter-correlative to a cause delimited by a property residing in what is opposed to defects (*doṣa*), because it resides in what is produced by defects,
like erroneousness (*bhramatva*).
Since that which is opposed to defects consists of both excellences (*guṇa*) and the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*), the self-validity (*svatastva*) [of knowledge] is established.

He states a counter-inference to that which was asserted by the *Maṇi*: "The nature of non-eternal valid cognition (*anityapramātva*) is the delimitor of the effectness that has as its counter-correlative a causality delimited by a form which is the delimitor of the causality of the cause of invalid cognition; because it is a delimitor of effectness that does not reside in error, like potness. [In this context], "defect" (*doṣa*) refers to bile (*pitta*) and so forth.
The property of being a state opposed to that [valid cognition] consists in the nature of being a quality (*guṇatva*) and so forth; the meaning is "delimited by that.
The rebuttal of the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the reason—namely, "because it is a state produced by a defect" (*doṣajanyavṛttitvāt*)—is as explained previously.

Now, one might object: even if the aforementioned inference establishes that a quality (*guṇa*) which is the opposite of a defect (*doṣa*) is the cause [of validity], it does not preclude the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*) from being a cause as well; thus, since validity (*prāmāṇya*) would be produced by more than just the causes of cognition, its status as being produced solely by the causes of cognition would be undermined. To this, he says: "the opposite of a defect" (*doṣavirodhī*).

The commonality between the two [types of opposition] is either the state of being unable to coexist (*saha-anavasthāna*) or the state of being the object of a certainty that obstructs the certainty [of its opposite].
And the meaning is that the nature of being an obstructor (*pratibandhakatva*) consists in being pervaded by the non-arising of that [opposite].

Section 212:
Invalidity is not delimited by being an effect,
because there is a subverting argument against such being the case.
It is like the nature of the cognition of a jar;
nor is there a lack of proof, because an opposing argument has been stated in the form of the absence of a recurring cause.

On the view that there are distinct excellences (*guṇa*) inherent in each individual means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, the property of being a valid perception that is non-eternal is not the delimitor of being produced by an object,
nor is it the delimitor of being produced by any one of the six types of contact;
for [the former] subsists in what is not produced by those [excellences].
It is like potness (*ghaṭatva*). Nor is it non-existent,
because it is produced by one of the six types of contact with its object, such as the direct perception of a yogin.

He states a counter-inference against what was said in the *Maṇi*: "The state of being a non-eternal valid cognition (*anityapramātva*) is the delimiting property of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), because—provided there is no subverting evidence—it is a property residing in all effects, just like the state of being an invalid cognition (*apramātva*). This is expressed as:
"The state of being a non-eternal valid cognition... and so forth.

In this and the preceding case, the qualification "non-eternal" is applied to the nature of validity (*prāmāṇya*) in order to exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*); such being the case.
The meaning is "the state of being a delimitor of effect-ness"—this refers to the phrase "due to an obstructing factor" (*bādhaka*).

The meaning is: "because of possessing an obstructing factor in the form of the impossibility of a single cause residing in that which possesses the counter-correlativity of an effect delimited by itself"—as in the case of a jar (*ghaṭa*).

The meaning is that it has been established above that "pot-cognition-ness" is not a delimiting factor (avacchedaka), because there is no common cause (anugata-kāraṇa) for all instances of the cognition of a pot; this is because it has already been stated.
The meaning is: "the refutation of the quality that accompanies every valid cognition"—this is the position.
It should be construed as: "contradictory inference is being stated."
Adopting the position that "being an object" (*viṣayatva*) is the quality (*guṇa*), he says: "Not by being an object.
Adopting the position that "contact with the sense organs" (*indriya-sannikarṣa*) is the quality, he says: "Not by the sixfold [contact]."
"Other than that."
The meaning is "any one of them.
One should keep in mind that its validity was stated previously;
he merely reminds us of what has already been established—namely, [the validity] of yogic perception and so forth.
The category of "pramā" and so forth consists of those things whose perception arises from the perception of a universal (*sāmānya*).

The theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*): [Thesis 1] The state of being a valid inference (*anumitipramātva*) is the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) relative to the cause-ness (*kāraṇatā*) delimited by the state of being a correct consideration of the middle term (*satyaliṅgaparāmarśatva*), because it resides in what is produced by an incorrect consideration of the middle term (*asatyaliṅgaparāmarśajanyavṛttitvāt*) and because it is an error (*bhramatvāt*). [Thesis 2] The state of being a valid verbal cognition (*śābdapramātva*) is not the delimitor of the effect-ness relative to the cause-ness delimited by the state of being a knowledge of the reality of the intended object (*vivakṣitārthatatvajñānatvāvacchinnakāraṇatāpratiyogikakāryatānavacchedakaṃ*), because it resides in what is not produced by a knowledge of the reality of the intended object (*vivakṣitārthatatvajñānājanyavṛttitvāt*) and because it is an error (*bhramatvāt*).

Nor should it be argued that, because it is necessary, the mere existence of the object (*viṣayasattva*) alone is the cause of valid cognition (*pramā*), and not the requirement for the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*);

for at the time of the error of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, even though the object—namely, the "shell-ness" (*śuktitva*) and so forth—is present, there is an absence of the valid cognition of "shell-ness" due to the obstruction caused by the defect.

The validity of perception of impermanence (*anityapratyakṣapramātva*), the validity of inference (*anumitipramātva*), and the validity of verbal testimony (*śābdapramātva*) are not the delimiters of the effectness (*kāryatā*) that is counter-correlative to a causality delimited by a property residing in what is opposed to defects (*doṣa*), because they reside in what is produced by defects, like erroneousness (*bhramatva*). (3) "By either one... [as stated in the commentary].
The meaning is "by one or another.
Since inferential and verbal cognitions are also not produced by a *guṇa*, he states [the definition] for inference in sequence with the words beginning "anumiti" (inferential cognition).
According to the view that the knowledge of the reality of the intended meaning is a merit (guṇa), he says: "The intended... and so forth.
Having stated [the arguments] individually, he says "pratyakṣa... in order to show that even when combined, they lack the capacity to prove the absence of defects.
"An antidote to the defects."
The meaning is that since that quality is the absence of defects, the self-validity [of cognition] is established; [the opponent's objection that it is] "unestablished" is thus refuted.

The meaning is: "of the reasons already stated. [Note: The phrase *satyaliṅgaparāmarśajanyavṛttitvāt* is also present in the Kuṇḍalita version; this portion of the text is absent in the Kuṇḍalita, Cha, Ga, and Kha versions; it is also absent from the middle of the Ka version. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 214) [End of section]
Nor is there a lack of proof [for our position],
because the quality of being a valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) exists in the cognition of a person produced by the error of [mistaking] a hand for a foot and so forth.
A cognition of fitness that is not in accordance with reality does not produce verbal valid cognition (*śābdapramā*).
Because [the reason] is not the counter-positive of an absence whose locus is the occasioning factor for producing the exclusion of that [quality],
like the prior absence of taste in the case of odor produced by cooking.

[This is stated] in order to refute the charge of "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) against the second reason, following the previous text beginning with "in the part of the subject (*dharmyaṃśa*)" regarding the cognition produced by the speech of a parrot or similar beings that is consistent [with reality].

And since, in the case of a cognition produced by a sentence whose mode is erroneous, [the object] is established as existing according to the previously mentioned direction, he clarifies that first [point]—he says "karoti" (it produces).

Nor should it be suspected that there is a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) because even the cognition produced from the words of Śuka and others possesses the quality of being generated by such a divine cognition;

for it has already been stated that while His [the Lord's] cognition acts as a cause by virtue of being a cognition whose object is the material cause and so forth—common to both error and truth—it does not act as a cause in the specific form of a cognition of the reality of the intended meaning, which is what is intended here.
According to the view that the knowledge of fitness (*yogyatājñāna*) is a quality (*guṇa*), he says: "as it truly is" (*yathārtha*).

And the meaning is that "fitness" (yogyatā) is either the existence of the relation that constitutes the sentence-meaning, or something else pervaded by that [existence], according to the direction previously stated—this is indicated by the word "tat" (that).
The meaning is: that which is the cause (nimitta) for bringing about the exclusion of verbal valid cognition (śābdapramā), and the object of that bringing about (āpādana).
The manner of this bringing about will be made clear later—namely, "produced by cooking" (pākaja).

In that regard, if the prior absence of taste (*rasaprāgabhāva*) did not exist, then odor would not exist; however, this is not the case. Since the prior absence of taste is asserted to be the cause, it is "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*) by virtue of its association with the prior absence of odor, which has already been postulated as the cause according to the method stated by Maṇi. Consequently, it lacks the capacity to bring about the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of odor, and for this very reason, it is not the producer of it.
The state [of being]—according to the manner described above.

The meaning is that, according to the method already stated, there is a refutation of the persistence of a quality (guṇa) in perception and other [means of knowledge]. [Note: The variants indicate that the word "ca" is absent in manuscript Kuṃ; that the phrase "because of the absence of being a producer" is present in manuscripts Mu and A; and that the phrase "as the object of the reductio ad absurdum" is additionally present in manuscript A. [End of section]—In the case of intrinsic validity (svatastva)—inference.
Regarding the theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*), page 215:
Nor is there a lack of proof [for our position].

For, according to the method already stated, since verbal cognition (*śābdapramā*) is established by the mere absence of a certainty regarding non-connection when compatibility (*yogyatā*) exists in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), if there were no knowledge of compatibility that accords with reality (*yathārthayogyatājñāna*), then there would be no verbal valid cognition (*śābdī pramā*).
Because it is impossible to raise the objection that [the result] would not exist.
Regarding the term "yajñapati" (lord of the sacrifice):

For in that view, having accepted that the extrinsic nature (*paratastva*) of truth consists precisely in the property of residing only in that which is the locus of the effect as delimited by a property residing only in its own substratum, it is stated that this is established even by being produced by non-uniform qualities (*ananugata-guṇa*).

Then, the following inference is stated: "The truth of an impermanent [cognition] resides only in that which is the locus of the effect as delimited by a property residing only in its own substratum," and so forth.
He states a counter-inference against that: "impermanent... [etc.].
The term "impermanent" is stated in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established.

"Of its own" (svasya): the meaning is that [the property] such as perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*), which resides merely in the locus of its own non-eternal truthfulness (*anityapramātva*), has a causal nature (*kāryatā*) delimited by that [property]; and that [causal nature], while residing in various instances—that is, residing in multiple loci—does not reside merely in the locus of that [causal nature]. Here, the first occurrence of the word "merely" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of avoiding a contradiction, because [the property] exists only in the locus of a causal nature delimited by "non-eternal cognition-ness" (*anityajñānatva*), which resides in a domain larger than itself, namely the locus of non-eternal truthfulness.
The second [definition] is also for the sake of excluding that very [fault].

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of a contradiction (*bādha*), because the property of being an impermanent valid cognition (*anityapramātva*) would reside in the locus of the effect delimited by such properties as perceptuality, inferentiality, and visual-cognisability.

Here, since the property of being an impermanent valid cognition exists only in that which is the locus of the effect co-located with properties such as perceptuality that reside solely in its own substratum, it lacks residence in that [other locus]; thus, the probandum (*sādhya*) is established.

Because it is sublated. [Notes on variants: 1. "Atre" is not present in manuscripts Mu, Ca, and Kha. 2. [Variant] Śa and Cha. 3. "Yapra" in Ka and Kuṃ. 4. "Tyabhipre" in A. 5. "Tre vṛttidharma" in Mu. 6. "Yā" is not present in Kuṃ. 7. "Vartinā" in Mu. 8. "Eva" is not present in Kuṃ. *Tarkatāṇḍava* with *Nyāyadīpa* (First Chapter, p. 216). [End of section] The term "vṛtti" (function/operation) here refers to the operation of a word; its property (*dharma*) is its capacity to denote a meaning. Since that property does not exist in the case of a non-existent object (*asat*), the cognition of such an object would be baseless. Furthermore, if one were to claim that a word has the power to denote an absolute non-entity (*atyantābhāva*), that too is untenable, as it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that every word could denote anything at all. Therefore, the cognition of a non-existent object is necessarily sublated by the cognition of its existence. Thus, the opponent's position is refuted.

For one who holds the view that the Lord is the master of sacrifice (*yajñapati*), the state of being a non-eternal knower (*anityapramātva*) does not reside solely in that which possesses a causal nature (*kāryatā*) delimited by a property residing only in its own locus and occurring in multiple instances.
This is because it is a property whose limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the object alone,
just like the state of being the cognition of a jar (*ghaṭajñānatva*).

The point is that the conclusion regarding the probandum (sādhya) follows precisely from the absence of the status of being a delimitor (avacchedakatva) as postulated by the opponent in the case of the "truth" (pramātva) of produced perception and so forth. The term "sva" (itself) refers to that which is co-uttered [in the same sentence].
Therefore, in order to exclude deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of non-truth (apramātva), the reason (hetu) is qualified by the phrase "having as its only adjunct (upādhi) the object itself."

Although invalidity (*apramātva*) is a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) because it resides only in various effects that are delimited by various non-universal properties (*ananugata*) which serve as the delimiters of being produced by defects such as bile (*pitta*), there is no absence of the reason (*hetu*) since it is constituted by the object of error and its absence. Even if one were to say "conditioned by the object" (*viṣayopādhika*), the aforementioned defect would remain unchanged; therefore, the word "only" (*mātra*) is used.
The meaning of that [definition] is: being qualified by the object while not being qualified by anything other than it.
In this context, the sense to be understood is "being different from cognition and not being qualified by anything other than that.

By this, the proof that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is qualified by a cognition other than its own object is established; thus, there is no room for the objection that the illustrative example lacks the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*).

And the term "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to its own object. Therefore, in the case of "being either a jar or a cloth" (*ghaṭapaṭānyataratva*), the reason is the mere adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the jar and cloth that are the objects of the cognition. Since this [reason] exists only in that which is the locus of multiple instances of effecthood delimited by jar-ness and cloth-ness residing solely in their own substrata, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the probandum is absent [in such a locus].
Thus, there is no room for such doubt.

Alternatively, since the intention to treat [the object] as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) by virtue of being its object will be made clear later [in section 4], the word "itself" (*sva*) need not be supplied;
for by that much alone, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the aforementioned instance is excluded.
It is like the nature of the cognition of a jar.

In that case, because there is no delimitor of effectness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) that is pervaded by it, the probandum— in the form of the absence of residing solely in that which possesses an effectness delimited by a property residing solely in its own locus—
is present. Nor should it be suspected that even there, such things as "perception of a jar" or "inference of a jar" constitute a pervader of that [effectness].

Because there is no single, common cause corresponding to the effect-nature delimited by "being the perception of a jar" and so forth, [the property] "being the perception of a jar" and the like cannot serve as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). [End of section on intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) and its necessity.]
Regarding the discussion on validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*), p.

217: To dispel the doubt that there is a contradiction because [the probans] would be the locus of an effectness (*kāryatā*) defined by the respective prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*) of those [individual instances], it is stated that [the property] "subsists in many" (*nānāvṛtti*).
There is no lack of establishment (*asiddhi*) here.
Because validity has as its limiting adjunct (upādhi) merely the object [of cognition].
Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the status of being perceptual knowledge in the view that knowledge produced by an object is not perception;
for what is intended is that the object functions as a limiting adjunct (upādhi) by virtue of its being an object,
whereas in the case of perceptual knowledge, it functions as a limiting adjunct by virtue of being its producer.

However, since validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in having as its object an entity exactly as it exists, that [object] is taken as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) by virtue of being its object. Alternatively, let it be a delimitor (*avacchedaka*);
nevertheless, the point is that the cognition of a jar, which is common to the knowledge of God, does not reside in that [cognition] alone.

Now, one might ask: since the property of "occurring in various things" (*nānāvṛtti*) has not been stated by the opponent regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), for what purpose is this additional qualification of "being an effect" (*kāryatā*) employed? To this, he says: "That and that... (*tattad...*).

The delimitor of the effectness (kāryatāvacchedaka) qualified by the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of each specific instance of valid cognition (pramā) is the "being that specific instance of valid cognition" (tattatpramāvyaktitva).
And the effectness delimited by that [property] resides only in that specific individual instance, not in two instances.
Thus, if one were to prove the absence of that [effectness] on the grounds that it subsists only in the locus of such effectness, there would be a contradiction (bādha).

The point is that by the statement "existing in various substrates," only its being the effect of something other than those [substrates] is obtained; therefore, there is no contradiction when proving the absence of existence in merely those substrates.
Thus it is considered.
The meaning is that, according to the view [of some], the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) is "being produced by an object" (*viṣayajanyatva*); thus [it is said] "perception" (verse 5).

The point here is that, because [the reason] exists only as residing in various substrata delimited by properties such as being visually perceptible (*cākṣuṣatva*) or being tasted (*rāsanatva*), which are pervaded by itself, the property of having "having only the object as its limiting adjunct" (*viṣayamātropādhikadharmakatva*) exists in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

He states, "non-validity" (*apramātva*), etc., to show that even though non-validity is the locus of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the reason itself is absent there.

However, the "alterity of the object" (*viṣayānyathātva*), which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for invalidity (*apramātva*), is not the object of invalid cognition; thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding invalidity. 1. *vṛtti-ka*. 2. *nacā-cha*. 3. *patvetu-ka*. 4. *tvaṃ-kuṃ*. 5. *kṣajñāneti-mu*; *kṣajñānatveti-a*. 6. *vatvena-a*. 7. *syāsiddhatvāt-a*. *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 218). [End of section] The "alterity of the object," which constitutes the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for invalidity (*apramātva*), is not the object of that invalid cognition; therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to invalidity.
In the view that, just as in the case of a visual illusion caused by bile and so forth, the qualities (guṇas) are indeed the causes of valid cognition (pramā),

the property of being a valid cognition subsequent to doubt is not a delimitor of the effect-ness (kāryatā) whose counter-correlative is the causality delimited by the state of having a true perception of a distinguishing feature (viśeṣadarśana).

[The cognition following doubt] is not produced by the perception of a specific feature, because it possesses the property of being a mental state [produced by doubt], like [the cognition following doubt]. Furthermore, the valid cognition (pramā) that follows doubt is not produced by the perception of a specific feature,
because it can be accounted for even without that [perception], like an error (bhrama).
The lack of proof in this case has already been extracted [and refuted] above. Thus ends the view.
It should be understood that "contradictory inference" (virodhyanumāna) is stated as the proof for intrinsic validity (svatastva).

To the proponent who claims that in the case of a subsequent valid cognition following a doubt, the excellence (guṇa) consists in the cognition of a specific feature (viśeṣapramā), he replies with the words beginning "saṃśaya."

And this qualification is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). If it were stated simply that [the cognition] is not produced by the perception of a specific object subsequent to doubt, and if "like knowledge" (*jñānavat*) were given as the example, there would be a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in that case; therefore, the term "validity" (*pramātva*) is used therein. "Satya" means "corresponding to reality" (*yathārtha*).

The meaning is that it is because [the cognition] occurs in a valid cognition (*pramā*) that follows a doubt produced by a false and non-correspondent perception of specific features (*viśeṣadarśana*), such as the erroneous apprehension of a hand and so forth as being a foot and so forth.

Now, it might be objected that in every case of valid cognition following doubt, the knowledge of a specific feature is not the cause; rather, this occurs only in instances distinct from cases where a valid cognition follows a doubt produced by the error of taking a hand for a foot and so forth. Therefore, in accordance with that [objection], he says: "valid cognition following doubt."
"Even without that."
The meaning is: "because it is established even in the absence of defects"—thus [it is said] here.
The meaning is "in two types of causes"—referring to the word "previously" (*prāk*).

By means of the passages beginning with “‘arising from the error of [perceiving] feet etc. in the hands etc. and “‘thus, even in the case of a valid cognition following an error’,” the author shows that there is no failure of the non-uniformity of the quality (*guṇa*). This is the sense.
In the discussion on the intrinsic nature (*svatastva*) of validity, page 219:
Furthermore, the contact of the sense organ with many parts is not the uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*) of valid cognition.
Because it produces error,
like the contact of the mind [with the soul].
Valid cognition (*pramā*) is not produced by causes other than those common to both valid cognition and error.

[The cognition in question] has error as its nature, because it is not the counter-positive of an absence [of error], and because it lacks the conformity to the positive and negative concomitance of that [repeated contact] which is established otherwise; just like an error.
He states the inference that refutes the position that "the repeated contact of many parts with the sense organ" is a quality (*guṇa*), beginning with the word "bhūya" (repeated).

The point here is that the lack of proof [for the opponent's position] has already been established by the reasoning that [the opponent's argument] produces errors such as the perception of a yellow conch shell.
He states a counter-inference against the ancient inference—"valid cognition is produced by causes other than those of [ordinary] cognition"—with the words "pramā" (valid cognition).
The inclusion of additional causes is intended to mean both a quality (*guṇa*) and the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*).
Furthermore, the reason [stated as] "having an object that is the locus of error" (*bhramadharmika*) and so forth is also unestablished (*asiddhi*);
the sense is that this has already been refuted previously by the passage beginning with "even in error, there is valid cognition regarding the aspect of the locus" (*bhrame 'pi dharmyaṃśapramāyām*).

Even in the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), since absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), both validity (*pramātva*) and its absolute non-existence can exist within an error through a distinction of parts;

however, because mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) lacks non-pervasiveness, the mutual non-existence of validity is entirely absent in error. This is the intended meaning of the phrase "not otherwise" (*ananyathā*).
The point here is that there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*), because it has already been stated that the qualities (*guṇas*) serve the purpose of eliminating the opposing defects (*doṣas*).

In all these cases, it is the very destruction of the reason (*hetūcchitti*) that constitutes the sublation (*bādhaka*), and not [the mere absence of] a motive (*aprayojakatā*); this is the general direction.
This has also been stated by the words beginning with “otherwise” (*anyathā*).
The meaning is that the stated probanda cannot exist in the subject (pakṣa) without the stated reasons.

1. Inferences [proving] that validity arises from itself (svatastva) regarding its production. // 16 // The word "dig" (direction/indication) means: "Valid cognition is not produced by a quality (guṇa), because it possesses the nature of valid cognition (pramātva), like the valid cognition of God. One should infer similar arguments, such as:
"Valid cognition is not produced by something contrary to defects (doṣa), because it possesses the nature of valid cognition, like the valid cognition of God. This is the intended meaning.

Inference [establishing] that validity arises from itself (svatastva) regarding its production: Regarding invalidity (*apramā*), however, a defect (*doṣa*) is the cause, because it possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with it in a way that is not otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*).
Even when defects such as similarity (*sādṛśya*) and so forth exist in certain cases—

Now, one might object: "Since there is a deviation from the rule of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) regarding defects even in the case of error—just as there is for excellences (guṇa) in the case of valid cognition—and since the defect is otherwise accounted for by its exhaustion in the removal of excellences that oppose error, the defect is not the cause [of error]; therefore, error too would be intrinsic (svataḥ). To this, the author states that the defect is indeed the cause of error in the passage beginning with "But in the case of invalid cognition," in order to refute the aforementioned objection and establish that validity is extrinsic (parataḥ), as stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya* and other works. He does so by demonstrating that the defect is the cause of error. "But in the case of invalid cognition... [etc. [The full argument continues: However, in the case of invalid cognition, the positive and negative concomitance with the defect is unerring; it is not otherwise accounted for by its exhaustion in the removal of excellences that oppose error, because excellences are not present in invalid cognition. Therefore, the defect is the cause of invalid cognition, and thus invalid cognition is extrinsic. This is what is meant by the statement: "But in the case of invalid cognition, however, the positive and negative concomitance with the defect is unerring. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the word "but" (tu) is used to indicate a distinction between the two cases. It is not that the positive and negative concomitance with the defect is unerring only in invalid cognition; rather, it is also unerring in valid cognition with respect to excellences. If that [capacity for valid cognition] were innate, then the capacity to produce error would also be so.

If, by virtue of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with defects, the capacity to produce error is dependent upon defects, then, because it follows the presence of excellences (*guṇa*), the capacity to produce valid cognition (*pramā*) would likewise be dependent upon excellences. For if the excellences are otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*) as merely serving to eliminate opposing defects, then the defects are equally accounted for as merely serving to eliminate opposing excellences. Furthermore, if an instrument (*karaṇa*) accompanied by the absence of excellences produces error, then the invalidity of that instrument is extrinsic (*parataḥ*); and since an instrument accompanied by the absence of defects produces valid cognition, the production of valid cognition must likewise be extrinsic.
If it is argued that this might be the case—

that the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*) is merely a causal factor (*prayojaka*) and not the conferrer of the capacity to produce valid cognition (*pramā*), and that the same applies to the absence of excellences (*guṇābhāva*)— we say no.

This is because the entire collection of arguments stated for the intrinsic (*svataḥ*) and extrinsic (*parataḥ*) nature of the validity and invalidity of cognition must also be applied to the intrinsic and extrinsic nature of the validity and invalidity of the instrument (*karaṇa*).

He says "dig" (the direction/point) with the intention that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because, even in the absence of a consideration of excellence (*guṇa*) in the case of a state of practice (*abhyāsadaśā*), one experiences the cognition that [the means] produces valid knowledge; furthermore, it has been stated that in an error such as "the conch is yellow," although an excellence in the form of a perception of particulars (*viśeṣadarśana*) exists, the error is produced by a defect in the instrument (*karaṇadoṣa*) such as bile, and thus it is impossible for excellence to be exhausted merely by its removal.

The fact that the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice is a means to attain heaven is either the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the Veda or is established by a means of valid cognition other than human-authored speech—[as indicated by the following]: “Nor should it be said that there is no such thing as a non-human-authored sentence (*apauruṣeya-vākya*). Having stated the conclusion of the "residual method" (*pariśeṣa*) regarding universals as set forth in the *Jijñāsādhikaraṇasudhā*—beginning with "because it is a real entity" (*vastutvāt*) and so on—he first refutes the reason "due to the absence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāvāt*) by saying: "of the Jyotiṣṭoma... and so forth.

Since the lack of authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) is not established for the sentence that indicates that specific [particular] subject (*pakṣa*) when it is pointed out in this particular way, but rather for the Veda as a whole, he states the general subject as "the Veda" (*veda*).

Alternatively, the general statement "the object of the Veda's purport" (*vedatātparyaviṣaya*) is a presentation of the subject for the purpose of refuting the statement of the author of the *Maṇi* (Gadādhara), who says: "Or rather, whatever word is employed by a speaker with a particular intention, that word has that as its purport; thus, the fact that the object of a word employed by a speaker is determined by his intention constitutes the very nature of a word’s purport—and it is through this consideration of purport that the Veda possesses human authorship.
To refute this, there is the general indication of the subject as "the object of the Veda's purport."

Alternatively, with the intention that in this view the reason "because it possesses a means of valid cognition" has its constituent parts established by the reason "because it is a real entity" (vastutva) and so forth, he says: "Veda... and so on.
In order to exclude sublation regarding that which is to be established by the prima facie view, [the author] says: "by way of intention" (tātparya).
The word "Veda" is used to exclude sublation regarding the intended meaning of worldly speech.
Now, what indeed is this that is called "Veda"?
(1) If "Veda" is the referent of the word "Veda," then there would be a contradiction regarding the subject matter of the purport of the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*;

(2) Nor is the Veda that which has the primary sense of the word "Veda," because no basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*)— which would establish its primacy and distinguish it from works such as the *itihāsas*— can be determined.
(3) Nor is the Veda a collection of recensional branches (*śākhā*).

If it is argued that [the definition] would over-extend to the words of Śuka, Bālāki, and others which are consistent with reality, resulting in the fallacy of sublation (*bādhā*), and furthermore, that according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it would also over-extend to the *Mahābhārata* and other works composed by Vyāsa, who possesses eternal knowledge; [Response: This is not so. For, in the case of the words of Śuka and others, there is no sublation because they are in agreement with reality. Furthermore, regarding the *Mahābhārata* and similar texts, although they were composed by one possessing eternal knowledge, the definition does not apply because those works do not possess the nature of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) in the same sense as the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Moreover, the term "eternal" (*nitya*) is used here in the sense of being uncreated (*akṛtaka*), and since the *Mahābhārata* was created, it is excluded from the scope of the definition. Thus, there is no over-extension. Consequently, the definition is faultless. Therefore, it is established that the Veda is the sole means of valid cognition for Dharma. Hence, the statement that "Dharma is known through the Veda alone" is proven. Thus ends the section on the means of valid cognition for Dharma. Now begins the section on the refutation of the opponent's position (*parapakṣanirākaraṇa*). It has been stated: "Dharma is that which is beneficial and is characterized by the performance of sacrifice. Now, the following doubt arises: Is this Dharma to be understood through inference (*anumāna*) and other means of valid cognition, or is it to be understood solely through the Veda? To resolve this, the author first presents the view of the opponent: "Some say that Dharma is to be understood through inference and other means. The word "some" refers to the Mīmāṃsakas. They hold that Dharma is to be understood through inference and other means, and not through the Veda alone. Why? Because it is possible to infer Dharma through the observation of its effects. For instance, when one observes that a person who performs sacrifices such as the *Agniṣṭoma* attains prosperity, one infers that the sacrifice is the cause of that prosperity. Having thus inferred the causal relationship between the sacrifice and prosperity, one concludes that the sacrifice is indeed Dharma. Similarly, one may infer that abstaining from killing (*ahiṃsā*) is Dharma by observing that a person who practices non-violence attains happiness. Furthermore, one may infer that eating meat is non-Dharma by observing that a person who eats meat experiences suffering. Thus, since Dharma can be understood through inference and other means, the claim that it is known through the Veda alone is incorrect. This is their view. To refute this, the author says: "That is not so, because it is impossible to establish a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). That is not correct. Why? Because it is impossible to establish a necessary connection between Dharma and its effect. What is this "necessary connection"? It is the state of being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitva*). For example, smoke is necessarily connected to fire, and the rise of the moon is necessarily connected to the swelling of the ocean. However, in the case of Dharma, it is impossible to establish such a necessary connection with prosperity and the like. Why? Because Dharma is imperceptible (*parokṣa*). Since Dharma is beyond the senses, one cannot perceive its connection with prosperity and the like. Therefore, it is impossible to establish a necessary connection. Furthermore, even if one were to perceive a connection, it would be uncertain. For instance, when one sees that a person who performs a sacrifice attains prosperity, one cannot be certain whether that prosperity arose from the sacrifice or from some other cause. Thus, because it is impossible to establish a necessary connection, the view that Dharma is to be understood through inference and other means is untenable. Therefore, it is established that Dharma is to be understood solely through the Veda. Thus ends the section on the refutation of the opponent's position. Now begins the section on the establishment of the Veda's authority (*vedaprāmāṇyasamarthana*). It has been stated: "Dharma is to be understood solely through the Veda. Now, the following doubt arises: Is the Veda itself authoritative (*pramāṇa*) or not? To resolve this, the author first presents the view of the opponent: "Some say the Veda is not authoritative. The word "some" refers to the Cārvākas. They hold that the Veda is not authoritative. Why? Because it is composed by humans. Whatever is composed by humans is not authoritative, just as the words of ordinary people are not authoritative. The Veda is also composed by humans, therefore it is not authoritative. Furthermore, the Veda contains contradictory statements. For example, it says, "One should sacrifice a cow," and also, "One should not kill any living being. Since it contains such contradictions, it is not authoritative. Moreover, the Veda is full of errors. For example, it says, "The earth has seven islands," whereas we see that the earth has only four continents. Since it contains such errors, it is not authoritative. Therefore, the Veda is not authoritative. This is their view. To refute this, the author says: "That is not so, because there is no composer. That is not correct. Why? Because there is no composer of the Veda. Who could have composed the Veda? No human being has the capacity to compose such a work. Therefore, the Veda is not composed by humans. Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the Veda. The apparent contradictions are merely due to differences in time, place, and circumstances. For example, the injunction to sacrifice a cow refers to a specific ritual context, while the prohibition against killing refers to ordinary times. Thus, there is no real contradiction. Moreover, there are no errors in the Veda. The statements about the earth having seven islands are based on ancient traditions and are not contradicted by direct perception. Therefore, the Veda is authoritative. Furthermore, the Veda is eternal (*nitya*). It has existed from beginningless time and will continue to exist until the end of the world. Since it is eternal, it is not composed by anyone. Being not composed by anyone, it is free from the defects of human fallibility and is therefore authoritative. Thus, it is established that the Veda is the sole means of valid cognition for Dharma. Hence, the statement that "Dharma is known through the Veda alone" is proven. Thus ends the section on the establishment of the Veda's authority. Now begins the section on the eternity of the Veda (*vedanityatva*). It has been stated: "The Veda is eternal. Now, the following doubt arises: How is the eternity of the Veda established? To resolve this, the author first presents the view of the opponent: "Some say the Veda is non-eternal. The word "some" refers to the followers of the Nyāya school. They hold that the Veda is non-eternal. Why? Because it is perceived to have a beginning in time. We observe that the Veda was taught by teachers to students at various times. Since it has a beginning, it cannot be eternal. Furthermore, the Veda contains names of persons and events that occurred in the past. For example, it mentions the sage *Vasiṣṭha* and King *Purūravas*. Since these individuals lived in the past, the Veda must have been composed after them. Therefore, the Veda is non-eternal. This is their view. To refute this, the author says: "That is not so, because there is no memory of a creator. That is not correct. Why? Because there is no memory of anyone having created the Veda. If the Veda had been created by someone, there would certainly be a tradition or memory of that creator. However, no such memory exists. Therefore, the Veda was not created. Furthermore, the Veda is recognized as the same across all regions and times. Just as the letter 'A' is recognized as the same everywhere, so too the Vedic sentences are recognized as identical regardless of the teacher or student. This uniformity proves its eternity. Moreover, the Veda is not dependent on human effort. It is revealed spontaneously, like the light of the sun. Since it is independent of human composition, it is eternal. Furthermore, the Veda is traditionally handed down without interruption. From beginningless time, it has been passed down through an unbroken lineage of teachers and students. This continuous transmission proves its eternity. Therefore, it is established that the Veda is eternal. Thus ends the section on the eternity of the Veda. The doctrine of the non-human origin of the Vedas (*vedāpauruṣeyatvavāda*): By the method to be explained hereafter, the status of the Vedic word as non-human in origin is established through the force of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatābala*).
Alternatively, the probandum (*sādhya*) is that [the Veda] has as its means of valid cognition words that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

In that case, the reason (*hetu*) is "having a means of valid cognition" while being characterized by the absence of sense-faculties, inferential marks, or human-authored words as means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is that [the Veda] is subordinate to the production of that [knowledge], as will be made clear later.
The meaning is that it refers to [scriptures] such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
The term "pauruṣeya" (composed by a person) is stated to prevent a contradiction regarding the probandum;
its meaning is "a word preceded by an independent person."

If it were stated merely as "other than human" (*pauruṣeyetara*), it would be logically consistent even by virtue of being based on any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) that is other than human;

therefore, the word "sound" (*śabda*) is included to exclude the possibility of proving something else [than sound]. As agreed upon. In the *Maṇikṛta-jñaptiprāmāṇyavāda*: “If it is asked, ‘How can there be an inference qualified by validity (*prāmāṇya*) without knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)?’—[the answer is:

The intention is that this is because of the statement: "Just as after a cognition whose qualificandum is an absence, there arises the knowledge 'the ground possesses an absence'.

The point is that because it would be contradicted (*bādhā*) if the probandum were to reside in [non-eternal things] such as the sky, it is ultimately established as residing only in non-human (eternal) words. Regarding the reason (*hetu*), there is a reference to that same non-human [nature].

Because it serves to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) within one's own system regarding non-existent things such as a rabbit's horn.

Consequently, there is no room for the objection that—since the relation that serves as the basis for the world's substratum allows for the cognition "Veda-ness exists now," "pot-ness exists now," and so on—the Veda-ness and other such properties also possess occurrence in time; thus, the reason would suffer from the fallacy of proving what is already established (arthāntaratva), and the qualifier [in the reason] would be redundant.
"That it is so."
Whatever, while not occurring in others, does occur [in a given locus], occurs in that [locus].
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (First Chapter, p. 236) (Note: Variants: 1. *kevala-kuṃ-ca*; 2. *ṣya-mu*; 3. *eveti nāsti-kuṃ*.)
Nor is there a failure to establish the qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) even in these three reasons:
because our own direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not operate with respect to dharma and adharma in the subject matter of the Veda;
and because the direct perceptions of Īśvara and yogins are themselves unestablished without the Veda, just like dharma and so forth.

In arguments such as "Dharma and so forth are perceived by someone because they are real entities, like a jar," even now [the argument fails] due to the unestablished nature of Dharma and so forth, which involves the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). The meaning of the phrase "being a jar" (*ghaṭatva*) is: being a locus of occurrence while not occurring in anything other than a jar. Regarding the first reason (*hetu*), the author will refute the unestablished nature of its qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) with the passage beginning with "na ca" (3). As for the second reason, there is an additional qualification consisting of the state of not being established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as sensory perception or inference.

4. Having first refuted the non-establishment of the six [means of knowledge] by means of the qualification stated in the *Sudhā*, he now considers perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is intended as the foremost among the senses:
is it the perception of people like us, or is it the perception of Īśvara and the yogins? 5. Regarding the first case, he says: "The meaning of the Veda," and its elaboration is "Dharma," etc.
Dharma consists of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites.
The last [author] says: "By God," etc.
"Because it is unestablished."

The idea that dharma and so forth are established by the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of Īśvara or by the direct perception of a yogin is untenable, because such things are not perceptible to people like us and must therefore be understood through the Veda alone. Thus, having first learned of the direct perception of Īśvara and others through the Veda, and then relying on that [perception] to understand the nature of dharma and so forth, one should simply determine them by means of the Veda itself—following the direction stated by Jaimini, "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction" (codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ). Why, then, engage in this futile effort like "catching a crane"? Such is the sense: that dharma is not an object of direct perception.
"In that case, let it be that the perception of God and so forth, whose objects include dharma and the like, is established through inference. To this he says: "Dharma and the like..."
The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "knowability and so forth" (*prameyatvādi*) refers to the logical reason (*hetu*); this is indicated by the word "even now."

This means that it is not only [the case] previously; even at the time of presenting the inference that establishes perception—such as that of the Lord (Īśvara)—which is adduced as the means for establishing dharma and so forth, against one who asserts that "there is no establishment of dharma and the like without the Veda," [the same objection applies]. This is expressed by the word *anyonya* ("mutually"). [Notes on variants: 1. *thadha-cha-ga*. 2.
The word *adharma* is absent in *cha-ka*. 3. *gre uddha-a*. 4. *ṣyasyā-mu*. 5. *iti vikalpo*.

[The phrase] "having kept in mind" is an addition found in the Kuṃ. manuscript; it does not exist in the Mu. manuscript. [The phrase] "by the Veda" does not exist in the Mu. manuscript. [The word] "reason" (*hetu*) does not exist in the Mu. manuscript. The Discourse on the Non-human Authorship of the Vedas (*Vedāpauruṣeyatva-vāda*), page 237. [The phrase] "in the state of being non-human-authored" (*vedāpauruṣeyatve*) is present in the Ni. manuscript. The Discourse on the Non-human Authorship of the Vedas, page 237.
