Furthermore, for people such as ourselves, dharma and so forth are not established by those two [the Veda and the Smṛti];

for even if one infers merely that there is a fruit—on the grounds that the activity of a discerning person toward *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrifices and works of public utility) would otherwise be inexplicable—it is impossible to infer the specific detail that "this is the fruit of this particular sacrifice or oblation. Such a subtle distinction is beyond the reach of inference.

The engagement of many discerning persons in specific rituals such as the Jyotiṣṭoma for the sake of attaining specific fruits is indeed possible, just as in the case of venerating a *caitya*; this was stated by the Blessed Teacher (Śaṅkarācārya):

"The meaning is that if dharma and so forth are established, then by taking them as the subject (*pakṣa*), the inference proving the perception of God and other entities is established; and if the inference is established, then through the perception established by that inference, dharma and so forth are established—thus there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)."

Or, even if it were granted that there is a perception of God regarding dharma and so forth through both scripture and inference, nevertheless, the determination of dharma and so forth useful for the performance [of rites] by people such as ourselves is not established by the perceptions of God or yogis;
thus he states another defect with the words "by those two."

Thus, the implication is that since the Veda alone must be accepted as the means for the knowledge of persons such as ourselves, what is the point of introducing the direct perception of God and so forth?

Having thus established the qualification consisting in the fact that [the self] is not proven by the sense organs (*indriya*), he removes the objection regarding the non-establishment of the qualification consisting in the fact that it is not proven by an inferential mark (*liṅga*)—with the words "iṣṭa" etc.

"Sacrifice" (yāga) and "pious works" (pūrta), such as the construction of tanks and so forth, are seen [in the texts]. Because of the rule "it is also seen after other [roots]" (*anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyate*), the lengthening of the vowel in the term *iṣṭāpūrta* is correctly established by the addition of the suffix *iti*. This applies to this [term] as well.
The intended meaning is that it is precisely the knowledge of that [object] which is useful for its practical application.
To show that the establishment of the specific qualification of the activity [is not possible], he says: "Because of the specific result," and so forth.
The meaning is "having the form of heaven and so forth"—this is what is meant by the word *caitya*.

Just as many who are outside the Veda engage in what is non-dharma—where there is no cause for a fruit—due to the delusion that it is dharma and so forth, so too [this tradition] has arisen through a succession of the blind;
it does not, however, determine the true nature of dharma and the like. This is the meaning, as it has been said: "taduktam" (it has been stated).

The meaning is that it has been stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya* that the establishment of dharma and so forth cannot occur through another means, such as perception or inference, because [the Veda] consists of words that are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).
The meaning is that in the absence of that [author], there would be an absence of the statement regarding its being non-human-authored (*apauruṣeya*).

*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 238) (Note: The variants provided—*syeti* for *syeti* (Kuṃ.), *tathāca* for *tathāca* (Mu.), and *tatparam* for *tatparam* (Mu.)—indicate textual differences in the respective manuscripts.)
"Because in the absence of that, all dharmas and so forth desired by any philosophical system would be unestablished. Thus [it is said].
Nor can that [reality] be established by means of human speech,
because there is no confidence in it due to the possibility of human factors such as ignorance, false knowledge, deception, negligence, and lack of proficiency in the instruments of cognition.

To prevent that [charge of circularity], if one accepts the Lord’s eternal omniscience and so forth, then for that very purpose, let it be postulated that the Word which makes known dharma is merely non-human (apauruṣeya).

Thus, by the very passage intended to establish the qualifying attribute consisting in having the senses or inference as its means of valid cognition, it should be understood that the proof of the non-human nature of the Word in the first thesis has also been established through the force of the reason's presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Furthermore, the qualification "provided that non-human words are not established as authoritative" in the first two reasons, and the qualification "provided that [the property] does not reside in anything other than the non-human" in the third reason, are unestablished (*asiddha*). He rescues [the argument] by clarifying the meaning of the passage from the *Tattvanirṇaya* beginning with "Nor can its establishment be through human speech, because ignorance and deception would follow," using the words beginning with "And not... (*na ca*).
"Pauruṣeyī" means created by Īśvara.
Even knowing it to be a deception intended to mislead others, such a deceptive act is [an instance of] delusion;
whereas stating "there is a cloth" when one ought to say "there is a jar" is negligence—this is for the purpose of excluding that [latter].
The meaning is: for the purpose of establishing the absence of lack of confidence caused by such defects as the suspicion of ignorance in persons—[this is expressed by the word] "eternal" (nitya).

The word "eternal" (*nitya*) is an attribute of omniscience (*sārvajñya*) for the purpose of removing the status of being an error (*bhramatva*) due to its being produced by the three defects (*doṣa*).
In the phrase "only in sound" (*śabda eva*), the word "sound" (*śabda*) ends in the locative case.
To the question "What is the distinction [of this]?", it is said: "merely" (*mātra*).
In that regard, however, [attributes] such as omniscience are numerous; this will be made clear later.

[Regarding the phrase] "false knowledge" (*mithyājñāna*): [the reading] *kuṇḍavalitaṃ* is found in manuscript Kuṃ., while the word *ādi* (etcetera) is not present in manuscripts Mu. and Ca. [The reading] *ṣāja* is found in manuscript Mu.
[This concludes the section on] the non-human authorship of the Vedas.
The doctrine of the non-human authorship of the Vedas [is untenable],
because presumption (*arthāpatti*) by its very nature has as its object that which directly accounts for the fact in question;
it does not, however, concern an indirect account such as the omniscience of a speaker.

Otherwise, having accepted that the Veda was not composed by an omniscient being, one would have to postulate that it is based on another word-composition produced by an omniscient being, for the sake of gaining confidence in its authority.
This has been stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda: “In accepting the non-human origin of a statement, nothing need be postulated.
He states another distinction as well: “from presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).”

For the authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the word that makes known dharma and so forth is the direct subsumer (*upapādaka*) of that which is called "presumption" (*arthāpatti*)— which consists of the ascertainment of dharma and so forth and which would otherwise be untenable without a validating cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes it.
However, eternal omniscience and so forth are merely indirect supports for establishing the certainty regarding dharma and other matters in that [Veda].

Being composed by a person free from defects such as ignorance is what directly establishes it; and omniscience is what establishes that [freedom from defects]. Thus, many such things must be postulated in a successive chain of supports.
The meaning is that, because it is simpler and because it serves as a direct means of proof, that alone should be postulated.
Now, one might object: "Since no word is ever observed in the world to be non-human in origin, a traditional succession [of teachers] is more reasonable. To this, he says: "Otherwise..."

The meaning is this: when a direct proof is available, to resort to an indirect relationship based merely on the observation of the coexistence of "being a word" (śabdatva) and "being non-human-authored" (apauruṣeyatva)—this is what is meant by the phrase "having granted" (aṅgīkṛtya).
The meaning is that in the world, it is observed that mere words are composed by those who are not omniscient; thus it has been said.
The meaning is that it has been stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya* that the mere postulation of authorlessness is the simpler [position].

Alternatively, regarding the claim that one should simply postulate the mere lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) as having been accepted [by others], he states—under the guise of citing an authoritative opinion—that even that is certainly not to be postulated: "That has been said."
"Nothing at all":
the meaning is that even the authorlessness of the Veda is established simply because no author of the Veda is known.

To dispel the misconception that the acceptance of the authorless (apauruṣeya) Vedic statements— which indirectly convey dharma and other truths by establishing the omniscience of the speaker, which in turn proves the absence of defects in the person who composed the Vedas— is merely for that purpose, he states the actual point relevant to the present context with the word "directly" (sākṣāt).

The meaning is that [the Veda] is the direct communicator of Dharma and so forth. // @--------------------------------------------------------------------------- Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava (First Chapter, p.

240) @------------------------ ---------------- --------- The meaning is that in a sentence which is a direct communicator [of truth], one accepts its merely being non-human in origin (*apauruṣeyatva*). //

Furthermore, there would be a burden of conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava) if one had to postulate for the Veda that it was composed by such [an author], as well as the qualities of being a teacher who is free from error, capable of acting without negligence, and who possesses the power to deceive regarding omniscience—all of which are unproven.
Furthermore, there is no establishment of non-deception and so forth in the case of omniscience;
for even in the case of the incarnations of an omniscient Lord, deception and the like are observed.

Thus, by demonstrating the parsimony (*lāghava*) in our own position, [we have refuted] the nature of being unestablished as a means of valid cognition for human-authored words, and the nature of not occurring in anything other than the non-human-authored.

And having established the qualification, he further establishes it by demonstrating the burden [of the opponent's position] as stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna* regarding the opposing view, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).

Alternatively, it is incorrect to say that nothing needs to be postulated, because the quality of being authorless (apauruṣeyatva) itself must be postulated; therefore, let this much stand for now. Nevertheless, with the thought that [the Veda] is not so extensive as you claim, he says: "Furthermore" (kiñca).
Is it not the case that omniscience and so forth are not lacking in authority, since they are established by inference from such reasons as "being an effect"?
And by means of omniscience itself, the absence of all defects is established.
For instance,
in one who has directly realized the Dharma and so forth, defects such as passion cannot arise;
this is because, according to Patañjali’s statement that "ignorance is the field for the subsequent [defects]," they have their root in nescience (*ajñāna*).
Because ignorance is impossible in one who is omniscient;
because it is impossible for one free from passion and the like to be deceived regarding its effects;
and because defects such as impairment of the sense organs cannot be suspected in one of such great majesty.
One might object: "Since he is a man of knowledge, why would he not teach the ignorant world?
Moreover, since the assumption that such teaching is established in the Vedas is simpler,"—anticipating this, the author replies with the words beginning with "na ca" and ending with "nirasiṣyate."

By the word "and so forth" (*ādipadena*), qualities such as vigilance (*apramāda*) and the status of being a teacher are included; and in the case of the Veda, its authorship [by that teacher] is also grasped—even though it possesses a body.
[This concludes the section on] the inference regarding the non-human origin of the Veda.

Regarding the doctrine that the Vedas are not of human origin (apauruṣeya): even in the case of an omniscient being, bodily defects such as physical frailty or lack of proficiency in the instruments of action are unavoidable; furthermore, it is observed that even those possessed of knowledge may turn away from providing instruction.
Because there is no established proof that the Veda was created by him, it too must be considered as something to be inferred.
Furthermore, the proof of the omniscience of God through inferences such as "being an effect" will be refuted.
Nor can his omniscience and other qualities be established through the Vedas alone;
for since the authority of the Vedas depends upon the establishment of God's omniscience and so forth, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Otherwise, his omniscience and other attributes could likewise be established through the scriptures of the Buddha and others.
This has been stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda:

“Your knowledge is non-deceptive, and those [other qualities] as well are to be postulated because of that; however, due to the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava), human speech is not a means of cognition. Thus it is said.
Therefore, there is no establishment of the qualification [of being composed by a person].
Furthermore, the fact that [the Veda] was created by such a person is apprehended even in the case of the body.
The meaning is that, in your view, the omniscient Lord has no body, even if a body were admitted for the sake of providing instruction;
this applies to the wise as well.
This means "of the perfected ones" (siddhānām).
All of this is clearly explained in the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā* [in the passage beginning] with "mutually" (*anyonya*).

The meaning is that once omniscience is established, the authority of the Veda is established because it was composed by him; and once that [authority] is established, omniscience is established by means of it.
Thus it has been said.
The meaning is that this refers to the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the *Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa*.
"Knowledge of that" means the valid cognition (*pramiti*) of dharma and so forth.
"Being produced by that" means being produced by that person.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), proficiency in the instruments [of perception] and so on are included. "Jñāpaka" means that which makes known or determines [the nature of] dharma and the rest.
The particle "ca" (and) is used in the sense of "since" or "because."
4. *Tat* means "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

[End of commentary] *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (First Chapter, p. 242) [End of section] (Note: Variants indicate that the commentary on *rasā*, *mu*, *ca*, *ṇasi*, and *kuṃ* is present, while the text following "3. ayaṃ granthaḥ" and "4. idaṃ" is absent in manuscript *a*.)

Alternatively, according to the view that the knowledge of God (*īśvarajñāna*) is not valid cognition (*pramā*), the Veda lacks a fixed sequential order due to differences in time; this is because, while it is not rooted in defects, it is devoid of being rooted in valid cognition, like the sky. According to the view that [God’s knowledge] is valid cognition, the reason is: "while not being rooted in defects, it is not rooted in the instruments of valid cognition.
He says "Alternatively" (*yadvā*) in accordance with the statement in the *Sudhā* that "the state of having one fixed mode [of expression] constitutes authorlessness" (*apauruṣeyatva*).
It was stated—"not valid cognition"—in order to refute the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*).
"Mother," he said.

The meaning is that, according to the view [of some], only that which is produced by a quality (guṇa) possesses the status of valid cognition (pramā); since the knowledge of God (īśvarajñāna) is not produced by such a quality, it is not considered valid cognition.
The phrase "by means of a difference in time" is stated in the probandum (sādhya) in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā).
This means by way of the distinction between the prior and subsequent cosmic cycles (kalpa).

When it is stated that "the sequence is fixed," if the probandum were taken to be the state of having a single type of sequence, then because the example would lack the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), the opponent's position could not be established; furthermore, the two negative particles (*nañ*) are used to achieve the refutation of the probandum as stated by the opponent.

In the *Tattvanirṇayaṭīkā*, having accepted that the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) in the phrase "neither perception and other means of valid cognition, nor deception and the like, are found to be its source; thus, being the object of common consensus is 'Veda-ness'" (*vedatvam*), [the author] states the reason for that very purpose by extracting it: "due to defects," etc. (*doṣa*...).
The meaning is "due to defects such as deception.

The mention of the qualifier and the qualified, respectively, is for the purpose of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a sentence rooted in error and a human statement rooted in valid cognition—hence the term "prameti" (rooted in valid cognition).

The meaning is that [the definition] is considered to be "valid knowledge" (pramā) because, even if not produced by a quality (guṇa), it is a cognition not produced by a defect (doṣa) and possesses the property of having a qualifier corresponding to its object;

furthermore, since the property of being a cognition (jñānatva) is pervaded by either validity (pramātva) or error-ness (bhramatva), it would follow that for that which lacks error-ness, there would be an absence of the property of being a cognition if validity were absent. Thus, it is held to be valid knowledge.
Now, having accepted that the term "pramāṇa" (means of valid cognition) has the sense of being the instrument for valid cognition, he says: "the instrument of valid cognition."

The point is that, according to the opponent's view, even though the Veda is rooted in the knowledge of God, it is not unestablished [as a means of valid cognition], because—due to its being unproduced—it lacks an instrument (*karaṇa*), and because it is itself not an instrument.
[The section on] the doctrine of the non-human origin of the Vedas (*vedāpauruṣeyatvavāda*). Page 243.
Although in the case of space—which has a nature inherently containing a sequence—there is no non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) in the sense of being eternally and uniformly sequential;
nevertheless, it certainly possesses that [non-human origin] in the form of being devoid of an indefinite sequence.

Although this [property of being produced by a person] is not excluded from impermanent things such as jars, nevertheless, because it is excluded from non-personal (apauruṣeya) speech, its absence—which consists in the lack of that "personality" (pauruṣeyatva) common to both intentional and non-intentional speech—does not constitute a different object (arthāntara) when proving its exclusion. Even in this view, according to the previously stated direction, since God’s knowledge functions as a cause everywhere only as a cognition whose object is the material cause and so forth (common to error), it is not a cause as a valid cognition (pramā); thus, even when the aforementioned reason is stated...

There is no lack of proof; nevertheless, this statement of another reason is made either as a concessive argument (*abhyupetyavāda*), or because the intention to distinguish [this case] from being rooted in a valid cognition (*pramā*) has not yet been stated previously.

Anticipating the objection that there might be a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in a case where the probandum has been fully established, he refutes it with the words "Even though... (*yadyapi*).

One might object: "Since the two aforementioned reasons exist even in the case of a jar and other such things, it is possible that they would terminate in 'impermanence' alone—just as they do there—even in the present subject (pakṣa); thus, the establishment of the probandum (sādhya), which consists in having a sequence of a single, eternal form, would not occur. For the absence of a qualified entity can be established by the mere absence of its qualifier. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words: "Even though... (*yadyapi*).

Regarding the term "pauruṣeya" (human origin): since it must be stated that the exclusion of human speech is caused precisely by the absence of necessity regarding the sequence [of syllables], there is a contradiction in the present case as well; for while the reason exists in the subject when accompanied by the sequence, it results in its absence [when that sequence is excluded].
The intended meaning is that the conclusion is reached precisely because there is an absence of necessity regarding that [object]; this refers to what was stated by the opponent.

The meaning is that the definition of "being of human origin" (pauruṣeyatva) is "the state of belonging to a class of utterances produced independently of the utterance of a similar [instance]," as stated in the *Maṇi*—namely, "intellect... and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: the speech of Caitra and others is preceded by intelligence (*buddhipūrvaka*), while the speech of Śuka, children, and others is not preceded by intelligence (*abuddhipūrvaka*).

That which is common to both of these—namely, the absence of a fixed sequence (*niyatānupūrvīkatvābhāva*)—is what is meant by "spoken by another" (*parokta*). (Note: Variants indicate that some manuscripts omit *abuddhipūrvaketi*, *tatpra*, *nai*, and the phrase *pakṣepyanityatvenaiva*.)

Alternatively, the probandum (*sādhya*) is: "not being the locus of an effect whose counter-correlative is a causality delimited by the state of being a cognition whose object is that which is to be propounded by itself.
In this context, the reason (*hetu*) is: "having as its root a valid cognition (*pramā*), while not having as its root an error (*bhrama*)."

Even under the view that the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), there is a contradiction (*bādha*) in attempting to prove its absence [of authorship], because the sequence of words (*padavalī*) in the Veda is the locus of an effecthood that is counter-correlative to a causality delimited by being a cognition whose object is [the sequence itself].
To exclude that [contradiction], the term "that which it itself expresses" (*svapratipādya*) was stated.

If it were stated merely that [the Veda] is produced by a cognition whose object is what it itself intends to convey, then there would again be a contradiction, because the cognition residing in God—which has as its object the things to be conveyed by the Veda—is indeed produced by a series of words.
To exclude that possibility, it is stated that [the cognition] must be "delimited by the nature of cognition" (*jñānatvāvacchinna*), and so forth.

Alternatively, according to the view that "being authored by a person" (*pauruṣeyatva*) consists in being produced by a cognition whose object is the meaning of a sentence, he states the following inference to prove the absence of that [authorship]: "Or rather, 'sva'... [and so on].
It should be understood that "the cognition of God is considered valid knowledge" (pramā) is what is intended; the word "Veda" is carried over [from the previous context].

The meaning is: that cognition which has as its object a thing such as Dharma, which is to be established by its own Veda—that is, a cognition whose nature of being an effect is not defined by a causal efficiency delimited by that [Vedic] reality—is not a locus of such an effect-nature.
The intended meaning is that the sky itself serves as the illustrative example.
He clarifies the function of the two qualifiers applied to the probandum with the words: "In [the case of] being authorless..."
"Of the Veda."
The meaning is that since the Veda consists of phonemes distinguished by a specific sequence, and since that sequence is produced, it possesses the status of being an effect; thus it has been stated.

The intention is as follows: even though it was stated that [the sentence] is "that which is to be conveyed" (*pratipādya*), since the sequence of words (*padavali*) and so forth also possess the quality of being conveyed by words, the term "itself" (*sva*) was used specifically to avoid that aforementioned fault.

But surely, even here, this reason (*hetu*) does not exclude [the property] from things such as the sky or a jar—which possess the stated probandum (*sādhyavat*)—since it is established therein precisely by being non-produced by a cognition of the aforementioned form; thus, it reaches the intended "non-human origin" (*apauruṣeyatva*), which consists in having an eternally uniform sequential order. Therefore, there is no [fallacy]. (Regarding the non-human origin of the Vedas...)
The doctrine of the non-human authorship of the Vedas (vedāpauruṣeyatvavāda) [is as follows]:

This too is the probandum, consisting of the absence of human authorship—that is, the absence of that quality common to both authoritative and non-authoritative sentences which is defined by having a person as its source (mūlaka).
Nor is there any deviation [from the rule] in the case of the speech of parrots, children, and the like according to the opponent's view,
because that too is equivalent to the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*).

Alternatively, the probandum (*sādhya*) is: "not being the locus of an effect whose counter-correlate is a causality delimited by being a true cognition regarding the object to be established by itself.

And in that case, the reason (*hetu*) is simply "not being rooted in a means of valid cognition" (*pramākaraṇāmūlakatvamātram*). [Objection: This proves something else [than the intended conclusion]. To this, he says: "This too... (*idamapi*).
"Of what has been stated by another."

The term "this Veda-ness" (etad-vedatva) refers to the state of being a Veda as recited by Caitra and others, which is established in Buddhism.
By the clause beginning with "satya," he clarifies the removal of the aforementioned defect—namely, that this Veda-ness [is not merely conventional]. 8. Indeed, this Veda-ness... [etc.]
Like the state of being smoke.
The meaning is that, just as "smokeness" (dhūmatva) is the delimitor of the pervasion by fire, this particular "smokeness" is not; this is the second [alternative].

In the second [definition], the exclusion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding "being this Veda" (*etadvedatva*) and so forth by means of the term "entirety" (*sakala*) is refuted; for "being this Veda" does not exist in a prior Veda that possesses the same sequential order (*anupūrvi*) as its own locus, namely this Veda. This is rejected because, according to the stated method, since "Veda-ness" (*vedatva*) exists in what was uttered by the Lord himself—without depending on a similar utterance—as well as in the Vedas manifested to Vasiṣṭha and others, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Since the property of being a sentence (*vākyavṛttatva*) is established by its being articulated, and since its being the delimitor of what is accepted by great people (*māhājanaparigrahya*) is established precisely by its residing in that which produces valid knowledge of dharma and so forth, the stated probandum (*sādhya*) is not a necessary consequence due to the complexity (*gaurava*) [of the reason]. Furthermore, as for the second reason, since it is established by the very same causes—namely, the throat, palate, and so forth—which produce the identical phonetic sequence (*tulyānupūrvī*) throughout all its own substrata, it is not a necessary consequence of the stated probandum due to complexity;
thus, he clarifies the exclusion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words "of this Veda-ness" (*etadvedatvasya*).
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is that by what has been stated regarding the jewel, this [objection] is refuted.
He clarifies what was stated by the words "by this" with the phrase "in the manner described."
The meaning is: "in the manner stated beginning with 'depending on me'"; the compound *svayaṃpratībhātavedaiḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi*.

He states, by means of the passage beginning with "vākya," that the reason is unestablished (*aprayojaka*) because both parts of the reason—the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)—are otherwise possible even without the stated probandum (*sādhya*).
The syntactical connection is with the phrase "by way of being established through the occurrence of what has been uttered.
The term "with gravity" (*gauraveṇa*) is illustrative;
it should also be understood as including "and by the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) in the contrary case (*vipakṣa*)."
The previously mentioned common defects, such as contradiction by scripture (*śruti*) and so forth, should also be considered here—on the grounds that the causes are equal.

By whatever cause the same sequence exists everywhere among the individual manifestations that serve as the substrata for the Veda, by that very cause the [existence of the] cause is established. (Note: The variants indicate textual differences: *samastapada* is found in the *ca* and *ka* manuscripts; *ccāri* appears corrected in the *cha* manuscript; *ktasā* is found in *cha*, *ca*, *ka*, *ga*, and *kha*; the word *gauraveṇa* occurs immediately after in the *mu*, *ca*, *cha*, *ka*, and *kha* manuscripts.)
Thus it is not [the case]—ga. (The Refutation of the Doctrine of the Non-Human Origin of the Vedas, following the examination of the marks [of authorship];
page 267.)

By this, the following argument is refuted: "The Veda, when recited by one who desires to inform others, is preceded by a cognition that has the same object as itself and is independent of [any other] authority;
because it is a sentence uttered by one desiring to inform, like a worldly sentence.

This is because the status of being a sentence uttered by one desiring to inform is established merely by its being preceded by a cognition having the same object as itself; therefore, due to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), an independent cognition is not a necessary causal factor (*aprayojaka*). Furthermore, [the argument is flawed] because of the excessive complexity (*gaurava*) involved in positing such independence.
By the very same reason stated otherwise, its dependence on the instrument of a cognition that has the same object as itself, while being independent of itself, would also be established.
In my view, since God’s knowledge is established as being independent of the Veda, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanāt*).
Nor is the Veda produced by a true cognition whose object is the meaning of a sentence;
it is not produced by anything else.
And that cause consists of the throat, palate, and so forth, but not the form of striking the palm and such;

thus, because the reason lacks the property of being based on the fact of occurring in what is uttered without depending on a preceding utterance of the same class, the meaning is that the reason is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*).
"Desiring to make [them] understand."
The meaning is that the Veda was recited by a teacher who desired to instruct his disciple.
The phrase "recited by one desiring to instruct" is stated in order to exclude the Veda recited by contemporary ignorant persons.
By the word "his own," the Veda recited by one desiring to instruct, which is proximate [to the author], is denoted.

The meaning is that [the effect] is independent of that [cause], i.e., not produced by it. And the meaning of "preceded by a cognition having the same object as that" is that there exists a cognition of that same object; and since such a cognition resides in God (Īśvara), the point is that the probandum is established through being produced by Him.

The phrase "desiring to inform" (*bubodhayiṣu*) is a qualification of the cause [of speech] in order to eliminate the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the property of being a sentence (*vākyatva*) in the case of words uttered by an ignorant person.
Following the statement in the *Sudhā* that "it is because inference is not a necessary factor," he says: "svasamāna... (equal to itself).
He rejects another formulation [of the argument] with the words: "Nor is it the Veda. [Notes: 1. *tvega* — *mu* and *ca*; 2.
*gauraveṇa* is absent — *cha*, *ka*, *kha*; 3. This much is absent — *ga*; 4. The phrase *svamānāviṣayakaraṇa* is added — *ka*; 5. The word *jñāna* is absent — *ga*; 6. *kami* — *kuṃ*.
From the *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava*, Prathama-pariccheda, p. 268.]
It should be stated that [the word] is a means of valid cognition because it is a word, like the *Mahābhārata*. However,

if one intends the mere cognition of the object as the probans, then in the case of a modern work recited with the desire to inform others of its meaning, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding that recent portion.

And if, in order to exclude that [fallacy], one qualifies the cognition by the property of "not being produced from words," there would still be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of a word rooted in another word.
If it is argued that this [objection] is equal to the [original] position (*pakṣa*), we say no;

for since validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), even when the Vedas are stated as the subject (*pakṣa*) in the *Maṇi*, it is stated in that very same work that what is read therein is equal to the subject. Thus, taking any portion of the Veda as the subject—

1. To indicate that the use of the plural number [in the opponent's argument] is rooted in a lack of discrimination regarding the establishment of the desired conclusion, the subject (*pakṣa*) is stated simply as "the Veda.

The phrase "having as its object the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārthagocara*) is included in the probandum (*sādhya*) in order to exclude the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*), since [the Veda] is produced by a knowledge of the sequence of syllables and so forth known by the reciters.

If it were stated merely as "produced by a knowledge having as its object the meaning of the sentence," then even if error were established in the case of God, the desired conclusion would not be proven; therefore, the word "correct" (*yathārtha*) is used to establish that specific nature—just as in the case of the *Bhārata*.
The meaning is: "like the Mahābhārata and so forth, which lack a foundation in direct perception"—this refers to the word "mere" (mātrasya).
The meaning is: "of that which is devoid of the qualification of being produced by sound.
Regarding the term "hetutve" (in the state of being a reason): [it refers to the following].
The meaning is "because of being a producer.

[Objection: But was it not precisely for the sake of removing this defect that the qualification "produced by words" was stated for cognition in the *Maṇi*? To this, he says: "for the sake of removing that."
Anticipating the intention of the statement in the *Maṇi* that "even such [an act] has two agents," he says: "He too... and so forth.

According to the ancient view, even in a case that is similar to the subject (*pakṣasama*)—where the probandum (*sādhya*) is doubtful—the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is considered a fault because the reason (*hetu*) is ascertained; however, according to the modern view, this is not a fault, as this has been clarified in the *Maṇi* (the *Tattvacintāmaṇi*) within the section on the proof of God (*īśvaravāda*).
Thus [ends the discussion] regarding validity (*prāmāṇya*).

In this context, it must be stated that the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) occurs through the qualified reason (*viśiṣṭahetu*), because either the subject (*viśeṣya*) or the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is untenable without the aforementioned probandum.
Among these, the subject, namely "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*), is certainly not untenable,
as it exists even in the case of what appears to be sound.

Because [the reason] exists. However, the establishment of the probandum must be stated by means of the very impossibility of the qualifier—namely, validity in the sense of being a producer of true cognition. (Veda-pautrānumāna-dīpaḥ)
Regarding the doctrine of the non-human authorship of the Vedas (pu-269):

Even if [the Veda] were dependent on another [source], it would be like a chance-correct statement; since the necessary factors such as semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and so forth are not established, and because of the resulting complexity (*gaurava*), the stated reason is not a probans for the proposed thesis.
Otherwise, by that very same reason...
It would also be established that [the cognition] is preceded by a means of valid knowledge whose object is the meaning of the sentence.
By this, the claim that "having the nature of knowledge corresponding to reality" (yathārthajñānatva) is intended as the delimiting condition for instrumentality (karaṇatāvacchedaka) is refuted.

This is because, whether the validity [of cognition] is intrinsic (svataḥ) or extrinsic (parataḥ), since the Veda is eternal—just as the knowledge of God is valid due to its eternity—it is logically established that the Veda possesses the status of being a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇaśabda).
By this, the argument that "if the Veda were not preceded by knowledge corresponding to reality, there would be a mere succession of books" is also refuted.

For even in the absence of such a prior [authoritative source], the occurrence of a blind tradition is established, just as in the case of knowledge produced by the qualities [of a person] or like the knowledge of God, which is not preceded by that [same kind of authoritative source].

For this very reason, the following [inference] is refuted: "The cognition produced by the sense-organ is preceded by a quality in its instrument, because it is a produced valid cognition (*janyapramā*), like visual valid cognition.
The meaning is that this [inference] is also non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) because it can be established otherwise.
The phrase "by way of intrinsic nature" (*svatastvena*) means "by the very power of being the generator of knowledge."
The logical connection is with the phrase "by way of being born"—that is, even if [the self] exists as something other [than the body].
The meaning is: "even though it is prompted by a quality.
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the knowledge of fitness, the absence of defects, and so on—because these are not the effective causes (*aprayojakatvāt*).
The meaning is that the probandum stated by you is intended to be understood—i.e., it is what is meant to be expressed.

This should be connected [to the previous statement] as being for the purpose of refuting the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) from the perspective of the previously mentioned portion.
He states another refutation regarding the eternity of the Veda, beginning with the words: "By this, [it is shown that] the Veda's... and "a succession of the blind."
And thus, the sense is that one would have no confidence in the Veda; this is why it says "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
Because it lacks probative force (*aprayojakatva*). *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, Part II, p. 270).

Nor should it be argued that "the Vedas were not composed by an omniscient being because they are Vedas, like worldly speech"— for this would entail the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
But then, is it not established that [the Veda] was composed by one who is not subject to saṃsāra?
And in this way, there is no fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
For, once a non-saṃsāric self is established by the inference: "Selfhood resides in one who is not subject to saṃsāra, because it is a universal (*jāti*), like potness."

If it is argued that the subject under dispute is the speaker of some statement because he possesses selfhood, just like myself—and thus, by this general reasoning, the fact of being composed by one who is not a transmigrating being (asaṃsārin) is established—this is not so.

For, according to the method already stated, due to the principle of parsimony (lāghava), the nature of the Veda and its validity are accounted for even without the author being a non-transmigrating being; therefore, the aforementioned reason is not logically necessary (aprayojaka).

Nor does the Vedic word "I" refer to an independent speaker; for the meaning is that the status of being a valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is established even in the absence of [such] qualities. He clarifies this very point.
Because it lacks a probative force.
Anticipating another ancient inference, he refutes it by means of the fault stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*:
"Nor [are they] the Vedas."

Accepting that the statement in the *Ṭīkā* is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), he anticipates another objection raised by others and refutes it with the words beginning "But then... (*nanu tarhi*).
"In the manner stated."
The syntactical connection is as follows: "by way of reasoning stated [in the passage] beginning with 'like perception' and 'like the knowledge of God which is not produced from qualities.
Having raised another formal argument (prayoga) stated by Udayana, he refutes it with the words "Nor also...
(nāpi).

"Tell me that: 'I am Brahman. "I myself indeed say this," and so forth; the meaning is that the word *aham* (I) and others are substitutes for the first-person pronoun (*asmad-ādeśa*). (Veda-pautvānu-diṅgaḥ)
It should not be argued that the authorship of the Veda is established by the [inference] "because it is a treatise, like the *Sammatasūtra*";
for if that were the case, then according to your own view, the Veda would contain such [authorial statements] as: "May my body be most wise..."
In passages such as "My tongue is most sweet," it refers only to the independent speaker, the Lord (Īśvara) himself; and in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, [it is said]:
"What have we to do with sovereignty, O Govinda?"...
Otherwise, in such passages as "I am your disciple; instruct me who has sought refuge in you," the referent of the word "I" would absurdly have to be Vyāsa himself;
and in worldly usage, in such phrases as "That king must be addressed by you with my words," the referent of "I" would absurdly have to be Kālidāsa and others.

While explaining the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā* with the words, "Because it would follow that sentences such as those expressing intention and prayer would be purposeless (*anarthakatva*) if that were the case," he states the reason: "If that were so" (*tathātve*).

In the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, the prayerful statement heard is: "May my body be possessed of distinguished subjects (viśiṣṭāścarṣaṇyaḥ)—that is, may it be endowed with distinguished offspring—and may my tongue be most honeyed (madhumattamā), that is, exceedingly sweet. Here, the word *asmat* (the form of the first-person pronoun) used in the sense of the sacrificer who performs the prayer refers to the meaning of the Lord. Likewise—
“Of what use to us is sovereignty, Govinda, or enjoyments, or even life?
Thus it is said in the *Gītā* when one is overcome by despondency:
“With my mind utterly bewildered regarding dharma, I ask you...”

In the statement made by Arjuna, “Tell me that which is the certain good; I am your disciple,” there would follow the absurd consequence that the referent of the word *asmad* (the first-person pronoun) as heard in the phrase *na aham* would be Vyāsa himself.
Similarly, in the *Raghuvamśa*, when [Sītā says] “at my word” (*mad-vacanāt*), the referent of the word *asmad* used by Sītā would be Kālidāsa. This is the meaning.
1. *Nayaḥ* – *Mu.* 2. *Maditi* – *Mu.* **Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava** (First Chapter, p.

272) Now, [an objection is raised]: although in passages such as “*śarīraṃ me*” (my body), the Lord (*Īśvara*) and others alone are the independent speakers, it is nevertheless accepted—on the basis of the indicative marks (*liṅga*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth—that the intentions of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and others are incorporated [into the mantra]. Thus, for the sacrificer, Arjuna, Sītā, and so on...

If you argue that the referent of the word "I" is the body itself, then even if the Vedas are not of human origin, I have also accepted— on the basis of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) within mantras such as "May my body [be firm]"— that the intention of the sacrificer or the Lord enters into those mantras; therefore, let it be that in such cases the referent of the word "I" is the sacrificer, while in passages such as "Worship Me," the referent is the Lord.
Furthermore, in my view, the Lord possesses independent speakership by virtue of being the utterer [of words] without depending on the utterance by another.

By this, the argument that the non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) of the Veda is established through the use of the first-person singular ending in expressions such as "may I not become" (*mā bhūvam*)—on the grounds that the number expressed by that [ending] cannot be connected to an independent speaker—is refuted. Anticipating the rebuttal stated in the *Ṭīkā*—"For we do not say that there is no entry of human intention whatsoever in the Veda"—the author speaks by way of another's mouth, beginning with the words "But the body... (*nanu śarīram*).
Regarding the phrase "mantraliṅga": it refers to the indicative mark of the mantra.
The technical definition of the Mīmāṃsakas and others is that the "indicative power of a mantra" (mantraliṅga) is its capacity to convey a specific meaning.
The nature of this indicative power, as well as context (prakaraṇa) and so forth, will be made clear later in the second chapter.

The meaning is that when a mantra possesses the capacity to convey a certain meaning, or when there is context, position, and so on, one accepts the entry of that [meaning] into the intended purpose of the mantra.

In that case, since [passages] such as "Worship me" (mām upāsva) would not be devoted to anything other than the independent speaker, they would have the status of proving what is already established; therefore, he states "furthermore" (kiñca) to show this.
"May we be so."

“May we be masters of riches; may I always be under your protection. (RV 8.48.1) [Note: The variants indicate that the word ‘anu’ is absent in the manuscripts Mu and Ca; the reading ‘tā’ is found in Ca; the reading ‘ma bhūvam’ is found in Mu and Cha; the reading ‘vanya’ is found in Kuṃ; and the variant ‘syāmiti’ in Mu refers back to the phrase ‘syāma hite sadamid rātau tava syām’.]
Regarding the doctrine of the non-human authorship of the Vedas (*vedāpauruṣeyatva-vāda*) [Puṇyarāja 273]:
because even in such passages as “I take your hand for the sake of good fortune” (*gṛbhṇāmi te saubhagatvasya hastam*), we observe the connection with speakers who are dependent on others.

On the contrary, it is precisely in your own position that the use of the plural and other such forms would be improper in passages such as “May we be lords of riches” and “We shall offer you the most abundant speech of homage,” because the independent speaker, the Lord, is a single entity.
By this, the argument that the Vedic use of the word *yuṣmad* (you) establishes its human authorship—
on the grounds that it denotes an independent speaker addressing someone— is refuted;

for in instances such as “*tvāṃ prapannam*” (“to you who have sought refuge”) and “*vācyastvayā*” (“it should be told by you”), the word is employed even when the speaker is dependent on another and the listener is merely being made aware [of something].

And in the third [case], the qualification "becoming an object" applies.

And here, in the *Bhāṣya* and other works, when defining "having an agent" (*sakartṛkatva*), the term "material cause" (*upādāna*) is inserted; furthermore, the terms "inhering" (*samaveta*) and "absence of material cause" (*upādānābhāva*) are employed within the subject (*pakṣa*), the probandum (*sādhya*), and the reason (*hetu*) in order to establish a "having-an-agent-ness" that excludes destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).

Likewise, because the potter’s action is the counter-positive of a prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) which is pervaded by a prior absence of a future unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) of the same class as the unseen force that produces the pot, the aforementioned defect remains as it was.

The sense is this: for that reason, following the direction stated by the *Ṭhakkura*, one would have to intend "causality" in the form of being a producer (*phalopadhāna*), which is a difficulty; and furthermore, to avoid confusion with the subsequent probandum (*sādhya*), one must intend "produced by itself" (*svajanya*).
Thus, [the opponent objects] that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

In this context, since the term "its own" (*sva-pada*) refers to the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) mentioned in proximity, the intention is that although the action performed by a living being such as ourselves may be the cause of the earth and so forth, it occurs only through the medium of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) and not directly; thus, because [the probandum] does not exist subsequent to the *adṛṣṭa* that precedes the production of the earth and so forth, there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*).
However, in the case of *Ṭhakkura* and others, there is [the fallacy] partially with respect to things such as the form of Kālī.

To prevent the over-extension [of the definition] to established sounds, it was stated that the qualification "preceded by the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of its own producer" is necessary; this is addressed in the third [case] as well.
The phrase "for the purpose of excluding [the fallacy of] proving what is already established" is to be supplied;
thus [is] the qualification.

The meaning is that [the qualities] are inherent in the material cause of the objects of his knowledge and so forth; the point is that in the case of the earth and other elements, there is an absence of inherence in the objects of the knowledge and so forth of beings such as ourselves.

Since the previously mentioned formulation would fail to establish the existence of a creator who is the maker of the entire world— because destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) would not thereby result in having a creator—

the alternative view stated in the *Maṇi* beginning with "Or else" (*yadvā*) is restated here by the passage beginning with "And here," after first clarifying the intended meaning of the previously mentioned position.
"By means of the mere [measure]," it says.
The meaning of the word *mātra* (only/alone) is "in the absence of being composed of [factors] such as grasping (*upādāna*)"; that is, in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth.
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 194). (Note: The word *prayukta* is not present in manuscript *ga*.)

However, when the destruction of the effect is intended to be proven merely by its having a non-agent as its cause, thereby establishing God, then words such as "inhering" (*samaveta*) and so forth need not be considered at all in the formulation of the thesis (*pakṣa*).

In this view, the destruction of the effort (*kṛti*) belonging to agents such as ourselves that produces jars and the like would lack the property of being "distinct from that [effort]"—because it is produced by an effort of the aforementioned nature—and thus it would not possess the status of being the subject of the thesis (*pakṣatā*).
To avoid this, the word "effort" (*kṛti*) should be replaced by "that which has an object" (*saviṣaya*) or "the triad" (*tritaya*).

And thus, although the destruction of an action (*kṛti*) is produced by its counter-positive—the action itself—and by a subsequent cognition that is a quality (*guṇa*) not incompatible with it, it lacks the property of being produced by a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*). Likewise, although the destruction of a desire to act is produced by both the desire to act and the action according to the aforementioned method, it lacks the property of being produced by a cognition (*jñāna*). Therefore, both of these [destructions] are established as the subject (*pakṣa*).

The meaning is that, among the subject (*pakṣa*), the probandum (*sādhya*), and the reason (*hetu*), words expressing the state of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) or a non-inherent cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) are not required.

"Now, if the definition of the subject (*pakṣa*) were stated simply as 'produced things distinct from those produced by an effort that does not have the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as its instrumental cause,' then the destruction of the effort that produces a jar would not possess the status of being the subject;

therefore, it has been argued that one must intend the property of 'not being produced by an effort or a desire that is not itself produced [by another effort],' thereby establishing that the destruction of effort and so forth do indeed possess the status of the subject."
Thus he says: "And in this..."
"Having an object" (saviṣayaka).

The meaning is that it must be stated that produced [cognitions] are distinct from those produced by the triad [of causes] which have an object and do not have the unseen (adṛṣṭa) as their mediate instrument—this is what is meant by "contradictory" (virodhī).
Because it is produced by a subsequent action that constitutes a specific quality of the higher self, he says: "the desire to act" (cikīrṣā).
"Knowledge," it says.

The sense is that, because the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) necessarily precedes it, [the volition] cannot be the producer of its destruction, since it is the producer of that [action]. This applies to both of them as well.
(The Refutation of the Theory that [Action] is Dependent on Desire)
Alternatively, let the earth itself be the subject (*pakṣa*). (Īśvaravādaḥ, p. 295)
But surely, in this case, there would be inconclusiveness due to doubt (*saṃdigdhānaikāntya*) regarding the sprout, which is other than the subject (*pakṣa*).

Nor should it be argued that the fault lies only in the doubt regarding the presence of the probans (*sādhana*) in that which is ascertained to lack the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*), and not also in the non-ascertainment of the probans in that where the probandum is doubted; for the seed of the fault—the doubt that the reason (*hetu*) applies to instances lacking the probandum—is present in both cases alike. And it is not so...

If it is argued that because such a doubt exists even regarding the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be the total abolition of inference itself— and that for this very reason the qualification "other than the subject" (*pakṣād anyatra*) was specified— that is not so. For if,

in the term "subject" (*pakṣa*) within the phrase "other than the subject," one intends to mean the subject as the object of the formal argument (*prayoga-viṣaya*), then there would follow the abolition of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
The meaning is that it applies to both the act of doing and the act of destroying.

But even so, not every destruction (dhvaṃsa) can be the subject (pakṣa), because the destruction of the final jar, pleasure, and so forth, must necessarily be excluded from the subject. Otherwise, since that [final destruction] is neither an object of enjoyment nor a means to it, it would not be produced by unseen merit (adṛṣṭa); consequently, as the unseen merit that produces it would be unestablished, the aforementioned probandum (sādhya) would be impossible, resulting in the fallacy of sublation (bādha) regarding that portion.

Following the direction already stated, since mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), it is unestablished in that [opponent’s] view, and thus there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Therefore, in accordance with the preference expressed by Pakṣadhara, the *Maṇi* states an alternative position—beginning with “Or rather, the earth alone is the subject”—and provides a justification for it; this he expresses with the words “Alternatively (*yadvā*)”.
The term "pakṣa" means a side or position.
The meaning is "the object of the thesis," because the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), characterized by doubt and so forth, exists elsewhere as well.

If the earth itself is the subject (*pakṣa*), then extract and explain the suspicion of a sublation (*bādhaka*) as stated by Maṇi, along with its refutation, from the words beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*) up to the end of "the establishment of what is desired" (*iṣṭasiddheḥ*).
It is stated that [the reason] must be "other than the subject" (*pakṣād anya*) out of fear of the total abolition of inference (*anumāna*).
