Since the sprout is also a subject (pakṣa) when there is an intention to state [the definition] as possessing the characteristics of a subject,
for this very reason the conventional designation "subject-equivalent" (pakṣasama) is applied to it.
However, the sprout is not mentioned because the desired conclusion is established even by taking only the earth as the subject.

Now, one might object: "In that case, even a doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—which is introduced by a doubtful qualifying condition (*upādhi*)—would not be a defect in the subject (*pakṣa*) itself. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that there is a disparity [between the two cases] because, while in that [other] case there is no certainty of pervasion (*vyāpti*) due to the absence of a supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*), here there is such certainty because the very destruction of the reason in the form of 'being an effect' (*kāryatva*) acts as a subverting factor (*bādhaka*). [Response: This should not be said.

If it is argued that, since doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) constitutes a defect [in an argument], then for the *tarka* (reductio) as well, its root would become weakened by the presence of doubt regarding deviation in the subject—this is not so;
for the true nature of the subject will be defined later, just like the definition of the subject itself.

The meaning is: "like the non-existence of form," because there is an absence of both proving and refuting evidence accompanied by the absence of the desire to prove [the probandum]. For this very reason—the sense being that the term *sama* (equal) is employed because of the absence of being the object of the proposition (*pratijñā*), precisely when the definition of the subject (*pakṣa*) is present—it is because the desired [conclusion] is already established.

The meaning is either that the existence of God is established by that alone, or else that because a logical mark (liṅga) whose pervasion is ascertained in the case of a jar and so forth is observed both in the subject (pakṣa) and in a similar instance (sapakṣa), inference arises in both cases.

Regarding the point that there is no fault in the ascertainment of the reason (hetu) in a locus where the probandum (sādhya) is doubtful, he states the refutation and the forthcoming resolution with the words beginning "nanu" and ending with "adoṣatvāt."
"Because it is doubtful."

The meaning is that [the statement] "He is dark-skinned because he is the son of Mitrā" involves even a doubt of deviation (vyabhicāra-saṃśaya), rooted in a doubt regarding the probandum (sādhya) due to the uncertainty of the exclusion of the probans from the subject (pakṣa-vyāvṛtti-saṃdeha) caused by the extraneous condition (upādhi) of being produced from the cooking of vegetables (*śāka-pāka-ja*) in the case of the eighth fetus.
The underlying intention is that if such a doubt were not a defect in that instance, there would be a certainty of pervasion (*vyāpti-niścaya*).
Anticipating the objection that the lack of certainty regarding pervasion in that case must have another cause, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
"Of reasoning as well."

The meaning is that even for an inference of the form "the reason would not exist in the absence of the probandum," there is doubt regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the consequence (*āpādya*) and the consequence-inducer (*āpādaka*), [due to] "disagreement" (*vipratipatti*) and so forth.
[Notes on variants: 1. *tvaṅku-kuṃ*; 2. *śayo-cha-kha*; 3. *nniścayaḥ -cha*; 4. *nniśca-cha*; 5. *śayasya-ka-cha-kha*; 6. *syādoṣatvāt / tasya dū -kuṃ*.
(The Refutation of the Dependence on God) The Doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), Part II, p. 297.

Even though doubt—which is produced by conflicting views (*vipratipatti*) and so forth, which serves as the basis for the subjecthood (*pakṣatā*) [of an inference], and which is conducive to inference—is not a defect, nevertheless, such doubt induced by a *upādhi* (limiting condition) is a defect because it functions in that [inferential] manner.

Is it not the case that this [argument] is inconclusive? For, since God’s eternal and all-encompassing activity is currently doubted, there is no certainty regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of activity in general—whether spatially or temporally—and thus the causality of activity in general toward effects in general cannot be apprehended.
However, in the case of fire and smoke in general, there is indeed certainty regarding their negative concomitance in places such as a lake; if this is argued, we say no.

Since there is no sublation when one perceives either the distinction or the causal status between the specific forms of the jar and the potter, the causal status of the two generalities is also established;
the word "etcetera" (ādi) refers to common properties and so forth—[the phrase] "by way of not being such" [refers to this].
The meaning is "by way of not being conducive to inference.

With the words beginning "Now, the apprehension of pervasion between effort and its effect is not [established] through positive and negative concomitance," he restates the very portion of the critique stated in the *Maṇi*, preceded by an objection—starting with "But this... and so forth.
The meaning is that this is an inference based on the nature of being an effect of a cause and so forth—[the word] "now" [is used].
The meaning is "prior to inference.

It should be understood that since the absence of God's activity is not [established] even in the Nyāya system, the objection and its resolution are stated solely with reference to the primary [absence], namely the mere negative concomitance (vyatireka).

Or rather, this is also an indication of the inclusion of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For if it were otherwise, there would be the total abolition of inference (*anumāna*) itself; therefore, he says: "Fire," etc., and "Jar," etc.
The meaning is: between the specific form of the jar and the specific form of the potter’s action—[this refers to] the state of being a cause.
The meaning is: "of the relation between cause and effect.
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 298) (Note: Variants from manuscripts: 1. *na tasyā* — Kuṃ; 2. *tasyeti nāsti* — Kuṃ; 3. *vā iti nāsti* — Cha-Kha.)

Otherwise, how could space and so forth be established as the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of sound and the like, given that their status as such is determined through the ascertainment of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the general category of inherent cause, since space and so forth are eternal and all-pervading?

If it is argued: "Even so, the example is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because there is no evidence to establish that the potter is not the cause when the causality of the potter's action alone is apprehended through positive and negative concomitance," we say: No.

Since the conjunction of the self with effort is a cause of the jar by way of [producing] motion, the self—just like the effort—is a cause as a qualifier of that [conjunction]. Even if one were to postulate [the existence of the self] on the grounds that it is an effect, such as being the speaker’s cognition of the sentence-meaning based on the sentence being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no sublation [of the self], because the general category of sentences and the general category of the speaker’s cognition do not sublate it; thus it is said: "the establishment of [entities such as] space."

The meaning is that, in this case, one must follow the very method already stated—namely, the apprehension of the exclusion (vyatireka) and so forth of the two qualifiers themselves, such as the jar and the potsherd; [the reason is] "because it is not a cause."
And thus, the meaning is that the probandum—in the form of being produced by some [specific cause]—is not present there.

The claim that there is a lack of evidence (*mānābhāva*) is unestablished; for one might argue that the potter is the cause of the jar because he delimits the conjunction that is its cause—just like the potsherd, or like the self-conjunction of the cause of the jar, or like [the body] possessing a single effort—and it is with this intention that he says [there is no such lack of evidence].
"With effort" means:
The phrase "of effort alone" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*);
it should also be understood as referring to things such as the potsherd, which is the substratum of the non-inherent cause (the conjunction) [of the pot].

[Objection: Surely, when there is conjunction with the self, movement does not occur without effort; therefore, effort alone is the cause, and not the conjunction of the self with that which possesses effort. To this, he says: "Of the conjunction...
(The Refutation of the Absence of Divine Will)
Regarding the proof for conjunction being a cause [of action], as stated in the *Īśvaravāda* (p.

299): "Action has as its non-inherent cause the conjunction of the self with that which possesses effort, because it is the counter-positive of a difference produced by the absence of a quality residing in something other than itself."
That which possesses an absence conditioned by the absence of its own non-co-substrate quality is the inherent cause of conjunction with that [quality].

— The connection with what follows is as follows: the proof for the fact that the conjunction of the self with the possessor of effort is the cause of the body's movement (ceṣṭā), which is the cause of the jar's production, is inference; thus [it is said] "movement" (ceṣṭā).
The meaning is "the vibration of the body"—that is, [caused by] effort.
The meaning is that [the action] has as its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) the conjunction of the self possessing effort and the body.
The qualification "possessing effort" and so forth is for the purpose of excluding other objects by means of the conjunction of impact.
In the reason, the word "sva" refers to motion.

The meaning is as follows: "having a different locus" means having a locus distinct from its own locus; "belonging to that" (tadīya) means its own quality, namely effort (*prayatna*); [the reason is] because it is the counter-positive of an absence whose occurrence is necessitated by the absence of that [quality].

The term "belonging to that" is stated in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the color of a jar produced from the color of a potter's wheel, which is its own [but not its own effort].
"Belonging to itself" (*ātmīya*) is the intended meaning.
Alternatively, the reason should be understood as "because it is an action whose counter-correlate has been mentioned";
therefore, there is no deviation [from the rule],
since the very reason [for such a deviation] is absent.
And thus, even though the word *tat* in the phrase *tadiya* refers to that which is co-referential with it, there is no fault;
the function of the word having a different grammatical coreference will be made clear later.

Although, in the *Maṇi*, it is stated that "the action which is produced by a quality residing in a different locus" and so forth—thereby implying that the reason (*hetu*) should be "because it is produced by a quality" and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) should be demonstrated in that very same way—nevertheless, even if an action were produced by a quality belonging to God (*īśvara*), it would not have the conjunction with God as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Therefore, in order to exclude such a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the meaning of that commentary is restated in the passage beginning with "caused by the absence of a quality," etc., where "that" refers to the action known as "motion" (*parispanda*). This is the sense.
Even in the case of a gem (*maṇi*), there is the statement: "the action [is] also... [The text continues:
"What is the inference regarding gravity? and so forth. [Note: The word *guṇa* is absent in manuscript *a*.
From the *Nyāyadīpāyutatarkatāṇḍava*, First Chapter, page 300.
For example, the inference that the movement of leaves and the like, which is caused by the impact of wind possessing touch and velocity, has the conjunction with wind as its non-inherent cause.

In order to exclude the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)— namely, that falling, which is the counter-correlative of the absence conditioned by the absence of gravity, is co-located with gravity, yet lacks having the conjunction of a substance possessing gravity as its non-inherent cause— the phrase "having a different locus than itself" (*svavyadhikaraṇa*) was stated in the reason (*hetu*).
Otherwise, motion (*ceṣṭā*) itself would not even arise.
Because there is no non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa),
and because effort cannot be established as a cause due to the absence of causal proximity (kāraṇapratyāsatti).
Nor should it be argued that, even so, the self is merely the delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) of the causal conjunction and not itself the cause;
for otherwise, there would be the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the color of a jar produced by the color of its potsherds—as follows.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "just like the action of a leaf, etc.
In that context, the term "possessing touch" (*sparśavat*) is used for the purpose of manifesting the existence of the probans (*hetu*).

The meaning is: the action of a leaf, etc., is the counter-positive of an absence (*vyatireka-pratiyogin*) whose own absence is necessitated by the absence of a quality consisting of motion belonging to air, which is in a different locus from itself—namely, in the case of falling.

The meaning is "the falling of mangoes, fruits, and so forth. If one were to state merely that [the subject] is the counter-positive of an absence whose own absence is necessitated by the absence of something residing in a different locus from itself, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the action of a mango tree falling; for in that case, the mango tree—which resides in a different locus from the action—is a whole (*avayavī*) because of its connection with the parts (*avayava*) that constitute it.

Even though it possesses the property of being the counter-positive of an absence conditioned by the absence of that [sound], because it lacks the status of having conjunction with the parts of the drum as its non-inherent cause, it was stated: "that which has a quality belonging to it."
He states the favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) for the reason (*hetu*), which consists in the sublation of the opposing side (*vipakṣabādhakarūpa*), by saying "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
The meaning is "the absence of the stated probandum"—namely, [the absence] of the cause.
The word "otherwise" (anyathā) is to be supplied [from the preceding context].
The meaning is "proximity that has become the cause.
The intention is that if that which is not proximate were to function as a cause, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

And because of the rule that "that which is the substratum of the non-inherent cause of conjunction is necessarily the producer of its effect," the author of the *Maṇi* clarifies this very point by way of an illustration—namely, "the cause of the jar"—in order to refute [the claim] that [God] is not the agent of creation. (Note: The word ‘samavāyi’ appears as an addition in manuscript *kha*. (The Refutation of the Claim that [God] is Not the Agent of Creation)
The doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), p. 301:
[This is] because it is observed that the potsherd, which is the substratum of the conjunction that serves as the cause of the jar, is itself a cause of the jar.

[Objection: "But surely, since knowledge is a cause of action toward a jar or the like only by way of volition (*kṛti*), and since volition itself has as its cause only the inference of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) is not a cause [of volition]; thus, there is a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). [Reply: This is not so.
For volition has an accomplished entity as its locus and an unaccomplished object as its domain.

In that regard, although there exists an inference of being a means to a desired end regarding the jar or the like—which constitutes the "probandum" portion—there is observed an absence of volition in the absence of direct perception of the "established" portion, such as the potsherds and so forth; therefore, direct perception of the material cause (*upādāna-sākṣātkāra*) is also [required].
Because it is the cause.

Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of an action directed toward the mind as its object caused by a mental operation, because a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the mind as its object—being co-located with the action—is not established; for [in such a case], an action arises in the channel (*nāḍī*) through an effort whose object is the channel carrying the mind, which is perceived by the sense of touch. "Now, the cognition that something is a means to a desired end, achievable through the effort to make a pot, is the cause [of action] by way of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*)."

And by the words "But that is not perception," etc., he restates the refutation of the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and its resolution as set forth in the *Maṇi* itself, but extracted in a different manner, starting with "Now, [is it]... and so on.
"To be proven" (sādhya).

The meaning is that the probandum (sādhya) consists of such properties as being produced by one who possesses knowledge, desire to act, and volition, which are not mediated by the sphere of grasping (upādāna); [the term] "inconstancy" (vyabhicāra) refers to this.

The meaning is that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) from the principle that "whatever action has a certain thing as its ultimate goal must be preceded by the direct perception (aparokṣa) of that object."
He clarifies that very point with the words: "of that which is in grammatical apposition."
By the phrase "from direct perception, etc.," the word "etc. includes the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).
The intended meaning is that [the mind] is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*); thus it is said, "carried by the mind" (*manovahanā*).

Due to the specific conjunction (*saṃyogaviśeṣa*) in the form of a push (*nodana*) within the *vega-nāḍī*, the production of mental activity (*manasikriyā*) occurs. *Note: Variants: 1. tvāt - mu-ca; 2. 'na' is not present - cha-kha; 3. kṛtyasiddha- cha-kha.* *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (First Chapter, p. 302). --- Through a particular conjunction in the form of a propulsion within the *vega-nāḍī*, the production of mental activity arises.
Even though the mere material cause is established,
nevertheless, because it is to be proven as possessing the quality of being an effect, a desire to act with respect to it is appropriate.

Nor should it be argued that, because we observe in a jar both the production of a direct perception whose object is already established and the production of an indirect (parokṣa) cognition whose object is not yet established, God’s eternal inference must likewise be eternal like His eternal perception;

for while there exists an indirect cognition of established objects such as atoms, we do not observe a cessation of effort apart from the absence of immediacy (aparokṣatva), just as we do not observe a cessation of effort apart from the absence of indirectness when there is a cognition of the portion to be accomplished (the sādhya).
The meaning is that [the mind] is the substratum of the action—because the production of the action occurs in the mind.
And thus, wherever there is volitional effort (*kṛti*), there is the state of being preceded by direct perception (*aparokṣa*) and so forth;
and where there is no direct knowledge in the mind, there is no volitional effort. The point is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Having restated the objection—"Even so, since the desire for action (cikīrṣā) is impossible with respect to a material cause when there is an absence of the desire for the instrument, the deficiency of the probandum (sādhyavaikalya) remains"—he refutes it by saying "yadyapi" (even though).

Having thus refuted the arguments regarding the lack of necessity (*aprayojakatva*) and the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), he restates the response to the doubt concerning the subversion by the *tarka* (reductio) mentioned in the *Maṇi*— namely, "In that case, since the production of inferential cognition is observed in the case of a jar and so forth, there would likewise be an inference regarding God"— with the words beginning with "And not" (*na ca*).

Since there is an absence of produced knowledge in God, how could there be knowledge produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*)? To this he says: although perception is produced by the senses, just like eternal perception, so too, although inference is produced by a logical mark, it would be eternal.

The sense is that if inference were non-eternal, the production of the first dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth at the beginning of time would not occur, because of the resulting absence of bodies and sense organs which are invariably concomitant with such [non-eternal] cognition. This remains true even regarding its being immediate (*aparokṣa*).
The meaning is "in that knowledge"—that is, "the one who has accomplished [his purpose]."
The meaning is that it has the atom as its object of operation— this refers to the phrase "the part to be established" (*sādhyāṃśa*). (The Refutation of the Deficiency of the Lord’s Will)
The Doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda), Part II—303.
Objection: Is there not a deviation [in the inference] regarding that which is produced by an effort born of hatred, due to the absence of desire to act (*cikīrṣā*)?
Nor can it be assumed that even in such cases, the Lord’s desire to act is the cause.

If it is argued that, by this very reasoning, since the examples established by effort (*kṛti*) originating from aversion would apply to earth and so forth as well— resulting in their being produced like aversion and thus leading to the consequence of eternal aversion— the answer is no. For even in those cases, since the absence of aversion itself is desired,

just as when there is a mediate cognition in the form of an inference where the object to be accomplished— such as a jar or a cloth— is the means to a desired end, one observes effort residing in the potsherds and other materials which are its causes.

When there is a direct cognition (*aparokṣajñāna*) of the object to be accomplished (*sādhyāṃśa*) as being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), one never observes the absence of an effort directed toward that cause which has the object to be accomplished as its domain; therefore, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is simply the fact that the object to be accomplished is known as a means to a desired end that is the causal factor for the effort directed toward that cause, and not the indirectness (*parokṣatva*) of the cognition of the object to be accomplished as a means to a desired end.
Because of [the Lord's] veneration:

the sense is that, in this way, even for Īśvara, there exists a direct (aparokṣa) cognition of the fact that the portion to be accomplished—consisting of the earth and so forth—is produced by its own creator; thus, his activity regarding the atoms and other materials which are the causes of those things is logical, and consequently, there is no fault of falling into the consequence of [his] being subject to constant inference.

Having thus removed the fallacy regarding the fact that action is preceded by immediate knowledge, and having rejected the excessive consequence (atiprasaṅga) that followed from it, [the author] now states the very argument mentioned in the *Maṇi* to refute the objection concerning the fallacy regarding the fact that action is preceded by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*): "But [what about] aversion... and so forth.
The meaning is: [the object] is that which is to be accomplished by an effort conducive to the cessation of suffering caused by aversion, such as the absence of suffering and so forth.

He says "for in this way" (*evam hi*) because, although there would be no deviation [from the rule] if one were to postulate a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) on the part of God (*īśvara*), there would nonetheless be the consequence of an undesirable result.

In that regard, there is no such thing as being produced from hatred in the case of an action, by virtue of which—through that example—it might follow that even in the case of the earth and so forth, there would be a state of being produced [by an agent] just as there is hatred. Nor is there a lack of evidence for aversion (*dveṣa*), because there is no absence of an effort toward cessation (*nivṛtti-yatna*)—which is distinct from the effort toward activity, is conducive to the exclusion of action, and is prompted by aversion;
for there is the uncontradicted experience: "I am averse."

The meaning is that even in the case of a means for the absence of suffering, when there is the cognition of it as a means—that is, as a means for the absence of what is detested—only a desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) directed toward that means is possible; thus [it is said] "distinct" (*bhinna*).

The meaning is that because the hatred directed toward an enemy and the volitional effort (kṛti) directed toward the means of killing him have different objects, hatred toward the enemy is not the cause for the volitional effort directed toward the means of accomplishing the absence of the object of hatred.
Anticipating the objection that if hatred were not a cause of action, then hatred would be entirely unreal, he states its non-establishment by means of perception: "And it is not so."

Thus, the logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: since hatred is the cause [of action] only when it is produced with respect to the means and the object of activity, there is a lack of evidence for hatred in relation to its own object [the thing hated].

Because hatred alone is the cause of an effort in the form of cessation (*nivṛtti*) toward things such as the means to suffering—even though that effort has a different object—therefore, the evidence for hatred consists solely in the effect, which is cessation; hence it is said "in activity" (*pravṛtti*), meaning an effort in the form of activity, i.e., action (*kriyā*).
The meaning is that it is to be inferred from the gestures of the limbs; [this is stated] because of its absence [otherwise].

The meaning is that there is an absence of effort in the form of cessation—which is produced by aversion toward the object of suffering—because such effort must be conducive to the non-existence of effects such as suffering.

If there were a twofold nature of effort, consisting of both the form of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and the form of cessation (*nivṛtti*), then the effort of engagement would be accomplished through the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), which in turn depends on the cognition of something as a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*);
whereas the effort of cessation would be accomplished by aversion. In that case, aversion would be established as having a valid basis (*prāmāṇika*).
But it is not so;
for cessation is simply the absence of effort in the form of activity.
Nor should one suspect the opposite— that activity is merely the absence of effort characterized by cessation— for that would be a contradiction. (The Refutation of the Absence of Desire)

[Objection: Even so, since it has been ascertained that in the case of a jar and the like, volitional effort (*kṛti*) characterized by purposeful activity (*ceṣṭā-vyāpāraka*) alone is the cause, [it follows that] in the case of the earth and so forth, volitional effort is not the cause, because it is sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi-bādhita*). Nor is this the case— [End of fragment]
For, in the state of deep sleep, since there is an absence of cessation [of activity], there would follow the occurrence of effects such as physical movements accomplished through active engagement.
Nor is it correct to say that at that time there is simply no absence of cessation;
for since there is then an absence of the cognition that [the object] is a means to suffering, the cause of cessation—namely, aversion—is absent, and thus cessation itself is absent.
Nor does this contradict the argument of Kusumāñjali, which states that "the effort toward activity arises from attachment, but cessation [from it] arises from aversion";
for while that is the case in his view, it is not so in the view of the author of the *Maṇi* (Udayana), as otherwise one would ask: "From where, then, does aversion arise?"
This is because it contradicts the statement in the *Maṇi*: "I hate my enemies," which is an uncontradicted perception.

By this, it should be understood that the laborious interpretation of the meaning of the *Maṇi* passage beginning with "kutaḥ" (from what?), which was offered by Pakṣadhara in accordance with the words of the *Kusumāñjali*, is rooted in a lack of knowledge regarding the intention of the author of the *Maṇi*.

Having thus established, by refuting the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), that action (*kṛti*) is preceded by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) which arises from immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), [the author] addresses the doubt regarding sublation (*bādha*) and its resolution as stated in the *Maṇi*—namely, that "in the case of a jar and the like, the state of being achievable through action (*kṛtisādhyatā*) occurs only through the mediation of the operation of the hands and so forth, and not directly"—by saying: "But even so... and so on.

The meaning is: even in the absence of defects such as being irrelevant (*aprayojakatva*), deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), deviation (*vyabhicāra*), contradiction by a reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*) consisting in the undesirable consequence of eternal inference and eternal aversion, [there is] "activity" (*ceṣṭā*).
The meaning is "movement of the limbs"—that is, the state of being causeless.
And thus, the sense is that [the object] produced by volition is sublated.
It is not by virtue of having become a door to both effort and action that [the pot] is the cause in the case of a jar and so forth, but rather each one individually.
Nor does this entail an impossibility of priority and posteriority between the action and the effort;
for even though father and son have a relation of priority and posteriority, it is possible for both to be independent causes with respect to a single jar.
And thus, with the intention that there is no sublation (*bādha*) regarding the aforementioned probandum (*sādhya*), he raises an objection and refutes it, saying: "Not so" (*na ca*).

*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 306) [Note: The text provided contains various manuscript variants indicated by the abbreviations *gyopa*, *ca.*, *tvena*, *kṛ*, *mu*, *ca..*, *ṇaika*, and *mu.*]

Nor can it be [the case] that, as with father and son in a single jar, effort (*ceṣṭā*) and volitional action (*kṛti*) are independent causes; for then even a person who is present as the substratum of an effort conducive to the jar, who possesses a volition conducive to it, but whose body is rendered motionless by shackles and is thus devoid of effort, would incur the status of being its cause. If you say this, it is not so.
The causality [of the agent] as the performer of purposeful activity does not apply to the mere effect, such as the earth and so forth,
because you yourself do not accept it as such due to the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra).
Nor [is it a cause] in that which is delimited by being produced by an effort (*kṛtijanyatva*),
because effort-produced-ness cannot be its own delimiting property due to the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Furthermore, while such causality may exist in specific effects like jars, according to the maxim of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*), effort is the cause of effects in general precisely as "effort-ness" (*kṛtitva*).
For this very reason, limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as "being produced by effort" or "being produced by a body" are also not [valid] reasons.
He states that they are not individually reasons because of their deviation (*vyabhicāra*), saying: "The pot... and so forth.

Mentally considering the alternatives— whether [the probans] refers to "effect" in general, or to "effect produced by volitional effort" in general, or to specific effects such as a jar— he rejects the first two and states that there is no sublation (bādha) in the final case because the desired conclusion is established, beginning with the words "ceṣṭā" and ending with "tvayāpi."
"Even by one who does not accept a Lord (nirīśvara) and so forth"—the meaning is:
"not only by me who maintains that the Lord is bodiless."—[Thus it is said: "limited" (avacchinna).
The phrase "in the mere effect" is carried over [from the previous context]—namely, "the universal."

The meaning is as follows: according to the principle that "if there is a causal relationship between two particulars in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it exists between their universals as well," since there is no subverting factor in the form of a deviation regarding the causal relationship between the particular effect, such as a jar, and the effort-mediated volition (*kṛti*), one may postulate a causal relationship between "effect-ness" (*kāryatva*) and "volition-ness" (*kṛtitva*). Even in this position, volition alone is the cause; therefore [it is said] "for this very reason."

The meaning is: precisely because it is established by logic (*nyāya*) that being produced by an agent (*kṛtijanyatva*) follows from the fact of being an effect (*kṛtitva*). (The Refutation of the Absence of Desire to Act)
The doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), page 307:
Due to the weight [of the evidence], the adjunct (*upādhi*)—by virtue of its form as "being an effort" (*ceṣṭātva*) and so forth—is not a necessary condition for causality.
If it is argued that there is nevertheless a sublation of the pervasion (vyāpti) such as "knowledge is necessarily non-eternal" or "the agent is necessarily embodied," we say no;
for since there is no causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) or the like between the property of being knowledge and the property of being eternal, there is no pervasion at all.
Furthermore, [the pervasion holds] because of the causal relation between the effect and its function.
Otherwise, by the pervasion that "the part is either large or [otherwise]," even the ultimate atom (paramāṇu) would not be established.

For this very reason, the counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) based on [the reason] "not being produced by eternal cognition that does not have the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) as its instrument" and so forth is also refuted.
The phrase "produced by one possessing non-eternal cognition, etc. is the meaning of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*); [the conclusion] is "no" (*na*).
The meaning is that it does not exist—as [defined] by such properties as being an action (ceṣṭā) and so forth.
The category of "body-ness" (śarīratva) and so forth.

It might be argued that this is contradicted by the perception of the initial apprehension of pervasion—such as "the agent is indeed embodied" and "knowledge is indeed non-eternal"—and so forth; thus, he restates the answer to the aforementioned objection by extracting its essence, beginning with "But surely...
and ending with "otherwise."

The meaning is that there is an acceptance of pervasion even in the absence of favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*), such as the non-occurrence of the reason without the probandum (*sādhya*) due to the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) which necessitates pervasion.

The proof of atoms (paramāṇu) through such inferences as "the dyad (dvyaṇuka) is pervaded by a substance possessing a dimension smaller than its own, because it is an effect, like a jar" would not be possible; for there would be a sublation (bādhāt) by the following reasoning: "whatever is an absence [of grossness] is large, as in the case of a triad (tryaṇuka) and so forth; and this atom is a constituent part. This is the meaning.

But even so, one might argue that the earth and so forth do not possess the aforementioned probandum, because they are not produced by a non-eternal cognition mediated by the unseen (adṛṣṭa), just like a pot; thus, there is a counter-argument (satpratipakṣatva).

To show that the two reasons [in the counter-argument] are stated with the qualification "not mediated by the unseen" in order to avoid the fallacy of the unestablished (asiddhi), he says: "For this very reason."

Because it lacks probative force;
for since "being unproduced" alone can serve as the reason, any further qualification that is not useful for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is redundant.
For this very reason, even the counter-objection regarding the horn of a hare is refuted;
for in that case, there is an absence of supporting reasoning (*anukūlatarka*), whereas here, oneness [of the substrate] follows from parsimony (*lāghava*).

Now, it may be argued that since an inference possesses as its qualifier only the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*) with respect to the pervaded aspect, here too the pervader—the agent—would not be established as being qualified by the property of agency (*kartṛtva*), which is the delimitor of pervasion. If you ask, "How then can he be established as being one?", do not say so. For although it is thus through the power of the general causal complex for inference, it is possible for this [oneness] to be a qualifier through the power of the causal complex of valid cognition, which has the form of the auxiliary principle of parsimony (*lāghavatarka*).

That cognition and so forth, which have the earth and other elements as their material cause and object-domain, is one and eternal due to parsimony (*lāghava*), because there is no factor to restrict its scope; thus, [the argument] that color and so forth residing in potsherds and pots [are distinct] is unproven (*aprayojakatva*).

[Objection: "But in that case, if one were to prove what is unestablished, then by the argument 'A rabbit has horns because it is an animal, like a cow,' the existence of a rabbit's horn would also be established. [The author] replies: "Precisely for this reason..."
The meaning is: "precisely because it lacks a [logical] probative force.
He clarifies that very point with the words: "anukūla... (favorable...).
Now, even if the mere existence of an agent is thus established, from what is its oneness established? To this he says: "But the oneness of the agent... and so forth.
He clarifies that very point through a question and answer, beginning with "nanu" and so forth.
Let it be so; however, how is the oneness and other qualities of the cognition and so forth residing therein established? To this he says: "And that... (tacceti).

Refutation of the Absence of Desire for Sovereignty (*īśitva-anukūlatva-bhaṅga*).
Regarding the doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), p. 309:

Because gravity and so forth must necessarily have God alone as their agent, and because [that agent] must necessarily have as its object the potsherds and other materials that serve as the substrata for color and other qualities, [the knowledge of God] has everything as its object.
To this it is replied: How can there be "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) in the case of mountains and the like, which were not perceived prior to their arising?

If you say it is because they possess parts (*sāvayavatvāt*), then if "possessing parts" means having constituent portions (*sāṃśatva*), it is inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
He undertakes to refute the inference stated in this way, saying: "To this, it is replied."

Regarding the statement by the venerable teacher, “The contradiction of the reason (*hetuvirodha*) is twofold: non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*),” since non-establishment is primary between the two defects of the reason—non-establishment and the absence of pervasion—and because others also accept the primacy of non-establishment through the traditional enumeration beginning with “non-established, contradictory,” and so forth, [the author] first demonstrates the non-establishment of the intended reason of "being an effect" (kāryatva) by means of the passage beginning with “provided that it is inherent” (*samavetatve sati*), citing the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*: “Furthermore, how is ‘being an effect’ established in those cases where no instance is perceived? and so on.
He elaborates: "non-apprehension."
Prākkotiḥ is prior non-existence (prāgabhāva).
[Objection: But surely its existence is established by the inference: "Earth and so forth are effects because they possess parts, like a jar.

Nor should it be argued: "Why establish 'being an effect' as an intermediate step when one could simply prove that [the subject] is produced by an agent possessing the aforementioned form on the basis of having parts alone"? For, according to the reasoning stated previously, just as there is no supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*) for "being an effect" regarding production by an agent, there is likewise none for "having parts."

With the thought that there is an absence of favorable *tarka*—such as the destruction of the reason (*hetu*)—due to the probandum (*sādhya*) consisting of the nature of being an effect, the following objection is raised: "If it be argued that [the world] has parts" (*sāvayavatvāt cet*).

Keeping in mind the statement from the *Sudhā* commentary on the *Śāstrayoni* Sūtra—beginning with, “In that case, it would follow that even space and so forth are effects”—he says: “[the reason] is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*) with respect to space and so forth.”

He elucidates that very point with the words: "gaganeti" (the sky, etc.). [The commentary on the verse beginning with] "tvad" [is as follows]: *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam*, First Chapter, page 310. Because the possession of parts (*sāṃśatva*) is established for both ether (*ākāśa*) and the atom (*paramāṇu*) by virtue of their being conjunctions;
and this has been explained in detail elsewhere.
Furthermore, if [the property] "being a substance originated by substances" is asserted, it is unestablished (*asiddha*) against one who maintains that [ether] is not an effect.
Space and so forth possess parts because they are conjunctive, like a jar.
Nor is the reason unestablished (*aprayojaka*);

for since it is impossible for [conjunction] to exist pervasively in space and so forth—given the uncontradicted cognition that "the bird is here" and "the bird is not here"—conjunction must be non-pervasive, being co-located with its own absolute absence.

The point is this: because it is contradictory for a single entity to exist partially in one place while existing pervasively everywhere else—such as in the case of space—it must be admitted that conjunction exists only as a partial, localized occurrence.

Furthermore, if that partiality were itself adventitious (aupādhika), it would lead to an infinite regress; thus, apart from an inherent partiality, the very nature of being a conjoined entity (saṃyogitva) is untenable.

But surely, if space, time, atoms, and so forth are likewise possessed of parts because they are conjuncts— since the same logic applies— then a part of [space] would also be a conjunct and thus possess parts, and that part of a part would likewise [possess parts], resulting in an infinite regress even for the parts of an atom.
And in that case, it would follow that space and an atom are equal in dimension.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction of its being an atom (*paramāṇu*).

Moreover, since there is no evidence for the existence of a portion consisting of form distinct from the constituent parts such as the material cause (*upādāna*), and because if one were to admit that even space and so forth possess such portions of form, it would follow that they are impermanent; therefore, he says:
"And this has been explained in detail elsewhere."
"Therefore, all objects always possess parts, because they are connected in all directions; thus, indivisibility is the state of being an ultimate atom."
The meaning is that this has been established in the section refuting the Vaiśeṣika school in both the *Anuvyākhyāna* and the *Sudhā*. (End of the refutation of the desire to create.)

311: If [the reason] is "inherence in a substance" (dravyasamaveta) because it is "substance-ness" (dravyatva), then it is non-conclusive (aprayojaka), as it can be accounted for even by being non-produced, like a universal (jāti) and so forth.

If, on the other hand, it is "having a medium dimension" (madhyamaparimāṇatva), then too it is simply non-conclusive—since that [dimension] can be accounted for by having parts, just like a portion of space (gaganapradeśa).
Furthermore, the intermediate dimension of a substance is established merely by its being the substratum of an intermediate magnitude, without depending on its parts;

for if one were to accept that a mustard seed occupies as much space as it does when perceived, and that the same applies to the sky with an equal succession of non-exceeding parts, it would follow that they possess identical dimensions.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction in the statement, "Since there exists nothing independent of its own parts, partless in form, and of minimal dimension, that is an atom," because such a definition is not self-contradictory; furthermore, the existence of a portion distinct from the material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth has been explained in detail in the *Bhāvaprakāśikā*, a commentary on the *Upādhikhaṇḍa*.
"Like genus and so forth."

The point is this: although universals (*jāti*), singularity, number, dimension, and so forth—which lack substantiality (*adravya*)—are inherent in substances (*dravyasamaveta*), they are not effects; likewise, let it be that even a substance inherent in a substance is not an effect. This is because there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against such a position, just as in the case of a spatial region of the sky (*gaganapradeśa*).

Just as here, by the cognition "a bird" and so forth, although the region serving as the substratum for the bird possesses a middle-sized dimension, that region likewise possesses multiple parts according to the aforementioned reasoning; similarly, even though the sky lacks the nature of being an effect— defined as being composed of constituent parts— it nonetheless possesses multiple parts, because it lacks the state of having infinite parts devoid of prior and posterior limits, and thus it possesses more parts than an atom which also possesses multiple parts.
And the meaning is that it is possible for there to be a middle dimension, which is neither the dimension of those two [extremes] nor a lack of dimension.
This was stated by accepting that dimension is caused by the accumulation of parts;
however, [the author] says "parts," etc., to suggest that in reality, let that very [notion] not exist.

Just as in the case of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth, there exists atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*) and large dimension (*mahat-parimāṇa*) independently of parts, so too let there be intermediate dimension (*madhyama-parimāṇa*).

The portions perceived in the earth and other such substances are not constituent parts (*avayava*) in the sense of being non-pervasive forms; rather, let them be considered mere divisions (*aṃśa*), like the distinct regions of space or like the moments (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth of time.
For this very reason, the argument that the earth is established as an effect because another whole (avayavin) arises through the destruction of its prior parts via digging and so forth, is refuted;
for by the same logic, time would also result in being an effect due to its destruction moment by moment.
[This is further supported] by the observation of light (prabhā), which is a quality of a lamp.
The sense is that it is not logical to claim that light is neither a quality nor a substance;

for in the *Sūtra-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-candrikā*, its status as a quality is established through arguments such as its conforming to [the nature of] a quality, and so forth, according to the sūtra: "Or [it is a quality], like light."
Having raised the objection that the aforementioned object of knowledge is contradicted by perception because it is independent of parts, he refutes it with the words "of earth and so forth."

Now, an objection is raised: "Is there not a disparity [in the examples], since the destruction of space-points is never observed, whereas the destruction of the constituent parts of the earth is observed? To this, he says: "Of time... [and so forth].

The intention is that if spatial divisions, moments, instants, and so forth are merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), then the parts of the earth must likewise be so; thus, it says "the previous whole" (*pūrvavayavī*).

The meaning is that because the status of being an effect is established through the *pīlupāka* (external heating of atoms) process— wherein, due to actions such as pushing or striking, a disjunction of the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) occurs down to the level of the atoms via the medium of action in the parts; once the prior substance has been destroyed, a new effect such as a fragmented earth-mass arises again through the medium of atomic conjunctions governed by unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)— the fact of being an effect is proven.

Nor should it be argued that because the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is established in the case of a fragmented earth (*khaṇḍakṣiti*) and so forth, yet it is not established for an unfragmented earth (*akhaṇḍakṣiti*) and so forth, there is thus a "partial unestablished" (*bhāgāsiddhi*) fallacy;
for the point is that by means of destruction (*nāśa*), that [property] is inferred there as well.
(Refutation of the claim that [the world] is an imitation of God: The doctrine of God (īśvaravāda) [is untenable],
because it would follow that even a mere digger and the like would be the creator of the earth and so forth.
Furthermore, because it would contradict recognition,
and because it would entail the fallacy of momentary destruction.
This has been stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda: “Because it is possible to infer [the opposite] even by way of contrariety.
He clarifies what was said with the words “ata eva” (for this very reason) by stating “kṣaṇādīti” (momentariness, etc.).

Nor is it correct to say that because moments and so forth are adventitious (*aupādhika*), their destruction there consists simply in the destruction of the adventitious condition (*upādhi*); for when the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is destroyed, the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) is also destroyed.
Furthermore, the intention is that the parts are not adventitious—since their being adventitious has been refuted in the *Upādhikhaṇḍana* and other works—but are rather intrinsic (*svābhāvika*).
With the intention that even the acceptance of the destruction of the earth through digging and so forth has already been stated, he says: "of the digger and so forth."
The sense is that, in that case, there would be proof of what is already established (siddhasādhanatā) in part.

As for what was stated in the *Maṇi*: “In that case, agency consists in the destruction of the earth itself, and not in a fragment of the earth, because its production arises solely from [the destruction of] the prior state and conjunctions”;
that is not correct, because if that were so, it would follow that one would lack agency even when a fragment of the earth is destroyed.
Because the contradiction with experience is equal for both positions.

But if there were an agent who causes the destruction of only one part [of the earth], then the production of an indivisible earth would not occur at all; therefore, how could the earth and other things possess the property of being an effect? With this intention, he says: "Pratyabhijñā... (Recognition).
"Kṣaṇa" means "moment."

The meaning is that, since in earth and the other elements there is at every moment the departure of individual parts due to impacts from wind and so forth, one must accept the arising of destruction caused by that departure at every moment.

Thus, having analyzed "possessing parts" (*sāvayavatva*) by way of its forms such as "having constituent elements" (*sāṃśatva*), the fallacies of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*), unestablishedness (*asiddhi*), and being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) have been stated.
Let there be some [property] regarding the state of possessing parts;
nevertheless, there is still subversion by reasoning (*tarka*).
