The intention is that it should simply be understood as a technical term (*pāribhāṣika*).

In the case of various objects such as a jar, since the status of being a primary agent (*mukhya-kartṛtva*) is established for the potter—who possesses the relevant volition (*kṛti*)—by observing the absence of the jar where there is an absence of that [volition], it might follow here as well that the one possessing the volition regarding the material cause (*upādāna*) of the earth and so forth would be the primary agent alone. To this, he says: "In the case of a jar, etc. (ghaṭādau). (Note:
The word *kṛti* is absent in the Kuṃ. manuscript.)
(The Refutation of the Alleged Nature of God as a Potter): Regarding the doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), page 319:

If one were to postulate [an agent] for a jar and other such objects merely on the basis of their being perceived, then—contrary to the "activity" (ceṣṭā) mentioned by you—one would have to postulate an activity that is the opposite of "effortless action" (nirapekṣakṛti), namely, an activity mediated by a door (dvārakakṛti).

And if, when this is done, it is argued that the causality of action is established as being the generator [of the world] precisely by virtue of its being an action delimited by the nature of "action" (*kṛtitva*), then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of actions such as our own.
To exclude that, if one introduces qualifiers such as "produced by itself" (*svajanya*), the argument becomes unproven (*aprayojakatā*),
because action in that specific form is not the cause.

And the statement "nor is its establishment through inference" is a restatement of the meaning of the preceding sentence—namely, that if one were to postulate that [inference] based on mere observation in the case of jars and the like.
The meaning is: "in the conceptualization of its own material cause and its object.
This is to be construed with the phrase "in earth and so forth.
Stating the meaning of the word *viparyaya* (contrariety) found in the subsequent sentence, he states the consequence (*apādya*) as follows: "as stated by you..."
It is indeed volition (kṛti) mediated by effort (ceṣṭā).

If it is argued that it has already been stated here that, although an effort mediated by activity is observed in specific effects such as a jar, there is nonetheless causality with respect to effects in general by virtue of being an effort (*kṛtitva*), according to the principle of the "general and the particular" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*), we say: no. The point is that since the production of the earth is accounted for by the very effort observed to produce its [own] cause, the postulation of an unestablished effort serves as a sublation; thus, the claim that "there is no sublation" is unproven.
In order to refute the [objection] that there are six further [consequences], he states the flaw in the inference after extracting it: "If this is so... and so forth.
The meaning is: "given that mere perception leads to an over-extension [of the argument]," because it lacks causal efficacy.

The meaning is as follows: because mere observation [of a person] in relation to a jar and such objects would lead to the over-extension [of the inference] to bodily movements and so forth; and because the principle of "the particular of that which is common" (*yatsāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*) is sublated by the consequence of having to postulate many unseen factors (*adṛṣṭa*) not previously established, it will be refuted later and thus does not apply here.

Furthermore, if the term "material cause" (*upādāna*) refers to any material cause whatsoever, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) with respect to sound, blowing, and so forth;

for even these are produced by the knowledge and other qualities residing in ourselves and others, which have as their object clay, drums, and so on— [objects] that serve as some kind of material cause for them.

If, however, in accordance with the linguistic usage established by all the world, one were to take the term "immediately preceding" (*samabhivyāhṛta*) as referring to the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*)—abandoning the specific portion of the definition that specifies it as the "inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*)—then one might argue: "Let the probandum (*sādhya*) then be simply 'not having the material cause as its object' and so forth. Therefore, keeping in mind the *Ṭīkā* which states, "For the generality of effects depends upon the generality of causes," he refutes the probandum as intended by the opponent, stating:
"Siddha... (established).
The meaning is that there is proof of what is already established in part (*aṃśataḥ-siddhasādhanam*).
Nor should it be argued that knowledge and desire do not possess causality in this regard,
but rather that only volition alone [is the cause], because these [three] combined produce an effect inherent in their own respective objects;
for such an argument fails to avoid the aforementioned defect, since the author of the *Maṇi* intends this very triad of things to be established as being constituted by knowledge and the rest.

Regarding what was stated concerning the *Ṭhakkura* and others— that the probandum is a cognition produced by such cognitions as have the status of being the cause of [their own] material cause (*upādāna*)—
there is no fault, because in that form they are causes only with respect to effects inherent in their own substratum.

As for the qualification "produced by itself" (svajanyā) and so forth [in the definition of perception], it is intended to exclude partial *siddhasādhanatā* (proving what is already established) regarding the form of time (*kāla*).
That is not correct;

for, according to the direction that will be explained, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), causal agency is never postulated in the stated form—namely, as being a producer by way of being a cognition whose object is the cause (*kāraṇagocarajñāna*) and so on.
"Whatever it may be."
The meaning of "depending" (*pratītya*) is that which is superior to its own inherent form (*svagatarūpa*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "mṛdaṅga etc.," the palate and so forth are included—referring to that which has become the object of the term "material cause" (*upādāna*).

Because, unlike the Vedāntin position, the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmika-kāraṇa*) is not accepted, the term "inherent cause" (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) is employed. (The Refutation of the Absence of Divine Agency)

Regarding the doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), page 321: Since the causality [of the earth] is apprehended precisely as an action whose object is the cause of the earth and so forth— which is the opposite of what you have stated— then even in proving such an instrument of action, it is merely a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).

This is because the knowledge that produces the earth, which itself produces the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), has as its object the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) and so forth that produce the earth, by way of that unseen merit.
Nor should it be argued that the oblation and such are merely the "instigators" (*prayojaka*) of the earth but not its "causes" (*kāraṇa*).

For even in that case, it is far more parsimonious to hold that the cause consists precisely in an effort whose object is the "instigator"—defined as having the nature of being invariably antecedent and not otherwise established—once the part consisting of the "unestablished" (*anyathāsiddha*) elements within the body of the cause has been excluded. This is the opposite of what you have asserted.

In order to demonstrate that the fault stated by [the opponent] is firmly rooted in the original position, he explains the meaning of the word "contrary" (*viparyaya*) in the subsequent sentence—taking it to mean that the proof of [the world's] being produced by that [Intelligent Cause] through the aforementioned inference (the previous statement) is not established, because [the world] consists of earth and so forth which are the objects of [His] material cause, knowledge, and so on—by saying: "tvadukteti" (as stated by you).
Because of the apprehension of causality.

The meaning is as follows: because, in the case of a jar and so forth, by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), causality is apprehended solely through the fact of being an effort directed toward the causes of the jar and such; and since, for the sake of parsimony, causality is likewise postulated for the earth and so forth in exactly that same way.
Let it be granted that the term "material cause" (*upādāna*) refers merely to "cause" in general; even with that much, God is established. To this, he says: "tathābhūta... (of such a nature).
The meaning is that this refers to establishing the nature of the cause as being the agent (kartṛ) with respect to the objects such as the earth and so forth.

With the intention that one should consider the same fault to apply here—namely, that [the effect] is produced by one possessing desire-to-act (cikīrṣā), which itself is produced by one possessing knowledge of the aforementioned form—it was stated "of knowledge and so forth," even though previously only "mere volition" (kṛti) had been mentioned.
Nor should it be said that the qualification "not seen to be produced by its own [agent's] unseen merit" (adṛṣṭa) and so forth was stated solely for this purpose.
The point is that, in his view, the fault of the reason being "non-probative" (aprayojaka) has already been stated; therefore, [the reason] is indeed probative (prayojaka).

The sense is that [the agent] is like the potter’s father with respect to the jar. The expression “contrary to what you have said” is used to demonstrate that [the point] is firmly established in the root [of the argument]. The same applies further on in the phrase “within the scope of the instigator.”
The meaning is "as stated by you.

*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, Page 322) (Note: Variants from manuscripts *thā*, *ga*, *kuṃ*; *vṛtti*, *cha*, *kha*, *kuṃ*; *ddhi*, *a*; and *nepī*, *mu*—regarding the reading 'ca', it does not exist in manuscript *a*.)
As for what was said— that because there is no positive or negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) between particulars, the universal must also be the cause as a causal factor—
therein, first of all, the initial position is not tenable;

for it is established that the capacity [of a cause] consists precisely in the apprehension of a causal relation between causes and effects of the same class, which is the opposite of what you have stated regarding positive and negative concomitance.
Furthermore, there is no basis for postulating an additional capacity [in the individual souls].

Now, an objection may be raised: "It has not been observed that the exclusion of effort directed toward the material cause of the earth and so forth occurs; by what means, then, could that [effort] be a probans?"
That is not so;
for since one observes the concomitance and so forth between two particulars, one may likewise postulate it for the two universals. To this he says: "And as for what was said..."

The meaning is that the preceding text, which consists of an objection and its response beginning with "Is this not [the case], so that [the reason] would be ineffective," refers to what is the opposite of what you have stated.

The meaning is this: as for what you have stated—that there is a causal relation between the general effect and the general volition based on the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth between the jar and the potter’s activity—this is contrary [to our view].

For it has been established in the case of the staff, the jar, and so forth, that "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) consists precisely in a causal relation between the specific effect and the specific volition, characterized by a commonality of form through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) in the forms of "jar-ness" and "potter-volition-ness."
Regarding the "seed" [of doubt]: if it is argued that the very absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is the seed, we say no;
for in the postulation of such a capacity, the postulation of numerous unobserved entities (*adṛṣṭa*) itself serves as the subverting factor.

This is because, in the case of a jar and so forth, one would have to postulate numerous things, such as its being produced by an effort independent of manual movement, and its being produced by an eternal knowledge whose object is everything.

However, by accepting the mere possession of established capacity, there is parsimony (*lāghava*). Otherwise, based on the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between the form of the threads and the form [of the cloth], one would have to postulate either that the general property of form residing in the cause is the cause for the general property of form residing in the effect, or that the mere quality residing in the cause is the cause for the mere quality residing in the effect.
The sense is that whatever objection may arise therein, all of it should be resolved by postulating a process consistent with that [position]. (Refutation of the charge of partiality)

Nor is the second [alternative] tenable: in the case under dispute, the generality (*sāmānya*) is subject to the relation of cause and effect because, in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is connected with particulars that stand in a causal relationship, just like the generalities of smoke and fire. In this argument, the property of possessing a form that delimits the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is itself the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Nor is there pervasion by the probans (*sādhanavyāpakatā*),

because in your position, the property of being an action (*kṛtitva*) does not delimit the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), since it subsists in the actions of God, which are devoid of spatial and temporal exclusion.
[The term] "in the universal" (*sāmānye*) ends in the dual number.
The meaning is: "in the case of the general nature of the effect and the general nature of the volitional effort (kṛti)," provided that there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka).
The meaning is: "without a subverting factor consisting of deviation regarding the general property.

When a causal relationship exists between two specific instances presented as possessing a certain property, that which is to be understood is their being characterized by that property—that is, their relatedness to it—as in the case of a jar and a potter.

Regarding the causal relationship between the generality of the effect and the generality of the person, even if one were to postulate "being an effect" and so forth based on the speaker’s sentence being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the sentence-meaning being a valid cognition, there would still be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because that [status] is absent in the case of the generality of sentences and the generality of the speaker’s knowledge.
To exclude this, he states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) beginning with "vyatireka... [in the verse].
In this context, the word "form" (*rūpa*) refers to a property (*dharma*).
For the causal relationship between the general property of smoke and the general property of fire is not based on their connection to specific instances of smoke and specific instances of fire;

rather, it is caused solely by the possession of the properties known as "fire-ness" (*vahnitva*) and "smoke-ness" (*dhūmatva*), which serve as the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) for the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) expressed as: "wherever there is an absence of fire, there is an absence of smoke."

Since such a [relationship] is observed everywhere in cases such as the pot and the staff, which have entered into a cause-and-effect relationship, the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) is evident; thus, he clarifies the non-pervasion of the probans (*sādhanavyāpakatva*) with the words "And not," etc.

If, in the context of causality, the possession of a nature that delimits the negative concomitance (*vyatirekāvacchedakarūpavatva*) alone were the governing factor, then the establishment of space (*ākāśa*) as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of sound would not occur;
likewise, the establishment of the self (*ātman*) as the inherent cause of cognition and so forth would also not occur.
Furthermore, there would be no establishment of spatial and temporal priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*), as they would lack a cause.

(Note: The variants indicate that the word *eva* is absent in the manuscripts *ca*, *cha*, *ka*, and *kha*; the phrase *viśeṣayoḥ* is absent in *kuṃ*; the word *bhūta* is absent in *a*; and the reading *nāt/ sādhyavyāpakatvaṃ vyanakti* is present in *kuṃ* but this line is absent in *a*.)
Nor does this result in the non-establishment of ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth;
for these are established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) itself.

Even if that [ether] is not established as the cause of sound and so forth, it is nonetheless established as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of sound precisely because the quality [of sound] is pervaded by being inherent [in a substance]. Anticipating the objection that this is not so because those [qualities], being eternal and all-pervading, lack a form that could serve as a delimiting factor for their absence (*vyatireka*), he refutes it with the words: "And it is not thus."
"By the witness alone."
The meaning is: "by the witness alone, in the form of the knowledge of the nature of the Self.

It is stated "by the witness alone" because there is no such rule that the cognition of space arises solely through its being the cause of sound; for even those who are deaf due to the absence of auditory knowledge of sound still have a cognition of space.

And this has been explained in the *Anuvyākhyāna*, the *Sudhā*, and the *Vādāvalī* on the section concerning inference (*anumānika-pāda*), beginning with: "The reality of the sky and so forth is established by the perception of a witness. This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, just as the state of being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*) is not to be understood as a distinct [category], so too the state of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) is not to be grasped as something specific; rather, the state of being an inherent cause is simply causality (*kāraṇatva*) that is co-located with the state of being an inherent substratum (*samavāyitva*).

Thus, according to the principle stated by Pakṣadhara and others—that "when both [factors] are grasped through a convergence of the means of apprehension, there is a convergence of the objects (*arthasamāja*)"—it is possible to grasp even that alone through the operation of a means that apprehends mere inherence.

With this intention, he states "sound... (*śabda...*) in order to establish the existence of space (*ākāśa*) in another way for one who is in disagreement regarding the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).

"By way of inherence" means by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya-vṛtti*), that is, as being the substratum of sound. Once the general existence of its substratum is established through the inference "Sound is dependent on something, because it is a quality," [the specific nature of the substratum is established] by the argument: "Sound is dependent on a substance other than the eight substances, because, while there are subverting arguments against its subsisting in those eight substances, it is nonetheless dependent."
The meaning is that proof is possible precisely by virtue of [sound] being an inherent property (samavāyin) of sound and so forth.

Even according to the view that the status of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) must be understood as specifically qualified, he demonstrates the manner in which space (*ākāśa*) is established by that very form, as stated in the *Maṇi* (the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*), beginning with "nimitta" [etc.]. (Note: The text fragments provided—"vye sama," "vārthaḥ samā," "nārthaḥ samā," "śabdapadaṃ na," "tyarthaḥ," and "sva"—appear to be marginalia or variant readings from different manuscript traditions.)
Thus [ends] the additional [section]—Kuṃ.

For while in the case of grasping an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇatā*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the form of a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*)— namely, "where there is no staff, there is no jar"— is required, in the case of grasping an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*), the negative concomitance must be in the form of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) alone, namely, "that which is not an inherent cause does not have the effect. Consequently, it is possible to establish that [space] is the inherent cause of sound as well.

Furthermore, in your view, there is no entity established as distinct from the object of an action (kṛti) in the same way that an inherent cause (samavāyin) is distinct [from its effect]; for if such were the case, causality could be apprehended through a mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) distinct from the action itself.
This is because, according to you, everything is the object of God’s creative action.

Since even spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) is an object of God’s creative activity by virtue of being a cause—due to its inclusion within the type of proximity known as "qualificative relation based on inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavetaviśeṣaṇatā*) toward the direct perception of the absence of a pot residing in itself; and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), pervasion (*vyāpti*) and non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) are included—it follows that [the qualification] is of the nature of a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*).

The sense is that, because there is no relationship of locus and located between the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) and its effect, it is the absence of connection (saṃsargābhāva) that is the governing factor.

If this is so, then let the establishment of God’s agency also be established in this same way. Since the causal relation between action and its effect can be grasped through a negative concomitance (vyatireka) consisting of mutual absence—namely, that "where there is no object of action, there is no effect"—the agency conducive to the production of the earth as an effect is thereby established; to this he says: "And not... (na ca).
"Of everything as well."
The sense is that since the action of God has as its object merely the cause [of an effect], everything whatsoever is a cause with respect to something.
Granted that even the self, time, space, and so forth may be objects of God’s creative activity by virtue of being the material causes for their own inherent qualities;
however, the atomic dimension known as *pārimāṇḍalya* (sphericality) is not a cause for anything whatsoever.

In this regard, the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—namely, "wherever there is no object of creative activity, there is no effect"—is easily established; therefore, he says: "Even of sphericality... [and so on].

It should be understood that this is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the short dimension (*hrasva-parimāṇa*) residing in a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), as well as [the properties] such as having a suitable counter-correlate (*yogya-pratiyogikatva*).
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (First Chapter, p. 326) [Note: *tti bhū - cha - ka - kha.* refers to manuscript variants.]
Furthermore, the absence of a jar there is not non-perceptual;
for the conditions you have stated for the perceptuality of an absence—such as having a capable counter-positive (yogyapratiyogikatva) and so forth—are present there as well.

And thus, an inference would also occur based on its being produced by a delimited action, which is the opposite of your stated [thesis] that it is produced by an action undetermined by space and time.
As for what was stated— that the knowledge of the substratum (*upādāna-jñāna*) is a cause precisely by virtue of being a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*)—
in the case of the perception of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), indeed, the perception of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-pratyakṣa*) is the essential factor,
but not [the perception of the locus] in every instance of the perception of absence (*abhāva-pratyakṣa*).

For in the perception of absence, what is required is either the fitness of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)— as stated in the direction that "the existence of something in a particular place is opposed to its non-perception"— or the fitness of the non-perception itself, which consists in having a counter-positive whose presence has been projected by the logical consequence (*prasañjana*) of that very presence.
And since this [fitness] exists even when perceiving the absence of atomic dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*) and so forth, the meaning is that the absence would indeed be perceptible.

By stating "not the second," and so forth, he extracts and demonstrates the fault already mentioned—namely, that "it is possible to infer [the opposite] by way of contrariety"—thereby establishing it upon the root text: "If this is so," and so on.

The meaning is: "given that the state of possessing the nature of negative concomitance (vyatireka) is the cause [of certainty], provided that there is an absence of sublation"—this refers to the term "delimited" (paricchinnā).
The meaning is that it does not have all things as its object;
thus, the intention is that the reason "being an effect" (kāryatva) is inconclusive (aprayojaka).

Having thus stated that the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is non-conclusive regarding the aspect of being produced by an effort (*kṛti*) desired by the opponent, he now addresses the previously mentioned claim—that effort is preceded by immediate perception (*aparokṣajñāna*)—with the intention of showing that it is likewise non-conclusive regarding the aspect of being produced by immediate knowledge. He does so with the words beginning, "And as for what was said... (*yaccoktam*, etc.).
"the cause."
The meaning is: "in the making of skull-cups and so forth."

The meaning is as follows: thus, by virtue of the pervasion of the reason "being an effect" residing in the earth and so forth, it is established that even the Lord’s knowledge which produces the earth and so forth is indeed indirect (*parokṣa*);
this is what was stated in the passage beginning with "And in your view, [it would be] like [the effort]," and so on.
(The Refutation of the Alleged Dependence on God) The Doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda), Part II, p.

327. That too is not correct. For in your own view, although the body composed of air—which is the material cause of movement—is imperceptible, it is nonetheless necessary that the Self, as its presiding controller, possesses the volition (*kṛti*) which is the cause of that movement.
This is because the cause of purposeful action (*kṛti*) is precisely that state of knowledge which is the opposite of the immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) described by you.
As for the absence of purposeful action with respect to indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) of atoms and the like, it is not due to a lack of immediacy;
rather, it is due to a lack of having as its object a specific place and time whose existence serves as the condition for the suitability of purposeful action.

For this very reason, when a blind person possesses knowledge of what is to be avoided and what is to be acquired regarding specific places and times through the words of a reliable authority (āpta), their avoidance and acquisition are appropriate.

Furthermore, the point is that by means of the example of the potsherd, since the self is the substratum of the conjunction that serves as the cause [of action], even in the absence of immediate perceptual knowledge of the material cause in cases such as a body composed of air, volition (kṛti) exists as the cause of effort; thus, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) of "being required" (apekṣitatva) with respect to volition.

In that case, one might argue that even through knowledge produced by a mark (liṅga) whose object is atoms, space, and so forth, there would also be an effort directed toward those objects; therefore, he says: "atoms and so forth."
He teaches.
The meaning is that, like a skull or similar objects, there is an absence of existence at a particular place and time.

Since the atom is eternal, it lacks existence at a particular time; however, since space and so forth lack existence at a particular place, no creative action (*kṛti*) occurs therein—this is the intended sense. "Precisely for this reason" [refers to this].
The meaning is: "precisely because it is a cause of action by virtue of being knowledge itself"—this is what is meant by the word "heyā" (to be abandoned).
The meaning is: "when there is the cognition that 'there is shell here' and 'there is silver here.

Now, one might argue: "Granted that there is no proof for [the Lord] possessing non-conceptual (aparokṣa) knowledge; nevertheless, the existence of the Lord must still be established by way of being the cause of an effect, just like a potter, since the potter's status as the cause of a jar has already been proven. To this, [the author] replies by restating and refuting the previously mentioned removal of the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example, beginning with the words "And that which... (*yacceti*).

The meaning is that this has been stated in the passage beginning with "because we observe that the potsherd, which is the substratum of the conjunction that serves as the cause of the pot, is itself a cause of the pot"—namely, [the argument] regarding "that which is lighter.
[That is not so.
(Nyāyadīpāyutatarkatāṇḍava, Prathama-pariccheda, p. 328)
That proof for [the status of] being a cause is not tenable;
for if the potsherd and so forth were the cause, it would be simpler to hold that the locus of the effect itself is the decisive factor, which is the opposite of what you have stated.
This is because, compared to being the locus of the conjunction that is the non-inherent cause of the effect, being the locus of the effect is simpler.
Thus, the sense is that the example— namely, the self being the cause of a jar that has attained non-existence— is indeed devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*).
Nor does it follow that past time and so forth would also be causes of the jar,
because [the status of being a cause] is intended to consist in being its substratum by way of inherence (*samavāyavṛtti*).
This was stated having provisionally accepted [the opponent's position];
however, in reality, since inherence will be refuted later on.
"Whose direct perception has ever reached a cloth that is distinct from its threads?"—
by such a recollection, since there is no jar existing apart from the two potsherds characterized by their specific conjunction, the illustrative example is unestablished.

Furthermore, even if one accepts that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is the cause [of action], the self (*ātman*) cannot be the cause because it is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) as merely the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of that conjunction.

Nor is it correct to argue that, just as the effort which is the cause of a jar is otherwise established as the delimiting factor of the self’s conjunction with the self (via the medium of volitional movement), so too the self is otherwise established, and therefore effort itself is not the cause;

One might object: "Let it be that, by virtue of being an effect, there is the establishment of knowledge and so forth through independence [of the agent], just as in the case of volitional action (*kṛti*), because the probans cannot be excluded by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of 'being produced by a body'—since that condition does not pervade the probandum but does pervade the probans. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*).

Alternatively, is the accomplishment of knowledge and desire due to its being an incidental accompaniment of volitional effort (*kṛti*), or is it through its own independence? Or is it because that which is already known is the object of volitional effort, and since volitional effort is not inherently connected to its own purpose, [knowledge] serves as the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) for the effort with respect to its object? The answer to the first [alternative] is: "Of the self," and so forth.
Anticipating a second objection, he refutes it with the words "And not," and so forth.
"Conjunction with the self."
The sense is that, according to your own view, because of the omnipresence of the self (*ātman*), there is always contact [with all objects].

(Note: 1. The word *eva* is absent in the manuscripts *cha*, *ku*, and *ga*. 2. The phrase *kṛtivat* is absent in *ga*. 3. *reva* in *kuṃ*. 4. The word *atha* is absent in *a*. 5. *na* in *kuṃ*. 6. The word *vedya* is added in *a*. 7. *ndhāt* in *mu* and *a*. 8. *gabhāvāsaṃbhavā* in *mu*.)

(The Refutation of the Dependence on Desire: The Doctrine of God, Part 2, p. 337. Nor should it be argued that knowledge is required for the sake of the proximity between the action and its object, because knowledge itself is the very means of proximity between the action and its object.

If the cognition that produces the effort were the proximate cause [of the relation], it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); furthermore, since the cognition that produced that effort has perished at the time of the effort, it cannot be the proximate cause. Therefore, just as the nature of the cognition itself is the proximate cause for the cognition, so too the nature of the effort itself must be the proximate cause for the effort. Otherwise, because the cognition would be absent at the time of the effort, there could be no cognition of the relation between the pot and the action, such as "I am making a pot."
Therefore, there would also be an inference based on the mere possession of an activity that is the opposite of the triad of activity and so forth as stated by you.
Furthermore, let it be granted that knowledge is established as a causal proximity (*pratyāsatti*) by virtue of being a proximity to the action (*kṛti*).

[Objection: Let it be that, for fear of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the knowledge that produces [an effect] elsewhere serves as the proximity to the action produced there; and thus, once it is established that knowledge is a proximity to action in some instance, let it be accepted here that even such [knowledge] is a proximity by necessity. To show that this is not the case elsewhere either, he says: "tajjanaka... (that which produces it...).
But for one who has no other recourse, even though he is lost, there is still that same state; therefore, he says: "In knowledge."
And it has been stated in the *Adhikaraṇasudhā*: “Not so, because [the world] possesses a purpose.”

Regarding the occasion for explaining the phrase "and because [the scripture] possesses a great purport," [the objection is raised]: "If it is argued that intelligence must be admitted in order to restrict the scope of effort, we say:
no."
But how could desire be established?
And thus, there would also be an inference based on the presence of the two factors that are the opposites of the three [factors] you have mentioned.

On the view that a qualifying condition (*upādhi*) indicates a deviation [of the reason from the probandum], there would be a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣatā*), because it is possible to infer the opposite of your stated "having an agent"—namely, "not having an agent"—by means of "being produced by a body.

Nor is the reason "not being produced by an agent" irrelevant (*aprayojaka*), since in the case of "not being produced by an agent," the mere fact of "not being produced" (*ajanyatva*) is the essential factor. Furthermore, whether "being produced by a body" or "being produced by an agent" is the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) in the case of being produced by an agent—[the former is not the case].

Since it has been established that there is doubt as to whether [the mind] is an effect, the reason for its establishment is equal [to the opposing view].—The sense of "because, like cognition, its inclination toward objects is possible by itself" (verse 3) is: how could it be proven?
Is it by way of being a secondary consequence of an action, or independently, or by way of the existence of volitional effort?
Not even one of these three positions is possible;
the sense is that this is due to the faults already mentioned.

Having thus stated that the reason "being an effect" (kāryatva) is vitiated by a limiting condition (sopādhika), he states its counter-balanced nature (satpratipakṣatā) with the words beginning "Furthermore" (kiñca).

[Objection: But surely, since it was stated in the definition of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) that "that very thing is also a defect consisting of a limiting condition" (*upādhi-doṣa*), and since the status of a defect is accepted precisely as being the counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*) to the probandum, and because according to the older Nyāya school this is likewise accepted, the statement "furthermore" (*kiñca*) introducing another defect is improper, given that the counter-argument in the form of its absence has already been stated by the mention of the limiting condition itself. To this, he says: "Because of deviation" (*vyabhicāra*). The sense is that, according to the author of the *Maṇi* (Rucidatta), since the mention of the limiting condition is accepted as a bringer-forth of deviation (*vyabhicāra-unnāyaka*), only the cognition of deviation regarding the reason arises from the mention of the limiting condition, and thus the cognition of a counter-argument does not arise; hence [the term] "contrary" (*viparīta*).
The meaning is that it is possible to infer: "The earth and so forth are without an agent, because they are not produced by a body, like space.
Here, there is no room for the objection that the reason—"not being produced by a body"—is unestablished (asiddha), for it is not an irrelevant (aprayojaka) reason.
The meaning is that, since being uncaused (*akartṛkatva*) is the sole determinant for everything that is not produced;
[the phrase] "of doubt" was stated in order to establish its status as a counter-position (*pratipakṣatā*).

(The Refutation of the Alleged Invariable Concomitance with Non-Agency) The Doctrine of God, p.

339. Now, it may be argued that because the pervasion (vyāpti) is grasped between non-producedness—such as that of space—and non-agency, there is no proof that [the property of] being qualified by a body is pervaded by the absence of that [non-agency].

Thus, the meaning of the term "qualified pervasion" (*viśiṣṭavyāpti*) is either that there is a single pervasion residing in both the qualifier and the qualified (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), or that the pervasion residing in the qualified alone is delimited by the qualifier. In that regard, if it were a pervasion residing in both, the reason would be the impossibility of its not occurring in the qualified alone.

If [the property] were to be delimited by a qualifier, it would be impossible for the delimitor of the qualificand (*viśeṣyatāvacchedaka*) to be the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*). However, in the present case, neither of these two conditions applies.
In reality, moreover, "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is not the delimitor of "being produced by an agent" (*kartṛjanyatva*).
Because that [effect-ness] can occur even without it;

otherwise, as has been stated, the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) would be non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*), since even "being an effect" would have to be the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of being produced by karma, and so forth— this is because of their equality.
And thus, the sense is that there is no lack of a probative reason (*aprayojakatva*).

Furthermore, he restates what was stated in the *Maṇi* and other works—such as "If [the probans] were produced by a body, the qualification would be redundant; for by parsimony (*lāghava*), being non-produced alone is the pervaded (*vyāpya*)"—extracting the essential point, from the words "Now, if it is thought... up to "...it is said here," namely: "the qualified pervasion" (*viśiṣṭavyāpti*).
The meaning is that the word's referent is "pervasion" (vyāpti) as residing in a specific cause; this is what is meant by the phrase "therein."
The meaning is "two kalpas"—this is the reason.
As in the case of "Sound is eternal because it is an effect of an existent entity" and so forth—[this is] by means of a qualification, etc.

The meaning is as follows: for example, in the inference "the fire is black aloe-wood because it possesses fragrant smoke," and so forth—this refers to the phrase "delimited by the property that qualifies the subject" (*viśeṣyatvāvacchedaka*).
The meaning is: "that which has non-produced-ness as its delimiting property (*avacchedaka*).

*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 340) (Note: Variants for the footnotes provided in the source text are as follows: 1. *hi* – Kuṃ-cha-ga-rā; 2. *ptya* – Kuṃ-cha-ga; 3. *rā-mu*; 4. *tiparyaṃ* – a.)

For it is possible for the state of residing in that which is not produced by the form of the bare qualificandum (*kevalaviśeṣya*) and the state of being delimited by the delimitor of the qualificandumhood (*viśeṣyatvāvacchedaka*) to exist within the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Nor should it be argued that, just like pervasion, the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is also a constituent of inference, and therefore a qualifier is required to establish it;

because only that [property-of-the-subject] which is co-locative with the pervasion is a constituent, whereas here, the property-of-the-subject residing in the qualificandum—which is non-co-locative with the pervasion and exists in the qualified whole—is not a constituent.

Nor should it be argued that in such cases as "the eye is not composed of light (*taijasa*) because it is a substance that perceives only color (*rūpa*) among the five objects beginning with color," the "property-of-the-subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*) consisting in a qualified occurrence is seen to be a factor for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurring in the qualificand;

for even there, by the force of the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), the reason is "being a perceiver of color while not manifesting other specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) besides color. Since the mere qualificand (*manas*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the pervasion must likewise be qualified.
Furthermore, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) here regarding the qualified object (viśeṣya), which consists in the state of not being born from parents (ajānyatva).
Considering that "in the case of color and so forth, which are the subjects" (rūpādiṣu pakṣeṣu) is a statement of their essential nature (svarūpa), he says: "Even there... (tatrāpi).

Now, if the phrase "of color alone" (*rūpasyaiva*) and so forth were to mean "a specific quality other than color" (*rūpetara-viśeṣa-guṇa*) and so on, then the mention of "in the subjects such as color" (*rūpādiṣu pakṣeṣu*) would be redundant.
Therefore, its meaning must be stated as "not manifesting anything other than color.

In that case, since the eye also manifests the universal *rūpatva* (color-ness), the reason (*hetu*) would result in being unestablished (*asiddha*); thus, the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) must be qualified by a specific attribute that excludes that [manifestation of universals].

Thinking that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and considering that [the previous definition] lacks purpose because it does not exclude what is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), he says "or else" (*yadvā*).
"Of that which has not attained self-nature."

The sense is that because [the property of] "being color" (*rūpatva*) is apprehended even by the mind and other [faculties], it is not established anywhere [as being exclusively perceptible by the eye].

[Note: The phrase "in the middle" (*madhye*) is an interpolation in manuscripts Kuṃ and Cha. Here, there is a line—"Because a single qualifier [does not entail] the pervasion of the property residing in the qualified, due to its particularity"—which expresses dissatisfaction with [the opponent's position]. (The Refutation of the Non-omniscience of Īśvara)
The doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), page 341:

Alternatively, since the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) which excludes deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the mind cannot exclude deviation unless it is supported by the qualification "with regard to color and so forth" (*rūpādiṣu*), the qualification itself serves only as a means to achieve that support, thereby functioning to exclude deviation.
But "unproducedness" (ajanyatva) has already established its existence in space and so forth, even without the qualification of being "bodiless."
Now, it may be thought that even in the case of blue smoke and the like, pervasion (vyāpti) resides specifically in the qualified [entity],
because there is an absence of deviation (vyabhicāra) and adventitious conditions (upādhi) therein;
otherwise, if the qualifiers were not themselves pervaded, pervasion would be without a substratum.
However, "being blue smoke" is not the delimiting property (avacchedaka) because it is cumbersome;
rather, it is simply "smokeness."

Nor should it be argued that, because the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs only when the object is unknown as possessing the qualifier "blue" (which serves to exclude deviation), there is an absence of valid knowledge of pervasion when the object is known as possessing that [qualifier];

for even when smoke is not known as possessing substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth, the apprehension of pervasion—in the form of non-deviation and the like—occurs provided there is observation of concomitance and no observation of deviation. If this is said, it is not so.
[For] pervasion certainly exists in the case of "blue smoke" and the like.

Otherwise, if the qualifiers were not pervaded, the pervasion would be without a substratum; with these words, he restates the objection regarding the position that pervasion resides in the qualified [subject] as stated in the *Maṇi*, beginning with "Now, it might be thought... and ending with "...not so," including the phrase "even in the case of blue smoke, etc."

And thus, even though [the effect] is produced by the body, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) certainly exists within the qualified probans (*viśiṣṭahetu*); therefore, the intention is that it is improper to raise the objection that the pervasion is unestablished (*asiddhi*) in that case.

For the "unestablishedness due to lack of pervasion" (vyāpyatvāsiddhi) is indeed the absence of the pervasion that serves as the causal condition for inference. And the pervasion that serves as its cause is characterized by the possession of a nature that delimits co-occurrence with the probandum (sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇyāvacchedakarūpavatva); it is not, however, of the nature of non-deviation (avyabhicāra) or the absence of a limiting condition (anaupādhikatva), because of the resulting complexity (gaurava).
If it were not the meaning of a word, it would not be the meaning of a sentence either, because that [meaning] is not perceived through the example-sentence (*udāharaṇavākya*).

Furthermore, its absence [as a property of the subject] occurs either due to the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in the case of a thing lacking a locus (*niradhikaraṇa*);
or, even when that [coreferentiality] exists, due to the absence of its being defined by the probandum (*sādhya*), as in the case of a contradictory [reason].

Alternatively, it may be because there is an absence of non-delimitation (*anavacchedakatva-viraha*) for the property (*dharma*) that is present in both [the reason and the subject], as in the case of "this earth [is non-eternal] because of being a substance" (*dravyatva*).

The proponent of the view that there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti-viraha*) in the qualified reason (*viśiṣṭa-hetu*) refutes the objection regarding the pervasion residing in a subordinate qualified entity by accepting the definition of pervasion favored by the author of the *Maṇi* (Raghunātha Śiromaṇi), stating "not so," etc.,
on the grounds of "cumbrousness" (*gaurava*).
The meaning is that it is because it is not composed of a negative particle (nañ); this refers to the "example."

The meaning is as follows: by means of a statement such as "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire," there is a cognition of the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probandum (fire) with the reason (smoke), as well as the possession of the property that delimits that [co-occurrence], namely "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*); however, there is no cognition of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) and so forth. This is what is meant by the phrase "in the case of a real entity" (*vastuni*).
The meaning is: "in the object called 'sky' [in the inference] 'the mountain possesses fire because it possesses sky-ness'"—that is, "in that [object]."
The meaning is "co-referentiality"—that is, "contradictory."
The meaning is: "in cases such as 'the mountain possesses fire because it is a lake,'" [and] "because it is a substance."

In this context, the meaning is that for co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), earthness (*pṛthivītva*) is the delimitor of that [co-occurrence] with respect to substancehood (*dravyatva*); for substancehood lacks co-occurrence with earthness alone. (Note: Variants: 1.
*rūpā* – kha; 2. *da* – kuṃ; 3. *mava* – kuṃ; 4. *vyavatvaṃ* – kuṃ.)
(The Refutation of the Dependence on God): Regarding the doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda), p. 343:

Furthermore, in the case of "blue smoke" and the like, even though there is co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and that [co-occurrence] is defined by the probandum (*sādhya*), because "blueness of smoke" lacks the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the co-occurrence as defined by fire, there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Now, in this context, delimitorhood (*avacchedakatva*) is not, first of all, the state of being a cause for the cognition of delimitation and so forth,
because that would involve the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
Nor is it the state of subsisting in a locus that is neither less nor more extensive than the delimited (*avacchedya*).

Because [the property of] having a common locus with fire does not exist in smoke-ness (*dhūmatva*) and so forth—which do not exist in things like pots—it would follow that [the definition] is absent there as well;
however, what is required is that [the two properties] occupy no more extensive location than one another (*anatiriktadeśakatva*).
And this [condition] exists even in the case of blue-smoke-ness (*nīladhūmavatva*).

Nor, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case, is it qualified by the condition "being not composed of another property whose locus is not distinct from the delimited [locus]"; for what purpose would this be in the present context? To this he says: "useless" (*vyarthā*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), [qualities such as] being produced by the body and so forth are included—because [the body] lacks the status of a delimiting factor (avacchedakatva).
The meaning is "out of respect.
And thus, the meaning is that the qualified reason is indeed devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The proponent of the theory that pervasion (vyāpti) resides in the qualified [locus] (viśiṣṭa-niṣṭha-vyāptivādī), while restating the refined definition of "delimitor" (avacchedakatva) as set forth by Pakṣadhara and others in his discussion of pervasion, raises the following doubt— that even in cases such as "blue smoke-ness" (nīladhūmatva),
there exists the status of being a delimitor of co-presence with the probandum (sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇyāvacchedakatva)— in the passage beginning with "nanu" and ending with "maivam."

By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi-padena*), there is the inclusion of such properties as being pervaded by the delimitandum (*avacchedya-vyāpyatva*) and being co-extensive with the delimitandum (*avacchedya-samaniyatatva*); [these are excluded] because of the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

The meaning is as follows: since the nature of being a cause (*hetutva*) consists in having a necessarily prior existence, and since this necessity is itself pervasion (*vyāpti*), the knowledge of pervasion is indispensable for the knowledge of pervasion; thus, there is the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

Nor should it be argued that "the state of being blue smoke" (*nīladhūmatva*) cannot serve as a delimiting factor because it is composed of other such properties, namely the state of being smoke (*dhūmatva*) itself;
for if this were the case, the body of the definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) would involve two absences, resulting in excessive complexity (*gaurava*).
If it is argued that [the definition] is also absent from the illustrative sentence, we say: not so.
For delimitorhood (*avacchedakatva*) is indeed a specific form of qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*), which is a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*).
Nor is this [delimitorhood] not apprehended from the statement of the example (*udāharaṇavākya*);

for there exists a relation in the form of delimitorhood between the "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) presented by the word "smoke" in the example-statement and the "co-occurrence with fire" (*vahnisāmānādhikaraṇya*) residing in the smoke as presented by the example-statement.

The meaning is as follows: because [the property] appears by way of relation (*saṃsarga*), there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) even in the case of "being smoke that is a probandum" (*prameya-dhūmatva*), "being smoke that is a substance" (*dravya-dhūmatva*), "being blue smoke" (*nīla-dhūmatva*), and so forth; for in these cases, there exists the state of having a locus no larger than that of the delimitable (*avacchedya*)—namely, the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with fire.
This is provided that [the definition] consists in being composed of another property whose locus is not larger than that of the co-occurrence with the probandum (*sādhya-sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Regarding the definition "having a locus no larger than that of the co-occurrence with the probandum" (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇyānatiriktadeśakatva*), although there are three absences due to the inclusion of three negative particles (*nañ*), it is nevertheless stated that there are two absences because the term *anatirikta* is employed twice;
or else, it is stated that there are two absences in relation to the two negative particles contained within the "existence" (*satya*) portion [of the definition].
Some, however, say that its meaning is "the state of being co-located with the probandum while not being composed of such other properties";
and thus they claim it consists of only two absences. That [view] is to be considered.
Because there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such things as knowability (*prameyatva*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*).

What is the specific nature of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*)? If it were defined as being the object of a cognition that produces a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Therefore, he says: "It is a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*)."
If it is asked, "Why is this so?", they reply:
"Because of the definition of delimitation (*avacchedakatva*). To explain:

As for the statement that "the nature of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) consists in not occupying a space distinct from that which is to be delimited (*avacchedya*)," that is not correct. (Refutation of the Theory of Non-Perception of Desire)

Regarding the doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), p. 345: Furthermore, that essential relation (svarūpasambandha) is postulated only for the simpler property of "smokeness" (dhūmatva), and not for the more complex property of "blue-smokeness" (nīladhūmatva); thus, there is no pervasion (vyāpti) in the case of blue smoke.
Nor should it be said that even the state of being light smoke exists in blue smoke;

for it must be stated that the delimiting factor of the causal status (*hetutāvacchedaka*) itself is the delimiting factor of the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is because it is the most proximate [factor], and because postulating another property would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

In this case, however, there is the fallacy of unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), because *nīladhūmatva* (the state of being blue smoke) and *śarīrajanyatva* (the state of being produced by a body), which are presented as the delimiters of the reasonhood (*hetutāvacchedaka*), do not serve as the delimiters for the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [of the probandum and the reason]. Furthermore, [this definition] would over-extend to such cases as "This is happy, because it is a self" (*idaṃ sukhi ātmatvāt*), where the reason is deviant (*vyabhicārin*) since it co-occurs with the absence of happiness in the self of God (*īśvara*). This is because the property of being a self (*ātmatvatva*)—which exists in the individual soul (*jīvātman*) in co-occurrence with happiness—is not something that occurs in a domain no larger than the co-occurrence with happiness [in general]. Thus, the delimiter of the reasonhood (*ātmatvatva*) does not qualify the co-occurrence [of happiness and the self] in the way required.

Nor can it be said that "delimitingness" (*avacchedakatva*) consists in not occurring in what is co-locus with the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*); for *ātmatva* (the nature of being a self) is indeed co-locus with the absence of pleasure in the self of God (*īśvara*). This must be stated [as a counter-example], because such a definition fails in the case of a reason (*hetu*) where the probandum is purely positive (*kevalānvayin*).
Because there is no [reason] that possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyaka*) therein;
for in that case, the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhyābhāva*) is not established.

Nor can it be said that "delimitingness" (avacchedakatva) consists in not residing in the locus of the absence of co-location with the probandum; for, although *ātmatva* (the nature of being a self) is indeed the locus of the absence of co-location with pleasure—delimited by its subsistence in the self of God—it would still result in the fallacy of over-extension (*avyāpti*) in an inference such as: "This tree possesses contact with this monkey, because it is this tree."
This is because even this "tree-ness" (vṛkṣatva) is the locus of the absence of co-location with this monkey-contact when delimited by its root.
If it is argued that since this "tree-ness" possesses co-location with this monkey-contact [in its upper parts], how can there be an absence of it?
Then the same applies to "selfhood" (ātmatva) as well.
This is because the same principle applies here as well: that even two contradictory things are not contradictory when distinguished by different limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*).
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (First Chapter, p. 346) [Notes: 1. *matve* — *ga*, *kha*; 2. *ca* — *ka*, *rā*, *kha*.]

Nor should it be argued that, in cases such as "the subject of dispute is smokeless because it lacks fire produced from wet fuel," or "it is free from fragrant smoke because it lacks fire produced from sandalwood," there would likewise be a failure to establish the pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*).

For in those instances, the pervasion is ascertained through non-contradictory reasoning (*anuttarka*) based on the causal relationship between effect and cause, which applies even to the absence of fire produced from wet fuel and the like.
Nor is it the case that [the definition] consists in not occurring in that which lacks co-presence with the probandum (sādhya) without being delimited by a single part of the locus.

For in the case of "being this tree" (etadvṛkṣatva), co-presence with the probandum exists only as delimited by a single part of the locus, namely the root; thus, since the absence of the qualified [probandum] exists there as well, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti).
However, in the case of "selfhood" (ātmatva), the state of lacking co-presence with the probandum exists only as delimited by occurrence in the locus consisting of God (īśvara).
However, since it is not [the case] by way of delimitation by a single part of that [locus], there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that instance.

Furthermore, in the case of a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) inference, the absence of such co-occurrence with the probandum (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇyābhāva*) is well-established in space (*gagana*) and so forth; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

This is because pleasure (*sukha*) and the like are non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*); even in the individual self (*jīvātman*), since the absence of co-occurrence with pleasure is present in respect to "selfhood" (*ātmatva*), the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for that [absence] is precisely its occurrence in a single part of that [locus]. This is the general direction of the argument.
Therefore, since a definition of "delimitingness" (*avacchedakatva*) cannot be established, delimitingness is simply the relation of identity (*svarūpasambandha*); thus, it exists in blue smoke.
And so, because it possesses such a delimiting property, even blue smoke is indeed pervaded—this is the intention of the objector.
And it is not thus.

The meaning is that if the property of being a Guru were not a pervader (*vyāpaka*), then there could be no inference of the absence of a specific effect from the absence of a specific cause. (The Refutation of the Charge of Non-observation by the Lord)
Regarding the doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), page 347:
Here it is said—
For it is established by experience— and is also accepted by you— that the cognition of a deviation (vyabhicāra) acts as an obstacle to inference;
and this is not, like sublation (bādhā) and other such defects, due to its directly having a subject matter that is contradictory to the probandum (sādhya).
Rather, it is by way of subverting the knowledge of pervasion which has become the instrument [of proof].

And that [subversion] is appropriate only when pervasion consists in a concomitance qualified by the absence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in a state contrary to the property of possessing a nature that delimits the co-presence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the probandum as stated by you.

Thus, when the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been established—that the quality of being produced by a body is unestablished as a pervaded (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*) by means of the example of a blue-cognition (*nīladhīmat*).

The nature of pervasion as stated by Maṇi is not a constituent of inference; rather, it is something else entirely, and that [other nature] exists in blue smoke and in the state of being produced by a body.
Therefore, with the intention that there is no lack of pervasion, he establishes the final position with the words "To this it is replied," and so forth.
And [it is] with your approval.

The meaning is that this refers to the definition of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), such as "inconclusiveness" (*vyabhicāra*), which states: "being the object of a true cognition that is the counter-positive of an absence which serves as the cause of inference."
Indeed, the state of being an obstacle to inference is twofold:
either by having as its object something that is contradictory to the object of the inference itself, or directly;

or else, by apprehending the absence of an object that is the content of the cognition which serves as the cause of that inference, or by being a constituent part of the instrument (karana) of that [inference].

In this regard, the first [type of invalidity] applies only to sublation (*bādha*) and its counteragent (*pratipakṣa*), but not to anything else; however, the second may apply to others as well. With this intention, he says: "And that," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "vyāptijñāna": [it refers to] the cognition of pervasion.

Although, according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), the subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) alone is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of inference— as it has been said: "Inference is the subsumptive reflection of the mark" (*liṅgaparāmarśo 'numānam*)—

nevertheless, because of the rule that an instrument must possess an operation (*vyāpāra*), since there is no operation when the subsumptive reflection is the instrument, the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāptijñāna*) [is required].

In the theory that the logical mark (*liṅga*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), where the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), it is stated—according to the method explained by the author of the *Maṇi*—that "it is the knowledge of pervasion which has become the instrument"; this is what is meant by "and that" (*tacceti*).

The meaning is that it is the subverter of the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*). The expression "contrary" (*viparīta*) is used to show that this is firmly established in the root text. (Note: Regarding the variants: *sā ca* is found in manuscripts ka and kha; *dvā ca* in ga and rā; the word "sati" is absent in manuscript kuṃ.)

4. [The term] *katve*—*kuṃ*—*a*. Even if there is a contradiction regarding the objective aspect (*viśeṣyāṃśa*) consisting of coexistence with what is contradictory (*viruddhasahacāra*), there is a contradiction in terms of the sphere of experience (*vaiṣayika-virodha*) with the qualifying aspect (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*) consisting of the absence of deviation (*vyabhicārābhāva*). This is from the *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava*, First Chapter, page 348.

However, it is not tenable [to claim] that [the property] consists in being qualified by the nature of possessing color (rūpavatva) as the delimiting factor for co-inherence with the probandum (sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇyāvacchedaka);
for there is no direct contradiction [between them], since they do not consist in mutual exclusion (parasparaviraha).

Nor does there arise an indirect contradiction [of the reason] by way of inferring that the delimitor of the reason (hetutāvacchedaka) is not the delimitor of the co-presence with the probandum (sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya) due to deviation;

for there is a contradiction with experience, since one experiences the cognition of the absence of pervasion immediately after the cognition of deviation, and thus postulating such an indirect sequence would contradict experience.
He clarifies this point by saying "like a contradictory [reason]."
The meaning is: "like a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) that is contradictory because it is connected solely with the absence of the probandum. Regarding the term *vaiṣayika*:
the meaning is "produced by an object (*viṣaya*) consisting of a contradiction between existence and non-existence. Thus, [the opponent's] position is correct.
The meaning is that it is logical for [the counter-example] to be a subverter of the cognition of pervasion—indirectly.

In the case of "The mountain possesses smoke because it possesses fire," the delimitor of the causal state (*hetutāvacchedaka*)—namely *fire-ness* (*vahni-tva*) and so forth—is not the delimitor of the co-presence with the probandum (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇyāvacchedaka*), because it subsists in that which is co-present with the absence of the probandum. Thus, there arises an inference that [the *hetutāvacchedaka*] is not the delimitor of co-presence with the probandum. Consequently, there is no cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of possessing such a delimiting property. Therefore, the meaning is that the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra-jñāna*) acts as an obstacle to the cognition of pervasion by means of the cognition that [the *hetutāvacchedaka*] is not a delimitor.

1. *katvātmakatve* – *cha*. *rūpapadaṃ na* – *ga*. 2. *katvena* – *kuṃ*. 3. This passage does not exist – *a*. (The Refutation of the Theory that [the World] is Created by a Lord) The Doctrine of God (*Īśvaravāda*), page 349. First, because there is no contradiction [in the definition], and second, because—unlike fallacies such as *asiddhi*—there is an absence of the status of being an object of the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) that directly obstructs inference, there is an absence of the status of being a "fallacy of the reason" (*hetvābhāsa*) or a "limiting condition" (*upādhi*), just like a true *upādhi*.
Furthermore, since these [two characteristics] are not perceived through the illustrative sentence (*udāharaṇavākya*), they are not perceived therein.

Regarding the view that the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) exists [in the term *vyāpti*], according to the rule “*nityavīpsayoḥ*” (Pāṇini 8.1.4), when there is a desire to convey pervasion (*vyāpti*), the singular form is prescribed for a single referent—@---------------------------------------------------------------------------
He says "like the sublation of a dream" (bādhādivat) in response to one who disputes [the existence of] experience.
The state of being a fallacy of the reason and the state of being a limiting condition.

The meaning is as follows: since being the object of a true cognition that obstructs inference constitutes the nature of a "fallacious reason" (hetvābhāsa), and since this [nature] is absent even in the case of a fallacy where a limiting condition (upādhi) indicates deviation— just as it is absent in a limiting condition that indicates deviation because it does not serve as the delimitor of co-presence with the probandum— the deviation itself would not be a fallacious reason, just like the limiting condition.
"Therefore, it is not cognized."
The meaning is: the non-apprehension of concomitance qualified by the absence of deviation.
"Therein" [refers to that].
The meaning is "in the illustrative statement" (*udāharaṇavākya*).
This is because both positions are stated in the *Avayava* treatise.
The expression of two views—namely, the view that there is repetition (*vīpsā*) and the view that there is not—is thus presented.
"By the sūtra" means by the grammatical sūtra.
He states the meaning of the word *vīpsā* found in the Sūtra: "pervasion" (*vyāpti*).
Regarding that which is "enjoined" (*ādiṣṭasya*), meaning prescribed as an *ādeśa* (substitute):

in the Grammar (Pāṇini), in the first quarter of the eighth chapter, under the rule *“nityavīpsayoḥ”* (P. 8.1.4), there is the recurrence of two words from the governing rule (*adhikārasūtra*) *“sarvatra dve”* (P. 8.1.1).

The meaning is that for every preceding word consisting of a collection of phonemes (varṇasamudāya) which occurs in the sense of "eternal" (*nitya*)— in the form of the repetition of an action— as well as in the sense of "distribution" (*vīpsā*), a double occurrence takes place.
And here two alternatives are possible:
either two substitutes, identical in form both phonetically and semantically, occur in place of the previously existing word;
or rather, there is a double utterance of the preceding word.

*Nyāyadīpayutatarkabhāṣā* (First Chapter, page 350) [The text continues from here.]

—because the word *yaḥ* (‘who’), which takes the form of a single word, is established as a constituent of inference by virtue of its being expressive of pervasion (*vyāpti*), which consists in a concomitance characterized by non-deviation.

In the view that there is no need for repetition (*vīpsā*), the knowledge of the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*) is possible through the mind alone, aided by the observation of concomitance produced by the example.

Thus, since the pervasion—consisting of concomitance qualified by the absence of deviation—is present in both "blue smoke" and "being produced by a body," how can there be a lack of establishment of their being pervaded (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*)?
In this regard, it is stated that [the reason] is "that which has been pointed out," because the first position alone is established as stable in both the *Bhāṣya* and the *Mañjarī*.
In that case, because it possesses meaning through the status of being a substitute (sthānivadbhāva), it has the nature of a nominal stem (prātipadika).
And because there is unity of meaning, the entire complex constitutes a single word; it is with this intention that the expression "having a single meaning" and so forth is stated.
"Of the word."
The connection [of the word] is by way of denotation (*vācakatvena*).
Since the substrata of all the means (*sādhana*) are presented by the word "each" (*vīpsita*), there is the prescription of the presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) therein;

thus, there arises the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of a relation between the probandum and every locus that depends upon its own substratum. The point is that it is precisely this [cognition] which is determined to be a constituent factor (*aṅga*) of inference.

As for what was stated in the *Maṇi* during the discussion on the definition (*nirūpaṇa*)—namely, "But we [hold] that even in the case of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), the state of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains as it was"—that is incorrect.

For when there is a desire to demonstrate pervasion (*vyāpti*), the phrase "whatever [is the locus]" (*yo yaḥ*), which is employed, possesses the capacity to convey the connection of the probandum (*sādhya*) with every locus of the probans (*sādhana*); since this is well-established through linguistic convention (*vyutpanna*), there is no room for the suspicion of deviation.

Having thus established pervasion (vyāpti) by way of its commonality with "blue smoke" and the like, [the author] now addresses the following objection: even if there is no pervasion in the case of "blue smoke" and so forth, there is pervasion in the case of "being produced by a body. Furthermore, since the term "body" (śarīra) serves to exclude the unestablished (asiddhi) rather than excluding deviation (vyabhicāra), it is redundant; therefore, how can there be pervasion in that which possesses a redundant qualifier? To this, [the author replies] that it is because [the term] expands the scope of the locus of pervasion.

With the intention that there is no "useless qualification" (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*) because [the qualification] serves as a means for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), he establishes that point there with the words beginning "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). (Note: The manuscript variants indicate the following textual details: *caritasaha* is found in Kuṃ and Rā; the phrase 'grahasambhavāt / tathāca' occurs in Ka; *psāśa* is in Kuṃ; and the word 'nirūpaṇa' is absent in A.)
(The Refutation of the Dependence on God) The Doctrine of God, Part 2, p.
351. Furthermore, that which constitutes the body of the reason (*hetu*) is of two kinds.
Some [qualifiers] are restrictive,
such as "blue" in the expression "blue smoke";
some are expansive.

For example, in the case of the reason "because it is an object of knowledge" (*prameyatvāt*), which has the sense of "because it is the object [of a cognition] that is the locus of validity," the term "object" (*viṣayatva*) is included.

Since no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) occurs when "because it is an object of knowledge" is stated, there is no redundancy (*na vyarthatā*). This is because the final term, which would otherwise be restricted by its opposite, serves as a means for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the very place where it is expanded by itself.

Otherwise, if the definition were merely negative (*vyatirekin*), a qualification would not have been employed to exclude the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*). [The term] "restrictive" (*saṃkocaka*) means that which brings about a reduction in the scope of the locus of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the definition of the logical reason (*hetu*).

By the term "smoke" (*dhūma*), the status of being the locus of pervasion is obtained for the mere substratum of the property of smokeness (*dhūmatva*) common to both blue and non-blue smoke. However, when the qualification "blue" (*nīla*) is added, it applies only to blue smoke; thus, blueness serves to restrict the locus of pervasion.

In the argument "The pot is denotable, because it is the object of that which is the locus of truth," if one were to state only "because of truth" (*pramātvāt*), one would obtain the status of being the locus of pervasion for that [truth] alone, and not for anything else.

However, when the qualificand portion (*viśeṣyabhāga*) is also stated, one obtains that status even for mere knowability (*prameyatva*); thus, the meaning is that it serves as a qualifier that expands to a different locus.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therein."
The meaning is "between the two components that constitute the causal body";
[this refers to] "of the last."
The meaning is "of that which causes the expansion of the locus of pervasion. The phrase "also of that which excludes non-establishment" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
"Otherwise" means...

If [the definition] were redundant simply because it is unestablished (*asiddhi*), then in the case of the definition of substance (*dravya*) as "that which is the locus of qualities" (*guṇāśraya*), the qualification "absolute non-existence" (*atyantābhāva*) would not have been employed. For although the property of "not being the locus of qualities" exists in a jar at its first moment of existence, it is absent in that same jar during its second and subsequent moments; thus, without the qualification "absolute," there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*). To avoid this, the term "absolute" was indeed introduced.

Furthermore, the term "body" (*śarīra*) serves to exclude [the definition] from sprouts and the like, wherein "unproducedness" (*ajanyatva*) is impossible; thus, it is not redundant. *Note: Variants noted in the manuscript collation: 1. *cājanyatvasyāṅkurādāvasambhāvitasya* (kha, cha); 2. *ktepi* (cha, ga, ka, rā); 3. *vyāptigrahānaupayikatvādvayarthatā* (kha, cha); 4. *ntene* (a).* *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam*, First Chapter, p. 352.
