The translation focuses on the core philosophical argument regarding the definition of God.*
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because of being produced by a body" (*śarīrajanyatvāt*), it is not the absence (*abhāva*) qualified by the body that is the reason;

rather, it is the absence of "being produced" (*janyatva*) as qualified by the body. [This is because] in the argument—"Substance is distinct from others because it is not the locus of the absolute non-existence of qualities (*guṇātyantābhāva*); otherwise, like qualities and so forth"—this [qualification] serves to exclude partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*) in the case of jars and the like existing at the second moment and beyond.

The point is that since it has been stated that even a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*), a definition is a purely negative inference when it establishes both exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that if one were to state only "because it is not the locus of the absence of qualities," the qualification "absolute" (atyanta) would not need to be added in order to avoid the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*) in the case of a jar existing at its first moment of production.
Granted that this may be so, what follows for the subject at hand? To this he says: "The body," etc.

If it were stated merely as "because of being unproduced" (*ajanyatvāt*), there would be a suspicion that the reason is unestablished (*hetvasiddhi*) due to the impossibility [of the reason] applying to sprouts and the like; therefore, this [qualification] expands the reason by establishing its existence even in those cases and by ensuring a multiplicity of substrates for the reason.
This is because, in those cases, the absence of being produced by a body mediated by *adṛṣṭa* can indeed be apprehended through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Hence, it is not [unestablished].
The meaning is that the qualification "of the body" is useless.

Not only is the body meaningful as a cause that brings about expansion, but—as stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*—it is also useful for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by way of presenting the nature of the reason (*hetu*) as the absence of the qualified [condition], since "the qualified condition indeed possesses pervasion of the probandum (*sādhya*), and its absence is here stated as the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*). Thus he says: "Moreover... (*api ca*).
"Non-existence."
The meaning is the absence of being produced; that is, it is not a cause.

For if that were the case, the term "body" (*śarīra*) would be redundant; because the mere absence of being produced (*janyatvābhāva*), which is pervaded by the state of not having an agent (*akartṛkatva*) as seen in the ether (*gagana*) and so forth, could be presented by the word "unproduced" (*ajanyatva*) alone, which constitutes the very nature of the reason (*hetusvarūpa*). (The Refutation of the Absence of Desire [to Create])

The doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), page 353: Furthermore, that [qualified cognition] is indeed distinct from both the qualifier and the qualified, whether one holds the view that the "qualified" is the relation between the qualifier and the qualified, or the view that it is a separate category of reality (padārthāntara); this is because of the difference in their respective counter-correlates (pratiyogin).

According to the view that the qualified (viśiṣṭa) is simply the qualificand (viśeṣya) as delimited by the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), [the absence of such a qualified entity] differs according to the difference in the delimiters of counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedaka). Furthermore, the cognition of the absence of such a qualified entity is not possible without the cognition of the qualifier,
because the cognition of an absence is necessarily produced by the cognition of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) as having the delimiter of counter-correlativity as its mode (prakāra).

And thus, the qualification of the body (*śarīraviśeṣaṇa*) is not merely useful for presenting the absence of the qualified (*viśiṣṭābhāva*)—which is the locus of the counter-pervasion (*viparītavyāpti*) regarding the absence of the qualificand (*viśeṣyābhāva*); rather, it is precisely useful for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*).
This is because pervasion cannot be apprehended without knowledge of the locus (*āśrayajñāna*).
The meaning of "not even so" (*na caivam*) is as follows.
Nor is there a positive concomitance (anvaya) such that [the qualified absence] is simply non-different [from the constituent absences].

If it were not non-different, then, by parsimony, since the absence of the qualificand and so forth would alone be the pervaded (vyāpya), the absence of the qualified (viśiṣṭābhāva) would not be the pervaded;
and this is not the case—this is the meaning.
Why is this so? He clarifies that point with the words: "By the qualification... (viśeṣaṇeti).
He says "it is a distinct category" in accordance with the opponent's view.
To the question, "Let there be a distinct absence; what follows from that?", he says: "tādṛśa... (of such a kind).
"Having as its qualifier the delimiting condition of counter-correlativity."
And thus, the meaning is that since [knowledge] is produced by the body by virtue of being "body-produced," knowledge produced by the body is not possible without knowledge of the body.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And so it is."
Regarding what was stated here in the *Maṇi*: "The absence of being produced by a body is not an unconditioned (*akhaṇḍa*) reason.
For if being produced by a body were the determinant (*prayojaka*) of having an agent, then the absence of having an agent would be necessitated by that [absence]."

The word *puruṣa* is not present in manuscripts Kha and Rā. 2. Read as *yathā* in manuscript A. 3. The phrase beginning with *dhṛtyādeḥ* introduces an inference (*anumāna*) in manuscript A. 4. Read as *ktam* in manuscripts Mu and A. 5. Read as *nirāsāya* in manuscripts Ku, Mu, and A. (The refutation of the claim that [the Lord] lacks desire.)
The doctrine of God (īśvaravāda) [is untenable]:

because, by means of the analogy of one who has awakened from sleep, the creation and so forth of the world can be explained simply as the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) belonging to another eon—just as the production of jars and other objects [is explained]—and thus the reasons [adduced for an eternal creator] are not probative (*aprayojaka*). This is established with greater parsimony (*lāghava*), since it avoids the postulation of a creator whose nature is contrary to what you yourself accept.

Otherwise, there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a Lord (*īśvara*) and his subsequent body and so forth, which are produced through a sequence beginning with binary atoms (*dvyaṇuka*).
Just as one who has been asleep and subsequently awakened performs, after sleep, such acts as the making of a pot that he experienced prior to sleeping; [so too does the transmigrating soul].

The meaning is as follows: by the same logic, since the potter and others at the beginning of creation—who have obtained a body through the force of past unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth—construct jars and the like and engage in their usage at the start of creation by recollecting what was previously experienced through the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by experiences prior to the dissolution (*pralaya*), your intended [thesis] that these things are created by an independent person (*svatantra-puruṣa*) is not established; thus, your reason is "inconclusive" (*aprayojaka*).
And he states the refutation by reasoning (tarkaparāhati): "Otherwise... [he says].

If it were assumed that at the beginning of creation a single independent person alone produced the various diverse constructions such as jars and so forth, then the Lord himself would have to assume various bodies—such as those of a potter, a weaver, and others—to perform those respective diverse constructions; thus, there would be the assumption of infinite bodies for the Lord.

Furthermore, one would have to assume that these [bodies] are themselves produced through a sequence starting from dyads (*dvyaṇuka*); the meaning is that this involves the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) due to the assumption of numerous unauthoritative entities.

Having extracted and restated this very object of knowledge— that the Lord is established through valid cognition— as expressed in the *Kusumāñjali* passage beginning with, “By the word ‘valid cognition’ (pratyaya), here what is meant is authority (prāmāṇya) as an object of confidence,” and ending with, “and one who is not omniscient does not possess independent power over dharma and adharma,” [the author] refutes it.

1. *Ādipadam na* — Kuṃ. 2. *Prasi* — Mu. Furthermore, it should not be argued that because at the beginning of creation there is no knowledge of qualifications such as Brāhmaṇahood, and thus the performance of rituals would be impossible, one must necessarily accept some being who is inherently cognizant of those [qualifications].

This is because, for those such as infants who have just begun to suckle at the breast, there is the possibility of recollection (smṛti) of both the action performed in a previous kalpa— such as that which causes one to be born as a Brāhmaṇa— and the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) between that action and the state of being a Brāhmaṇa, just as there is a recollection of pervasion (vyāpti) which serves as the cause for the inference of "being a means to a desired end" (iṣṭasādhanatā), which in turn is the cause for the inclination toward sucking the breast.
And it should not be said [that there is no proof], as indicated by the words beginning with "nacavācyam" (nor should it be stated).
"Self-cognition of that [cognition]" means: [the cognition] of that [object].
The meaning is that otherwise, due to a lack of confidence, there would be the consequence of abandoning the performance [of the rite].
Thus ends the section on "the breast."

The meaning is: it is like the recollection of pervasion (vyāpti), which is the cause of the inference that [an action] is a means to a desired end—the very cause for the initiation of suckling at the breast.
"At creation" (sarge) [is the beginning of the verse].
The meaning is: "of those such as Brāhmaṇas who have arisen in [this] creation.
Regarding the word "tasya" (of that):
The meaning is "of karma."
The meaning of the reason "because of scripture" (*śruteḥ*) is as follows:

the Vedas were composed by an omniscient being because they possess the nature of being scripture, unlike the speech of commoners; thus, the existence of God is established through a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) based on the effect in the form of scripture.

As for the phrase "because of [being] sentences" (*vākyāt*), the existence of God is established through a positive inference (*anvayin*) based on the reason of being sentences, as in: Vedic sentences are of human origin because they are sentences, like the sentences of ourselves and others.

Having accepted that both of these [objections] have been refuted in the discussion on the non-human authorship of the Vedas, and extracting and restating what was said in the *Kusumāñjali*— specifically in the passage beginning with “Furthermore, because of a particular number” (*saṅkhyāviśeṣāt khalvapi*)— which is intent upon elaborating on the verse “And because of a particular number, the imperishable Creator of the universe is to be proven,” the following doubt is raised, beginning with “Now, however” (*nanu*).

When it is established that the triad (tryaṇuka) possesses dimension by means of the reason "being a substance" (dravyatva), and given that this dimension is produced because it is an effect-quality (kāryaguṇa),
then— since any positive effect (bhāvakārya) is produced from three causes— even though the material cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of the triad is constituted by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa),
its non-material cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) must be stated to be the number three residing in the dyads (dvyaṇuka).

With the intention that a triad (*tryaṇuka*) is produced by three dyads (*dvyaṇuka*), he establishes the fact that number is something produced (*janyatva*) by stating the application [of the reason] as a property of the subject (*dharmin*): "The dimension of a triad...
[Notes on variants: 1. *rājñā*—kha; 2. *tsvargā*—kha; 3. *sarvatrāpyevamasti*—ka; 4. *bhuvām*—cha; *bhāvānām*—kha-ka.

[The refutation of the lack of dependence on a creator (īśvarānapekṣatva-bhaṅga): The Doctrine of God (Īśvaravāda), p. 335. ...of future things—[the suffixes] -rā, 4. ṇatvādi, va-cha-ka-kha, 5. ādi [are added]—ga-kuṃ. 6. Like a jar that possesses a superior dimension within its interior, though initiated by a mere skull—kha. [End of section] (The refutation of the lack of dependence on a creator: The Doctrine of God, p. 335. [End of section] --------- --------- (Note: The bracketed portions represent editorial notes or variant readings from the manuscript sources indicated by the abbreviations rā., ga., kuṃ., and kha.)
Is it not the case that the dimension of a triad has as its cause a number inherent in its parts, because it is a dimension not produced by dimensions or by aggregation,
like the superior dimension found in another jar composed of three potsherds which possess the same dimension as the two potsherds that constitute the jar under discussion?
Nor is the qualifying attribute unestablished.

Regarding the dimension of a triad (*tryaṇuka*), which has as its cause the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)— according to the aforementioned reasoning, even if one accepts the dimension of a dyad as the subject (*pakṣa*) and establishes the probandum (*sādhya*) in the stated manner, the existence of God (*īśvara*) is nonetheless established by virtue of His being the substratum of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) that serves as the instrumental cause for the number "two" residing in the atoms, following the direction that will be explained hereafter.

Nevertheless, since both the dimension of another atom (*paramāṇu*) and the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) are minute dimensions (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), it would be impossible—following the direction to be stated—to avoid the fallacy of the qualification being unestablished (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) for the reason (*hetu*) if the dimension of the dyad were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*). Therefore, the dimension of the triad (*tryaṇuka*) is stated to be the subject. By specifying "not produced from a [prior] dimension" in the reason, [the fallacy of being unestablished] regarding the dimension of a jar and so forth is avoided; and by specifying "not produced from accumulation" (*pracaya*), [it is avoided] regarding the dimension of a tuft of cotton.

By using the term "produced" (*janya*), and by stating "because it is a dimension" (*parimāṇatvāt*) rather than "because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*) with respect to the dimensions of atoms and so forth, the suspicion of a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the color and other qualities residing in a jar is dispelled.
Nor should the reason (*hetu*) be suspected of being irrelevant (*aprayojakatva*).
The meaning is that since the dimension of the product is produced by a triad consisting of number, dimension, and aggregation,
it is impossible for its state of being produced— given that it is not produced from two [factors] alone— to be established without its being produced by number.
He himself demonstrates an example, even though one was already stated starting with the word *vardhamāna*, by saying: "this jar... and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: when a certain pot situated in a buddhi (intellect) is denoted by the word "pot," it is evident that there exists within it—namely, in a pot possessing a larger magnitude—the probandum (the form produced) which is generated by the number three residing in its shards, as well as the aforementioned reason; [this is stated] because [otherwise] the consequence would be that [the pot] would become atomic.
And thus, the implication is that a triad (*tryaṇuka*) would consequently fail to be perceptible.
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (First Chapter, p. 366) [Notes: 1. yī-ka-kha-ga; 2. ṣṭādernimitta-kuṃ.]
If [the triad] were produced [from atoms], then, for that very reason, it would follow that it too is atomic.

Furthermore, in a dyad composed of partless parts, accumulation—in the form of being conjoined with those [parts] while not being conjoined with the greater number of parts residing in another dyad—is impossible.
Therefore, the dimension of an atom is not the originator of the dimension of a triad, because it is an atomic dimension, just like the dimension of a dyad.
Nor is this argument unproven; for if the dimension of a dyad were not caused by the dimension of the atom, it would follow that the dyad possesses the same dimension as the atom.
Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the dimension of a dyad is simply the duality residing in the atoms.
By stating the nature of the aggregate, he reveals its non-produced status with the words "partless" (*niravayava*).
The meaning is that [the object] is originated by parts in the form of atoms which are themselves partless.
He states another formal argument (prayoga) mentioned by Vardhamāna, beginning with "evam" (thus).

The point is that since number alone is the producer [of dimension], the production of the dimension of a dyad occurs through that number and not through its own dimension; thus, neither a contradiction nor the non-production of the dyad's dimension should be suspected.
And this formal argument applies to the dimension of the dyad;
the aforementioned argument should be understood here as well.
To avoid the objection that the desired conclusion is already established by accepting minuteness (*aṇutva*) in the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), he says: "minutenest" (*aṇutamattva*).
Therefore.

The meaning is that [the Lord cannot be established] because dimension (parimāṇa) is not a producer [of effects], and because accumulation (pracaya) of the kind previously described is impossible. Therefore, to address the question of what follows for the proof of the Lord, he states the formal argument (prayoga) as set forth in the *Kusumāñjali*: "And those... [te ca].

1. tvavat-ka. 2. bdha-kuṃ. 3. garu-ka. 4. ntarā-cha-ka-kha-rā. 5. ṇavada-kuṃ. 6. prāyaḥ ‘yī’ ityevāsti - ka-rā. (The Refutation of the Mimicry of God; The Doctrine of God, p. 367. The text contains various manuscript variants as follows: 1. *tvavat* (variant: *tvat*) 2. *bdha* (variant: *bda*) 3. *garu* (variant: *guru*) 4. *ntarā* (variants: *ntara*, *ntarā*) 5. *ṇavada* (variant: *ṇavad*) 6. The reading *prāyaḥ ‘yī’* is found in manuscripts *ka* and *rā*. (This concludes the section on the refutation of the imitation of God, within the treatise on the doctrine of God, page 367.)

Furthermore, those [qualities of] three-ness and two-ness are produced by enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi), because they are numbers residing in multiple substrates, like the two-ness and so forth residing in a jar. If it is argued that enumerative cognition—which is impossible in [inanimate things] such as atoms—thereby postulates God as its substrate, this is not so.

Even though number is eternal, it is possible for the two units residing in the atoms—which are the opposite of the duality residing in the atoms as you have stated—to serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to the dimension of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*);
and likewise, it is possible for the unities residing in the dyads to serve as the non-inherent cause with respect to the dimension of the triad (*tryaṇuka*). [Note:
"Residing in the dimension of the dyad" is the intended meaning.]
The term "subsisting in many" (*anekavṛtti*) is stated in the reason to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of oneness (*ekatva*).
The term "because it is a number" (*saṅkhyātvāt*) is stated to exclude that [deviation] in the case of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.
Thus, the Lord is the substratum of that [number]. This concerns duality (*dvitva*).

The point is this: although there is a rule that destruction is caused by the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) which serves as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), since God’s cognition is eternal, the destruction of duality and so forth residing in atoms and the like must be brought about solely by the destruction of other causes; thus, there is no suspicion of its being eternal.

With the intention that the first reason is non-conclusive because it can be established otherwise—namely, by being the locus of the "relative cognition" (apekṣābuddhi) as intended by you, which does not prove the existence of God—the author states the final conclusion (siddhānta).
"Not so," and so forth.
"Even though number is its source."
The meaning is: "even though the dimensions of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) and the triad (tryaṇuka) are produced by the number residing in the atoms.
The word "api" (even/also) indicates an admission (*abhyupagamavāda*)—namely, that they are indeed produced by the number in the atoms. This is what is meant by "dvyaṇuka... etc.
The meaning is that it resides in three dyads (dvyaṇukas).
But is it not the case that this is impossible?
Because unity is not manifold;
whereas, since duality and triad each consist of individual unities, there is simplicity regarding both of the two dimensions of size belonging to the dyad and the triad.

Since there is no distinction in the fact that [the size] is produced by the number one residing in its own constituent parts, it would follow that even the magnitude of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) would be atomic (*aṇutva*); therefore, he refutes the first [position] with the words: "of the unities" (*ekatvānām*).
Because unity,
even when there is multiplicity, is already established [as a known entity],
whereas duality and triality, although each consists of a single unit, must be postulated [as new entities].

Nor should it be argued that if the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of a triad were caused by the non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) consisting of the individual unitary natures (*ekatva*) residing in the dyads, then it would follow that it possesses minuteness (*aṇutva*) like the dimension of a dyad.

This is because it is logically consistent for eternal number (*nityasaṅkhyā*) to be the cause of the specific quality of minuteness, while produced number (*janyasaṅkhyā*) is the cause of the specific quality of largeness (*mahattva*).
Anticipating this final objection, he refutes it with the words "nor should it be argued" (*na ca*).
"Perpetual."
The meaning is as follows: because the singularities residing in the atoms are eternal, the dimension of the dyad produced by them is minute (*aṇu*);
and because the three singularities residing in the dyads are produced, the dimension of the triad produced by them is large (*mahat*), which is logically established.

Although it could easily be said that the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of a triad is "large" precisely because it is produced by three unities, while the dimension of a dyad is "minute" because it is produced by two unities;

nevertheless, since the production of the dimensions of a tetrad and so forth is also possible through number alone— following the direction of the *Vaiśeṣikādhikaraṇasudhā* which establishes a uniform nature for all effect-dimensions— it must be that [these larger dimensions] are produced solely from the multiple unities residing in their respective inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

The point is that, according to your own view, every dimension (*parimāṇa*) residing in effects such as triads is produced by a "produced number" (*janya-saṅkhyā*) characterized as "largeness" (*mahattva*), and thus its distinction from atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*) is established; it is with this intention in mind that the phrase "by being a produced number" was stated. Now, one might object: although the number "oneness" (*ekatva*) residing in the cause is invariably antecedent to the dimension in the effect, numbers such as "duality" (*dvitva*) and "trinity" (*tritva*) have already been established as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) for those [dimensions]. Therefore, like the color of the threads (*tantu-rūpa*), they are "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*) and cannot be the cause of dimension.
If it is asked, "Whence [then] its status as a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for that specific [quality]?"—no; [this is not so]. (The Refutation of the Absence of Divine Agency) *Note:
In this text, the letter *ka* does not appear everywhere (as noted in manuscript kha). The reading *pavi-ka-rā-kuṃ* is found in manuscript ka.* *Note:
The reading *pratijanyasaṃkhyātvena* is found in manuscript kha.* (Refutation of the Absence of Divine Agency)

Furthermore, rather than postulating a single conjunction— contrary to the number [of atoms] you have stated— which is assumed to be the initiator of a substance, it is more parsimonious to postulate that conjunction alone, as already established by its necessary antecedence, is the cause of dimension (*parimāṇa*),
since this would avoid the mere assumption of something else [i.e., a specific number].
But not so for duality;
for there is parsimony in postulating that its own nature is merely non-otherwise-established,
whereas this is not the case for duality.

Because it would involve the conceptual complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating the essential nature of that [magnitude], as well as its being invariably established as not otherwise possible and its existence as a prior antecedent.

Furthermore, even if that were the case elsewhere, it is more appropriate to postulate a material cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) for magnitude than to postulate that the number "one" residing in atoms— which is impossible— serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the numbers "two" and "many" produced by enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) residing in those same atoms.
By the principle that "let the causality belong to that very cause [which is already established]; what is the use of that [other]?",
it has been stated that multiplicity is simpler to postulate than duality and so forth, because it is already established.

If you consider that [the explanation] is unsatisfactory because unity is not manifold, then, since it is already established, let dimension itself be the originator of dimension as the originator of substance;
what is the use of number? To this he says: "Furthermore," etc.
"Of one" means:
Although the conjunction of the three dyads that initiate a triad is manifold, it is stated as "of one" because the conjunction of the two atoms that initiate a dyad is singular;
for this very reason, it is stated later: "but not of duality."
Now, one might ask: "If [the number] is otherwise established by the production of the substance itself, how can it be the cause of dimension? To this, he says: "Niyata... (restricted).
"Without alteration."
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "non-otherwise-establishment," "invariable concomitance," and "antecedent occurrence" belong to them.
He states—beginning with "Furthermore, [regarding] the present..."—that even though dimension (*parimāṇa*) is produced by duality (*dvitva*), this does not establish the existence of God (*īśvara*).
1. *dvatva*—kha-ka; 2. *dvimātra*—kuṃ-ga; [due to] the necessity of being preceded by *ddha*, *niyata*, and *pūrvavartitva*—ca-kha-rā; [due to] the necessity of being preceded by *niyama*—pūrva-ga.

Furthermore, although a Brāhmaṇa of the present time is preceded by a [previous] Brāhmaṇa, a Brāhmaṇa existing at the time of the beginning of creation is preceded by elements conditioned by a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force). *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 370): [The commentary on the rule] *ṇvādi-a.* 4. Even though the duality and so forth of the present moment are produced by enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), let it be that the primordial [duality] is preceded solely by atoms endowed with a specific type of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Otherwise, one would have to postulate an eternal Brahmin as well, just like an eternal enumerative cognition.
And this is logical;

otherwise, since there would be an absence of causes for the destruction of (1) the inherence [of duality] and the destruction of the two-ness residing in the atoms (2), which depend respectively on the destruction of the inherence [relation] and the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), it would follow that those [two-nesses] could not be destroyed.

Since the enumerative cognition residing in God, as conditioned by a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), is the cause [of the production of duality], it is necessary that the destruction of that [cognition] leads to the destruction of the duality (3). Therefore, let the specific *adṛṣṭa* itself be the cause.

(The refutation of the charge of being a non-probative reason: The doctrine of God (īśvaravāda), page 373. Furthermore, the reason is not non-probative.
The reason is that it is a general rule (*utsarga*) that qualities residing in the cause do not produce a quality of the same kind in the effect;
furthermore, at the time one grasps the causality with respect to the generality of dimension (*parimāṇasāmānya*), the property of being a dimension (*parimāṇatva*) necessarily presents itself.

The intended meaning is that [the property of being a dimension] pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) in the dimensions of space and time, yet it does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*) because it is absent in the subject (*pakṣa*) which possesses the probans.

Nor should it be argued that this is not an *upādhi* because it is the absence of the previous probans (*sādhana*), for that would lead to the undesirable consequence of the total destruction of all counter-arguments (*pratipakṣa*).

This is because, when the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhya*) by the previous reason is ascertained through the presence of a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*), its absence is then ascertained as being a pervader of the probandum within the counter-inference.

However, in a case where the formulation [of the reason] is fallacious—specifically, in the state of a counter-balanced argument (*satpratipakṣa*) due to the non-perception of a distinguishing feature—the absence of the original probans (*pūrvasādhana-vyatireka*) is not a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*).

For example, in the argument "Sound is non-eternal, because it is a quality (*guṇatva*)," which is countered by the counter-argument "Sound is eternal, because it possesses a unique quality like space (*vyomaikaguṇatva*"), the absence of "being a quality" (*guṇatvābhāva*) is not a limiting condition;
for it does not pervade the probandum in the case of the color of a water-atom (*jalaparamāṇu-rūpa*).

Here, with the intention that there is no fault whatsoever even if the absence of the previous probans (*pūrvasādhana*) is also a limiting condition (*upādhi*), he clarifies— through favorable logical reasons (*anukūlatarka*) consisting in the apprehension of the causal relation characterized by unconditional concomitance— in the proof (*sthāpanā*) by means of the passage beginning with "Nor is the reason unestablished" (*na cāprayojako hetuḥ*).
Because it is the general rule.
The sense is that since this [cognition] is obtained by its very nature (*jātita eva*), it is also a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the absence of an exception; furthermore,
because any sublater (*bādhaka*) will be refuted here later on, this too is indeed within the scope of the general rule (*utsarga*).

Nor should it be argued that, even so, the probans for the establishment [of the conclusion] is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the dimension of a tuft of cotton and the like— since such dimension is produced merely by the accumulation (*pracaya*) consisting of the conjunction of many loose parts, and thus deviates from the dimension residing in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the tuft of cotton;
for that too is included within the scope of the thesis (*pakṣatulyatvāt*).

In the first case, if the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) were the inherent locus of the counter-positive (*pratiyogisamavāyin*), then the destruction of a jar resting on the ground, produced by the destruction of its substratum, would not be perceptible.
If, however, the locus were merely the substratum itself, then the locus of sound would likewise be perceptible;
for in cognitions such as "the lion's roar in the forest," the forest—the locus—is also perceptible due to the proximity consisting of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇarūpa*).
Not the second,
because it would follow that the mutual absence of a *piśāca* and Īśvara would be perceptible even when there is a pillar and a living being.
Not the third.
If it is argued that this would lead to the absurdity of perceiving the absence of color, bitter taste, and fragrance in air, molasses, and stones, we say no;
[the objection] is that [those qualities] would not be perceptible.

In this regard, [the ground] is not the substratum because, due to the destruction of the inherent [atoms], there is an absence of the capacity that serves as the basis for the superimposition of "sensory-ness";
furthermore, the bare ground is not an inherent cause—this is the sense. [This is stated] because even a forest is perceptible.
And thus, the point is that the non-existence of that [object] is likewise nothing but perception itself.
Regarding the phrase "because it is not perceptible":

For at the end of the section on proximity (*sannikarṣa*) in the *Maṇi*, it was established that the perception of the non-existence of a piśāca’s identity with a pillar is a case of "perception of absence" governed by "suitable non-apprehension"—that is, non-apprehension in the form of the non-perception of the counter-positive, which is incompatible with its existence. Thus, the perceptibility of the mutual absence of a piśāca in a pillar and so forth was demonstrated. That would not be possible [in your view], because in that case there is an absence of the "fitness of the locus," which according to you consists in the locus being perceivable by the same sense organ that perceives the counter-positive.
The meaning is that this is because the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) in that case is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).
"Vāyuguḍa," and so forth.

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: because color, bitter taste, and odor are respectively apprehended by the faculties of sight, taste, and smell, whereas wind and the others are not apprehended by those same faculties—sight, taste, and smell—as their objects, there is no apprehension of their absence by those respective faculties. Thus, there is no apprehension of their absence by the faculties that would otherwise apprehend them.

Since it is accepted that the "fitness of the locus" (adhikaraṇayogyatā) consists in the locus—whether it be of the nature of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) or of something else—being perceivable by the sense organ intended to apprehend the absence, as that which is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) through whose being the absence is known; [this constitutes the definition].

And thus, the perceptibility of the destruction of a jar— which arises from the destruction of the pot-sherd and resides in the ground— as well as the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of a ghost and God, which reside in a pillar and a living soul, is established;
for the ground and the pillar are grasped by the visual and other senses that apprehend the destruction of the jar and the mutual non-existence of the ghost,
respectively, and the living soul is also grasped by the internal witness (*sākṣin*) that apprehends its difference from God.
For this very reason, it has been stated in the Anuvyākhyāna:
“Because it is distinct from that which is known through scripture and is subtle, a difference from one’s own self is perceived;
how can oneness be asserted in the face of contradiction with direct experience?

He refutes the aforementioned objection with the words: "If this were so... (evam ca iti).
In order to dispel the misconception that [the self] is mental according to the logic of the dialecticians, he says: "of the individual soul" (jīvasya).

Alternatively, since the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is apprehended through scriptures such as "Two birds... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), how can it be apprehended by the senses? To this, he says: "Of the individual soul... (jīvasya).
Because difference and mutual non-existence are one and the same, it is said "difference"—namely, the witness (sākṣin).
The meaning is: "because it is perceivable by the senses through its own nature"—for this very reason.
The meaning is as follows: because, in the perception of absence, the unfitness of the locus—characterized by being perceptible through the sense organ of sight—is the decisive factor;

and because it was stated in the third pāda of the second adhyāya, under the aphorism "Because of the separate teaching" (*pṛthagupadeśāt*), that the difference between the Lord, who is knowable solely through scripture, and the individual soul (*jīva*) is established by the direct perception of the witness (*sākṣi*). Thus it is concluded.
The meaning is that it is known by a witness. (The refutation of the [notion] that the nature of the letters is perceived.)

Furthermore, since the praise of qualities (*varṇavāda*) and so forth are not perceived by the ear— which is held to be the grasper of the absence of sound— they do not constitute the auditory nature of the absence of sound.
As for the argument that the non-perception of the absence of color and other qualities in air and so forth would result in their being imperceptible, that is not so.

For in your own view, cognitions having air as their qualificandum—such as "air is colorless" or "air is not bitter"—are accepted as inferential; likewise, in my view, cognitions having air as their qualifier—such as "there is no color in air" or "there is no bitterness in jaggery [in air]"—are also accepted as inferential, and thus the desired conclusion follows.

In that case, just as there is an absence of the probans in the form of perceptibility—which consists in the fitness of the qualified object—in the present instance as well, such as length and so forth, there is an absence of the probans in the form of fitness belonging to the established substratum; therefore, one must postulate the consideration of a mark (*liṅga*) in the form of non-apprehension of what is otherwise fit (*yogyānupalabdhi*).
Furthermore, in my view, unlike the Bhaṭṭa school, even non-apprehension is not itself to be inferred;
for if non-apprehension were to be inferred by another non-apprehension, an infinite regress would result.
Nor is there any pointlessness in the operation of the eyes and other senses if the absence of color and so forth in air and the like were to be inferred;
[the author] refutes what was previously stated—that even the locus of sound is indeed perceptible—by stating: "the forest and so forth."
He refutes another previously mentioned fault with the words "yat tu" (as for that which...).

Regarding the term *śālīn* as a specific variety of fine rice, [the author] says "this is indeed knowledge, not [something else]" and therefore states: "of recognition" (*pratyabhijñāyāḥ*).
"The permanent [self]."
The meaning is that this is established by experience, as in the case of "This is Devadatta" and so forth, where one recognizes, "This is that very same letter *ga*.
Since such an experience exists there as well, the existence of the experience of recognition is not present because of a contrary perception;
even if it were present, it would be nothing but an error.
But since it is not so in the present case, he says [the following] with this intention:
"Those are rice grains. [Notes: 1.
*nyabhuñjata* (Ga), *nyabhuñmahe* (Cha-Ka). Corrected to *abhrajāma* (Cha). *nbhuñjānaḥ* (Kha). 2. The word *ca* is absent (Ga). 3. *pūrvapūrvatapamapyeva* (I);
*pūrva pūrvatamamapy* (A). 4. *tibhe* (I).
Nor is it the case that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has as its object the non-difference between the *ga*-sound present before one and the *ga*-sound presented as a universal (*gatva*);
for that [recognition] is equally accounted for by the identity of the *ga*-sound present before one with itself.
However, it should not be said that [the recognition] has as its object the non-difference from the letter *ga* as presented through the delimitation of time and so forth;
for, like other recognitions, this [recognition] "this is that" is a cognition of the non-difference between the substrata of "that-ness" (*tattā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*).
One might object: "Surely this [cognition] has as its object the non-difference between the universals *gati* (motion) and so forth;

and if that were the case, it should take the form 'this belongs to that same class' (*tajjātīyo 'yam*). This objection is not valid, for such a form would occur only when there is a cognition of the universal-ness (*jātitva*) residing in the genus—which is something in addition to the non-difference of the universals—and here, universal-ness is not cognized. To this we reply: no.
Having restated the second position, he refutes it with the words: "And this is not [the case]."
This is called recognition.
The meaning is: "it is intended by you to be recognized"—that is, it is established.
The meaning is that, in this way, it is simply a case of recognition (*abhijñā*) and not re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*); thus [it is said] "at that time."
The meaning is "in the past time."
He raises the third alternative with the words "But surely" (nanu).
He refutes what was stated in the *Maṇi*—namely, that "if that were the case, it would follow that this [object] belongs to that same class"—with the words: "And not so, because of its being such."
The meaning of the statement "this belongs to that class" is indeed "this possesses the universal (jāti) residing in that";
the point is that this form [of cognition] is logically possible only when there is the manifestation of the universal-ness (jātitva), and not otherwise.

This is stated by accepting the reality [of the universal] based on the support of his own view, namely, that the eternality of the universal is not contradicted by any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Even though a refutation has been stated in the *Ṭīkā*, he himself states a refutation following the perspective of others: "by means of highness (*tāratva*) and so forth. (Note: The commentary on the non-eternality of phonemes [varṇānityatva] concludes here.)

Because of the [logical] confusion (*sāṃkarya*) that will be stated on account of properties such as high-pitchedness (*tāratva*), there is an absence of a universal (*jāti*) such as "ga-ness" (*gatva*).

Furthermore, since this would lead to the same conclusion regarding statements such as "this is that very jar," it would follow that the non-difference of individuals (*vyaktyabheda*) is never established anywhere.
Furthermore, in some cases, this would result in the non-occurrence of error in recognition;

moreover, it would entail the undesirable consequence that even when a difference from another jar has been apprehended, there would still arise the recognition "this is that very same jar" with respect to a given jar.

Furthermore, regarding the sentence "This is that very letter *ga*," which generates recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), if the word "that" (*saḥ*) were intended to refer to the universal (*jāti*) and the word "this" (*ayam*) were intended to refer to the individual (*vyakti*), then only the identity of the individual with the universal would be perceived,
and not the identity of the universal with the universal. Consequently, this [view] would be included within the category of error (*bhrāntitva*), which will be refuted later.
The meaning is that in cases such as "This is Devadatta," it is possible to assert that the object is the universal (jāti). [The phrase] "from another jar" [is used].
The intended meaning is that even there, the universal (jāti) persists.
To one who might think that the production of such recognition is intended with reference to the universal itself, he says: "And what... (kañca).
Whatever determination of the object applies to verbal recognition will apply to [perceptual] recognition as well.

And so, in that case, it must be stated whether by the two words "that" (*saḥ*) and "this" (*ayam*) in the expression "this is that" (*so 'yam*), both the genus and the individual are expressed, or only the genus, or only the individual;
for no other alternative is possible.
Even if there were non-difference between the individual (vyakti) and the universal (jāti), would that [non-difference] be direct or indirect?
Regarding this, he refutes the first alternative with the words: "that which generates recognition" (*pratyabhijñājanaka*).
Nor should it be argued that there is no error because even the non-difference of the universal exists in the individual through a mediated relationship (*paraṃparā-sambandha*).
In some cases, there is no establishment of non-difference between individuals due to the previously mentioned faults.
Furthermore, when both [the word and the perception] refer to the genus (*jāti*), the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the letter *ga* as denoting the individual has been explained.

But when both refer to the individual, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) produced by the word has as its object the non-difference of the individual; likewise, perceptual recognition also has that very same object.

For although there is a distinction between those two based on their being mediated by an instrument (*karaṇa*) and thus indirect (*parokṣa*) versus direct (*aparokṣa*), no distinction based on their objects (*viṣaya*) is experienced.
And this is not an error, such as [the cognition] "this is that mass of hair" and so forth;
thus, the objection regarding its being an error is refuted.
And thus, by the refutation of that [position], this present position will also be refuted; such is the intended meaning.
Anticipating the final objection, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not).

The meaning is that the non-difference of the universal from the universal [is established] directly in the case of the universal itself, whereas in the case of the individual, it is through a mediated succession by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "In both cases, [it would be] the universal."
He states the third [point]: "of both also, [there is] manifestation" (vyakti).
Now, let it be granted that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has as its object both the individual phoneme *ga* and the universal;

nevertheless, let that [recognition] be an error. This is like the recognition "this is that same mass of hair," which occurs due to the cause of similarity between a mass of hair that was shaved off and one that has grown back again. Anticipating this fourth position, the author says: "Not so."

In this regard, he says "bādhaka... [referring to the absence of a subverting cognition], just as when one sees a mass of shorn hair fallen on the ground, the subverting cognition arises that "this is not that person," whereas here such a [subverting cognition] is absent. Nor is the cognition of difference a sublater [of the identity],
because there is no cognition of difference regarding the specific substratum in the form "this *ga*-sound is not that *ga*-sound."

The cognition that "the high-pitched *ga* sound is not the low-pitched one" has as its object the difference between the qualified [entities] (*viśiṣṭabheda*), and not the difference between the qualificanda (*viśeṣyabheda*). This is like [the cognition] "the jar is not black when it has become red through baking," or "the boy is not one with a topknot when he has been shorn.
It does not have the difference between the qualificanda as its object.

However, there is this distinction: for me, that qualified [object] is a distinct category (padārthāntara), whereas for you, it is either the qualifier-tinged object or simply the relation between the qualifier and the qualified.

In either case, there is no loss of the non-difference of the qualified entity (*viśeṣya*). [Objection: But is it not the case that [the reason] "because a sublater is seen" or "because a sublater is absent" is unestablished (*asiddha*)? [Response: What then constitutes this sublater—is it the cognition of difference, or the cognition of arising and destruction, or the cognition of possessing contradictory properties, or rather the cognition consisting in the experience of specific universals (*jāti*) pervaded by *gatva* and so forth?
Anticipating this initial objection, he replies: "Not so."

Since it is not subverting [the object], one might ask: does that [cognition] have as its object a difference between the qualified (viśeṣya) itself, or rather a difference characterized by qualities such as "highness" (tāratva)? Having thus raised the dilemma, he refutes the first alternative with the words "saḥ" (that).
With the intention that in the second case there is the occurrence of a specific attainment (viśiṣṭāpatti), he says: "Tāra" (the Savior).

With the intention that the cognition of a difference between the qualifiers does not have the difference between the qualified entities as its object because it is sublated, it was stated: "by means of the knowledge of the non-difference of the qualified."
The word "by the cause" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Now, one might object: "In the view that the qualified (viśiṣṭa) is not something over and above the qualified entity (viśeṣya), let it be that [the cognition] has the difference of the qualified entity as its object. To this, he says: "But this is the distinction."
The meaning is that only the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is colored [by the cognition], and not the [cognition] alone.

Nor does the cognition of arising and so forth—such as "the high [pitch] has perished and the low [pitch] has arisen"—constitute a sublation [of the notion of identity].

This is because, in my view, such cognitions have the destruction of a specific state as their object (just as in the case of "the black [color] has perished" regarding something turned red by baking), whereas in your view, they have the destruction of a qualifier as their object; in both systems, however, they do not have the destruction of the substantive itself as their object.

Nor does the cognition of the association with contradictory properties such as "high-pitchedness" (tāratva) and so forth constitute a sublation [of the identity of sound]. This is because of the experience of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)— such as "that very same [sound] which was low (*mandra*) is now high"— which, like the cases of being "crested" and "shaven" in the case of Caitra, or "darkness" and "redness" in the case of a jar, or "sound" and its "absence" in the case of the sky, [demonstrates that these properties coexist in a single locus].
And it is like the perception of the absence of that [sound] in the self;

like sound and its absence in space; and like the perception of both [sound and its absence] in the self and in space, because there is no contradiction due to the distinction of time and other factors.
Nor should it be argued that the high pitch (*tāratva*) and low pitch (*mandratva*) of two *ga* sounds uttered simultaneously by Caitra and Maitra are not observed;
for [such simultaneous occurrence] is like the conjunction of a bird's body with the sky and its absence at the same time,
or like pleasure and pain within a single self.
Because there is no contradiction due to the difference in location (*pradeśabheda*).
And that difference in location is natural for me, whereas for you it is adventitious (*aupādhika*); thus, this is merely another form of difference.

Furthermore, the implication is that according to your own view, just as in cases such as "the inhabitant of heaven has perished," here too [the cognition] would have as its object only the difference between qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇabheda*).
He states the second refutation: "Nor is it the *tāra*."
He states the third [point]: "Tāratva... etc.
Is that [quality] such as high-pitchedness (*tāratva*) an adventitious property (*aupādhika-dharma*), or is it of the nature of a universal (*jāti-rūpa*)?
Regarding the first case, he says: "That which is the letter *ga*..."
Thus, by way of the distinction of time and so forth.

The meaning is as stated in the *Tattvanirṇayaṭīkā*: "Because it is possible for a single phoneme (*varṇa*) to be superimposed with contradictory properties due to differences in time, differences in the person uttering it, and differences in the articulatory locations such as the nose.

(Note: Variants in the manuscripts include: *mu*, *ca*, *cha*, *ka*, *rā*; the reading *sarvatra 'nda' ityevāsti* found in *cha*, *ka*, *ga*, *kha*; the absence of the word *ādi* in *cha*, *ka*, *ga*, *kha*; the absence of the word *ādi* in *cha*, *ga*, *kha*; and the additional term *āditya* in manuscript *a*.)
[This is] the refutation of the non-eternality of phonemes (varṇa), [classified under] the section on wisdom;
*Varṇavāda*, page 407.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that because qualities such as high pitch (*tāratva*) are universals (*jāti*), there is no contradiction with their varying according to differences in time and so forth.
In your view, this is because [the properties] would be conflated through [the act of] going and so forth, and because they are relative;
for a genus (jāti) is not relative.

Furthermore, it is because they share the same individual instances (tulyavyaktikatva), since "highness" exists in a high note in relation to another, and "lowness" exists in a low note in relation to another.
Because even degrees such as "higher" or "lower" are qualities conditioned by limiting adjuncts characterized by excellence, just like the quality of being "the best cook" and so forth.
Nor is there a lack of confusion [of properties] due to the multiplicity of "pitch" (*tāratva*) and so forth, which are pervaded by [the universal] "going" (*gati*) and the like;
for if that were the case, it would follow that this [alleged fault] is not a defect at all, as it could be easily avoided everywhere in the same manner.
Anticipating a second objection, he refutes it with the words: "Nor is there [a lack of confusion] of pitch and so forth."

The meaning is as follows: since "g-ness" (gatva) exists without the exclusion of "high-pitched-ness" (tāratva) in another letter [such as *ka*], and "high-pitched-ness" exists without the exclusion of "g-ness" in a low-pitched *ga*, both "g-ness" and "high-pitched-ness" exist together in a high-pitched *ga*; therefore, "high-pitched-ness" is not a universal (*jāti*).
The same applies to "low-pitched-ness" (*mandatva*) and so forth; this is because it is associated with a specific locus (*sāvadhikatva*).
The meaning is that high-pitchedness depends on the low-pitched, and low-pitchedness depends on the high-pitched.
"Equal," it is said.

The meaning is this: as many *g* sounds as there are that are high-pitched (*tāra*), so many are also low-pitched (*manda*). Therefore, because of their being high-pitched or low-pitched, *gatva* (the universal of *g*-ness) and the like do not constitute universals (*jāti*), just as *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness), *karīratva* (mango-tree-ness), and *kalaśatva* (jar-ness) do not.
Rather, it is *gatva* and the like alone that are the universals, and not high-pitchedness and the like.

Now, one might object: "If qualities such as high-pitchedness (*tāratva*) were not universals (*jāti*), then qualities such as the degree of high-pitchedness (*tāratamatva*) would likewise not be universals. To this he replies, "It would indeed be so," with the words beginning *tāra*.

Or, because there would be a gradation [of intensity] due to the incomparable distinctness of individual instances, it might follow that the universal (*jāti*) itself possesses degrees; therefore, he says: "The higher," and so forth.
"Of that" means:
The meaning is that there is no resulting contradiction regarding caste (*jāti*) due to the occurrence of *saṃkara* (intermixture).

[From] *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava*, First Chapter (Pra.pariccheda), p. 408. (Note: Variants from manuscripts: 1. *sāpatte* is noted as *mu.*; 2. the word *ādi* is absent in *i-a*; 3. the word *dve* is absent in *i*; 4. this introductory remark is absent in *i*.)
For this very reason, even "pot-ness" and the like, which are subsumed under "gold-ness" and so forth, are manifold.

This is because pot-ness can be established as a property based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika-dharma*), such as being co-located with a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*) consisting of a particular conjunction of parts.
[This argument applies] to the manifoldness of "high-pitched-ness" (*tāratva*) and other such qualities.
And because a cognition conforming to the appearance of stars is untenable.

Nor can there be a single uniform cognition based on the recurrence [of a property] as the cause for applying the term "high-pitched" (*tāra*) even to distinct classes, because even an infant who has not grasped linguistic convention possesses a cognition that conforms to the form of "high-pitched."
Nor can there be a unification [of the property] by way of "being a capacity" (*jñātitva*) as the delimiting factor for the obstruction of the direct perception of a homogeneous instance;

for since the linguistic usage and conventional practice [of the term] are already accounted for by the aforementioned obstructive capacity itself—which is indispensable—the postulation of a universal (*jāti*) would be futile.
[Objection: But if, in this way, the confusion (*sāṃkarya*) due to multiplicity remains unavoidable, then "potness" (*ghaṭatva*) could not be a universal in a golden pot.
Since the confusion of classes (*jātisaṃkara*) must be avoided precisely by means of their distinctness (*nānātva*), he says: "For this very reason."
Regarding that, he says "of pot-ness" to show that pot-ness is not merely a genus (jāti). [He gives the example:
"the form of a star."
"This is Tārā, this is Tārā, this is Tārā, and this too is Tārā"—the meaning is that she has the form of Tārā; thus, she is "ungrasped."
The meaning is that even for one who does not know the cause of the word "tāra," there is observed a corresponding cognition in the form of "this is tāra."
"Of the same class" means:
The meaning is "of the same class" (sajātīya) with respect to the genus that pervades the quality.
The function of the word "pūrvavat" (as before) is to be understood as previously explained. Thus it is said.
The meaning is: by way of being an obstacle to the direct realization of that which is of the same class.
Regarding the word "sound" (śabda):
The meaning is "having the word *tāra*. (Note: 1. The term *jīti* is not present in manuscript kha; 2. *yāda* in the *mu* edition.
[This concludes] the section on the classification of phonemes (*varṇa*) and the types of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, it is not the case that when there is a desire to perceive a low (*mandra*) tone, the usage of the term "high" (*tāra*) would fail to occur because the perception of the effect— namely, the apprehension of the low tone— is present and thus lacks any obstructive capacity. Rather, the establishment of the universal (*jāti*) occurs through the absence of an obstruction characterized by the exclusion of its opposite.
It should not be argued that this is because there is no other delimitor (avacchedaka) than the genus (jāti);

for even in your own view, when that which is delimited by the delimitor of the state of being an inhibitor (pratibandhakatāvacchedaka) is present, the effect in the form of a weak apprehension cannot occur.

And if [the loudness] were an excitant (*uttejaka*) for the desire to know, then even according to my view, although the effect would be possible due to the presence of the excitant, the linguistic usage "loud" (*tāra*) would still be justified because of the presence of the obstructer (*pratibandhaka*).
Therefore, the relation with contradictory properties such as loudness does not constitute a sublation (*bādhaka*) of the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Anticipating an objection against the aforementioned intended meaning, he refutes it with: "And not... (*na ca*).

The meaning is that at the very moment of hearing a loud (tāra) sound, because one perceives a faint sound due to the desire to know [the faint one], there would be no application of the term "loud sound" to that loud sound being heard, since the perception of a sound belonging to the same class— by way of a genus pervaded by the quality of *guṇatva* (quality-ness)— would not be obstructed [and thus the loud sound would be perceived as faint].
"Even in my own view," [he says].
