The meaning is as follows: sound, however, inheres in such [substances] as earth, water, fire, and air, and it does not reside in two [different substrata]; thus, the reason exists within the property of "soundness" (śabdatva) which resides in them.
And these reasons are to be employed by way of reversal, because of the Teacher’s statement that "refutation is carried out by means of [reasons] established for the opponent."
For this very reason, the discussion begins with "those which have counter-arguments" (*satpratipakṣāṇi*);
otherwise, he would have said, "the proof for eternality.
This is because, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is an absence of non-inherence in that which is not contained within a recurring genus (*anugatajāti*).

For this very reason, in the *Sudhā* commentary on the section concerning primordial matter (*prakṛti-naya*), it is stated that sound arises even as a quality of earth and the other elements in the passage: “And [the existence] of ether and so forth.
This is said either by not intending the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa-prakriyā*) and accepting that the word ‘genus’ (*jāti*) refers to similar properties, or according to his own system.
They say that by this, there is no contradiction with the subsequent text beginning with “In my view” (*tena manmate*).
The function of the qualification will be made clear later on—namely, "like selfhood."
And that [existence] is clearly evident in some cases as the existence of both the reason and the probandum in a substratum where they do not reside in a non-inherent relation;
for according to the Nyāya system, the self, being all-pervasive, does not reside [in anything].

By means of the nose. The meaning is that the external sense organ, which is distinct from the nose—namely, the auditory faculty (*śrotra-rūpa*)—must exist, because it is that which determines and regulates those [cognitions].
For the effect, which is the cognition of sound, leads one to infer the nature of its cause, the sense organ called the ear;
for a non-eternal cognition cannot arise without a cause.
The meaning is that no other [sense organ], such as the eye and so forth, can function as the instrument for the cognition of sound;
for when sound establishes such a sensory modality, it is "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) that serves as the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*).

To ensure the logical consistency of the reason regarding those factors that establish the eye and other senses—such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and "taste-ness" (*rasatva*)—the general term "external sense organ" (*bahirindriya*) is employed.
But it is not so in the case of the auditory organ; thus it is distinguished—just as in the case of "possessing the nature of form" (rūpatva).

The meaning is: "like the nature of color (*rūpatva*), the nature of taste (*rasatva*), and the nature of touch (*sparśatva*). The meaning is: "because that which resides in two [entities] does not exist as a non-distributed occurrence (*avyāsajyavṛtti*). [In the term *katāvacchedake*, the reading is *katāvacchedake*; in the *mu.* manuscript it is *katāvacchedake*; in the *ca.* manuscript it is *tasya*.]
[The property of being a color-instantiation] is not non-eternal,
because it is a property that does not reside in what is co-located with both selfhood and corporeality, like temporality. (3)

(4) Because it resides in a perception that is not co-located with a specific quality distinct from its own substratum, like *ātmatva* (the nature of self). (5) Because, while not residing in earth and not residing in self, it is pervaded by a sub-class of existence (*sattā*) which is itself not directly pervaded [by existence], like *jalatva* (the nature of water). Even if one were to take as the subject (*pakṣa*) only one among the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) that establish the external sense-faculties—namely, color, taste, smell, touch, or sound—[it follows that] because smell is a quality belonging exclusively to earth...

Since qualities in earthly atoms are impermanent because they are produced by heating (*pākaja*), there is an absence of the probandum—namely, the state of not occurring in eternal things—in the case of odor. However, because color, touch, and so forth residing in water-atoms and the like are not produced by heating, the triad beginning with "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) does occur in eternal things. To avoid the fault of over-extension (*ādhikya*), it was stated specifically as "like color-ness" (*rūpatvavat*); this refers to "selfhood" (*ātmatva*).
The meaning is: because it resides in that which is located in two [loci] which are not co-located with both "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) and "corporeality" (*mūrtatva*).
Corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is defined as the possession of a dimension delimited by a finite measure;
it is a property of earth, water, fire, air, space, and the mind.

The meaning is that there is a concomitance between the reason and the probandum because of the eternity of time, which resides in both sound and time—those very things that constitute the subject and the example.
"His own" (sva): sound is the locus of its own property, "sound-ness" (śabdatva);
a specific quality different from that [sound] is color (rūpa) and so forth; and perception is that which does not have a common locus with that [color].
The meaning is: "only sound," because it possesses that [quality] and so forth.
In the example, the self is the locus of its own selfhood.

The logical concomitance of the reason (*hetvanugama*) should be understood as follows: the entity called "self" (*ātman*), which is perceptible and does not subsist in anything else, is not co-located with any specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) other than itself, because it subsists in that [entity].
This is because the word "own" (*sva*) refers to that which is mentioned in proximity (*samabhivyāhṛta*).
Even if it were taken to mean "soundness" (*śabdatva*) alone, there would be no fault—just as color and so forth subsist in earth.

The occurrence in the self is [the property] cognition and so forth. Given that it does not occur in either of those two (non-self and non-existence), "quality-ness" is the property directly pervaded by existence in the subject (pakṣa), while "substance-ness" is such in the example (dṛṣṭānta).

Therefore, sound-ness (*śabdatva*) and water-ness (*jalatva*), which are directly pervaded by that [impermanence], constitute the concomitance of the reason (*hetu*) in both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
[The self exists] because it possesses the universal that resides in everything other than ether;
(6) [the self exists] because it possesses the word "all" (kala), like existence (sattā). (7)

This is because [the opponent's position] is countered by such inferences as: "The auditory organ grasps a genus that is pervaded by a nature whose existence is eternally present, because it is a non-earthen sense organ, like the visual organ" (8);
and "Color is eternal, because—while being distinct from what is pervaded by the property of being a sound of noise—it is audible, like the universal 'soundness'" (9).
Thus, the argument is refuted by these and similar inferences.

In this context, regarding the first reason (*hetu*), the term "residing in two" (*dvistha*) is stated to ensure there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) with respect to the "duality residing in time and space" (*kālākāśagatadvitvaniṣṭhadvitvatva*).
In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the inference of the probandum (*sādhya*) should be understood as residing in a water-atom (*jalaparamāṇu*).
What is called "direct pervasion" (*sākṣādvyāpyatva*) is pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) itself, provided that it is not [indirectly] pervaded by what is already pervaded (*vyāpyāvyāpyatve sati*).

This is because there is no other intermediate pervaded property (vyāpyadharma) between the two properties of quality-ness (guṇatva) and substance-ness (dravyatva), nor between the universal of existence (sattājāti), nor between the two properties of sound-ness (śabdatva) and water-ness (jalatva).

"Vyoma" [means as follows]: In this ether (*vyoman*), there exists neither sound that possesses birth nor the self (*ātman*); and because the property of being sound (*śabdatva*) and the property of being the self (*ātmatva*) reside in those two respectively, the reason (*hetu*) conforms to both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"The ear" is the thesis.

The genus (*jāti*) which is sound (*śabda*), being pervaded by the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) that is itself pervaded by existence (*sattā*), has a function that is eternally active; by virtue of grasping this [genus] in the subject (*pakṣa*) and by virtue of grasping such a form in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is a concomitance with the probandum (*sādhyānugama*).
This is because even color-ness (*rūpatva*) resides in that which is eternal, namely the color of water-atoms (*jalaparamāṇu*) and so forth—therefore, it is said "non-earthly" (*apārthiva*).
According to the opponent's view, since the olfactory organ alone is composed of earth while the others are not, there is no fallacy such as "unestablished" (asiddhi) and so forth.

Regarding the term "dhvanīti": the meaning is "being distinct from both *dhvani*—which is a sub-class of *śabdatva* (the universal of sound)—and [qualities] such as high pitch (*tāratva*) and so forth. This is because of the contradiction (*pratirodhāt*).
The syntactical connection is "they are counter-balanced" (satpratipakṣāṇi); [this occurs] in the case of "duality-ness" (dvitvatva).

Regarding the non-eternality of the duality residing in both time and space— which is produced by a non-final enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) dependent on [the perception of] time, space, and so forth, as brought forward by inference—
[this is] the refutation of the [opponent's] claim [that such duality is eternal].
(Page 423)
The term "not inhering" (*asamaveta*) is stated to ensure there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) with respect to [properties] such as odor-ness (*gandhatva*) or suffering-ness (*duḥkhatva*).

The phrase "possessing a genus that is pervaded by substantiality" (*dravyatvavyāpyajātimat*) is stated to refute the opponent's objection regarding the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of "subsisting in what does not inhere."

In the second [definition], the term "distinct from the olfactory organ" (*ghrāṇabhinnā*) is used so that there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) regarding the nature of odor (*gandhatva*). The meaning is as follows: although the reason—namely, the existence of such duality (*dvitvatva*) residing in that [duality] which exists in substances possessing a genus subordinate to substantiality (*dravyatvavyāpyajātimat*), such as earth, water, fire, air, self, and mind, by virtue of being inherent in them—is present in duality, it lacks the property of "residing in eternal things" (*nityavṛttitva*); therefore, the term "existing in two" (*dviṣṭha*) is stated in order to eliminate such deviation.
If it is argued that one might as well simply say "because of existing in two [loci]," he says: "gandhatva... (starting with the word *gandhatva*).

The meaning is that there is no deviation (avyabhicāra) because the nature of odor (*gandhatva*) and so forth resides in odors and the like that are inherent in the self (*ātman*) of earth and so forth.

However, since the nature of color (*rūpatva*) and so forth resides in eternal [substances], the term "nature of odor" was used; the point is that odor is not eternal because the qualities of earth are produced by heating (*pākaja*).
In that case, let it simply be that [the universal] resides in two [loci] while being non-inherent; to this he says: "non-inherent."
"Towards the opponent" means with respect to the adversary.
The meaning is directed toward the logician (*tārkika*).

This is for the purpose of refuting non-establishment (*asiddhi*), because at the time when one employs a counter-inference (*satpratipakṣānumāna*), the proponent (*siddhāntin*) acts as the establishing speaker (*sthāpanāvādī*), while the opponent (*para*) alone functions as the respondent (*prativādī*).
Nor is the refutation of non-establishment (asiddhi) useless;
for since both pervasion (vyāpti) and the property of being a locus-feature (pakṣadharmatā) are constituent factors of inference, that which brings about the latter is also purposeful.
This is according to the principle: "A qualifier is purposeful when, without that qualifier, the pervasion residing in [the subject] as determined by [the probandum] cannot be ascertained."

The meaning is that, because the pervasion residing in a qualified cause cannot be apprehended without the aforementioned qualification, [the qualification] is necessary for the apprehension of pervasion.
"Olfactoriness."

The meaning is as follows: since the quality of earth (*pṛthivīguṇa*) is produced by maturation (*pākaja*), it lacks the probandum—namely, the property of subsisting eternally (*nityavṛttitva*)—insofar as it is odor (*gandhatva*); nevertheless, because it serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the establishment of the external sense organ consisting of the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇa*), there is no fault in the statement "distinct from the olfactory faculty" (*ghrāṇabhinnā*) regarding those [qualities] mentioned. — [Regarding the term] *duḥkhatva*.
The term "external" (*bahis*) was also stated in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*avyabhicāra*) with respect to suffering (*duḥkhatva*) and other such qualities.
In the third [reason] as well, the purpose should be understood to be like that of the first reason in the case of the "non-hatred" property:

to ensure non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) with respect to properties such as being suffering (*duḥkhatva*) or being velocity (*vegatva*), it is stated that [the property] must not be co-located (*asamānādhikaraṇa*) with selfhood (*ātmatva*) or materiality (*mūrtatva*).

In the fourth [definition], the term "not co-located with specific qualities" (*viśeṣaguṇāsamānādhikaraṇa*) is stated to avoid over-extension (*avyabhicāra*) to the nature of odor (*gandhatva*), suffering (*duḥkhatva*), and so forth. The term "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) is stated to avoid over-extension to the nature of velocity (*vegatva*) residing in the mind's velocity (*manogata-vega*), which is not co-located with specific qualities; for the nature of velocity in the mind is imperceptible (*apratyakṣa*).

When that much has been stated, [the reason] would be unestablished (*asiddha*) for the opponent, because the letter *ga* also possesses co-occurrence (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with the specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) in the form of the letter *ka*.
To avoid this, it is stated: "distinct from its own substratum" (*svāśrayabhinnā*).
The meaning is that [the property] serves as the delimitor (avacchedaka) for the establishment of the internal sense-faculty (antarindriya) within it.

Regarding the statement "because it exists in multiple locations while not being co-located with either selfhood (ātmatva) or corporeality (mūrtatva)," he says: "in the case of suffering-ness (duḥkhatva), etc."

Regarding the absence of the property of "subsisting eternally" (*nityavṛttitvābhāva*) in such things as "suffering-ness" (*duḥkhatva*), which resides in suffering and so forth that do not share a common substratum with corporeality (*mūrtatva*), there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) [in the reason] therein. The phrase "not sharing a common substratum with selfhood" (*ātmatvāsamānādhikaraṇa*) is a qualification for that which resides in two [entities]. The meaning is that if one were to state only "because it subsists in that which resides in two and does not share a common substratum with selfhood," then the quality of momentum (*vega*), which is a property of earth, water, fire, air, and mind, would also be included; therefore, the qualification "not sharing a common substratum with selfhood" is applied.
He states the fault if one were to state only "because it subsists in what is perceptible" (*pratyakṣavṛttitvāt*): "and in the case of suffering-ness, etc. (*duḥkhatvādau ca*).
In that case, taking the term "perception" (pratyakṣa) to mean "external perception," it was stated: "the nature of odor" (gandhatva), etc.
[This refers to] the cognition of another.

① "Because of being possessed of velocity (*vega*), etc."—this phrase does not exist in manuscript *cha*. It exists as "because of being possessed of velocity, etc. in manuscript *ga*. ② The word "velocity" (*vega*) does not exist in manuscript *cha*. ③ [The phrase] "in order to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this case" exists in manuscript *i*. ④ The word "existence" (*vṛtti*) is redundant in manuscript *i*.
[In the context of] the permanence of forests, etc., [there is] the inference...
And thus, since even the letter *ka* possesses the status of being a locus for the nature of sound (*śabdatva*), it is not non-existent (*asiddhi*) because it lacks difference from that [sound].

In the fifth [definition], the phrase "existing as not occurring in earth" (*pṛthivīvṛttyavṛttitve sati*) was stated to ensure non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) with respect to odor-ness (*gandhatva*) and so forth. The phrase "existing as not occurring in the self" (*ātmavṛttyavṛttitve sati*) was stated to ensure non-deviation with respect to suffering-ness (*duḥkhatva*) and so forth. The phrase "that same [quality]" (*sa eva*) and so forth was stated to ensure non-deviation with respect to luminosity (*prabhātva*) and so forth.

And thus, while *dravyatva* (substance-ness) is pervaded by existence (*sattā*) directly, it is specifically *tejastva* (fire-ness) that is directly pervaded [by substance-ness], and not *prabhātva* (light-ness) and so forth; therefore, there is no deviation [in the rule].
However, in my view, *śabdatva* (sound-ness) is directly pervaded by existence.
Furthermore, according to the opponent's view, "quality-ness" (guṇatva) is directly pervaded by "substance-ness" (dravyatva); thus, there is no lack of proof (asiddhi).
In the sixth [definition], the term "possessing a genus" (*jātimat*) is stated to ensure non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) regarding the prior non-existence of sound (*dhvani*).
The phrase "not subsisting in anything other than space" (*vyometarāvṛtti*) is stated to ensure non-deviation regarding [properties] such as odor-ness (*gandhatva*).
This is for the purpose of addressing the Logician (*tārkika*), meaning that there is no unestablished reason (*asiddhi*).
The purposefulness of the term "asiddhivāraka" (exclusion of non-establishment) is also as explained previously.
He states the fault in asserting [the self] as "self" and so forth: "In the case of odor-ness and so on."

Having stated that "the ether is distinct because its existence consists in the existence of a substance," he points out the fault [in that argument] by saying: "if it were the prior non-existence of sound."

[Objection: But surely, if one were to state simply "because it exists in all seven categories," there would be no deviation (vyabhicāra), since even in the case of "knowability" (prameyatva) and the like—which are purely positive (kevalānvayin)—the probandum (sādhya) also exists as something subsisting in eternal [categories]. Therefore, the term "sound" (śabda) would be redundant; for even if it serves to exclude the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the locus (svarūpāsiddhi), it is still superfluous. [Response: To this, he says "the seventh," with the intention that it is purposeful because, according to the method stated in the *Īśvaravāda*, it establishes the plurality of the substrata of the pervasion (vyāpti).
1. *gakāra*—*cha-ka*. 2. *ttetyā*—*cha-ka-ga-kha*. 3. This passage does not exist—*cha-ka*. 4. *tvasā*—*a*.

In the seventh [section], the term "word" (*śabda-pada*) is not redundant, because it serves as an inclusive expansion that encompasses even purely positive properties (*kevalānvayi*) such as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*). *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 426). [Note: The text provided contains various manuscript variants indicated by the abbreviations *cha*, *ka*, *ga*, *kha*, and *a*. The translation reflects the primary reading.]

1. In the eighth [inference], where the probandum (sādhya) is "having eternal existence" (*nityavṛttisattā*), the phrase "pervaded by what is pervaded by existence" (*sattāvyāpyavyāpya*) is stated in order to dispel the suspicion that there would be the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), since [the reason] would otherwise apprehend "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) or "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*).
2. The term "non-earthly" (*apārthiva*) is stated so that the reason does not deviate (*avyabhicāra*) in the case of the nose (*ghrāṇa*).

In the ninth [definition], the phrase "distinct from that which is pervaded by the nature of sound" (*dhvaniśabdatvavyāpyabhinnā*) is stated in order to avoid non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) with respect to [qualities] such as high-pitchedness (*tāratva*), which are pervaded by the nature of sound (*śabdatva*).
[This applies] to those [reasons] that are not purely positive (*akevalānvayin*).
The phrase "of that which resides in sound" (śabdaniṣṭhasya) is also to be understood;
the meaning is that it applies not only to [the property] of being an object of cognition (prameyatva), which is purely positive (kevalānvayin), but also to others.
The term "and so forth" (ādi) refers to such properties as inherence in space (ākāśasamavetatva).

"Regarding the eighth": this means that with respect to the probandum (sādhya) in the reason "because it is not an earthly sense-organ," namely "it exists eternally" and so forth—specifically, regarding the two [properties] of eternal existence and substantiality (nityavṛttisattādravyatvayoḥ).

If it is stated that [the definition] is "that which grasps a genus residing eternally," there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*), because [the definition] would also grasp the existence (*sattā*) inherent in words;
for even though a word is non-eternal, existence resides eternally in [the category of] space and so forth.
Therefore, [the definition must be] "that which grasps a genus pervaded by existence residing eternally."

When that much has been stated, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*), because [the property] would be apprehended as either "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) in the view that sound is a substance, or as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) in the view that it is a quality.
Therefore, the meaning is that it was stated [in the definition] that [the property] must be pervaded by [and yet not pervade] existence (*sattā*).

The sense is that it is clear that the qualification "occurring eternally" (nityavṛtti) is applied to the genus (jāti) in order to establish the eternity of sound and to exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā).

Regarding the ninth [point]: the function of the word "dhvani" in the statement "because it is audible while being distinct from that which is pervaded by the property of being the word 'dhvani'" is explained as "in the case of dhvani."

If one were to state only "because it is audible while being distinct from sound" (*dhvanibhinnatve sati śrāvaṇatvāt*), the fallacy [of the reason] would apply to *śabdatva* (the nature of sound), *tāratva* (high pitch), and so forth. (Note: This passage addresses a logical argument regarding the definition of sound. It points out that if the reason for something being "sound" were merely its audibility and its difference from noise, then properties like the generic nature of sound itself or specific qualities such as pitch would also inadvertently qualify as "sound," leading to an over-extension of the definition.)
Praise of the [theory of] phonemes (varṇavāda), p. 427.
Here, the subverting arguments against the opposing view are: (1) the impossibility of recognition [of the same sound], and (2) the principle of parsimony (gaurava).
However, some say: "The auditory organ perceives eternal substances, because it is a partless sense organ, like the mind."
Regarding the proofs for the eternity of phonemes (varṇa):
the meaning is that it has been stated [in the previous verse] that [phonemes] are distinct from both sound-in-general (dhvani) and space (ākāśa).

The intention is that the reason "because they are audible" (śravaṇatvāt) is clearly stated to avoid its deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to objects such as jars. [The phrase] "due to the complexity of conceptual construction" (kalpanā-gaurava) refers to the following.

This will be explained in the subsequent section on refutation (*uttarabhaṅga*): the conceptualization of the infinity of individuals (*vyakti*) and so forth—namely, that according to the analogy of waves and ripples, a preceding sound produces a different succeeding sound, a succeeding sound destroys each preceding sound, and the final and penultimate sounds destroy each other—will involve the complexity (*gaurava*) that will be described later. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), many contradictions and other such issues are included. [The term used is] "eternal substance" (*nityadravya*).
The term "substance" (*dravya*) is included to exclude other possibilities, such as [the property] of being a grasper of sound-ness (*śabdatva*) and so forth.
In this way, the probandum (*sādhya*) results in the establishment of both the substantiality and the eternity of sound;
for it is sublated [otherwise], since [the reason] would otherwise terminate in [merely] being a grasper of eternal substances such as space (*vyoman*).
The statement "without parts" is made because the mere quality of being a sense faculty (indriyatva) is found to deviate in the case of the eye and so forth; [the proof is] "like the mind."
The meaning is that this is because it grasps at a self.
The seed of dissatisfaction here, however, is as follows:

if the self were mental, there would arise doubts such as "Is this my self? or "Is it not?", which would result in the example being deficient in its probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), because the self is known through direct perception (*sākṣivedya*) in the form of a very firm ascertainment; furthermore, by the logic of conjunction as stated in the *Īśvaravāda*, any mere entity must possess parts.
One should reflect on the passage beginning with "because partlessness is unestablished" (*niravayavatvāsiddheḥ*).
These are the inferences regarding the impermanence of phonemes (*varṇa*).

*Tarkatāṇḍava* with *Nyāyadīpa* (Prakaraṇapāda-pariccheda, p. 428):
Now, an objection: if letters (*varṇas*) were eternal, they would be perceived at all times.
Nor should it be argued that there is no such fault because the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) in the form of sound (*dhvani*), which is produced by articulation (*uccāraṇa*), is only occasional.
For its nature as a manifestor is not, first of all, by way of bringing about the proximity of the sense organ like the removal of an obstruction;
because, whether on the view that it is a quality of the ear or on the view that it is omnipresent, the phonemes are always in contact with the sense organ.
Nor is it by way of imparting a refinement to the ear, as collyrium does to the eye and other senses.

If it is argued that this is not so because, by means of a refined auditory organ, there arises—as if by the eye—a single cognition that takes as its object the entire collection of phonemes connected to itself through successive discernment (*vividhya*), we say no;
for in your view, just as the producers of the phonemes are restricted, in our view, their manifesters (*vyañjaka*) are likewise restricted.

Now, regarding the doubt raised in the commentary on the *Tattvanirṇaya* statement—"Therefore, the phonemes and so forth are manifested in sound, which is a quality of space"—concerning an objection to the permanence of phonemes stated in the *Maṇi* and other works, he raises the following objection: "But surely... (*nanu*).
This refers to the position that [sound] is a quality of the auditory organ.
The meaning is that the ear is always connected with a word that possesses magnitude (*parimāṇavat*).
Having raised the objection that the desire to hear (*bubhutsā*) might be the determining factor, it is stated: "as by the eye"—meaning, "the ear, once refined, would manifest all sounds."
The meaning is that this is according to the statement of the ancients: "An eye opened by a jar does not indeed fail to perceive a cloth," [referring to] "in your own view."

Just as there is no production of all phonemes by that which produces a single phoneme, so too there is no manifestation of all phonemes by that which manifests a single phoneme; thus, the meaning is that there is no perception of everything [simultaneously].

In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the doctrine of the non-eternality of phonemes, the author of the *Maṇi*, having raised an objection, now suspects that even the inference [previously] refuted might be subject to another fault, and thus he raises a doubt with the words "But surely" (*nanu*).
"Specifically determined" (*pratiniyata*).
(The fact that phonemes are manifested by specific manifestors.)
[The opponent objects: But surely phonemes (*varṇa*) are not manifested by specific manifestors, because—

given that they occupy the same location and are apprehended by the same sense organ— they are manifested by a single delimitation (*ekāvaccheda*), just like the oneness (1) and dimension (2) of a jar.

And here, regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), by the term "manifesting agent" (*vyañjaka*), what is intended is a cause of cognition distinct from the contact between object and sense-faculty; thus, there is no sublation (*bādha*).

In the reason (*hetu*), the qualification "by the same sense-faculty" (*samānendriya*) is added to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as color and taste, which are apprehended by different sense-faculties.

In this context, "being manifested by a specific manifestor" means being manifested by manifestors that are mutually non-deviant; that is to say, they are objects of a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) that does not have the other as its object when there is no defect [in the cognition].

Therefore, they explain that there is no deviation [from the rule] in cases such as: (1) a cognition grasping magnitude that produces the error of duality in one place, and (2) a cognition grasping unity that produces the error of magnitude. Thus they say: "unity... and so forth.

In the first syllogism (kavarma), one should understand the presence of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject (*pakṣa*)—namely, that letters (*varṇa*) are perceptible by the auditory organ (*śrotrendriya-grāhya*) while occupying the same location as the auditory organ which is their delimitor (*avacchedaka*).
This will be made clear later that they share a single delimiting location and time.

Some maintain that the purpose of the two phrases "occupying no less and no more space" and "occupying no less and no more time" is to exclude [the auditory organ] from being the locus; thus it is said: "as in the case of a jar."

The logical concomitance (*hetvanugama*) is as follows: the oneness and the dimension residing in a jar occupy the same location and are apprehended by the same sense organ, namely the eye, by virtue of being delimited by the single jar-ness.

The intended meaning is that since oneness is manifested by light—which is the manifestor of dimension—there is an inference of the probandum, which consists in the absence of being manifested by a specific manifestor.

Now, an objection: if the term "manifestor" (*vyañjaka*) includes even "contact" (*sannikarṣa*), then even though inherence (*samavāya*) is one, the inherence of the auditory organ as determined by this or that particular phoneme is restricted; thus, in establishing the non-existence [of such a restriction], there would be a contradiction (*bādha*) in the example.
And because there is also the fallacy of the probandum being deficient, he says: "And here, the probandum..."
The phrase "there is no sublation" (*na bādha*) is an elliptical indication;
one should also consider that there is no deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example.
To the objection that "let mere truthfulness alone be the reason," he says: "In the case of the reason."
The meaning is that color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth are manifested by distinct manifestors such as light and salt.
He clarifies the intended purpose of the phrase "provided they occupy the same location" (*samānadeśatve sati*), as stated by Maṇi, with the words "by one" (*ekeneti*).

In the *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava*,
First Chapter (pu-430): [The conjunction] of a hawk with its two feet,
which exist simultaneously and are manifested by distinct conjunctions, [is produced] by the hawk’s contact with the post and its parts.
The qualification "provided they occupy the same location" (*samānadeśatve sati*) is added to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) between the two types of conjunction.
Here, "occupying the same location" is intended to mean "not having distinct locations.
Therefore, regarding the two [types of conjunction] mentioned:

Even though two conjunctions reside in a single hawk, there is no deviation [in the rule], because the conjunction with the post resides in the post—which is not the locus of the conjunctions with its parts—and the conjunctions with the parts reside in the parts—which are not the locus of the conjunction with the post—thus they occupy distinct locations. For this very reason:
"In a lamp, the universal is manifested, but not in water or a blue lotus."
Because this has been stated, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of blueness manifested by a lamp that manifests the quality of being produced from its causes (*uktapralatva*).
To establish the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), it was said: "of two things manifested by distinct conjuncts" (*bhinnasaṃyogivyaṅgyayoḥ*).

This is because, according to the position that conjunction is produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*)—namely, that from the conjunction of cause and non-cause arises the conjunction of effect and non-effect—the conjunction of the post and the hawk exists in the place where the conjunction of the parts of the post also exists; thus, [the conjunction] belongs to both the post and its parts.
It was stated that [the rule applies] to two conjunctions.
To the question, "In that case, how is there no deviation (vyabhicāra)? he says: "And here... and so forth.
Since the exclusion of deviation (vyabhicāra) is the result even in other cases as well, he says: "For this very reason."
The meaning is: "precisely because of making such an intention" in the case of [the word] *samādeśatve sati* (when there is the state of being a substitute). — Thus [it is said], "like a lamp."
The meaning is "only when the lamp exists.
"Jāti" refers to the state of being a blue lotus (*utpalatva*);
however, the grammatical connection is that it is not manifested.
The meaning is that, as stated by the ancients, "the dark blue of the lotus is manifested in that [face] by means of truth"—thus [it is called] *atirikta* (surpassing).

(Note: Variants such as *ekeneti nāsti*, *ne pādāva*, *śyenasyeti nāsti*, *vasaṃ*, *tyantasyaivaṃ*, and the omission of the passage ending with *ityuktatvāt* are noted; the reading *vanāṃ-prata-vyaṅka-vyantvam* is also recorded.)
Praise of the color [of the Buddha]—431.
Because the state of being a blue lotus (*utpalatva*) subsists in a location distinct [from the color itself].

The qualification "by a single delimitation" (*ekāvacchedena*) is added to exclude the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) between color and its destruction, which both reside in a single jar despite being delimited by different temporal forms.
And this single delimitation occurs not only temporally,
but also spatially;
by this, the deviation [of the reason] in the case of two conjunctions of wholes— each residing in two parts and each produced by two parts— is refuted.

Because the whole (*avayavin*) exists pervasively (*vyāpyavṛtti*), whereas the conjunction of its parts (*avayavasaṃyoga*) exists non-pervasively (*avyāpyavṛtti*), there is a spatial distinction between them due to their different delimiters (*avacchedaka*).

Furthermore, in this case, since number and other such qualities— namely, the general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*)— possess both the capacity for being included within the capacity for grasping a substance and the quality of being graspable by the external sense organs that grasp substances, there is no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Nor can the absence of a specific cause for production be established by that very reason already stated;
the point is that [the reason] exists even in the case of a red lotus—this is what is meant by "in the form of time."
The meaning is "called time"—that is, the whole (avayavin).

The term "avayavī ca saṃyogaśca" is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound. Since the whole (*avayavī*)—the cloth-form residing in two threads—and the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of the two threads are respectively manifested by light and by the two threads, [one might argue that] the reason exists even in the absence of the probandum; therefore, he says "no" in that case with the words "of the whole" (*avayavinaḥ*).
Regarding the term "avacchedaka" (delimitor): [it refers to that which delimits the locus of a property].
The meaning is that conjunction exists by way of delimitation through a portion of the individual, whereas the whole exists by way of delimitation through all its parts.

[Objection: "But even so, since there is non-deviation (of the reason) from the probandum—because the reason 'being graspable by the same sense organ' exists in length, breadth, magnitude, and separateness when they possess a common designation under a single delimitation, and the probandum also exists there"—to this he says: "In this case, let the reason be present. [That is, there is no fault, because the probandum is indeed present.]
"Because the causes are distinct."

The sense is that velocity (*vega*) is produced by action (*karman*), and action is produced by impulsion (*nodana*) and so forth; nevertheless—[the text continues with] "tathāpi" (nevertheless). (Note: Variants indicate that the word *sāmānyapadaṃ* is not present in manuscript *ka*, and *yāvadindri* is found in manuscripts *ga* and *kha*.
This passage is from the *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava*, Prameya-pariccheda, page 432.)

If it is argued that there is no such deviation because [the properties] produced by different causes—namely momentum (*vega*) and heat (*uṣṇatva*)—do not deviate from their respective causes, we say:
not so; for even then, there is a deviation between the touch and the distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) residing in a jar, both of which are perceptible by the skin.
This is because, in that case, the distinctness is manifested by a method other than that which manifests the touch.
Nor is it intended by the phrase "perceptible by the same sense organ" that [the two qualities] must not be perceptible by sense organs that do not perceive each other;

and thus there is no deviation [in the rule]. For although touch is not perceptible by a sense organ that does not perceive it (namely, the tactile organ), since it is perceptible only by the tactile organ which perceives touch, [the rule holds]; yet, because distinctness is perceptible by the visual organ which perceives touch, distinctness is not something imperceptible to that [visual organ]. Thus, there is no lack of perceptibility by that [organ].
This must be stated [as an objection]:

because there is deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of two dualities produced by two distinct relative cognitions (apekṣābuddhi) residing in different persons, or manifested at the same place and time.
[Response: This means that there is no such deviation in the cases already mentioned.
It was stated by Hetusatva: "Of the two things to be grasped by the skin."
The existence of the probandum (sādhyasattva), however, is clearly manifested by the existence of the truth; [the word] "there" (tatra) manifests that existence.
"By means of the limit."
The meaning is that the limit (avadhi) is indicated by a word ending in the fifth case (pañcamyanta), based on the cognition "this is distinct from that.
To the question, "Even so, how is there no deviation [in the definition]? he says: "of touch" (sparśasya).
"Broken."

The meaning is as follows: in a locus such as a jar and a cloth, where two duality-units are produced by Caitra’s cognition of "not being here" and Maitra’s cognition of "not being here," there exists—given that these two duality-units occupy the same location under a single delimiting condition—the reason consisting in their not being apprehended by sense-faculties that do not apprehend one another.
This is because, since the sense-faculty that apprehends the duality-units delimited by the property of duality is singular, there is no plurality [of such faculties].
With the intention that the probandum does not exist [in the example], it was stated: "and in the two suggested [meanings]."
The meaning is: "and of the two things manifested by the two types of cognition (buddhi) of the aforementioned nature.
(Note: The text contains fragments of commentary on the following terms: *sādhyā*, *śabdā*, and *vanāṃ-prata-vyaṅka-vyantvam*.)
Because you also accept that relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is the manifestor (*vyañjika*) of color.
Furthermore, it should not be intended that "being perceived by a specific individual" (*prati-niyata-pratipattṛkatva*) is also a qualification of the reason (*hetu*);
for if it were, one would have to say [the reason] is "perceived by two specific individuals.

This is because there would be a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the multiplicity of parts—which is not manifested by what manifests the whole—and due to properties such as separateness (*pṛthaktva*) and length (*dīrghatva*), which are not manifested by what manifests unity.
But surely, the probandum is that [the two] do not have mutually deviant manifestors or non-manifesteds; and thus there is no deviation.

Even though there is deviation from the manifestors of plurality and separateness in relation to the manifestors of the unity of the whole—@---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Since its being a manifester of that [object] is unestablished, he says: "By you."
It is the whole (avayavin).

The phrase "manifested by that which manifests only the whole" (*avayavivyañjakamātravyaṅgyena*) is stated in order to demonstrate that, although the plurality residing in the parts of a cloth shares the same location as the cloth itself under a single delimitation and possesses the same causal basis in the form of the sense organ, it nevertheless lacks the property to be proven (i.e., being a quality of the whole).
The point is that this [plurality] is accepted as being manifested even by enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). This is what is meant by the words beginning with "oneness" (*ekatva*).
The meaning is that this applies even to the delimited object (*avadhipadārtha*) as something suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Since the existence of the reason (*hetu*) is evident, the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) alone has been established.
Thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) between oneness and length, nor between oneness and separateness; such is the meaning.
To show how there is no deviation (vyabhicāra), he clarifies the presence of the probandum (sādhyasattva) in the aforementioned instance with the words: "the whole" (avayavī).
The meaning is: "of those two which are the manifestors of the whole (avayavin) and of unity (ekatva)"—that is, "even in the case of deviation."

The meaning is that there is no deviation [in the logical reason], because the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) which manifests plurality does not manifest the whole (*avayavin*), and likewise, the delimitation (*avadhi*) which manifests distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) does not manifest unity (*ekatva*). This is the sense of the phrase "by way of deviation."

—because, as stated in the *Maṇi*, the probandum—in the form of "not being manifested by a manifester that is mutually inconsistent" (parasparavyabhicāri-vyañjakāvyaṅgyatva)—is present due to the non-deviation (avyabhicāra) of the manifestors of plurality and separateness from the manifestors of the unity of the whole;

nevertheless, this is inconclusive (*anaikāntya*) because, just as there is a perception of the whole even in the absence of a perception of the plurality of parts, there is likewise observed a perception of the plurality of parts even in the absence of a perception of the whole.

The sense is that, since the perception of a whole (*avayavin*) and so forth is impossible when their substrates—the ground and light—are not perceived due to their having sparse parts (*viralāvayavatva*), it is necessary that the light which manifests the whole and so forth does not deviate [from its object]. This refers to the phrase "in the gem" (*maṇau*). Regarding the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) against the doctrine of the non-eternality of phonemes (*varṇa*), the phrase "at the edge" (*añcale*) is used. (Note: *bhinnapratiyogivyaṅgyayoḥ* refers to two things manifested by distinct counter-correlatives; *samavāyināśajanyayoḥ* refers to those produced by the destruction of their inherent causes; *samādeśāloka* refers to the light occupying the same location.)
The meaning is "the edge of a garment.

And thus, there is merely the state of being the manifested (vyaṅgya) of that which manifests mutual deviation (vyabhicāra), but not the existence of the probandum (sādhya) in the form of its absence; this is the meaning of "deviation" (vyabhicāra).

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntya) because the reason—defined as "being perceptible by the same sense organ while occupying the same location under a single delimiting condition" (ekāvacchedena samānadeśatve sati samānendriyagrāhyatva)—is absent? For plurality resides in only one part of the cloth's constituents, whereas the cloth resides in more [of them]; and because plurality is quickly destroyed, whereas the cloth persists for a longer duration. [The author] states elsewhere the instance of deviation (vyabhicāra): "bhinna... etc.
The words "distinct" (*bhinna*) and so forth are for the purpose of establishing the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).
The phrase "located on the ground" (*bhūtalagatayoḥ*) is for the purpose of expressing their co-location (*samānadeśatā*).
The word "inherent" (*samavāyin*) and so forth [is used to specify the relationship].
The syntactical connection is with "dhvaṃsayoḥ" (of the two destructions).
With the intention that if the two counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*) are co-located, their two destructions are likewise so, he says: "In the parts of the *virava*."
The meaning is: "in two light-particles located in the same place," because, unlike stones and the like, there is an absence of dense materiality (*nibiḍadravyatva*).
The underlying idea is that light is perceived even on a surface situated within clear water.
[Notes: 1. *maṇāv uktam iti* is not found in manuscript *cha*. 2. *vatayeti* in manuscript *i*. 3. *vimala* in manuscript *mu*.]

Furthermore, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of light and the destruction of water—which stand in the relation of counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) to water—and in the case of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of Brahminhood and the absolute absence that manifests it. [Note: *varṇavādaḥ* refers to the discussion on caste; page 435.]
Even if by the word "place" (*deśa*) one intends the inherent substratum (*samavāyin*), it remains unestablished for me, who maintain that phonemes (*varṇa*) are eternal substances.

Furthermore, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of oneness and singularity as they pertain to a jar, and in the case of cowness (*gotva*) and the property of being a substratum as manifested by distinct individuals;
for the position that a universal (*jāti*) is omnipresent (*sarvagata*) is indeed authoritative.
[This refers to] the absolute non-existence of Brahminhood and the absolute non-existence of its manifesters.
The phrase "of the two [properties] residing in the ground, which are manifested by their respective distinct counter-correlates," applies here as well.
Brahminhood is the manifestor, while being the son of Brahmin parents and so forth is the manifested; this is what is meant by the word "place" (deśa).
The meaning is that by the word "place" (*deśa*) included within the body of the reason (*hetu*), it is meant "while being in the same place.

Thus, the intention is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case because the reason is absent. Now, one might object: let the meaning of the reason be "because of the absence of being perceptible by the same sense organ while being in the same place as delimited by a single [limiting adjunct] (*ekāvacchedena*). To this, he says: "of the two belonging to a jar" (*ghaṭagatayoḥ*).

The point is this: since oneness is not manifested by a limit (*avadhi*), whereas singularity-in-distinction (*ekapṛthaktva*) is so manifested, the reason [the opponent] has stated exists even though the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is absent, because they are manifested differently.
Furthermore, the reason is qualified by the phrase "not manifested by a limit"; therefore, he says "distinct," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: "How can there be the presence of the reason (hetu) in cases such as 'cowness' and 'horseness,' given that they lack the quality of being co-extensive? To this, he says: "The universal (jāti) is omnipresent."

In the view that the universal *gotva* (cowness) resides in multiple individual cows separated by space and other factors, it is impossible for it not to be connected with horse-objects and the like situated between them; therefore, since its connection with horses and so forth is established by reason, one must admit that it exists there as well.
The non-perception of *gotva* and other universals in horses and the like is explained by the absence of the manifesting agents (*vyañjaka*) in the form of individual cows.

Thus, the point is that because a universal such as *aśvatva* (horseness) is related to individual cows and the like, and because a universal is omnipresent (*sarvagata*), there is co-location (*samānadeśatva*).

Furthermore, there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatā*) based on the following inference: "The colors (*varṇāḥ*) are things that prove and are proven by one another through mutual deviation, because they are perceptible by the same sense organ as their substratum, just like smell and taste.

For it has been stated in the *Tattvanirṇayaṭīkā*: "Since even others accept that [universals] such as cowness (*gotva*) and horseness (*aśvatva*) are pervaded by specific individuals, [the opponent argues that] cowness and the like..."
If it is argued that there is no co-location [of universals] because they are all-pervasive with respect to individuals, we say no; for proximity is unavoidable,
and because the absence of inherence exists even in the case of phonemes (*varṇa*), and so forth.
But surely, the reason is further qualified by the condition: "provided that its own determination is not dependent on the determination of another.

Since all the previously mentioned instances of deviation are indeed such that their own determination is dependent on the determination of something else, there is no deviation due to the absence of the reason. To this prima facie argument, he states the counter-objection already mentioned in the *Maṇi*: "The letters... [and so forth].

The sounds, which are mutually deviant, are the means of valid cognition; the establishment of the probandum occurs through their being the objects to be cognized by those [sounds]. [This is] "by means of the substratum."

Although sound is perceptible by a single sense organ according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), [the reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*) because, insofar as it resides in the letters (*varṇa*), it is perceptible by the same sense organ as the ether (*gagana*); yet, since the ether is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it is not perceived by the sense organ that perceives its substratum—this being the established meaning.

Nor should it be argued that the portion ending with "saha" (together) is redundant because it excludes the unestablished (*asiddhi*), since [the probans] remains a pervaded (*vyāpya*) even without it;
for [the qualification] also serves to exclude the unestablished.
Because it has been stated that [the qualification] is meaningful precisely as a means of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*),
and because it is not redundant even in the case of an indivisible absence (*akhaṇḍābhāva*),
just like "not being produced from a body" (*śarīrājanyatva*).
Nor should it be said that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth;

for some say this is because the logical reason is qualified by the condition "provided it is perceptible" (pratyakṣatve sati). Others say the meaning is "because it is perceivable by a sense organ that does not perceive its own substratum."
Regarding "gandha" (fragrance):

because fragrance and taste are apprehended by the nose and tongue respectively, whereas their substrata are apprehended by the eye and other [senses], they are distinct—[from the substratum]. (Note: This passage addresses the distinction between qualities such as smell and their physical substrata, based on their respective modes of sensory apprehension.)

The possession of a fitness included within the fitness for grasping a substance, and the state of subsisting in corporeal things, are also limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Furthermore, this being the case, why is it not also established by inference that the *varṇas* (phonemes) do not stand in a relationship of mutual producer-and-produced (*vyabhicāry-utpādaka-utpādya*),

because they are qualities of the elements (*bhūtaviśeṣaguṇa*) while not being producers [of other qualities], just like color and taste in water? Such an inference would demonstrate a lack of fixed rule regarding their production.
In the case of the color, taste, and other qualities residing in produced water, since they are preceded by the qualities of their causes, there is no mutual deviation among those which produce them.
Furthermore, because both the probans (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) are pervaded by valid cognition (*pramā*), their concomitance is manifest.
The mention of "counter-thesis" (*satpratipakṣatā*) is merely illustrative.
In the Nyāya view, because phonemes are produced sequentially and are non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), they lack identity of place and time;

therefore, the reason "by way of a single delimitation" (*ekāvacchedena*) and so forth is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Furthermore, it should be noted that there is also sublation (*bādha*), since direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) occurs with respect to each individual phoneme alone.
He states the "single delimitation" (*ekāvacchedena*) as the reason and the "limiting condition" (*upādhi*) as "substance" (*dravya*), etc. The sense is this:

where there is the state of being manifested by a single manifestor for both the singularity and the dimension residing in a jar, there the limiting conditions such as "the apprehension of a substance" exist; thus, they pervade the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*).

Furthermore, since these stated limiting conditions—such as "the apprehension of a substance"—do not exist in the locus (*pakṣa*) of the phoneme which possesses the probans (*sādhanavat*), their non-pervasion of the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*) is evident. This is the intended meaning.
Because the previously stated reason was declared to be inconclusive, he states another reason: "provided that it is not produced by fire" (apākajatve sati).

If it is stated [as a reason] "because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*), there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the general qualities such as number and dimension residing in a jar and so forth, which are produced by a producer distinct [from them]; therefore, the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is added.
The word "bhūta" is used to ensure non-deviation with respect to the qualities of the self, such as knowledge and so forth, which are both produced and producers.
The term "existent" (sat) is included to ensure that there is no deviation with respect to visible form and so forth that reside in the earth.

If it is argued that since the cognition of a qualified object and so forth is established by the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*) alone, there is no need to postulate a single [additional] relation—this applies equally to the case at hand. This will be explained further below, in the section on the refutation of the inference stated in the *Nyāyamañjarī* beginning with "nor by quality or action" (guṇakriyā). This is the intended meaning.
The consideration (*parāmarśa*) of conjunction as being the subject (*pakṣa*).
Any conjunction other than this is "conjunction other than this" (*etadanya-saṃyoga*). [Regarding] the pillar—[Note: 1. *api* is added in manuscript *ka*. 2.

*bhagavatā* is absent in manuscripts *ca*, *ga*, and *kha*. 3. *ghaṭavat* is added in manuscript *kha*. 4. *ca* is absent in manuscript *i*. 5. The intermediate word is absent in manuscript *i*. 6. *etadanya-saṃyoga*].
Thus, [the argument] "there is no [such thing as] non-existence" is refuted.
In the inference,

"Color and so forth are connected with a sense organ because they are perceptible, like a jar," there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*), due to a relation such as *saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇatā* (qualification of the conjoined), just as in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*) and the like.
The state of being a conjunction with that [jar]—namely, "conjunction with something other than this"—is what is meant by *etad-anya-saṃyogatva*.
A relation that is devoid of that [state] is both the relation that constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*) and some other relation different from it.

Thus, since in the subject there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the property of being other than the relation constituting the subject, the conclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) is reached by taking its difference from some other, unprecedented relation; hence, the establishment of inherence (*samavāya*).

Furthermore, in the example such as a jar, one should understand that the concomitance with the probandum (sādhya) occurs through its being distinct from the relation consisting of conjunction, which constitutes the subject (pakṣa); this is the meaning of "qualified negative inference" (viśiṣṭavyatirekyanumāna).
"Contradicted by itself."

Even now, since another relation in the form of an aggregate has not been established, there would be a contradiction (*bādhā*) if the conclusion of the probandum were reached by taking that [aggregate] as the basis; therefore, it must be stated that the conclusion of the probandum occurs only through its being other than itself (*svānyatvena*).
This is the meaning of [the statement] "that is contradicted."

Alternatively, by taking conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) themselves as the subject of the argument, one could employ such formal arguments as: "This [conjunction/inherence] is other than a relation that lacks being a conjunction or inherence with anything other than itself, because it is cognizable (*meyatva*), like a jar";

or "This jar is other than a jar that lacks being a jar other than itself, because it is cognizable, like a cloth. Since such applications are possible, it would follow that a relation other than conjunction and inherence, as well as a novel jar and so forth, would be established;
thus, the position is self-contradictory. This is the meaning.
With the words "But others," etc., he raises the very objection stated in the *Maṇi* and refutes it.
"Form and so forth."
The meaning of the word "etcetera" (ādi) is action, genus, and so forth.
"Because of being perceptible" means because of being an object of perception.
The underlying intention here is that when conjunction is ruled out, inherence (samavāya) is established as the factor that constitutes the connection with the sense faculty.
Regarding the phrase "in the case of non-existence, etc. (abhāvādau): it refers to non-existence and so forth.
Just as, in your own view, when "the ground is devoid of a jar" is perceived, the absence of the jar and so forth is perceived as a qualifier of the ground conjoined with the eye;

and just as the inherence of color and so forth in a jar and the like is perceived as a qualifier of the jar and so forth conjoined with the eye— because there is no inherence of absence or inherence in [the case of] absence and inherence respectively.
In the same way, let form and the other [qualities] also be [inherently related to their substrata].
And thus, since inherence (*samavāya*) is not established, the meaning is that [the argument commits] the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*).
(There would be a destruction of one's own position.
The theory of inherence (samavāyavāda), page 449:

Nevertheless, as stated by Maṇi, cognitions that are true and qualified by qualities, actions, and universals, along with their possessors and so forth, must have as their object a relation distinct from [the objects themselves].

"The [inference] is: 'Because it is a qualified cognition whose object is merely an entity devoid of conceptual construction,' or 'because it is a qualified cognition not definable by anything other than itself,' like the cognition of 'the man with a staff'.
This is not correct.

Because there is a deviation [from the rule] in cognitions such as "the form of a jar at time," he states what was said by the author of the *Maṇi* with the words beginning "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).
"By means of the possessor of qualities (guṇin) and so forth."

The category of action (kriyā) and so forth constitutes the referent of words such as "existence" (sat). The term "corresponding to reality" (yathārtha) is included in order to exclude erroneous cognitions that might otherwise be sublated.
The term "as it is" (*yathārtha*) is stated to exclude other objects by specifying that the object must be one to which a relation has been attributed;
the term "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) is used to eliminate sublation in cases where there is a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of such things as qualities and their possessors.
The meaning is that it penetrates the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa).

The expression "distinct from the relatum" (sambandhibhinna) is stated regarding the probandum (sādhya) in order to exclude other objects by means of the relation of essential identity (svarūpasambandha).
In the first reason (hetu), the qualifier "qualified" (viśiṣṭa) is added to ensure there is no deviation (avyabhicāra) in cases such as indeterminate cognition (nirvikalpaka).
In the cognition "the ground is devoid of a jar," [the qualification] "having as its object mere non-existence" is included to ensure there is no deviation.
The qualification "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*) is added to the term "existence" (*bhāva*) in order to ensure non-deviation in cognitions such as "the jar is known.
[The word] "others" (*itare*)...
The meaning is that [the object] is not definable by means of the definition of anything else, because it is a cognition whose objects are both the qualificandum and the qualifier.

The phrase "not definable by the definition of anything else" is included to avoid over-extension (*avyabhicāra*) to cognitions such as "the ground is possessed of absence" or "the jar is known," where the object is indeed defined by something else.
Here, "definition" (*nirūpaṇa*) refers either to cognition or to verbal expression.
"and so forth."
Now, the phrase "the ether," "the sound in the lute," and so forth, constitutes the meaning of the word "etcetera" (ādi);
[this is stated] because of deviation (vyabhicāra).
The meaning is that [this applies] to both reasons as well.

In your view, there is no relation distinct from the related entities between the color residing in a jar and time.

In his own view, since there is no sublation to the conjunction of every mere entity with time, he uses the expression "in your view";
for conjunction, being either different or non-different from its relata, possesses the quality of difference as well.

If it is argued that "because it is a cognition" (buddhitvāt) means "because it is perceptual" (pratyakṣatvāt), even so, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of such a perceptual cognition that has been presented [to the mind].

Nor should it be said that the meaning [of the reason] is "because it is a worldly perceptual cognition," for in the case of non-worldly qualified cognitions such as "fragrant sandalwood," the reason is unestablished (bhāgāsiddhi). Furthermore, if one takes other qualified cognitions as the subject (pakṣa), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (arthāntaratā).
This is because there is a dispute regarding whether every particular cognition has such a relation as its object;
furthermore, if this were the case, the qualification "objectless" would result in being redundant.

This is because, in cognitions such as "the jar is known," since the cognition qualified by the presented (upanīta) knowledge and so forth is non-ordinary (alaukika), no deviation (vyabhicāra) can possibly arise.

Nor should it be argued that at the time when cognition is the object, the cognition "the self is cognition" is a qualified cognition of the self in the present; and that due to a defect, because of the absence of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), there is merely the appearance of the subject-object relationship, and the term "objectless" (*nirviṣayaka*) was used therein to ensure non-deviation.
For even so, the deviation remains unremedied in your view regarding cognitions qualified by inherence, such as "color is inherent."
Nor should it be said that the proof of that [inherence] is impossible at the stage when inherence itself is unestablished;

for, since there is an initial cognition [of it], one who perceives an instance of deviation regarding the relation might still be capable of grasping the pervasion (vyāpti) due to an aversion to grasping it [otherwise], as will be stated later as a fault.
Furthermore, in reality, an inference produced by a deviation must necessarily be erroneous.
The sense is that since the non-sublation of the object has not yet been established, it is also untenable to claim that validity consists in the non-sublation of the object.
Thus it has been said.
(End of section 1.2.13 of the Brahma Sūtras,
regarding the refutation of the sleeping state.)

The meaning is that the theory of inherence (samavāyavāda) is untenable because, just as with the reason (hetu) in relation to the subject (pakṣa) and the similar instance (sapakṣa), there is no fixed rule regarding the connection with the probandum (sādhya). This is due to the lack of stability, since even when there is a desire to express the cognition "the form of the jar exists at this time," there is an equality of existence (sattvasāmya) [between the cognition and the object], and thus the connection would [erroneously] apply to the probandum itself.
Furthermore, even after the establishment of inherence (*samavāya*), it is easily provable that [the cognitions] have as their objects a relation distinct from the relata other than inherence;
likewise, after that is established, it is easily provable that they have as their objects a relation distinct from the relata other than those two;

and similarly, after that is established, it is easily provable that they have as their objects a relation distinct from the relata other than those three. Thus, there follows the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress of relations.

This has also been stated [in the *Ślokavārttika*] under the heading "Because of non-abiding" (*anavasthiteḥ*). The meaning is that, just as one could qualify the probandum (*sādhya*) by saying "distinct from its relata," it is equally possible to qualify it by saying "non-distinct from the inherence of its relata"; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress of relations.
This constitutes the point that the reason proving inherence (*samavāya*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as stated in the section on the Vaiśeṣikas in the *Samayapāda*.

Now, one might ask: "How is this meaning obtained from the words of the Sūtra? To this, having accepted that the Vaiśeṣika doctrine is untenable because it admits of *samavāya* (inherence), as clearly stated in the earlier section [of the Śrībhāṣya], he himself clarifies another meaning of the latter part [of the Sūtra] which was not mentioned by Sudhā and others, beginning with the word "hetoh" (from the reason).
The meaning is that because the Sūtra faces all directions (*viśvatomukhatva*), having multiple meanings is not a defect; on the contrary, it is indeed a merit.

Since the term "cognition" (*buddhi*) refers here to ordinary perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*), there is no fault. Therefore, he states another defect—the sublation by reasoning (*tarka*)—of the inference, beginning with "furthermore" (*kiñca*).

The intention is that [the opponent's position] will be refuted by the passage beginning with "This [objection] is destroyed by the refutation of the logical reasoning (tarka) based on whether inherence (samavāya) is established or not established," which is merely superficial; thus [he says] "inherence and other... etc.

The qualification of the relation (*sambandha-viśeṣaṇam*). [Notes on variants: 1. *Vaprasaṅgādi* — *ka*, *ga*. 2. Regarding "from that" (*tataḥ*), only "due to the infinity of relations" (*sambandhānantye*) exists. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "in this way" (*evam ityādi*) does not exist in *ca*, *ka*, or *rā*. From the beginning, the passage beginning with "in this way" (*evam ityādi*) also does not exist in *ga*. 3. *vasama* — *a*. *Nyāyadīpāvalī-tarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 452).
Furthermore, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the specific cognition that "the cloth is inherent in the threads," which you yourself accept.
If one were to admit another relation even between the inherence and the inherent—as one does between the thread and the cloth—then there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā).

Nor should it be argued: "What can a deviation do when the inherence is established? And if it is not established, where is the inconclusiveness (anaikāntya)? For [the existence of] the inherence is precisely what is in question.

Because for one who perceives a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in a relationship that appears to hold at first glance, it is impossible to grasp that [relationship] due to an aversion toward grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*);

otherwise, in your own case regarding the reason "because it is a qualified cognition" (*viśiṣṭapratyayatvāt*) where the probandum is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), the word "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) would be redundant. [Regarding the phrase] "following after inherence" (*samavāyānantyam*):...
The point is that even after the non-establishment of duality and inherence, it is equally easy to say "distinct from that" [i.e., distinct from inherence].
He states the very same deviation that was well-expressed [by others] with the words "api ca" (furthermore).
The meaning is: a cognition whose qualifier is the inherence of the threads and whose qualificandum is the cloth.
He states the answer to the objection exactly as expressed in the *Sudhā*, beginning with "And not... (*na ca*).

If it is argued that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because inherence (samavāya) is defined by the definition of another, whereas the reason (hetu) was stated as "not being defined by the definition of another," [we reply:
this is because that passage proceeded with the intention of referring only to the first reason;
for this very reason, the deviation mentioned in the *Sudhā* is stated later.
"It is useless."

The meaning is as follows: in the inference "the cognition qualified by genus and so forth is produced by the knowledge of the qualifiers, because it is a qualified cognition," the word "qualified" (viśiṣṭa) is intended to exclude deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of indeterminate perception (nirvikalpaka). For if that [indeterminate perception] were established, what could deviation do there? But if it is not established, how can one speak of inconclusiveness (anaikāntya)? Thus it is easy to say.

"As in the first case" means that in place of the phrase "the cognition in the form of 'the color of the jar at a particular time,'" one should understand it as "the cognition in the form of a qualified knowledge [that] 'the cloth is inherent in the threads.'"

This has also been stated [in the sūtra] as "because of non-abiding" (*anavasthiteḥ*); however, the meaning should be understood as being the same as in the first position. Furthermore, [the text reads] *na* (not), with *ityadhikam* (it is added) in the *mu* manuscript and *tat* in the *i* manuscript. (The Refutation of the Theory of Sound as the Manifestation of the Word-Sound)

Furthermore, just as the cognition "the ground is characterized by the absence [of a jar]" is explained by way of an intrinsic relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*), and just as cognitions such as "the jar is known" or "the jar is desired"— which involve objects of knowledge and so forth— are explained by way of an intrinsic relation, so too is the cognition of things characterized by qualities and the like explained by way of an intrinsic relation; therefore, the argument for the existence of inherence (*samavāya*) lacks logical necessity.
Otherwise, there would be specific true cognitions (*viśiṣṭa-satya-buddhi*) regarding knowledge, desire, aversion, and volition in relation to their respective objects.
In the *Sudhā*, however, regarding the first sūtra, "Because of non-termination" (*anavasthiteḥ*), it is explained how this applies to this position:

if, in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), one were to postulate yet another inherence (*samavāya*) for inherence itself, then there would be "non-termination" (*anavasthiti*). Thus it is construed.
He states, beginning with "Furthermore," that both reasons are likewise non-conclusive, preceded by the statement of examples in due order.

The word "api" (also/even) in the phrase "guṇādiviśiṣṭabuddherapi" has the sense of: even though [the cognition] has only the substance itself as its object, and even though it is a qualified cognition that cannot be defined without defining the other [qualifier].
The underlying intention is that this is because there is an absence of supporting arguments (*anukūlatarka*) and so forth.

If it is argued that the proof of the stated probandum is established by a mere reason associated with a qualifier that excludes the cognition qualified by absence and so forth— even in the absence of supporting arguments (*anukūlatarka*) and the like— then,
since the stated probandum would also follow as being established by a mere reason associated with a qualifier that excludes the cognition qualified by qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth,

it follows that there is an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) in the cognition qualified by qualities and so forth, whereas in the cognition qualified by absence and so forth, there is a distinct relation (*atirikta-sambandha*).
Thus he says "it would be so," [introducing it] with the words "otherwise."

The meaning is that the probandum in the form stated is established by the mere reason (hetu) endowed with qualifiers that exclude cognitions qualified by non-existence and so forth. The connection [of the sentence] is "the opposite would occur. He clarifies this opposite as follows: "jñāna... [etc.].
The pot is known;
the pot is seen;
it is desired.
The term "kṛta" (made) means true cognitions whose qualificandum is a pot and whose qualifiers are [properties] such as knowledge;
the inclusion of the word "satya" (true) is for the purpose of excluding other [types of] objects by ensuring that the object is not a superimposed relation.

He states the formulation of the thesis (*pakṣa*) in a manner common to both cognitions qualified by absence and cognitions qualified by name: "unconnected," etc. *Note: In this version of the text, the phrase "in this thesis" (*asmin pakṣe*) is absent; the reading *dabhā* is found in the manuscript (mu.), while *dasvabhā* is in the edition (a.); the portion beginning with 'abhāvaḥ' and ending with this point is absent in the manuscript (i.). The reading *abhāvaviśiṣṭabuddhināmaviśiṣṭabuddhisādhāra* is present in the manuscript (i.).*
