Alternatively, cognitions of qualified entities regarding things that are unconnected and separately established (*asaṃyuktayutasiddha*) have as their object a relation distinct from the related terms, because they are cognitions of qualified entities whose objects are separately established (*yutasiddha*), like the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*). Thus [it is argued].

By the definition [of inherence], there would be the opposite: for things that are established separately (*yutasiddha*), such as cognitions and the like, their relation with their own objects would be a relation between distinct correlates, like that of a staff with a person; whereas for things that are not established separately (*ayutasiddha*), such as qualities and the like, their relation with the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) and so forth would be a relation of essential identity (*svarūpasambandha*), like that of a jar's non-existence with the ground.

Thus, by the following inference— "Cognitions qualified by a reality whose object is not [intrinsically] connected [to it] have as their object a relation distinct from the relata, because they are qualified cognitions, like the cognition 'the man with a staff' (daṇḍin)"— it would be established that qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth have a relation distinct from the possessors of qualities (*guṇin*) and so forth, cognitions (*jñāna*) and so forth have a relation distinct from the objects of cognition (*jñeya*) and so forth, and non-existence (*abhāva*) has a relation distinct from its locus (*adhikaraṇa*), just as the staff has a relation distinct from the man.
"Mutually distinguished."
The meaning is that there are also such qualified true cognitions as "the ground is devoid of an absence," "this is Ḍittha," or "the jar is known.
[This refers to] "of cognition and so forth."
The meaning is: of those [faculties] named knowledge, desire, aversion, effort, and mental formation;
"by their own objects" means...
This was stated with reference to [the cognition of] knowledge and so forth;
however, it should be understood that in the case of non-existence and the like, [the cognition] occurs together with its own qualificand.
Having thus established the opposite [position], he states another over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) characterized by the same uniformity everywhere, beginning with the word "evam" (thus).
The term "otherwise" (*anyathā*) is carried over [from the previous context].

The meaning of the word "thus" (*evaṃ*) is that, just as there would be the opposite case, so too, if no specific qualification were provided regarding the reason (*hetu*), there would be uniformity in all cases.
Having refuted the lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*) of the reason, he states the conclusion: "And if this is so... (4).

1. And by this, [the reading] *ca-ka-ga-rā* [is established]. 2. Only "of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth" exists; "of cognitions (*jñāna*) and so forth" does not exist—this is the *ka* [manuscript]. 3. By this, *ca-ka-ga-rā*. 4. "Of the cause (*hetu*)" and so forth does not exist—this is the *mu* and *i* [manuscripts].

And thus, since the state of being a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhitva*) alone is the governing factor when the object is a relation distinct from its relata, there is both parsimony (*lāghava*) and uniformity (*ekarūpya*).
This has also been stated [in the verse] "because of abiding in the mind" (*manasthiteḥ*).

Regarding the similarity in terms of being established separately (*yutasiddhatva*): for cognition and so forth, there is an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) with their own objects, whereas for Caitra and the staff, there is conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Likewise, regarding the similarity in terms of being established inseparably (*ayutasiddhatva*): for the ground and absence, there is an essential relation; for quality and the qualified, etc., there is inherence (*samavāya*).
The meaning is that this results from the subversion of the established system (vyavasthiti) stated by you, beginning with those [words].

Nor do cognitions qualified by qualities, actions, or universals have as their object a relation with those qualifiers, because they are qualified cognitions, like the cognition "the man with a staff.
Furthermore, there is no deviation [in the rule] regarding cognitions such as "the jar is known," for these also have as their object a relation with its own nature (*svarūpa*).

Nor should it be argued that even here there is the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*) by means of that same [reason], on the grounds that since individual natures are infinite, it would be cumbersome; rather, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), only one single relation is established.

Furthermore, according to the maxim that "the postulation of a property (dharma) is better than the postulation of a substratum (dharmin)," since the nature of inherence (*samavāya*) and its status as a relation residing therein are both merely conceptual constructs, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to postulate only the property of being a relation—which is already established—for things like the absence of a jar on the ground, whose own natures as qualities and so forth are already established.
With the words beginning "It is said" (*ucyate*), the author [Śrīharṣa] refutes another inference established by the author of the *Maṇi* (Udayana), stating: "Nor... (*nāpi*).
The application of the terms of truth (satyapadakṛtya) is to be understood as before.
He elaborates on this according to the aforementioned method, beginning with the words "jñāta" (known), and so forth.
"Of one" means:

In the inference for [the existence of] an agent, the sense is "as if there were a single agent. Otherwise, even though [the conclusion] could be established in another way, he states a counter-example (pratibandī) in the form of an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), following the logic of parsimony (lāghava-tarka), with the words "otherwise" (anyathā).
The word *mātra* (only) refers to all types of non-existence, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth.
Otherwise,

if one were to take as the subject (*pakṣa*) the cognition of "truth" qualified by mere non-existence and prove that it has a relation as its object, then— due to parsimony (*lāghava*)— a single, eternal relation would be established as that which is common to all instances of mere non-existence.
1. Thus, by taking as the subject (*pakṣa*) the cognitions of things qualified by absence, substance, quality, action, and genus— as well as cognitions such as "the jar is known"—

and proving that they have a relation as their object, there would be established, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), a single, eternal relation existing in the case of absence, quality and its possessor, and so forth, as well as in cognition, desire, and the like.

This has also been stated [in the verse] "because it would lead to an infinite regress" (*anavasthiteḥ*). The meaning is that since there is no distinction between the two cases—namely, the principle that "it is better to postulate a property (*dharma*) than to postulate a substratum (*dharmī*) when aided by parsimonious reasoning"—there can be no fixed rule that the relation is an essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*) in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*) and so forth, whereas it is something other than that in the case of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.

[Objection: But in this context, for both [types of relations], the state of being a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhitva*) or the state of being a determinate cognition (*savikalpakabuddhitva*) culminates in a cognition whose object is the relation.

If it is argued that this results in the fallacy of the probandum being identical to the reason (*sādhyāviśeṣa*), we say no; for it is logically possible to define the reason as either "being a cognition produced by the cognition of a qualifier" or "being a non-qualified cognition. Otherwise, this same fault would apply to your own formulation as well, since it is common to both cases. Furthermore, if you argue that the property of being produced by the cognition of a qualifier, or the state of being a generator of a cognition that pervades its locus, is difficult to ascertain without knowing the object-relation of the cognition, then the same fault applies to you as well.

The point is this: it is the same [in both cases]. Since the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is the object of the cognition that grasps it, and since that [qualifier] alone must be the cause because it is that upon which the [cognition of the qualified] depends, this [argument] is likewise equal [to the previous one]. 4. Or, "the state of being a cognition that produces a cognition of recurrence" is the qualifier—this is an addition [in manuscript *i*]. 5. "Because of similarity"—[manuscript *i*].
6. "You also"—[manuscript *a*]. 7. "And you"—[manuscript *a*]. 8. "Even though blind"—[manuscript *i*]. 9. "The object of the senses"—[manuscript *i*].

Regarding the theory of inherence (samavāyavāda), page 457:
But if that were the case, then in a place containing a jar where there is an absence of cloth, there would arise the cognition of the absence of a jar;
for the relation of inherence (vaiśiṣṭya) is one and the same in all absences.

If it is argued that, in this way, a jar or the like would possess the nature of a self (*ātmatva*) because of its eternal relation with the cognition and so forth that have those things as their objects,
then for you as well, there would be a cognition of color in the wind— which possesses touch but lacks color—
because inherence (*samavāya*) is a single entity.
In this way, even a jar and the like would possess the nature of the self;
for the inherence of "jar-ness" is identical to the inherence of "cognition"—the argument is the same.

If it is argued that even though the inherence (*samavāya*) of color exists in air, there is no cognition of color because of the absence of a specific relation in the form of a qualifier-qualified (*viśeṣaṇatā-viśeṣya*) relationship with color, then [we reply]: even at a time when a jar exists on the ground, although the qualification by the absence of the jar (*ghaṭābhāva-vaiśiṣṭya*) exists, there is no qualifier-qualified relationship with the absence of the jar. Therefore, it is improper to apply the same logic—by way of a counter-argument—to the case of cognitions qualified by absences and the like, suggesting that they must involve a single, eternal, and constant relation.
There, with the thought that "because there exists a subverting argument," he anticipates the very subverting argument stated by Maṇi, beginning with "But surely" (nanu).
In that state.
The meaning is: "given the existence of a single, eternal relation with non-existence.
It is stated that "it possesses the non-existence of a cloth" in order to establish the existence of the relation with the non-existence of a jar.
In such a case, the phrase "possessing a jar" is stated in order to exclude the over-extension [of the definition] to the cognition of the absence of a jar.
It would follow that it possesses the nature of a self.
The sense is: "as in the case of the self.

Therefore, with the thought that it is precisely the abandonment of *samavāya* (inherence) that is logical, he provides a resolution by means of a counter-argument: "Then [the same applies] to you as well."
The meaning is: even for one who asserts a single, eternal relationship [of inherence] with respect to qualities and so forth.
“Even though there is an inherence of color in air, there is an absolute absence of color [in it], whereas this is not the case in a jar.
How can this be so?”

Anticipating the objection raised by Maṇi—that "because of the nature of the substratum (adhikaraṇa), there is a cognition that determines an uncontradicted form"—he refutes it, saying: "But even in that which possesses the inherence of color (rūpasamavāyavat)..."
The meaning is: because of the nature of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) consisting in its own incapacity (*ayogyatva*).

[The opponent argues:
"Because there is no specific [condition], there is no cognition of the absence of a jar"—but this is the same [as our position].
But surely, even though air possesses the inherence of color, there is no cognition of color because of the nature of the substratum;
yet such a nature cannot be postulated here,
because immediately after a jar is removed, the absence of the jar is cognized in that very same place.
If it is argued that there is never any cognition of color in air, then [we reply]:
in that case, since the inherence of the future red color exists in a jar during its state of blackness, there would likewise be a cognition of red color at that time; thus the two cases are equal.
Nor should a nature characterized by contradiction be postulated here for the wind,
since at that very same time, a red form is sometimes perceived therein.
But surely, at that time, there would be no cognition of it due to the absence of the red form,
since in worldly perception the object itself is also a cause [of cognition].

For you, however, since the absence of the jar exists even at the time when the jar is being brought in— just as it existed at the time when the jar was being removed— the cognition of that absence would be unavoidable.
"And not here" means "not in the case of the ground, which is the locus of the absence of the jar.

With the intention that, if that were so, the cognition of the absence of the jar on the ground would never occur—just as there is no cognition of color in the air—he says: "by the obstruction of the jar."
Because at times there is the cognition of a red form.
The point is that even in the case of air and so forth, if one were to postulate a locus characterized by unfitness (ayogyatā), that [inherence] would not exist there either.

Now, [it may be argued that] in the case of an unbaked jar, at the stage when it is black, the cognition of a red color is produced as either a presented perception (*upanītapratyakṣa*) or a non-presented perception (*alaukikapratyakṣa*).
It cannot be the first, because that would entail an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

With the intention that, in the final case, because the existence of the object (*viṣaya-sattva*) is the cause [of perception], the non-perception of the red form there is established simply by its absence, he addresses the objection raised by Pakṣadhara and others, beginning with "But surely... and so forth;
and since it might be argued that "I too can say this," he says: "But for you... and so on.
The meaning is: even in the case of a cognition qualified by non-existence, for one who maintains a single, eternal relation [between the qualifier and the qualified].
"Time" (kāla) refers to this.
The meaning is "at two times. [Notes: 1.
*svarūpasambandhāḥ* is added—Rā. 2. From here until *svābhāvaḥ kalpyaḥ* is absent—Cha. 3. *tadā* is added—Mu. 4. *tāvat* exists—Cha, Rā, Mu;
*tu* is absent—Ga.]
(The refutation of the doctrine of inherence: For at the time when a jar exists, its non-existence has not gone elsewhere.
If it is argued that [the self] does not perish because it is formless,
nor does it perish because it is eternal, we say: no.

Because, at the time when the pot is brought near or removed by me, there is an absence of the non-existence of the conjunction with the pot on the ground, which [non-existence] was present at the time of its prior concealment.

Furthermore, even if one adopts your position, is it the cognition of absolute non-existence that is being attributed [to the self], or rather that of a fourth kind of non-existence characterized by arising and perishing?
[The phrase] "because it has been accepted" [is used].

This is because of the statement in the *Tattvasaṅkhyānaṭīkā*: "The absence of contact with this ground for that which has gone there is also included, as the case may be, within [the categories of] antecedent non-existence and so forth," and likewise because of the statements of Vardhamāna and others.
And this matter has been explained in the *Nyāyāmṛta* in the section titled "The Argument Establishing that the Non-existent is the Counter-correlative of Negation"; such is the sense.
Because of non-existence.

If it is objected: "Since the prior absence of the conjunction with the jar about to be brought near—which existed previously—is indeed a *prāgabhāva* (antecedent non-existence), and since the absence of that [conjunction] which exists later at the time the jar is being removed is of the nature of the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of the jar's conjunction, and thus exists even at the time of the jar's removal, how can there be no perception [of the jar]?"—we reply: No.

The point is that if one were to take the destruction of the prior conjunction with the jar as the basis for the undesirable consequence that [the spot] would now be perceived as possessing the jar even when it does not, this is an instance of "accepting the desired" (*iṣṭāpatti*).

This is because the cognition "this jar was previously here, but having been moved elsewhere, has been brought back here" is indeed a cognition of that very nature, just like the cognition "it was carried elsewhere."
Granted, there may be no fault in your own position—namely, that the cognition "there is no jar on the ground" has as its object the absence of the contact between them;
however, this fault would certainly persist in the systems of the Logicians (Tārkikas) and the Bhāṭṭas. Therefore, he says: "Furthermore... (kiñca).
"O you two, come hither! Thus [it is said].
The meaning is: "O maker of jewels, [I am] yours.

[From the *Tarkatāṇḍava* with the *Nyāyadīpa*, First Chapter, p. 460] (Note: Variants indicate that the word "ghaṭa" is absent in manuscript *mu*; "tvadīya" is the reading in manuscript *i*; and "dīye" is the reading in manuscript *i*.)

Not the first [alternative], because according to your position, since that [pot] exists there even at the time of the pot’s non-existence by virtue of its proximity consisting in its own nature (*svarūpa*), the cognition of it would be unavoidable. Nor the last, because just as the red color does not exist during the state of blackness, so too [the cognition of the pot] would not exist at the time when the pot exists— @---------------------------------------------------------------------------
Now, even according to the ancient view, when it is stated that "there is no jar here on this ground," it is the conjunction with it that is negated;

thus, following the opinion that there exists a fourth kind of non-existence of relation—distinct from the triad beginning with prior non-existence—which is subject to production and destruction, he says:
"subject to production and destruction."

And it has been stated by Vardhamāna: "Since non-existence differs not only through the difference of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) but also through the difference of the delimitors of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), this 'absence of a jar conjoined [with a surface]'—like the absence of other qualified entities—is subject to production and destruction, and is of the nature of its own specific form."

By this, the argument that "because the two [entities] existing at that time lack the capacity to produce a qualified cognition, they do not possess the status of essential proximity (*svarūpa-pratyāsatti*)" is refuted;
for it is an incoherent statement to claim that when both exist in their own right (*svarūpasattve*), they do not constitute proximity.

As for what was stated by Vardhamāna— that the relation between the absolute non-existence of a jar and the ground is simply the destruction of their conjunction, and thus there is no resulting cognition [of that non-existence] at that time—
that is not correct;
for it is impossible for there to be a relation between an absence and its locus without some other relation.

The point is this: if one were to postulate a relation such as the destruction of the conjunction with an object—thereby abandoning the relation established by the nature of being essentially conjoined—then there would be an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar in its shards.

However, when the jar exists, since there is no absence of a relation consisting of the destruction of the locus-located relationship (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), the non-perception [of the jar] is logically accounted for, and thus there is no sublation [of our position].

Consequently, it follows that even the absolute non-existence of a jar and so forth would be a purely positive entity (*kevalānvayin*), just like the absolute non-existence of space and so forth. This is the intended meaning.
As for what was previously stated— that there is no cognition [of redness] at that time because of the absence of the form of redness— that is not so;
for while a jar is in its dark state, since the form of redness exists in a hibiscus flower,
the cognition "the jar is red" would indeed be unavoidable.

(The refutation of the theory of inherence: The doctrine of inherence, page 461.)
Because the absence of the fourth state is equal [to its presence] in terms of existence;
and because even a red color exists in things such as the *japā* flower precisely during the state of its being dark blue.
If you say, "It does not exist here," [we reply: no.
When there is a relation between the qualifier and that which is qualified, it is impossible for the absence of the qualifier to exist in the qualified;

for when the counter-correlate (pratiyogin), the delimitor of counter-correlation (pratiyogitāvacchedaka), and the relation [of the counter-correlate] are present in a form, the absence of the relation of that form is not possible.

Furthermore, just as air possesses the nature of being devoid of color even due to its inherence in color, one must postulate that the locus containing the counter-positive also possesses the nature of not producing a cognition qualified by the absence of that counter-positive within itself at the time of that counter-positive's existence. With the intention that—given the oneness of inherence—the inherence of black color exists in a jar at that very time when the inherence of red color existing elsewhere also exists, he says: "of the red color also."
"Here," he said.
The meaning is: "If it is argued that the red color does not exist in the jar.
[This refers to] the qualifier.
The word "sat" (being) is the logical concomitant (anvaya).
Of that qualifier,
[the term] is "the delimitant of counter-correlativity" (pratiyogitāvacchedaka).
In the statement "form is not inherent," it is said thus because the relation itself serves as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka).
It was previously stated that it is improper to establish the cognition of non-existence through a counter-argument based on the assumption of existence;

now, he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*) to explain how the cognition [of non-existence] does not occur during the state of the jar, even though there exists an eternal relationship between existence and non-existence.

By the statement beginning with "the time of the counter-positive," one should consider that such an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not to be postulated here; for the aforementioned fault—that the non-existence of a jar is perceived immediately after another moment of the jar—is thereby avoided.
Furthermore,

just as for you [the Naiyāyika], there is no relation between the absence in the courtyard and the nature of the house at the time of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), because the absence is not then perceived,
but rather [the relation exists] only at some other time; likewise [it is for us].
Likewise, although the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) exists at the time when the jar exists, it does not possess the status of a relation at that time;
thus, there is no undesirable consequence of a cognition of the absence of a jar in a place where a jar is present.
[Objection: If the absence has an eternal relation with its own substratum, then upon the destruction of the substratum, even the *dhvaṃsa* (destruction) would lead to the reappearance of the jar.

However, you who maintain the doctrine of absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) must state that— just as the absence of a jar on the ground is not perceived even when the jar is present because of some obstructing factor such as its being in a different location from the locus of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) or a relation consisting of the destruction of its conjunction and so forth—

so too it should be in this case under the view of an eternal relation; and thus, he says "Moreover" (api ca), indicating that there would be no room for the doubt that the cognition of absence would not occur after the jar has been removed.
Fourfold.
There are four.

The meaning is as follows: just as there is no relation between the two intrinsic natures (svarūpa) of that non-existence which is the limit of the four [negations] and that which is the house—at the time when the counter-correlate (pratiyogin), such as a cloth, is apprehended—likewise, in the present case as well, such a relation exists because otherwise an occasional cognition would be inexplicable.

In this way, even in the case of a cognition qualified by non-existence (*abhāva*), some single, eternal relation might be established; however, by the aforementioned counter-argument (*pratibandyā*), it would follow that there could be a cognition of the non-existence of a jar even during the state when the jar is present. Having thus set aside the objection stated by Maṇika and others, he now anticipates and refutes another objection as well, beginning with the words "nanvabhāvasya... ("But [it may be argued] regarding non-existence...").

Now, an objection: in the case of the destruction of an effect caused by the destruction of its substratum, the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) alone is the determining factor, as is observed in the case of cloth and the like.

And so, how can the destruction of an effect in the form of cessation (*dhvaṃsa*) be urged to occur merely through the destruction of its own substratum, which is endowed with an eternal relation as previously described?

For inherence (*samavāya*) is not established by the reason of being a cognition qualified [by its object] within a cognition of an absence qualified [by its locus]. (The Refutation of the Theory of Inherence)
Regarding the doctrine of inherence (samavāyavāda), p.
463: With respect to the destruction of an effect, the general principle alone—that it consists in the destruction of the cause characterized by a permanent relation—is the decisive factor;
however, the destruction of the inhering substance as a particular instance thereof is not.

If there is no subverting evidence, it is improper to abandon the universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, if it is argued that inherence-ness (*samavāyatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*), but rather a conceptual construct consisting of the state of being an eternal relation characterized by specific difference (*vaiśiṣṭya*), and thus involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), we say: no.
That being the case, since there is no obstacle to accepting a relation of inherence (*vaiśiṣṭya*) in an absence other than destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), [the opponent's position fails].
Nor can it be argued that if an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*) holds for one absence, it must likewise hold for other absences;

for if an essential relation were accepted in cases such as "the jar is known" where it pertains to an existent (*bhāva*), it would follow that the same would apply to cases such as "the color is the jar."
Because there is an absence of inseparable establishment (*ayutasiddhatva*), it is rather something else entirely.
To the question, "In that case, how can such a consequence be drawn?", he says: "For, with regard to the destruction of the effect... [and so forth].
He says "furthermore" (kiñca) to show that not only is there an absence of a cause for renunciation, but there is also a positive reason [for its necessity].
It is not birth.
The meaning is that [the relation] is one individual;
the sense is that in a cognition qualified by non-existence and so forth, the nature of being related to something eternal is simply the state of being qualified by whatever [qualifier] it may be.
"And not" [is the beginning of the next point].
And likewise, there is a positive concomitance (anvaya) with "even in the case of non-existence";
why is this? To this he says: "Even in the case of existence."
The logical connection is that [it would result] in the consequence of being identical to reality (*tathātva*).

If there is a distinction among positive entities (*bhāva-padārtha*) based on whether they are established separately (*yutasiddha*) or not established separately (*ayutasiddha*), then it is the same for negative entities (*abhāva*), as there is a distinction between them based on whether they are effects (*kārya*) or non-effects (*akārya*). Thus, the two cases are equal.

If it is argued that there would always be the manifestation of the jar because of its eternal relation with cognition and so forth, [we reply] that this is the same as the consequence that there would always be the cognition of dark or red color in the jar because of its eternal relation with the jar and so forth.
If it is argued that there is no fault because the dark color and so forth are only occasional, [we reply: the same applies here.
The same applies to cognition (*jñāna*) and so forth; thus, the two cases are equal.

Furthermore, if you argue that there is a dual nature (*dvairūpya*) in existence due to some kind of subverting argument (*bādhaka*), then let there likewise be a dual nature in non-existence due to the very same subverting argument already mentioned; therefore, the point is that [non-existence] is indeed identical [to existence].
Furthermore, if—

on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*)— the destruction of the eternal relatum were the cause of the destruction of the effect, then, for even greater parsimony, the destruction of that [relatum] itself would have to be the cause there. But this is not an acceptable conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*).
For it would follow that the form of the cloth is destroyed by the destruction of the pot;
indeed, although the pot is not a cause of the form of the cloth, it is the inherent substratum (*samavāyin*) of the cloth's form.
Thus, if a relation is destructible, what determines its destruction is simply the nature of being a relation (*sambandhatva*) due to parsimony (*lāghava*),
and not a specific variety thereof such as "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*); consequently, even inherence (*samavāya*) would be subject to destruction.

If, for the sake of preserving inherence (*samavāya*), the qualification "being a cause" and so forth is applied there, then let the qualification "being distinct from relation" (*vaiśiṣṭyānyatva*) also be applied for the sake of preserving relation (*vaiśiṣṭya*); for the two cases are equal. Now, it may be argued: "Let there be uniformity in the case of mere non-separation (*ayutasiddha*), but there is no uniformity in the case of mere relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*)."
Since it is accepted that only non-existence distinct from destruction possesses an eternal relation; therefore,
let the eternal relation reside in non-existence alone, and the aforementioned fault does not apply.

With the intention that the destruction of the effect is governed solely by the destruction of its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and that the [alleged] complexity (*gaurava*) is irrelevant, he refutes what was stated starting with "for the destruction of the effect... by saying "furthermore" (*kiñca*) and "possessing an eternal connection" (*nityasaṃbandhin*).
The meaning is that it is endowed with that relation which is eternal;
this is because of its greater parsimony (lāghava).
The meaning is: "because of the abandonment of the causal term."

Without stating that the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyin*) is the governing factor in the destruction of the effect, he points out another over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by accepting, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), that the destruction of only the eternal related entity is the efficient cause; he does so with the words "In this way" (*evam*).

The meaning is as follows: by following parsimony (*lāghava*) and abandoning specificities, when a universal (*sāmānya*) or the like exists, even if the effect is destroyed, just as there is destruction of that which is eternally related, so too upon the destruction of the relation, the property of being a relation (*sambandhatva*) alone would be the determining factor.
"Therein" (*tatra*) refers to this.

The meaning is that if the qualification "being a relation other than inherence" is applied to the condition of being a relation that causes destruction, such that it means "being a relation that serves as a cause," [then the following would occur].

Regarding the term *vaiśiṣṭya*: some, however, maintain that when postulating the destruction of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) as a cause [of the destruction of an effect], the property of inherence (*samavāyatva*) is not included [in the definition of that cause].
By which [definition] there would be respectability;
however, they say it is merely the individual (vyakti) as the substratum of the collection of shaven heads, so as not to over-extend the definition.

By this very [reasoning], cognitions qualified by real, non-sensory perception, universals, qualities, and actions have as their cause the relation with the qualifiers, because they are cognitions qualified by real, non-sensory perception.

Alternatively, let it be that the very fact of being a relation other than the *vaiśiṣṭya* (the relation of qualification) which is the object of a cognition qualified by absence is what governs the destruction of the relation.
And in this way, even in the case of absence (*abhāva*), there would indeed be an eternal relation; such is the intended meaning.

Although the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is simply "those who have the cognition of a qualified [object] regarding a jewel," the term "cognition of a qualified [object]" (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) in this context—within the thesis, the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—refers to ordinary perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*). This is because of the commentary on that [text], which states: "In the case of ordinary [perception]," etc.
The word "ordinary" (*laukika*) is used to exclude sublation (*bādha*) in the case of extraordinary perception (*alaukikapratyakṣa*).
The term "perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*) is used in order to exclude sublation (*bādha*) in the case of inference and other means of knowledge.
The term "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*) is used in order to exclude that [non-conceptual cognition] from being non-conceptual;
the term "real" (*satya*) is used in the reason (*hetu*) to prevent the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of error;
and the qualifiers of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are provided to avoid the deficiency of the probandum and the probans.

He states what was argued by Pakṣadhara and others: "In the case of the earth and so forth, there is indeed an agent."
Having said "for this very reason," he clarifies the subverting argument that cuts off the cause with the words: "the connection."

Regarding the phrase "having relation as their cause," does the relation function as a cause by virtue of being an object (*viṣayatva*), or by virtue of being inherence (*samavāyatva*)? In the first case, let the natures of qualities and so forth themselves—when followed by some common property—be the cause in that manner; what is the use of inherence?
In the final view, however, inherence (*samavāyatva*) consists in being an eternal relation; thus, by parsimony (*lāghava*), let its status as a cause be based simply on its being a relation.

Since that [quality of being a relation] is common even to essential relations (*svarūpasambandha*), let the status of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—unified by that very [property of being a relation]—be what constitutes the cause.

Regarding the theory of inherence (*samavāya*), [it is argued that] it is sufficient for the very natures of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—which are subsumed under the relation of identity-in-difference (*svarūpasambandha*) as established in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*) and the like—to serve as the cause for the production of a uniform effect. Thus, there is no need to postulate a separate category such as inherence.

Therefore, just as in the case of non-existence and so forth, since the relation is a conceptual construction upon the substratum even in the case of qualities and so forth, by the equality of this principle, the essential nature itself is the relation.

With the intention that, just as there are cognitions qualified by a staff and so forth which have two distinct entities related by a *yutasiddha* (separate) relation as their objects, so too there are cognitions qualified by a whole, a quality, an action, or a universal which have two related entities related by an *ayutasiddha* (inseparable) relation as their objects—and that in this case, due to the parsimony of the mutual delimiters (*avacchedaka*), the complexity of the individual entity (*vyakti*) is not a defect—he refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "In the case of non-existence, etc. (*abhāvādau*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), there is the inclusion of cognitions qualified by inherence as established in that [Vaiśeṣika] system.
This was stated on the assumption that "being a perception qualified by real, non-conceptual universals (*jāti*) and so forth" is the delimitor of the effect (*kāryatāvacchedaka*).
In reality, however, even such "perceptuality" is not a delimitor—just as "inferentiality" and the like are not—because there is a lack of evidence (*mānābhāva*).

Furthermore, it cannot be a delimitor because it is subject to sublation (*bādhaka*), similar to "the state of being an impermanent valid cognition" or "the state of being an impermanent perception," since a single, recurring cause corresponding to an effect delimited by itself is unestablished.
Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that inherence (*samavāya*), which consists of an eternal and uniform relation, is the underlying cause [of the notion of "existent"];
for this would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Moreover, it should be understood that this is because the fact that an object is not a cause with respect to perception has already been established in the discussion on the nature of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*).
Having restated what was asserted by Pakṣadhara and others, he refutes it with the words beginning "yat tu" and so forth.
[The word] "anyonyam" means mutually.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: the cognition qualified by parts has a mutual similarity (*sājātya*) with the cognition qualified by qualities and so forth, and that [cognition qualified by qualities] has a mutual similarity with the cognition qualified by a genus, and so on, in the form of "the cognition qualified by a genus" being similar to "the cognition qualified by qualities," and so forth. This similarity—consisting in the absence of a clear manifestation of distinction—is distinguished from other cognitions qualified by [other] attributes; it is an empirical fact established through experience.

And thus, just as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established as the cause for the cognition qualified by a staff and so forth, so too inherence (*samavāya*) is established as the cause for the uniform effect consisting of perceptual cognitions qualified by qualities and so forth.
This is because it does not have difference as its object,
or because it lacks the causal complex for a very clear manifestation.
Alternatively, [it is] by virtue of having as its object "inseparable existence" (*ayutasiddhi*), which is the regulator of the inherence (*samavāya*) postulated by you;
he states its nature: "clearly," etc.
Viveka means distinction (*bheda*).
The meaning is that it consists in the absence of being an object of that [distinction].
This refers to the mutual [distinction] between parts and wholes, and so forth.
The meaning is that, like two fingers, the difference [between them] is not perceived.
"Anyā" (other).

The meaning is as follows: there exists a mutual similarity (*sājātya*) among qualified cognitions such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and "the one with earrings" (*kuṇḍalin*), which is distinct from the mutual similarity found among other types of qualified cognitions involving inseparable entities (*ayutasiddha*). This [similarity] is established by experience (*anubhava-sākṣika*) as being absent in cognitions such as "the man with a staff.
Thus, it has been stated that such a similarity—distinguished from others and residing within qualified cognitions of qualities, actions, and so forth—is proven by experience.

Is that [invalidity] caused by its being a class (*jāti*), or rather by the absence of a very clear manifestation of discrimination, or by the non-distinction of the object from the sublation (*bādha*)?

Not the first, because there is no evidence for it being a class; for the nature of such a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) is otherwise intelligible. He addresses the third [objection] with the words "tvad" (your).
The meaning is that those [qualities] which you accept as the inseparable existence (*ayutasiddhi*) that regulates inherence (*samavāya*).

Furthermore, just as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) [is distinct] among things that are separately established (*yutasiddha*), so too would inherence (*samavāya*) fall into the error of being manifold among things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*), due to the symmetry of the underlying logic.

Now, one might object: "Inseparable establishment (*ayutasiddhi*) is simply the state of being related to a permanent relation. To this, he states another point of reference—namely, that it refers to qualities, actions, wholes, and so forth, which persist as long as their substance (*yāvaddravyabhāvin*)—with the words: "Because of difference" (*bhedāt*).
With the intention that qualities and so forth persist as long as the substance exists, he says: "saviśeṣa" (with its specific attributes).

Alternatively, it should be understood that the first statement of the object [of cognition] follows the Nyāya system, the second follows the Mīmāṃsā system, and the third follows the Siddhānta (established conclusion) system.

The point is that, according to the *Sudhā* commentary, the cognition of "threads and cloth" is intended as distinct from the cognition of "a bowl and jujube fruit," and is thus determined to have non-difference (*abheda*) as its object.
By speaking in this manner, you would be asserting that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) exists within a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*) endowed with a very clear manifestation of distinction.
And that is incorrect; thus he says, "In the absence... and so forth.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), things such as that which is desired to be attained are included. Regarding the term "Nyāya":

The meaning is as follows: just as "inherence" (samavāya) is posited in cases where there is an absence of the manifestation of a very clear distinction, so too would "conjunction" (saṃyoga) apply to a qualified cognition possessing such a manifestation, just as in the case of a cognition such as "one with a staff" (daṇḍī).

The Refutation of Inherence (Samavāya) as a Means of Cognition // 29 // The meaning is as follows: even if there exists a commonality (*sājātya*)—consisting in the aforementioned lack of manifestation—that is pervasive [in all instances] such as the cognition "one who possesses a staff" (*daṇḍī*), it would follow that inherence (*samavāya*) is also manifold, just as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is manifold in those cases. Thus, the means of valid cognition for inherence fails.

In cases where the destruction of an effect is caused by the destruction of its substratum, it must be stated that the cause of the destruction of the effect is specifically the destruction of the substratum in its capacity as an inherent cause (*samavāyin*), and not merely the destruction of the substratum. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the destruction of a jar residing in its shards could be destroyed even by the destruction of the shards, which would lead to the re-emergence of the jar; therefore, one must admit the existence of inherence (*samavāya*). This is not so.
For inherence-ness (*samavāyatva*) is simply the state of being an eternal relation, and not a universal (*jāti*), since universals are not admitted [by the opponent]. And thus:

If, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), one were to accept that either the destruction of the substrate’s form as the cause of the relation, or simply the destruction of the substrate which serves as the cause, is the cause for the destruction of the effect residing therein, then the destruction of the *samavāya* (inherence) would not follow upon the destruction of the entity; consequently, *samavāya* would not need to be postulated. In reality, however, according to the theory of dimension (*parimāṇavāda*), since destruction resides in the ground and so forth, its destruction would not follow even when the potsherd is destroyed.
For this very reason, it was previously stated that [the opponent's view] concerns the objects of difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*).

Furthermore, since you yourself have accepted that time has an essential relation with its own attributes such as number and dimension, what is the use of inherence (samavāya) in that case?

And if it is argued that because time possesses an inherence relation with that [jar], there is no relation by way of its own nature (*svarūpasambandha*), then how could a relation by way of its own nature not be established for time with respect to the jar? For the case is the same.

Having thus stated that inherence lacks scriptural authority, he states the refutation of the acceptance of another form of inherence as set forth in the *Anuvyākhyāna* and the *Sudhā*, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).

Alternatively, the establishment of inherence (*samavāya*)—which was intended in the previously mentioned inferences on the grounds that it is the relation serving as the cause for cognitions qualified by qualities and so forth—is not tenable;
for the cognition of "having teeth" can be accounted for otherwise.
He states the fourth alternative account with the words beginning "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
Alternatively:
"And inherence is a relation; it must be eternal and one.

Since inherence is thus defined as that which possesses the nature of being a relation while being eternal, [the author] refutes this "nature of being a relation" by means of four alternative possibilities, beginning with the words "Furthermore," and so forth.

In this regard, first of all, he says "of time" (*kālasya*), having accepted the meaning of the portion of the aphorism *sāmyādanavasthiteḥ* as follows: because there is a similarity in accepting an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) for time with its own internal qualities such as number, just as there is for other categories (*padārtha*), it would follow that inherence (*samavāya*) is non-existent due to the resulting infinite regress (*anavasthiti*).

The meaning is as follows: since it is accepted that time has an essential connection with all its own attributes and all other [attributes], based on cognitions such as "the measure of time always exists" and "the number one always exists in time," and because time is the substratum of the universe; and since, by that very relation, a single time possesses a delimited magnitude—thereby accounting for the qualified cognition "time is [of such] a measure"—it would follow that inherence (*samavāya*) cannot reside therein.

He says "yadi ca" (if, moreover), having accepted a different consequence: that because the existence of conjunction in a substance such as a jar is similar to the existence of inherence in [an entity] such as number through its own adventitious attributes (*svagata-saṅkhyā*), there would follow the non-existence of the relation of essential nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*) accepted by the jar and other things, on the strength of cognitions such as "this is a jar" at this moment.
By that [means], such as the number inherent within itself (*svagata-saṅkhyā*) and so forth.

Furthermore, in your view, even for qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, there exists an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) with their own non-existence, their own cognition, and their own time. Among these,

the status of being an essential relation that qualities and so forth hold toward their non-existence, cognition, and the like, does not consist in being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), nor in being an object (*viṣaya*), and so on.
Because it does not follow [the object],
and because it would involve prolixity;
whereas, because it follows [the object] as a qualifier, there is parsimony.

Since the status of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatva) is equally applicable to qualities and the like with respect to their substrata and so forth, the relation of essential identity (svarūpasambandha) between the quality and its substratum is already established; what room, then, is there for inherent relation (samavāya)?

Furthermore, since a specific relation of qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*) between color and the jar must necessarily be admitted to distinguish the cognition "the jar has color" from a collective cognition such as "the collection of pot and color," the qualified cognition is established by that very relation of qualification; what, then, is the use of inherence (*samavāya*)?
The same applies to taste and so forth; thus, there is no room for inherence.

[Objection: Let it be so; nevertheless, by the force of cognitions such as "the color of the jar" (ghaṭarūpam) and so forth, the jar has an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) with color and the like alone, and not with time. To this, he says: "Moreover" (*api ca*).

Alternatively, even if inherence (samavāya) is established as a relation that accounts for the cognition of a substance qualified by its qualities at a particular time, let it be established as such in other cases as well; therefore, he says: "Moreover" (api ca).
And that [relation] is the relation of identity (*svarūpasambandhatva*); this is the syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
By the phrase "by way of objecthood (*viṣayatva*) and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

A direct relation distinct from conjunction is not distinct from both conjunction and the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*), because it is a direct relation, just like conjunction.

Being a direct relation is pervaded by the property of being other than either conjunction or the state of being a qualifier, because it resides in all direct relations, just like the nature of conjunction (*saṃyogatva*).

If only "relation" (*sambandha*) were stated, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to relations such as the redness resulting from the connection between a crystal and a *japā* flower, or blackness resulting from the connection between a cloth and mud; therefore, the term "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used to exclude these.
Furthermore, the phrase "distinct from conjunction" (*saṃyogabhinnah*) is used to exclude the possibility of the definition applying to conjunction itself.
Some say that the word "directly" (sākṣāt) is stated in order to exclude other objects by means of the relation consisting in the nature of being a qualifier;
[it is] not [the relation of] conjunction (saṃyoga).
The meaning is that it consists solely in the form of either the qualifier or the qualified of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

When stated in that very way, the expression is made with two negative particles (*nañ*) because, otherwise, there would be the consequence of non-distinction from the probandum (*sādhya*) to be stated later.
For in that case, since there would be an absence of the state of being distinct from the conjunction, there would be a sublation (*bādha*) upon reaching the final conclusion of the probandum.

The point is that since the conclusion regarding the probandum (sādhya) is reached precisely through the absence of non-difference from the nature of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatā), it is established that a direct relation other than conjunction is indeed of the nature of being a qualifier.
The term "direct" (sākṣāt) is used in the reason to ensure non-deviation (avyabhicāra) with respect to the previously mentioned indirect (paramparā) relation.
"Directly" (sākṣāt): This statement of "directly" is made to exclude any sublation regarding the aforementioned indirect relationship. "Conjunction" (saṃyoga)... [etc.].

The explanation of the meaning of the phrase "being pervaded by either being a qualifier of conjunction or [being conjunction itself]" is as follows: the world is other than both conjunction and being a qualifier; the state of being other than that is the state of being pervaded by those two—namely, conjunction and being a qualifier.
Thus, only two direct relations, in the form of conjunction and being a qualifier, are established, and there is no separate entity called inherence (*samavāya*); this is the intended sense.
The function of the word "direct" (*sākṣāt*) when the reason is stated is as previously explained.

For even when there is a cognition of fire by way of [its universal] "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so on, that [cognition of "possessing fire"] is absent.
Nor [is it] by way of being a cognition of a qualifier that has the delimitor of the qualifier as its mode;
for by that [criterion], indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) would be unestablished,
and because [the definition] is overly complex (*gaurava*).
Rather, [it is] by virtue of being a cognition whose mode is the delimiting property of the qualifier;
and thus, there is no establishment of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*).
[Objection: But surely, in that case, there is also the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñānatva*).

And thus, with respect to a cognition that apprehends the qualifiedness of the qualified (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyāvagāhijñāna*), [the cause is] the cognition of the delimiting factor of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*)— [Objection:

Surely, if there is no cognition of the relatum, there can be no cognition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and power (*śakti*) as determined by it; having raised this doubt, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (nor is it the case).
Even while adopting the opponent's own method of analysis, he states the non-establishment of non-conceptual [perception] with the words: "Or let it be so."
To the objection, "Let it be so; what is the fault?", he says: "And thus, it is not non-conceptual."

The sense is that, since it is devoid of any specific mode (*niṣprakāraka*), even by the principle of "whatever is specific," only the knowledge of the qualifier as having a specific mode (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedakaprakāraka*) is established.
With the thought that even so, the establishment of non-conceptuality [is achieved], the objection stated in the *Maṇi* is anticipated: "But then... and so forth.
The meaning is "in the case of the cognition of fire" and so forth.
[The term] "viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyena" means "by way of the qualification of the qualified."
The meaning is: "the cognition that [the mountain] possesses fire," and so forth. (This concludes the refutation of the nirvikalpaka-pramāṇa.)
If it is argued that the status of being a cause will be established by the nature of the knowledge of a qualifier possessing a particular mode (*prakāraka*),
according to the maxim "that which [is the cause] of two specific [effects]," etc.;

For in this way, since the knowledge of the specific mark (liṅga) is the cause of inferential cognition, by the maxim "whatever is the case for two specific instances," the knowledge of the instrument in general would be the cause of all produced cognitions.
And if that were so, even in the case of perception, one would have to postulate a supersensuous non-conceptual [cognition] having the eye and other [senses] as its object.

Moreover, in this way, the cognition of the qualificandum would also have to be a cause for a perceptual cognition qualified by a qualifier, because it is established that the cognition of the locus (dharmin) and so forth is the cause in cases such as doubt, and the cognition of the subject (pakṣa) and so forth is the cause in inference and the like.
In that context, since there is the manifestation of the "qualifiedness by fire-ness" on the mountain, [the example] "this is a cow" and so forth is merely a qualified cognition; such is the meaning.
He states that the reasoning is fallacious due to over-extension: "For in this way," and so forth.
In order to avoid the contradiction with experience, he says: "supersensuous and non-conceptual."
By stating another over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he declares the fallacious nature of the principle that "the two particulars [are related]": "Moreover, in this way... (6).
The meaning is that, according to the maxim "that which [is required] for two particulars," the cognition of the qualifier is the cause for any qualified cognition whatsoever.
To the question "Why? he says: "In cases such as doubt," and so forth.

The cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) and the cognition of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhānajñāna*) serve as causes for both a specific qualified perception in the form of doubt, such as "Is this silver or not?", and a specific qualified erroneous perception, such as "This is silver.
Otherwise, the recollection of the alternatives (*koṭismaraṇa*) and the occurrence of a doubt with a predominant alternative (*utkaṭakoṭika-saṃśaya*) would be inexplicable.

Likewise, in inference (*anumiti*), the cognition of the subject (*pakṣa*) is a cause, and in verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the cognition of the word-meaning (*padārtha*) is a cause. Thus, by the maxim "that which applies to two particulars," since there is a causal relationship between the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*) and so forth and the cognitions consisting of doubt or perception, it follows that there would also be a causal relationship between their respective universals—namely, between perception in general and the cognition of a qualified object in general. This is the meaning.

*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (First Chapter, page 490) [The cognition of the qualifier is the cause of the cognition of the qualified object by virtue of being the cognition of the qualifier. This is an addition in Ca, Ka, Ga, and Rā. [Objection: It is not so; for if the cognition of the qualifier were the cause of the cognition of the qualified object, then even when one has previously cognized the qualifier and subsequently remembers it, the cognition of the qualified object would arise. [Response: This is not a fault, because we do not say that the cognition of the qualifier is the cause of the cognition of the qualified object in all cases. Rather, we maintain that it is the cause only when the qualifier is present at the time of the arising of the cognition of the qualified object. Furthermore, since the qualifier is not present at the time of remembering the qualifier, the cognition of the qualified object does not arise. Moreover, the cognition of the qualifier is the cause of the cognition of the qualified object only when it is a cognition of a qualifier that is currently being perceived, not when it is a cognition of a qualifier that is merely remembered. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition. Thus, the definition of perception is established as follows: "Perception is a cognition produced by the contact of the sense organ with its object, which is non-conceptual (*avyapadeśya*), non-erroneous (*avyabhicārin*), and determinate (*vyavasāyātmaka*). This is the conclusion. Nor should it be argued that this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because the staff also appears in its own form within a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) whose object is "staff-ness," since the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present; for this would entail [the acceptance of] the causality of the cognition of the qualificandum (*viśeṣya-jñāna*), which you do not admit.

Furthermore, on the view that there is no "universal proximity" (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*), the fire experienced at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot serve as a qualifier for the mountain.

Moreover, if the cognition of a qualifier belonging to one thing were the cause [of the inferential cognition], it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). He clarifies this unintended consequence with the words "stick-ness," etc. (*daṇḍatva*...).
It is called "the totality" (sāmagrī).
The meaning is that it has the form of the contact between the staff and the sense organ, and so forth.

The point is that, just as in the case of the cognition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), it is not undesirable for the cognition of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*)—in this case, the form of the staff—to function as a cause for the conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) qualified by "staff-ness" (*daṇḍatva*), precisely by virtue of its being a cognition of a qualified object.
This is indicated by the phrase "by virtue of being a cognition of the qualified object."
The sense is that it is just as the qualification-cognition possesses causality by virtue of its existence.

With the intention that even by way of the principle of specific determination (*viśeṣanyāya*), it is not possible to postulate causality on the basis of being a cognition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñānatva*), whereby the establishment of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpakatva*) would follow from its force, he says: "Furthermore... (*kiñca*).

In the view of the Nyāya school, it is stated that there is no such thing as "cognition through generality" (*sāmānyapratyāsatti*), because at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—in the form "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire"—the fire on the mountain is also manifested as a qualifier of the mountain; thus, the aforementioned defect does not arise. This is the sense [of the author], since the operation of inference according to this view will be demonstrated in the third chapter.

Moreover, you yourself [must admit] that in the cognition "the ground possesses the absence of a jar," there is the qualifier in the form of an absence; in cognitions such as "these two are conjoined" or "these two are inherent," there is the qualifier in the form of conjunction, inherence, and so forth;
in the after-cognition (anuvyavasāya), there is the qualifier in the form of the state of having silverness as its mode (prakārakatva) residing in the primary cognition (vyavasāya);
and in the cognition of an absence...
Furthermore, there is a deviation [in the rule] because it has been accepted that even a qualifier— such as having the nature of being a counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*)—
appears even when it was previously unknown.

According to the view that "there is an absence on the ground" is a cognition having absence as its qualificandum (viśeṣya), and immediately after that, "the ground has absence" is a cognition having absence as its qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), there would be a mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya).
This is because the establishment of this conceptualization depends upon the proof of the causal relationship between the qualified cognition and the cognition of the qualifier.

By this, the following is refuted: [the objection] that if the cognition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) that conforms to the object were not a cause, then the conforming effect in the form of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) would be accidental (*ākasmika*), because there would be no other conforming cause for it.

[This is incorrect] because there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) consisting of deviation (*vyabhicāra*); thus, even the application of the maxim "that which applies to two universals when no subverting argument exists" is inappropriate here.

With the intention that the establishment of indeterminate perception (nirvikalpaka) is achieved through the proof of its being the cause of the cognition of qualifiers by virtue of its own power, [the author] states the deviation [of the reason] in several places, beginning with "Moreover" (api ca).

As for the objection raised in the *Maṇi*—anticipating this very point and offering a resolution with the words "first, there is the cognition that 'the jar is not on the ground'" and so forth—the author restates that and refutes it with the passage beginning "the absence on the ground" and so forth.
He clarifies what was stated as "mutual dependence" with the words: "this."
The meaning is that it refers to the conceptualization [of cognition] as being first the object of qualification (*viśeṣya*).

For only when the causal relationship between the cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) and the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is established can one postulate an alternative explanation for the deviation (*vyabhicāra*); and once that alternative explanation is established, the causal relationship between those two is proven.
This is the intended sense.

Because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) has already been stated. *Note: Variants noted—1. *rūpapadaṃ na* (not present) in ka-ga; 2. *bhāvatvā-* in ka-ga-rā; 3. *vādi-* in ca-ga.* *Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍava* (First Chapter, p. 492).

Furthermore, since specific cognitions can arise solely from the general cause of cognition—namely, the contact between the self and the mind—which is accepted by both parties and excludes desire and other such factors.
For if the pair of cognitions consisting of the non-conceptual and the conceptual were as authoritative as the pair of cognitions consisting of non-inferential and inferential knowledge,

then— fearing that all cognition would become conceptual because a qualified cognition could arise from the very same general causal complex (sāmānyasāmagrī) that produces cognition— one might postulate a distinct specific causal complex (viśeṣasāmagrī).
But such a thing does not exist.
Because non-conceptual cognition remains unestablished even now, all cognition is indeed conceptual;
for every act of awareness is of the form "this is such-and-such.
This is because [the reason] has been stated to be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).
Thus, the sense is that because there is no common underlying cause, "being a qualified cognition" cannot even serve as the delimitor of the effect (kāryatāvacchedaka).
Even while accepting that [the property of being produced] is the delimitor of the effect-ness (kāryatāvacchedakatva), he states another universal cause: "ubhaya... (both...).

Now, one might object: "How can this be so? Since the common cause of indeterminate cognition (nirvikalpaka) is the cause of determinate cognition (viśiṣṭajñāna), otherwise even that [indeterminate cognition] would result in being a determinate cognition. To this, he says:
"For if," [it means: "if indeed."
"Specifically," it says.

thus, indeed.

Desire might also be something entirely formless and beyond the senses;
the same would apply to hatred as well.

By this very same deviation, the claim that the cognition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is established as the cause of an error such as the memory of silver—and therefore must be the cause in other qualified cognitions (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) as well—is refuted.
This is because its causality in that case is due solely to its being a necessary contact with the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇasaṃnikarṣa*).

Furthermore, since the causality of the cognition of the qualificand (*viśeṣyajñāna*) toward error has already been established, it would follow that it must also be a cause in other qualified cognitions.

Now, an objection: if [the indeterminate cognition] does not produce the knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), how can there be the rule that the qualifier alone possesses the status of a "mode" (*prakāra*)?
If it is argued that this is because the sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) exists with respect to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) as well, then [we ask]:
even if you accept the existence of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), how [is this rule established]?
In the same way, so too is hatred.
The meaning is that it would be devoid of activity and beyond the reach of the senses;
this is precisely what is meant by "by this very [reason]."
The meaning is: "precisely by stating [the fallacies of] non-deviation, qualification, cognition, being otherwise established, and over-extension.
The syntactical connection is: "because of the deviation of the memory of silver and so forth.

Since there is an absence of memory in cases of superimposition upon what is being perceived (*gṛhyamāṇāropa*), the cognition of the silver and so forth—which are the objects of superimposition—is not a cause by virtue of being a memory.
However, the meaning is "by way of being the cognition of the qualifier.
To the question "How then is it a cause?", he says: "Because it is necessary" (āvaśyaka).
And because it would result in [the self] being a cause.
The sense is that the objection of "acceptance of the consequence" (iṣṭāpatti) has already been refuted previously.

Furthermore, as for the argument that the status of the genus (*gotva*) and so forth as qualifiers is established because their status as qualifiers would otherwise be inexplicable, and that this is due to the fact that being an object which serves as a cause for a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭadhī*) is precisely what constitutes being a qualifier (*prakāra*); having raised this objection, he refutes it with the words "But surely... (*nanu*).

In your view, since the causal complex for indeterminate perception—such as sense-object contact—is present even with respect to the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), indeterminate perception would also exist with respect to the qualificandum.
Furthermore, how could "absence-ness" (*abhāvatva*) and so forth function as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition of an absence?

Furthermore, regarding the resulting cognition (*phalībhūtajñāna*), is the rule that "whatever appears as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the cognition of a qualifier is the object of a cognition produced by a cognition having that [qualifier] as its content" (1), or is it that "whatever cognition is produced by a particular cognition has that [cognition] as its mode (*prakāra*)" (2)? It is not the first.
Not the latter, because it would entail that pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth become qualifiers (*prakāra*) in inference and other such cognitions, due to [the qualifier] residing in itself.
Therefore, even by you, the restriction that [only] a qualifier is a mode (*prakāra*) must be stated as being due to the "experiencing" (*bhojaka*), "vision" (*dṛṣṭi*), and so forth.
"How so? [To this he replies: The ellipsis is "the restriction that only a qualifier is a mode.
Why? To this he says: "In your view... (*tvanmate*).
In the phrase "the cognition of absence and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes conjunction, inherence, and the rest mentioned in the context of prior linguistic usage.

This is because, even if—according to your own method—the initial cognition were one in which the absence is the qualificandum (viśeṣya), such as "the ground is the absence of a jar," the property of being an absence (abhāvatva) would still be the qualifier (prakāra) therein while remaining previously unknown.

Even if it were argued that this rule applies only to cases involving positive entities (bhāva), the point is that [the rule would fail] in instances such as "these two are conjoined," since there is no absence [therein].

Now, one might ask: "In that case, what is the basis for the restriction of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*), as in the case of 'cowness' (*gotva*) and so forth? "In the knowledge that has become the result" means in a qualified cognition;
"as a qualifier" means as a mode (prakāra).
[The objection] "because of self-dependence" [is raised].

Therefore... [tasmāt].

The meaning is that it is impossible for the state of being an object of a generative cognition (*janakajñānaviṣayatva*) to constitute the nature of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*). (The Refutation of Nirvikalpa [Cognition])

The doctrine of non-conceptual [perception] (nirvikalpakavāda) is refuted by the very same aforementioned deviation: that qualified cognition has the relation as its object, and that in the cognition of a relation, the cognition of the relata is the cause, and the relatum is the qualifier.

This is because it has been stated that when there is simultaneous sensory contact with the two relata and no apprehension of their non-connection, there arises a cognition of the relation itself, which is also in sensory contact with them.
However, this is the distinction:
the relation does not manifest without the two related entities, whereas those two do manifest even without it.
Furthermore, since the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) is also a relatum, its cognition too would have to be a cause [of the knowledge of the absence].

Nor can it be argued that even though the qualificandum is a relatum, it does not possess the status of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*), whereas the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) alone does; therefore, only the cognition of the qualifier is the cause. [This is rejected] by what has already been stated.
Furthermore, the meaning is that this has been stated by you yourself in the passage beginning with "by you also.

The point is that in cases such as "the ground is devoid of a jar," even when the related entity—the absence—is not known, a qualified cognition nevertheless arises; therefore, that [absence] cannot be the cause [of the qualified cognition].
And he states another fault: "of the two related [terms]," etc.
And because it has already been stated.
The meaning is that this has already been stated in your own system by the passage beginning with "viśeṣyapi" (even the qualified object).
Alternatively, the meaning is that it has been stated by the passage beginning with "daṇḍapuruṣayoḥ yugapad indriya-sannikarṣa" (simultaneous sensory contact between the staff and the person).
[Objection: If this is so, then like the related entities, the relation itself would also have an independent cognition; to this he says: "iyāṃstu" (but there is this much...).
The meaning is that this, O Venerable One, is produced by the intrinsic nature of things.

If it is argued that because the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), the cognition of the qualifier is the cause of the cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) by virtue of being its objective basis, then he states the flaw: "as in the case of the cognition of non-existence (*abhāva*) and so forth.

496): [This is] because, as in the case of cognitions of non-existence (*abhāva*) and so forth, it must be stated that only a cognition whose qualifier is the delimiting condition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka-prakāraka-jñāna*) is the cause; thus, indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is unestablished.

Furthermore, even granting that there is a cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), nevertheless, the establishment of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) does not follow. For instance, it cannot be the delimiting factor (*janyatāvacchedaka*) of [the qualified cognition],
because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakti*) to memory (*smṛti*).

Nor should it be argued that even in that case, the prior experience is the cause by way of being the cognition of the qualifier through the medium of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). For it is impossible for a latent impression to serve as a medium when the generative capacity resides in the cognition of the qualifier itself.
Indeed, in such cases, the "operation" (*vyāpāra*) is precisely that which, having first produced [its own effect], produces another of the same class.
Otherwise, even the staff and other such tools would be the activity of the potter.
The phrase "the cognition that these two are conjoined," etc., refers to the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).
He states that it is the cause by way of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) because [direct] experience perishes when there is an interval.
Regarding the phrase "of whatever kind":

it is observed that for an object of a certain class—such as the eye and other sense organs—the production of contact is precisely what brings about the production of a direct perception (sākṣātkāra) of a corresponding class, such as visual perception; thus, contact alone is the operation (*vyāpāra*) of the sense organ.

Similarly, it is observed that for an object of a certain class—such as a staff—the production of the rotation of a wheel is precisely what brings about the production of an object of another class, such as a jar; thus, the rotation is seen to be the operation of the staff. This is the meaning.
In some cases, the expression "of whatever kind" is used so that even a new staff or similar object, which lacks the presence of a result, may possess causal activity;
otherwise [it would not].
The meaning is that [something] is an operation simply by virtue of its being dependent [on something else].
"Let it be so; even such an operation may belong to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*). To this, he says: "And not here. (Note:
