Now, one might ask: even if, according to the stated manner, being a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) is the delimiting factor for the effect, why does this not result in the non-establishment of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*)? To this, he says: "And thus... (*tathāca*).
The meaning is: "provided that the property of being a cognition qualified by its produced object is not a delimiting condition (anavacchedaka)";
"therein" refers to this.
The meaning is "recollection.

Even the initial cognition of a cow as qualified by the universal "cowness" (gotva) in one who has not previously experienced an individual cow may be a recollection produced by impressions (saṃskāra) from a previous birth;
this is the point, just as in the case of suckling at the breast and so forth.
Now, one might object that since recollection is produced by the cognition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), there would be an infinite regress; to this, he says: "produced" (*janyā*).
It has been said.
The meaning is that this was stated in the preceding text beginning with "because of the over-extension of memory" (smṛtivatiprasakteḥ).

Having himself established that the delimitor of the effecthood (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) is indeed distinct from memory, he states another view—namely, that the delimitor of the effecthood should be common to both [memory and other cognitions]—with the words "Some say" (*kecid*).
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "so they say.
*Nyāyadīpayutatarkatāṇḍavam* (First Chapter, p. 498) (Note: Variants from manuscripts *i* and *mu*: 1. The word *janya* is not present; 2. The word *ādi* is not present; 3. The reading is *ttviti*.)
Or let it be that "being a produced cognition" (*janyajñānatva*), which is common to both [perception and] memory, is indeed the delimitor of the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedaka*).
Even so, there is still the very same complexity (*gaurava*) involved in introducing the relation of "qualificative distinction" (*vaiśiṣṭya*).
Nor does this lead to an infinite regress.
Like the seed and the sprout, an infinite regress of entities is not a fault because it is established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*).

This is because, through the first functioning means of valid cognition assisted by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), one determines that the knowledge of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*) is the cause specifically within the series of produced cognitions.
Otherwise, even an infinite regress would be a fault, as one causal complex would depend upon another causal complex, and so on.

Nor does the fault of infinite regress apply to cognition, for even if every produced cognition requires the cognition of its qualifier, there would be no interruption in the stream of preceding cognitions, which would otherwise render death and other such events impossible.
In this life, memory is the cause of the first experience; and in that case, an experience from a previous birth serves as the cause by way of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

Even in that case, if one accepts that there is an experience from another previous birth, then because there would be an absence of a continuous stream of uninterrupted cognitions, death and so forth would be logically possible.

Nor should it be argued that, in the case of the perception of a person qualified by the genus (*jāti*) residing in the word "prayojya," the cognition of the qualifier is not of the nature of memory because that genus was not previously experienced. This is expressed by the phrase "nor thus" (*nacaivam*).

The meaning is that even for remembrance, there is the state of being produced by a cognition of a particular qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*). He clarifies its status as being grounded in valid authority (*prāmāṇikatva*) with the words "the first," etc.
Regarding the term "lāghava": it means lightness.
The sense is that, in view of the requirement for entering into a specific distinction, the property of being a produced cognition (*janyajñānatva*) is simpler (*lāghava*).
"In another causal complex" means:
The meaning is: "within another causal complex that produces its own [effect].
Regarding the phrase "at the time of death, etc. (prāyaṇādīti):
The meaning is death, fainting, and so forth. (Nirvikalpa-bhaṅga)
The doctrine of non-conceptual [perception] (nirvikalpakavāda) [is untenable],

because after the recollection of a word as "word-ness" (śabdatva) and so forth, once a cognition arises having the genus (*jāti*) as its qualificandum and the word as its qualifier, it is subsequently possible for a cognition to arise having the word as its qualificandum and the genus as its qualifier;
this is just as, in your own position, a cognition having that [genus] as its qualifier can follow immediately after a cognition having absence (*abhāva*) as its qualificandum.
The same should be understood regarding the perception of specific objects such as color-form (*rūpa*) that have just arisen;

otherwise, even in your own position, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), since non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) would be produced by a cognition generated through an unperceived medium, they say.
The refutation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding non-conceptual [cognition] // 31 // [Regarding the phrase] "by way of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) in the case of produced cognition":
The meaning is: "the knowledge produced by having the sacrificial oblation (havis) and so forth as its object."

Others say that this is the seed of their lack of conviction; however, it should be understood as being exactly what was stated previously, beginning with the words "because of over-extension in the case of memory" (smṛtāv atiprasakteḥ).

if one accepts supersensuous knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*), it would be impossible to ascertain the absence of cognition due to the non-existence of "non-perception of the perceptible" (*yogyānupalabdhi*). Consequently, the cognition of the absence of jars and other objects, which is produced by the mark (*liṅga*) of non-perception, would not occur.
He says "moreover" (kiñca) to show that in the case of non-conceptual [perception], the mere absence of a prover is not a subverting factor.
"Fit."

The meaning is that it is due to the non-apprehension of the perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*), which consists in the fact that if knowledge were present in me regarding this [object], it would have been apprehended—thus implying the existence of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*).

It is produced by the *liṅga* (logical mark). (Note: The following textual variants are provided for reference: 1. Furthermore, the mere absence of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for the absence of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*);
because when non-conceptual cognition exists, there is no necessary presence of conceptual cognition, conceptual cognition is not a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of non-conceptual cognition.

Furthermore, at the moment when a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) produced by an indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) arises, because the causal complex for an extra-sensory indeterminate cognition (*atīndriya-nirvikalpaka*) is present, the two complexes— like two opposing arguments (*satpratipakṣa*)— act as mutual impediments, and thus no cognition arises at all.

Even though the absence of a jar or similar object is cognizable through perception aided by the non-apprehension of the perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*), nevertheless, in certain cases such as a place shrouded in darkness, [this does not occur].

Since it is accepted that the absence of a jar or the like, being apprehended through a conceptual reflection (*parāmarśa*), serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*)— in the form "the jar is not here, because, while conditions for perception are met, it is not perceived"—
it is stated that "the cognition of the absence of a jar is produced by a logical mark" in order to indicate the necessity of a cognition of the absence of the [perceptual] knowledge itself.

Nor should it be argued that the mere absence of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) must be the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the cognition of the absence of a jar or the like, since the absence of such a cognition is possible due to the [non-]existence of the conceptual cognition itself;

for the point is that only the general absence of apprehension (*upalabdhi-sāmānya-abhāva*) serves as the inferential mark for the non-existence of an object, otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

One might object: "Granted that non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is beyond the senses, so that its absence cannot be perceived; nevertheless, let the knowledge of it be of the nature of inference (*anumiti*). Since conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*) pervades non-conceptual perception, the absence of conceptual perception itself serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for the former, and this [absence] is known through perception. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words: "And not... (*na ca*).
Because conceptual construction necessarily exists.

The meaning is that there is only non-conceptual [perception], because conceptual perception is the causal complex for direct perception, and its absence is possible due to the lack of other causes and so forth.
He states another objection: "Moreover" (api ca).

Anticipating the objection that "in the state of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), the causal complex for non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) simply does not exist, because the causal complex for non-conceptual cognition consists precisely in the contact of the sense organs with their objects as aided by the absence of non-conceptual cognition—and thus the aforementioned fault does not arise"—he refutes it, saying: "And not [due to] the previous... etc.

It is not the case that a preceding non-conceptual cognition acts as an obstacle to a subsequent non-conceptual cognition;

for even in your own position, it is established by the observation of continuous (dhārāvāhika) direct perception that in the case of perception, one established cognition does not obstruct another established cognition.

Nor should it be said that, like a cognition with multiple objects (*samūhālambana*), there exists a single cognition arising from the collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*) due to the convergence of objects;
for in this case, there is no absence of contradiction regarding the result.

Indeed, it is not possible for a single cognition to have "pot-ness" as its qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to one and the same pot, while simultaneously having something other than that as its qualifier.

Furthermore, when there is contact with both the staff and the person, immediately after the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) of both the staff and "staff-ness," and prior to the cognition of the qualification of staff-ness in the staff, there would have to be a cognition of the person qualified by the shaven-headed staff.
[The author] raises the objection that there is no contradiction even if two causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) exist, and then refutes it: "Nor is it a collection... and so forth.

The meaning is this: even when there exists a multiplicity of causal complexes (sāmagrī) consisting of the contact of those respective sense-faculties, a single cognition arises having multiple objects as its domain, and it is not the case that there is an obstruction; thus, let it be so.
He clarifies the contradiction with the words "for not... (na hi).

Now, one might argue: "Let it be that from the causal complex of recollection (smṛti-sāmagrī), just as from the causal complex of direct experience (anubhava-sāmagrī), and from the causal complex of inference (anumiti-sāmagrī), just as from the causal complex of perception (pratyakṣa-sāmagrī), only indeterminate cognition (nirvikalpaka) arises. To this, he states another objection, beginning with "api ca" (furthermore).
"Like a lump of clay" (mṛtpiṇḍa) means:
the cognition of a person as qualified by a staff, without the specific delineation of "staffness" (daṇḍatva).

Because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) exists;
nor is this a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Because such a cognition is not experienced.

For indeed, immediately after the contact between the staff and the person, prior to the cognition of the qualification of "staff-ness" (daṇḍatva) in the staff, no cognition of a person qualified by a shaven-headed staff is experienced;
nor is this cognition itself beyond the reach of the senses.
Because [your view] involves conceptualization (*savikalpaka*).

For me, however, since the cognition of a qualified object as qualified (*viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyajñāna*) arises right from the beginning through sense-object contact (*indriyasannikarṣa*), this undesirable consequence does not apply.

Furthermore, just as there is a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) whose object is merely the intrinsic nature of both [the staff and the person] when they are in sensory contact, why should there not also be a non-conceptual cognition whose object is merely the intrinsic nature of the relation itself when that relation is in sensory contact?
[The answer is: because of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*).

The meaning is: by means of the causal complex for qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), which consists of the cognition of the qualifier, the sense-object contact with the qualificand, and the non-apprehension of the non-relation between those two.

[Objection: But surely, just as the causal complex for the cognition of a "shaven-headed man with a staff" exists, so too does the causal complex for the cognition of the qualification of "staffness" (daṇḍatva) exist in the staff; thus, at the moment of the arising of the cognition qualified by the shaven-headed man and the staff, the qualification of "staffness" also appears in the staff. Therefore, according to your view, let there be a cognition of the qualification of the qualified (viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyadhī) in the system of Nyāya. To this, he says: "Furthermore, [regarding] the staff and the person... etc.
"By means of proximity."
The meaning is: in the form of being a qualifier of that which is conjoined, and so forth.
If it is argued that, in the manifestation of a relation, mere sense-contact is not the cause,
but rather the cognition of the relata as well, we say no;
for while the cognition of the relation as a relation may require that, the cognition of the essential nature of the relation itself does not depend upon it.
Otherwise, since it is observed that the cognition of a relation occurs through the very cognition of the relata as delimited by the relation-delimiting property (*sambandhitāvacchedaka*),
it would follow that the relation does not even appear in the cognition of the qualified (*viśiṣṭajñāna*).

Furthermore, it is not logical for this [cognition] belonging to the class of non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognitions— which never produces the effects of cognition such as worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), mental impression (*saṃskāra*), desire (*icchā*), and so forth— to possess the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*).
Furthermore, it can never possess the nature of a certainty that is not contradicted by doubt and the like regarding its own object;
nor can it possess the status of a valid cognition (*pramā*) if it does not establish its own object.
Moreover, the establishment of any real entity has never been observed to occur through indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*).
And there is no cognition that is of a different genus from both valid cognition and erroneous cognition.
Moreover, in this way, just as there is a specific type of non-conceptual knowledge that is perception, there would also be a specific type of inference.
Alternatively, having granted [the opponent's position], he states another fault: "Furthermore, of this... and so forth.

Since even when no effect is produced, the property of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) and so forth is not contradictory in a mere non-conceptual [cognition] simply by virtue of the effect that is cognition within another non-conceptual [cognition], the gloss of "of this" (*asya*) is "of that which belongs to the class of non-conceptual [cognitions].
Furthermore, *natarām* and *natamām* are indeclinables expressing an intensification of degree.

The implication is: if that were the case, why would even a jar or similar object not be cognition?

Furthermore, the statement in the *Maṇi* and other works that "perception is of two kinds, namely non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and conceptual (*savikalpaka*)" is also incorrect; thus he says: "Moreover, in this way... (api caivam).

The meaning is that even for that which does not perform the function of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), it would follow that it is a specific kind of perception (*pratyakṣajñāna-viśeṣa*); and even for that which does not perform the function of inference (*anumiti*), it would follow that it is a specific kind of inference (*anumiti-viśeṣa*).

Because it is a cognition, like an inference;

and "immediacy" (aparokṣatva) is pervaded by the nature of being a qualified cognition, because it is a property that divides cognition, just like mediacy (parokṣatva)—this and similar arguments are to be observed.

The phrase "it is to be seen as such" connects with what follows.
By this, the claim that the establishment of the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) occurs simply because there is no evidence for its absence is refuted.

Furthermore, since even a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is distinct from other conceptual cognitions, the formulation of the probandum (*sādhya*) specifies "distinct from that which is delimited by being conceptual" in order to eliminate sublation (*bādha*).
The qualifier "all" (*sakala*) is applied to the term "conceptual" (*savikalpaka*) in order to exclude any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding whatever [cognition] is conceptual.
He clarifies that the aforementioned object of knowledge is established by the absence of any sublation (*bādhaka*) with the words beginning "yadviśeṣa" (whatever specific...).

The theory of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakavāda*): [This concerns] the logical principle beginning with "of two particulars" (*yadviśeṣayoḥ*), which consists of the impossibility of the production of a common effect without a common cause; the impossibility of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) in a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) due to the prior non-appearance of the qualifier; and the impossibility of the cognition of a relation (*sambandhajñāna*) without the cognition of the relata (*sambandhijñāna*).
And the meaning is: because, according to the stated method, there is no subverting argument (bādhaka) against the contrary position (vipakṣa).
And this is merely an illustration;

as well as the consequence of its being non-conceptual.

this [point] is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Demonstrating that the fruit [of this work] is the justification of the previously stated qualification—namely, "devoid of beginning"—by establishing the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) through primary and secondary digressions, he concludes the chapter with the words: "Thus, in this way.
